> Semispinalis extends and contralaterally rotates the head and vertebral column.

Library: Erector spinae muscles
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Vertebral Column and Back

![Posterior view of the deep back muscles labeled spinalis muscle (medial), longissimus muscle (intermediate), and iliocostalis muscle (lateral)](library/images/msk-week-13/vert-erector-spinae.jpg)

## Identify it

- Vertical column of muscles next to the spinal column, between the spinous processes and the angles of the ribs
- Three columns from medial to lateral: spinalis, longissimus, iliocostalis
- Longissimus is usually the widest

## Key features

| Feature | Erector spinae |
|---|---|
| Origin | Broad tendon from the posterior iliac crest, posterior sacrum, sacroiliac ligaments, and sacral and inferior lumbar spinous processes |
| Iliocostalis insertion | Angles of ribs and cervical transverse processes |
| Longissimus insertion | Ribs between tubercle and angle, thoracic and cervical transverse processes, mastoid process |
| Spinalis insertion | Upper thoracic spinous processes and skull |
| Action | Unilateral: lateral flexion of the column; bilateral: extension of the column and head |
| Innervation | Posterior rami of spinal nerves |

Deep back muscles help maintain posture and control movements of the vertebral column.

> Erector spinae columns from medial to lateral are spinalis, longissimus, and iliocostalis, innervated by posterior rami.

Library: Back sprain, strain, and spasm
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Vertebral Column and Back

## Key features

The handout separates three common back injuries by which tissue is involved.

| Injury | Tissue involved | Cause or trigger |
|---|---|---|
| Back sprain | Only ligamentous tissue, or the ligament-bone attachment | Excessively strong contractions with movements such as excessive extension or rotation |
| Back strain | Muscle fibers stretched or microscopically torn, especially the erector spinae | Weight not properly balanced on the vertebral column |
| Back spasm | One or more muscle groups contract suddenly and involuntarily | Protective response after injury or to inflammation, for example of ligaments |

- Back strain is the most common cause of low back pain
- Spasms cause cramps, pain, involuntary movement, and a distortion of the vertebral column

These link back to the structures in this lecture. Sprains involve the vertebral ligaments, strains most often involve the erector spinae, and the pain is carried by the meningeal branches and posterior rami that supply the back.

> A sprain involves ligaments; a strain involves muscle fibers (especially erector spinae) and is the most common cause of low back pain.

Library: Skin functions and the three skin layers
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Labeled diagram of the layers of the skin: epidermis, dermis divided into papillary dermis and reticular dermis, and hypodermis, with a hair follicle, sweat gland, and blood vessels](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-skin-layers-diagram.jpg)

## Key features

The skin (integument) has a tripartite structure: three layers plus appendages.

- **Epidermis**: stratified squamous cornifying (keratinizing) epithelium
- **Dermis**: mostly dense irregular connective tissue, divided into papillary and reticular dermis
- **Hypodermis**: adipose tissue (the subcutaneous layer), where the fat cells (adipocytes) are
- **Appendages**: epidermal derivatives, meaning hair, nails, and glands

## Function

1. Barrier (protection) against UV light, mechanical abrasion, heat, and chemical insult including water, which protects from dehydration. Unlike the shell of a turtle, skin is flexible and extensible.
2. Sensation: touch of various kinds, pain, and temperature.
3. Thermoregulation: skin acts as an insulator and as an evaporative cooler, depending on sweat (glands and ducts) and arteriovenous anastomoses in the dermis.
4. Storage and synthesis of nutrients: keratinocytes synthesize vitamin D, and adipocytes in the hypodermis store lipid from cholesterol conversion.
5. Self-repair (wound healing).

## Vitamin D

- Keratinocytes ("skin" cells) synthesize vitamin D
- Vitamin D3 is produced from 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC)

> Keratinocytes synthesize vitamin D3 from 7-dehydrocholesterol, and adipocytes of the hypodermis store lipid.

Library: Epidermal layers and keratinocyte differentiation
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![H&E section of epidermis labeled C (stratum corneum), G (stratum granulosum), S (stratum spinosum), and B (stratum basale), with a very thick pale corneum over a thin cellular epidermis](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-epidermis-layers-cgsb-he.jpg)

![Diagram of epidermal layers from basal lamina up: stratum basale, stratum spinosum, stratum granulosum with keratohyalin granules and lamellar bodies, and stratum corneum, with a red arrow pointing up for differentiation](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-epidermis-layers-differentiation-diagram.jpg)

## Identify it

- Stratified squamous cornifying (keratinizing) epithelium sitting on the dermis
- Deepest: a single row of cuboidal to low columnar cells on the basement membrane (stratum basale)
- Above it: many layers of polyhedral cells (stratum spinosum)
- Then 1 to 3 layers of flattened cells with dark basophilic granules (stratum granulosum)
- Outermost: layers of anucleate, lightly eosinophilic squames (stratum corneum)

## Key features

- The epidermis is made of keratinocytes at different stages of differentiation
- The keratinocyte is the most common cell type in the epidermis
- Keratinocytes differentiate as they move up from the stratum basale toward the surface, so the stratum corneum is the most differentiated layer
- Order from deep to superficial: stratum basale, stratum spinosum, stratum granulosum, (stratum lucidum in thick skin), stratum corneum
- The stratum corneum is the water impermeant barrier
- The epidermis is avascular. There are no tight (occluding) junctions between any living epidermal cells, so nutrients and oxygen released in the vascularized dermis can diffuse between cells of the basal, spinous, and granular layers.

| Layer | Main feature |
|---|---|
| Stratum basale | Stem cells; hemidesmosomes to basal lamina |
| Stratum spinosum | Thickest region; desmosome "spines" |
| Stratum granulosum | Basophilic granules; keratinocyte death |
| Stratum corneum | Dead squames; water barrier |

> Keratinocytes differentiate upward from the stratum basale, and the stratum corneum is the most differentiated layer.

Library: Stratum basale and epidermal renewal
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![High-power micrograph of the stratum basale with a red line along the epidermal-dermal border, arrows to two dark mitotic figures labeled stem cells, and the dermis below](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-stratum-basale-mitotic-figures.jpg)

![Diagram of epidermal renewal labeled from bottom: connective tissue of dermis, basal lamina, basal cell layer with a basal cell dividing and a basal cell passing into the prickle cell layer, prickle cell layers, granular cell layer, keratinized squames, and a squame about to flake off from the surface](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-epidermal-renewal-basal-cell-dividing-diagram.jpg)

## Identify it

- The innermost layer of the epidermis, right on the basement membrane
- Single layer of cuboidal or low columnar cells
- Mitotic figures can be seen here at high power

## Key features

- Keratinocyte stem cells are located in the stratum basale
- Basal keratinocytes are coupled to one another by desmosomes and keratin cables, and to the basement membrane by hemidesmosomes
- Constant renewal is needed because cells are constantly lost from the surface
- Division of basal stem cells "throws" cells outward, and these cells undergo terminal differentiation
- Stem cells can divide without limit
- When a stem cell divides, each daughter can either remain a stem cell or embark on a course that leads irreversibly to terminal differentiation
- The epidermis is regenerated approximately every 28 to 45 days
- "Exfoliation" is the removal of dying and dead cells from the surface

## Clinical relevance

- Basal cell carcinoma arises from the basal (stem) cells of the epidermis
- Bullous pemphigoid targets the hemidesmosomes that anchor basal cells to the basement membrane

> Keratinocyte stem cells live in the stratum basale, and the epidermis is regenerated about every 28 to 45 days.

Library: Stratum spinosum histology
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![H&E section of epidermis with a large black arrow at S (stratum spinosum), G (stratum granulosum) above and B (stratum basale) below, and a red arrow labeled differentiation of keratinocytes pointing toward the surface](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-stratum-spinosum-he.jpg)

![Two panels of stratum spinosum keratinocytes: A, light micrograph of cells with spiny borders, and B, electron micrograph of a keratinocyte edged by spines, with a label for tonofibrils (tonofilament bundles) anchored to desmosomes](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-spinosum-spines-tonofibrils-em.jpg)

## Identify it

- Multiple layers of keratinocytes just above the stratum basale (the thickest region of the epidermis)
- Polyhedral cells with prominent nucleoli
- A "prickled" or spiny look at the cell borders

## Key features

- The "spines" are actually desmosomes, with the keratinocytes "holding onto one another"
- Keratinocytes in the stratum spinosum express desmosomes and bind tightly to each other
- Dense interlocking of cells by desmosomes and keratin filaments
- Tonofibrils (tonofilament bundles) are anchored to the desmosomes
- Desmosomes serve as attachment sites for keratin filaments, giving structural support and mechanical resilience
- Transgenic knockout of keratin shows that the keratin filaments are important
- Melanocyte processes ("tentacles") reach into this layer and deposit melanin into the keratinocytes here
- Langerhans cells sit in the basal and spinosum layers

## Clinical relevance

Antibodies to desmosome proteins (desmogleins) cause pemphigus vulgaris, a loss of adhesion between keratinocytes.

> The spines of stratum spinosum keratinocytes are desmosomes anchoring keratin filaments between neighboring cells.

Library: Desmosomes vs hemidesmosomes in the epidermis
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Diagram of a desmosome: keratin filaments inserting into a cytoplasmic protein plaque to which intermediate filaments attach, with desmoglein and desmocollin (cadherin family members) crossing the intercellular space](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-desmosome-diagram.jpg)

![Diagram of basal epithelial cells attached to a yellow basement membrane (basal lamina) by anchoring junctions, with cytoskeletal filaments inside the cells and extracellular matrix labeled](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-hemidesmosome-basal-lamina-diagram.jpg)

## Key features

- **Desmosomes** bind keratinocytes tightly to each other, most visibly in the stratum spinosum
- Desmosomes are attachment sites for keratin (intermediate) filaments, giving structural support and mechanical resilience
- Desmogleins and desmocollin are the desmosome proteins that span the intercellular space; they're cadherin family members
- Inside the cell, keratin filaments attach to a cytoplasmic protein plaque
- **Hemidesmosomes** attach keratinocytes of the stratum basale to the basal lamina (basement membrane)
- Hemidesmosomes help the epidermal keratinocytes stick to the dermis to make a waterproof seal

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Desmosome | Hemidesmosome |
|---|---|---|
| Joins | Keratinocyte to keratinocyte | Basal keratinocyte to basal lamina |
| Main layer | Stratum spinosum | Stratum basale |
| Target proteins named | Desmogleins | BP180 (type XVII collagen), BP230 |
| Autoimmune disease | Pemphigus vulgaris | Bullous pemphigoid |
| Split | Between keratinocytes (acantholysis) | Below the epidermis (subepidermal) |

> Autoantibodies to desmosome desmogleins cause pemphigus vulgaris, while autoantibodies to hemidesmosome proteins cause bullous pemphigoid.

Library: Stratum granulosum: keratohyalin granules and lamellar bodies
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![High-power H&E of the stratum granulosum: a row of flattened keratinocytes packed with dark purple basophilic granules beneath the pink stratum corneum, red dots marking cell nuclei, and paler spinous cells below](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-stratum-granulosum-granules-he.jpg)

![Diagram of keratinocytes differentiating from stratum basale through spinosum and granulosum to corneum, with keratohyalin granules labeled for structural reinforcement and Odland or lamellar bodies labeled as lipids, and an inset of a lamellar body releasing lipids and enzymes at the lipid bilayer](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-odland-bodies-keratohyalin-diagram.jpg)

## Identify it

- 1 to 3 layers of flattened keratinocytes just under the stratum corneum
- Cytoplasm filled with dark basophilic granules

## Key features

The basophilic granules hold enzymes, lipids, and other components needed to build the stratum corneum. There are two types.

| Granule | Contents | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Keratohyalin granules | Sulfur-rich amino acids, keratin filament aggregates; not membrane bound | Structural reinforcement; form the water-free cytoplasm of dead corneum cells |
| Odland (lamellar) bodies | Lipids, with hydrolytic enzymes, phospholipids, ceramides, and sterols | Released by exocytosis to coat squame membranes; water repellent barrier |

- Keratinocytes die in the stratum granulosum
- The secreted lipid combines with keratin and other proteins to form the water impermeant squames of the stratum corneum
- The squames have no nucleus, and with their specialized envelopes they form the water repellent barrier of the stratum corneum
- The stratum corneum is the product of granulosum secretion and differentiation

> Keratohyalin granules give structural reinforcement, and Odland (lamellar) bodies secrete the lipid that makes the water barrier.

Library: Stratum corneum and the cornified water barrier
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Diagram of epidermis labeled basal layer, spinous layer with desmosomes, granular layer with keratohyaline granules, stratum corneum, and desquamating cells flaking from the surface above the dermis](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-stratum-corneum-squames-diagram.jpg)

## Identify it

- Outermost layer of the epidermis
- Cells with no nuclei, stained lightly with eosin
- Prominent and thick in thick (acral) skin, thin and "whispy" in thin skin

## Key features

- Made entirely of dead keratinocytes called squames, with no nuclei or other organelles
- A squame is a scale or flake of skin; squames act like water impermeant shingles
- Each squame has a specialized cell envelope instead of an ordinary plasma membrane
- Rather than a lipid bilayer held together by hydrophobic and hydrophilic interactions, the envelope is a complex of lipids and hydrophobic proteins (such as loricrin and filaggrin), all cross-linked by transglutaminase into a hydrophobic water barrier
- The water-tight complex is strengthened by a core of keratin filaments
- Squames at the surface are shed (desquamation, or "exfoliation")
- Lipid from Odland bodies and protein from keratohyalin granules in the stratum granulosum build this layer

## Clinical relevance

- Formation of the cornified envelope depends on many "effectors" (crosslinking enzymes, keratins, lipid enzymes), and many of them can be mutated, resulting in disease
- In psoriasis, cells of the stratum corneum keep their nuclei (parakeratosis)

> The stratum corneum is made of anucleate squames whose cross-linked lipid and protein envelopes form the skin's water impermeant barrier.

Library: Dermal papillae, epidermal ridges, and fingerprints
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![H&E of epidermis over dermis with labels for an epidermal ridge and a dermal papilla of loose connective tissue projecting up into the epidermis](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-epidermal-ridge-dermal-papilla-he.jpg)

![Micrograph of the dermal-epidermal junction labeled epidermal (rete) ridges, dermal papillae, papillary dermis (type III collagen, fine elastic fibers, lots of cells), and reticular dermis (type I collagen, thick elastic fibers, few cells)](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-dermal-epidermal-junction-friction-ridges.jpg)

## Identify it

- Dermal papillae: fingers of loose connective tissue pushing up into the base of the epidermis
- Epidermal ridges (rete ridges): downward projections of epidermis between the papillae

## Key features

- The interlocking of dermal papillae and epidermal ridges makes a tough yet flexible structure, like the dovetail interlock used in furniture building
- The interdigitations provide mechanical strength
- Papillae carry blood vessels and prevent shear stress induced failure
- They're especially prominent in thick skin
- Epidermal ridges are also called friction ridges, and in thick skin they produce fingerprints

## Fingerprints

- The dermal papilla and epidermal ridge interaction creates friction ridges that make each person's fingerprints unique
- The epidermis is regenerated about every 28 to 45 days, but the dermis doesn't undergo such regeneration, so the dermal papillae are critical to the fingerprint profile
- Permanent fingerprint damage takes a third-degree burn or other serious injury reaching the deeper layers where the pattern is "encoded"
- A minor burn or cut won't permanently change fingerprints, though it can take around a month for damaged fingerprints to show back up

> Fingerprints come from dermal papillae interlocking with epidermal (friction) ridges, and because the dermis doesn't regenerate, only deep injury erases them.

Library: Papillary vs reticular dermis
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Light micrograph of skin with E (epidermis) at top, P (papillary dermis) in loose tissue just below and between epidermal projections, and R (reticular dermis) deeper, beside a legend for E and P and drawings of dovetail joints](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-papillary-reticular-dermis-he.jpg)

## Identify it

- The dermis is the connective tissue (CT) below the epidermis
- Papillary dermis: the thin, loose, cellular layer right under the epidermis, including the dermal papillae
- Reticular dermis: the deeper, thicker layer of coarse, densely packed collagen bundles

## Key features

The dermis is a tough yet flexible and elastic connective tissue with two discernible layers.

| Feature | Papillary dermis | Reticular dermis |
|---|---|---|
| Tissue type | Loose | Dense irregular |
| Collagen | Fine, type III | Coarse, type I |
| Elastic fibers | Fine, randomly oriented | Thick |
| Cells | Lots of cells | Few cells |
| Other contents | Capillaries, nerve endings | Coarse collagen bundles |

- Papillae of the papillary dermis penetrate into the epidermis, carry blood vessels, and resist shear stress
- Meissner's corpuscles sit in the papillary dermis (dermal papillae)
- A blood vessel plexus forms at the reticular/papillary boundary, and another (the cutaneous plexus) at the dermis/hypodermis boundary
- The dermis is vascular, but the epidermis is not
- Unlike the epidermis, the dermis doesn't undergo constant regeneration

> Papillary dermis is loose connective tissue with type III collagen, and reticular dermis is dense irregular connective tissue with type I collagen.

Library: Hypodermis (subcutaneous tissue)
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![H&E of thick skin with brackets for epidermis, dermis, and hypodermis (subcutaneous tissue), and labels for dermal papillae, dense irregular connective tissue of the dermis, and adipose tissue of the hypodermis](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-thick-skin-three-layers-he.jpg)

![Diagram of four types of injections: intradermal, intravenous, subcutaneous (hypodermis), and intramuscular, each showing the needle depth in a block of skin](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-injection-types-diagram.jpg)

## Identify it

- Deepest of the three skin layers, beneath the dense irregular connective tissue of the dermis
- Dominated by large, pale, empty-looking adipocytes (adipose tissue)
- Skeletal muscle lies below it

## Key features

- A loose, adipose-rich connective tissue, also called the subcutaneous layer of skin
- Permits sliding of skin over underlying structures
- Adipocytes here store lipid from cholesterol conversion
- Pacinian corpuscles are found in the dermis and hypodermis
- The sweat gland coils sit at the base of the dermis and into the hypodermis

## Function

- Insulating the body
- Protecting the body from harm
- Storing energy (triglyceride storage)
- Connecting the skin to the muscles and bones

## Injections by depth

| Injection | Target layer |
|---|---|
| Intradermal | Dermis |
| Subcutaneous | Hypodermis |
| Intravenous | A vein |
| Intramuscular | Muscle below the hypodermis |

> The hypodermis is loose, adipose-rich subcutaneous tissue that insulates, stores triglyceride, and lets skin slide over deeper structures.

Library: Thick vs thin skin and the stratum lucidum
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Two stained sections compared: thick skin (acral skin) with a very thick orange stratum corneum and deep ridges, above thin skin (non-acral skin) with a thin corneum](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-thick-vs-thin-skin.jpg)

![Diagram of epidermal layers labeled stratum basale, stratum spinosum, stratum granulosum, stratum lucidum, stratum corneum, and dead cells flaking off at the skin surface, with an arrow showing keratinocytes move up as they age](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-stratum-lucidum-layers-diagram.jpg)

![H&E of epidermis lettered A to E from bottom to top, with D marking the thin clear stratum lucidum just under the stratum corneum](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-stratum-lucidum-he-labeled.jpg)

## Identify it

- Thick skin: very thick, prominent stratum corneum, and no hair follicles
- Thin skin: thin, "whispy" stratum corneum, with hair follicles
- Stratum lucidum: a thin, clear (translucent) band between the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneum

## Key features

| Feature | Thick skin | Thin skin |
|---|---|---|
| Other name | Acral skin | Non-acral skin |
| Stratum corneum | Prominent | Whispy |
| Hair follicles | None | Present, with sebaceous glands and arrector pili |
| Stratum lucidum | Readily visible | Not readily visible |
| Where | Palms and soles | Elsewhere |

- Stratum lucidum is Latin for "clear layer"; it's made of dead skin cells
- It's readily visible by light microscopy only in thick skin
- Dermal papillae are especially prominent in thick skin, where the friction ridges form fingerprints
- Sweat glands are found in both thick and thin skin

## Other regional variations

- Loose vs tight skin
- Muscular skin (scrotum, nipple, prepuce, glans penis, perianal region), where smooth muscle powers local contractions in response to environmental stimuli
- Pigment-rich skin: axillae, areolae, labia majora, circumanal region

> The stratum lucidum is readily visible only in thick (acral) skin of the palms and soles, which also lacks hair follicles.

Library: Psoriasis and failed keratinocyte differentiation
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Clinical photo of psoriasis plaques on the elbows and forearm with silvery scale, above an H&E section of psoriatic epidermis with a thick layer of nucleated surface cells](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-psoriasis-plaques-and-parakeratosis.jpg)

## Key findings

Psoriasis shows the clinical relevance of understanding keratinocyte differentiation. The lecture uses the Stedman's definition.

- Eruption of circumscribed, discrete and confluent, reddish, silvery maculopapules
- Lesions occur predominantly on the elbows, knees, scalp, and trunk
- Microscopically, characteristic parakeratosis: retention of nuclei in the cells of the stratum corneum
- Elongation of rete ridges

## Mechanism

- Caused by failure of terminal differentiation
- This failure allows cells in the stratum spinosum and above to continue to divide
- Normally, only basal stem cells divide, and their daughters that leave the basal layer commit irreversibly to terminal differentiation, losing their nuclei by the time they reach the stratum corneum

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Normal epidermis | Psoriasis |
|---|---|---|
| Dividing cells | Stratum basale only | Spinosum and above too |
| Stratum corneum nuclei | Absent | Retained (parakeratosis) |
| Rete ridges | Normal | Elongated |

> Psoriasis is a failure of terminal differentiation that lets spinosum cells keep dividing, giving parakeratosis and elongated rete ridges.

Library: Melanocytes: location and identification
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Diagram of epidermis over dermis with two blue dendritic melanocytes labeled in the basal layer, their processes extending between the keratinocytes above](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-melanocytes-in-epidermis-diagram.jpg)

![H&E of scalp epidermis with arrows labeling melanocytes and, separately, pigmented epithelial cells along the basal layer](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-melanocytes-vs-pigmented-epithelial-cells-scalp.jpg)

## Identify it

- Cell body located in the stratum basale
- Long processes ("tentacles") extend into the stratum spinosum
- You won't be able to tell a melanocyte from a keratinocyte on H&E
- Melanocytes, Langerhans cells, and Merkel cells all need antibodies (IHC or ICC) for definitive identification
- IHC (immunohistochemistry) is an antibody-antigen reaction on cells in a tissue section; ICC (immunocytochemistry) is an antibody-antigen reaction on cells

## Key features

- Melanocytes are one of the non-keratinocyte cell types of the epidermis, along with Langerhans cells and Merkel cells
- They produce melanin and pass melanin granules to keratinocytes
- So a darkly stained cell with melanin isn't necessarily a melanocyte; many pigmented cells are keratinocytes that received melanin
- Melanocytes are derived from the neural crest
- Melanocytes in the hair follicle give hair its color

## Clinical relevance

- Melanoma is a malignant tumor of melanocytes
- Vitiligo is destruction of melanocytes
- In albinism, melanocyte number is normal but melanin production is reduced

> Melanocytes sit in the stratum basale but can't be told from keratinocytes on H&E, and a pigmented cell isn't necessarily a melanocyte.

Library: Melanin synthesis and transfer to keratinocytes
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Diagram of a blue dendritic melanocyte with a developing melanin granule in its cell body, budding melanin granules at the tips of its processes, and melanin granules inside surrounding keratinocytes](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-melanocyte-melanin-granules-diagram.jpg)

![Two H&E sections compared: dark skin with brown melanin labeled throughout the lower epidermis, and light skin with little visible pigment](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-melanin-dark-vs-light-skin-he.jpg)

## Key features

- Melanin is a complex polymer that originates from the amino acid tyrosine
- It's a black-brown to red-yellow pigment
- Melanin determines eye, hair, and skin color, and it can absorb harmful UV rays
- Melanocytes synthesize pigment within melanosomes in the cytoplasm
- Granule-bound melanin travels through the melanocyte's processes and is deposited into the cytoplasm of keratinocytes in the spinosum layer
- In keratinocytes, the pigment collects over the sun-exposed side of the nucleus

## Regulation of pigmentation

Genetic variation in:

- Number of melanocytes
- Rate of melanin production by individual melanocytes
- Color of the melanin
- Size of the melanin granules
- Distribution of granules in the epidermis (more superficial deposition in darker skin)

Environmental (UV) effects, in order:

1. Darkening of existing pigment (rapidly reversible)
2. Increased melanin synthesis
3. Melanocyte division, giving a deep, long-lasting tan

> Melanocytes make melanin from tyrosine and hand it off as granules to keratinocytes, so skin color depends on melanin production and distribution rather than only melanocyte number.

Library: UV tanning mechanism: p53, POMC, and MSH
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Diagram of UV radiation from tanning beds hitting a keratinocyte, where p53 drives up-regulation of POMC; melanocyte-stimulating hormone and beta-endorphin are released, MSH binds the melanocortin 1 receptor on a basal melanocyte, and melanin made in melanosomes moves to the keratinocytes](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-uv-tanning-pomc-msh-diagram.jpg)

## Mechanism

1. Ultraviolet light triggers DNA damage in the nucleus of keratinocytes.
2. The damage activates p53.
3. p53 transcriptionally up-regulates the gene encoding proopiomelanocortin (POMC).
4. POMC is post-translationally processed to melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) and beta-endorphin.
5. After secretion, MSH acts on its receptor, the melanocortin 1 receptor, on melanocytes in the basal layer of the epidermis.
6. This induces pigment production in the melanocyte (synthesis within melanosomes).
7. Pigment is transported out of the melanocytes to overlying keratinocytes.
8. The pigment vesicles coalesce over the sun-exposed side of the keratinocyte nucleus, resulting in tanning.

## Key features

- UV damage is sensed in the keratinocyte, but the pigment is made by the melanocyte
- A UV-induced tan proceeds from rapid, reversible darkening of pigment to increased synthesis and then melanocyte division (deep, long-lasting tan)

| Step | Cell |
|---|---|
| DNA damage, p53, POMC | Keratinocyte |
| MSH secretion | Keratinocyte |
| Melanocortin 1 receptor | Melanocyte |
| Melanin synthesis | Melanocyte |
| Pigment cap over nucleus | Keratinocyte |

> UV damage activates p53 in keratinocytes to up-regulate POMC, whose product MSH stimulates melanocytes through the melanocortin 1 receptor.

Library: Langerhans cells of the epidermis
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Micrograph of epidermis with arrows labeled L pointing to two pale Langerhans cells among the keratinocytes and an arrow labeled CP](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-langerhans-cells-micrograph.jpg)

## Identify it

- Found in the basal and spinosum layers of the epidermis
- Pale cells with long processes among the keratinocytes
- Difficult to see in lab, and definitive identification needs antibodies (IHC or ICC)

## Key features

- An immune cell searching for antigens
- A unique population of tissue-resident macrophages, macrophage-like but with long processes looking for antigens
- They form a network of cells across the epidermis
- They can migrate from the epidermis to draining lymph nodes, where they present antigen to T cells
- They play a key role as immune sentinels

## Look-alikes

| Cell | Location | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Keratinocyte | All layers | Barrier, vitamin D |
| Melanocyte | Stratum basale | Melanin |
| Langerhans cell | Basal and spinosum layers | Antigen surveillance |
| Merkel cell | Basal layer | Light touch |

> Langerhans cells are tissue-resident macrophages of the epidermis that migrate to draining lymph nodes to present antigen to T cells.

Library: Merkel cells of the epidermis
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Two fluorescence micrographs of epidermis outlined by dashed lines, green epithelial cells with white arrowheads pointing to red-orange labeled Merkel cells along the basal layer](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-merkel-cells-immunofluorescence.jpg)

## Identify it

- Scattered in the basal layer of the epidermis
- Concentrated in the fingertips
- Difficult to see in lab; they need a specific detection approach such as an antibody (IHC or ICC)

## Key features

- Merkel cells are mechanosensory cells
- They're a highly sensitive mechanoreceptor for light (fine) touch
- Merkel cells are essential for light-touch responses
- They're part of the skin's innervation, alongside free nerve endings, Meissner's corpuscles, and Pacinian corpuscles

## Look-alikes

| Receptor | Location | Sense |
|---|---|---|
| Merkel cell | Basal layer of epidermis | Light touch |
| Meissner's corpuscle | Dermal papillae | Light touch |
| Free nerve ending | Into the middle of epidermis | Pain, temperature, light touch |
| Pacinian corpuscle | Dermis and hypodermis | Deep pressure, vibration |

## Clinical relevance

Merkel cell cancer is listed with the skin cancers, alongside basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma.

> Merkel cells are mechanosensory cells in the basal layer of the epidermis, mainly in fingertips, that detect light touch and need antibodies to identify.

Library: Nail structure and germinal matrix
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Section of a fingernail labeled E (eponychium, cuticle), F (nail fold), R (nail root, site of active growth), GM (germinal matrix, stem cell location), and DP (distal phalanx)](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-fingernail-section-labeled.jpg)

![Diagram of a fingertip in side view labeled germinal matrix, nail fold, eponychium, nail plate, nail bed, and distal phalanx](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-nail-germinal-matrix-diagram.jpg)

## Identify it

- A hard plate of cornified epidermis on the dorsal fingertip, over the distal phalanx
- The nail root tucks into an invagination of epidermis under the nail fold
- The eponychium (cuticle) covers the nail where it emerges

## Key features

- The nail is made of highly cross-linked keratin
- Structure: plates of especially hard, cornified epidermis
- It originates from the nail root, formed by invagination of the epidermis into the dermis
- At the base of the invagination is the germinal matrix, where the stem cells are
- The nail root is the site of active growth
- Generation: within the ingrowth of epidermis (the nail root), by cell division and then cornification

| Label | Structure |
|---|---|
| E | Eponychium (cuticle) |
| F | Nail fold |
| R | Nail root, site of active growth |
| GM | Germinal matrix, stem cell location |
| DP | Distal phalanx |

## Comparison with other epidermal derivatives

Nails, hair, and glands are all epidermal derivatives. Like hair, the nail forms from an ingrowth of epidermis with dividing cells at its base, followed by cornification.

> Nails are highly cross-linked keratin made at the nail root, with stem cells in the germinal matrix at the base of the epidermal invagination.

Library: Hair follicle and hair bulb
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![H&E of thin skin with oblique hair follicles labeled epidermis, dermis, arrector pili muscle, sebaceous gland, hair follicle, external root sheath, hair bulb, and dermal papilla](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-hair-follicle-bulb-he.jpg)

![Line drawing of a hair follicle in skin labeled epidermal layers (corneum, lucidum, granulosum, spinosum, basale), dermis, sweat gland, sebaceous gland, arrector pili muscle, follicle, hair matrix, dermal papilla, and bulb, with a hair cross section showing cuticle, cortex, medulla, and melanin](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-hair-follicle-bulb-diagram.jpg)

## Identify it

- A tube of epithelium running obliquely from the epidermis deep into the dermis
- Ends in a swelling, the hair bulb, with a dermal papilla of connective tissue indented into its base
- A sebaceous gland opens into the follicle, and a strap of smooth muscle (arrector pili) attaches nearby
- Found in thin (non-acral) skin, not in thick skin

## Key features

- The hair follicle is an invagination of the epidermis into the dermis (an ingrowth of the basal layer)
- It terminates in the hair bulb, where division and differentiation grow the hair
- The root lies below the skin surface and the shaft above
- Cells for terminal differentiation are made by division at the base of the follicle, followed by cornification with more extensive protein cross-linking than in skin
- The hair matrix sits at the base of the bulb around the dermal papilla
- External root sheath lines the follicle
- Erection: the arrector pili muscle is a smooth muscle strap
- Coloration: from melanocytes in the follicle
- Sebaceous glands and arrector pili muscles go with hair follicles (thin skin), while sweat glands are in both thick and thin skin

> The hair follicle is an epidermal invagination into the dermis that ends in the hair bulb, where cell division and differentiation grow the hair.

Library: Hair shaft layers and hard keratin
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Two hair diagrams: left, a hair in skin labeled cuticle, cortex, medulla, sebaceous gland, arrector pili muscle, bulb, outer root sheath, and dermal papilla; right, a follicle labeled hard keratin, soft keratin, medulla, cortex, hair cuticle, connective tissue sheath, external root sheath, glassy membrane, internal root sheath, matrix, hair root, and connective tissue papilla](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-hair-shaft-cuticle-cortex-medulla-diagrams.jpg)

## Key features

The hair shaft has three layers.

| Layer | Position | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Cuticle | Outermost | Protective shield |
| Cortex | Middle | Most of the hair's structure and color; strength and texture |
| Medulla | Innermost core | Soft core of loosely packed cells; only in thick hairs |

- Hair is a surface projection made entirely of dead, cornified epithelial cells
- Hair cells are dead squames, but harder and more strongly bonded to one another than skin squames, with complex cross-linking of keratin
- In the follicle diagram, the shaft is labeled hard keratin and the root region soft keratin
- The shape of the hair follicle determines whether hair is straight or curly: round to slightly oval follicles give straight to wavy hair, oval follicles straight to curly hair, and oval to elliptical follicles curly to coiled hair

## Comparison with other epidermal derivatives

| Feature | Epidermis | Hair | Nail |
|---|---|---|---|
| Final cells | Squames | Dead squames, harder | Hard cornified plates |
| Keratin bonding | Cross-linked | More extensive cross-linking | Highly cross-linked |
| Growth site | Stratum basale | Hair bulb | Nail root, germinal matrix |

> The hair shaft has an outer cuticle, a middle cortex holding most structure and color, and a medulla core present only in thick hairs.

Library: Sebaceous glands and holocrine secretion
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Three H&E panels of sebaceous glands beside hair follicles, lettered F, G, and M, with double asterisks on pale lipid-filled gland cells and a red arrow labeling M as the arrector pili muscle](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-sebaceous-gland-arrector-pili-he.jpg)

![H&E of thin (non-acral) skin with labeled hair follicles and a sebaceous gland below the epidermal surface](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-thin-skin-hair-follicles-sebaceous-gland.jpg)

## Identify it

- Clusters (acini) of large, pale, foamy cells right next to a hair follicle
- Cells stain lightly because of their high lipid ("oily") content
- Nuclei are centrally placed and condensed, or absent in cells near the opening into the follicle
- An arrector pili muscle often runs nearby

## Key features

- An outgrowth of hair follicle epithelium forms the gland, so it's associated with hair follicles (thin skin)
- It secretes an oily substance called sebum into the hair follicle
- Sebum is a mixture of fatty acids, cholesterol, squalene, triglycerides, and other molecules
- Holocrine secretion: the whole cell, with its contents, is sloughed into the gland lumen

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Sebaceous gland | Eccrine sweat gland |
|---|---|---|
| Secretion mode | Holocrine (whole cell released) | Merocrine (exocytosis only) |
| Product | Oily sebum | Watery, hypotonic sweat |
| Opens into | Hair follicle | Skin surface |
| Cell staining | Pale, lipid-filled | Clear and dark cells |
| Skin type | Thin skin with hair | Thick and thin skin |

> Sebaceous glands release sebum into the hair follicle by holocrine secretion, so their pale lipid-filled cells are shed whole.

Library: Eccrine sweat gland histology
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![H&E and diagram of an eccrine sweat gland: a coiled secretory portion deep in the dermis, a duct portion formed by stratified cuboidal epithelium in the dermis, and a duct portion formed by cells of the epidermis opening at the surface](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-eccrine-sweat-duct-and-secretory-portion.jpg)

![H&E of sweat gland coils in cross section at low and high power, tubules lettered S, D, and M, with a red arrow labeled Cl](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-eccrine-sweat-gland-cross-sections-he.jpg)

## Identify it

- Clusters of small tubules in cross section in the deep dermis and hypodermis (the coiled base)
- A thin duct that spirals up through the dermis and epidermis to the surface
- Found in both thick and thin skin

## Key features

- Eccrine (merocrine) sweat glands are the most common sweat glands and produce sweat, up to 10 L per day
- A simple gland: an invagination extending into the dermis, coiled at its base in the dermis/hypodermis
- It secretes a hypotonic (to blood) aqueous fluid onto the skin surface
- Secretory portion (in the dermis): a coiled tube of simple cuboidal epithelium made of light (clear) and dark cells, surrounded by contractile myoepithelial cells
- Conducting portion (the duct): stratified cuboidal epithelium in the dermis that stratifies as it approaches the surface; the part in the epidermis is formed by epidermal cells
- Ductal cells reabsorb Cl- ions, which makes the sweat hypotonic

## Apocrine glands

- Found in the axilla
- Make an ultrafiltrate with an odor
- To be covered in a later block (GI/GU/Endocrine)

> The eccrine sweat gland is a simple coiled gland: a secretory coil of clear and dark cells with myoepithelial cells, and a stratified cuboidal duct that makes sweat hypotonic.

Library: Eccrine sweat gland secretory cells
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Electron micrograph of the eccrine sweat gland secretory portion labeled dark cells with many dense granules near the lumen, a clear cell with an intercellular canaliculus, and myoepithelial cells at the base](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-sweat-gland-clear-dark-myoepithelial-em.jpg)

## Identify it

On EM of the secretory portion:

- Dark cells: packed with dense secretory granules, lining the lumen
- Clear cells: pale cytoplasm, with intercellular canaliculi between them
- Myoepithelial cells: at the base of the epithelium

## Key features

| Cell | Product or action |
|---|---|
| Clear cell | Ultrafiltrate of blood (bulk of the secretion) |
| Dark cell | Protein (mucous-like substance) by exocytosis |
| Myoepithelial cell | Contracts to expel sweat onto the surface |

- Eccrine (merocrine) secretion: no part of the cell architecture (such as the cell membrane) is secreted; proteins and fluid leave by exocytosis
- The bulk of the secretion is an ultrafiltrate of blood made by the clear cells, which are clearly visible by EM
- Sweat released onto the surface is hypotonic relative to blood
- Sweat proteins help form a chemical barrier on the skin and act in antibacterial defense

> In the eccrine sweat gland, clear cells make the ultrafiltrate, dark cells secrete protein by exocytosis, and myoepithelial cells contract to expel sweat.

Library: CFTR in the sweat duct and salty sweat
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Three-panel diagram: A, a sweat gland coil and duct opening at the skin surface; B, a normal sweat duct with CFTR and the epithelial sodium channel moving Cl- and Na+ from the ductal lumen to the interstitium; C, a cystic fibrosis sweat duct where CFTR is blocked and chloride stays in the lumen](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-cftr-normal-vs-cf-sweat-duct.jpg)

## Mechanism

- Sweat is hypotonic because of its low NaCl concentration
- The ductal cells absorb Cl- ions from the sweat and return them to the interstitium (the vascular connective tissue of the dermis)
- The ductal cells have the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR), a transmembrane chloride channel that reabsorbs Cl- back into the interstitium
- Na+ is reabsorbed through the epithelial sodium channel

## Clinical relevance

- If CFTR is defective, the ductal cells can't reabsorb Cl- efficiently, which gives "salty sweat," a characteristic of patients with cystic fibrosis
- Cystic fibrosis is an inherited disease caused by a defective CFTR gene
- It affects the cells that produce mucus, sweat, and digestive juices, and it can lead to lung and pancreatic dysfunction
- The lecture ties the CF sweat test to this finding

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Normal sweat duct | Cystic fibrosis duct |
|---|---|---|
| CFTR | Functional | Defective |
| Cl- reabsorption | Efficient | Poor |
| Sweat | Hypotonic, low NaCl | Salty |

> Ductal CFTR reabsorbs chloride to make sweat hypotonic, so defective CFTR in cystic fibrosis gives salty sweat.

Library: Dermal blood supply and thermoregulation
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Injected specimen of skin vessels with the papillary plexus near the surface and the cutaneous plexus deeper](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-papillary-and-cutaneous-plexus.jpg)

![Diagram of skin blood supply labeled papillary loops, papillary plexus, arteriovenous anastomosis, sebaceous gland, sweat gland, cutaneous plexus, arterial supply, and venous drainage](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-dermal-vasculature-av-anastomosis-diagram.jpg)

## Key features

- Blood vessels are in the dermis but not the epidermis (the epidermis is avascular)
- Plexuses (dense networks) form where supply is needed:
- Cutaneous plexus at the hypodermis/dermis boundary
- Papillary plexus (called the sub-papillary plexus in the handout) at the reticular/papillary dermis boundary, feeding papillary loops in the dermal papillae
- Arteriovenous anastomoses control blood flow and so provide thermoregulation
- Blood flow is controlled by the CNS and the sympathetic nervous system

## Thermoregulation

| Condition | Blood flow | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Body hot | Shunted to the papillary plexus | Heat exchange with the outside |
| Body cold | AV anastomoses shunt blood away from the papillary plexus | Prevents heat escape |

- Skin acts as an insulator and an evaporative cooler
- Sweating relies on the "heat of vaporization": it takes energy (heat) to evaporate sweat off the skin, so converting sweat to vapor uses excess body heat and cools the body
- Thermoregulation depends on sweat (glands and ducts) and arteriovenous anastomoses in the dermis

> When the body is cold, arteriovenous anastomoses shunt blood away from the papillary plexus to prevent heat loss; when hot, blood goes to the papillary plexus.

Library: Cutaneous sensory receptors and free nerve endings
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Silver-stained section at the epidermal-dermal border with an arrow to thin dark fibers labeled free nerve endings reaching up among the epidermal cells](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-free-nerve-endings.jpg)

## Identify it

- Free nerve endings: thin, branching fibers reaching up into the epidermis

## Key features

- Free nerve endings are the most common nerve endings in skin
- They extend into the middle of the epidermis
- They're terminal axonal processes of afferent sensory neurons
- They're sensitive to painful stimuli, to hot and cold, and to light touch
- They're slow to adjust to a stimulus, so they're less sensitive to abrupt changes in stimulation

## Receptors compared

Sensation is one of the skin's functions. Fine touch uses Meissner's corpuscles, free nerve endings, and Merkel cells, and deep pressure uses the Pacinian corpuscle.

| Receptor | Location | Sense | Structure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free nerve ending | Into mid epidermis | Pain, hot and cold, light touch | Bare axon terminals |
| Merkel cell | Basal layer of epidermis | Light touch | Mechanosensory cell |
| Meissner's corpuscle | Dermal papillae | Light touch | Stacked flat Schwann cells, capsule, axon |
| Pacinian corpuscle | Dermis and hypodermis | Deep pressure, vibration | Onion-like lamellae around one axon |

> Free nerve endings are the most common nerve endings in skin and sense pain, temperature, and light touch.

Library: Meissner's corpuscles
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Two micrographs of Meissner's corpuscles in dermal papillae: left, H&E with M marking an oval corpuscle in a papilla under the epidermis (E); right, a silver stain with an arrow at M near the epidermis (E)](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-meissner-corpuscle-dermal-papilla.jpg)

## Identify it

- An oval, encapsulated structure tucked into a dermal papilla, right under the epidermis
- Inside, a stack of flattened cells with an axon winding between them

## Key features

- Meissner's (tactile) corpuscles sense light (fine) touch
- Located in the papillary dermis, within the dermal papillae
- Three primary components: elongated Schwann cells, a connective tissue capsule, and a central axon
- The flattened Schwann cells are stacked in a background of interlamellar matrix made largely of collagen and microfilaments
- The axon is intertwined with the stack of highly flattened cells
- Thought to be exquisitely sensitive to pressure
- Fine touch, as in reading braille, relies on Meissner's corpuscles along with free nerve endings and Merkel cells

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Meissner's corpuscle | Pacinian corpuscle |
|---|---|---|
| Location | Dermal papillae | Dermis and hypodermis |
| Sense | Light touch | Deep pressure, vibration |
| Structure | Stacked flat Schwann cells around an axon | Concentric fluid-filled lamellae |

> Meissner's corpuscles sit in the dermal papillae and sense light touch, with stacked flattened Schwann cells around a central axon inside a capsule.

Library: Pacinian corpuscles
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Two micrographs of Pacinian corpuscles labeled PC: top, two large oval corpuscles with concentric layers in connective tissue (blue stain); bottom, H&E cross section of one corpuscle with onion-like concentric lamellae around a central core](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-pacinian-corpuscles-micrographs.jpg)

![Diagram of a Pacinian corpuscle labeled capsule, single nerve fiber in the central core, and myelin sheath on the fiber as it leaves the corpuscle](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-pacinian-corpuscle-diagram.jpg)

## Identify it

- Large, oval structure deep in the dermis or hypodermis
- In cross section it looks like a sliced onion: many concentric layers around a small central core

## Key features

- Also called Vater-Pacini or lamellar corpuscles
- Sensory receptors for vibration and deep pressure
- Essential for proprioception
- Found throughout the body, but most numerous and tightly grouped in the hands and feet
- Located in the dermis and hypodermis
- Structured like an onion: a central core containing a single myelinated nerve fiber, surrounded by concentric layers of fluid-filled lamellae (membranes) that form an outer capsule
- The concentric layers are made of helper cells surrounding the axon

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Pacinian corpuscle | Meissner's corpuscle |
|---|---|---|
| Location | Dermis and hypodermis | Dermal papillae |
| Sense | Deep pressure, vibration | Light touch |
| Structure | Concentric fluid-filled lamellae around one myelinated fiber | Stacked flattened Schwann cells with an intertwined axon |
| Look | Onion in cross section | Oval stack inside a papilla |

> Pacinian corpuscles are onion-like lamellar receptors in the dermis and hypodermis that sense deep pressure and vibration.

Library: Skin cancers by cell of origin and melanoma
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Diagram titled types of skin cancer: a skin block showing squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, and melanoma growing from the epidermis into the dermis](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-skin-cancer-types-diagram.jpg)

![Clinical photo of sun-damaged skin with an irregular dark gray-brown melanoma among smaller brown spots](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-melanoma-clinical.jpg)

## Key findings

| Cancer | Cell of origin |
|---|---|
| Basal cell carcinoma | Basal (stem) cells of the epidermis |
| Squamous cell carcinoma | Keratinocytes of the epidermis |
| Melanoma | Melanocytes of the epidermis |
| Merkel cell cancer | Merkel cells |

## Basal cell carcinoma

A slow-growing, locally invasive, but rarely metastasizing neoplasm derived from basal cells of the epidermis or hair follicles (Stedman's).

## Melanoma

- A malignant tumor produced by malignant transformation of melanocytes, the cells that produce the melanin coloring skin, hair, and eyes
- Melanocytes are derived from the neural crest, so melanomas, although they usually occur on the skin, can arise in other places neural crest cells migrate, such as the gastrointestinal tract and brain
- Melanoma doesn't always have a pigmented appearance
- People with albinism have an increased risk of skin cancer

> Melanocytes come from the neural crest, so melanoma can arise outside the skin, such as in the GI tract and brain, and it isn't always pigmented.

Library: Oculocutaneous albinism
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

## Key findings

- Albinism is a group of inherited disorders that results in little or no production of the pigment melanin
- Melanin determines the color of the skin, hair, and eyes
- Melanocyte number is normal; the problem is reduced tyrosinase activity and/or transport, affecting melanin production
- Multiple genes are involved in melanin production
- Albinism affects all races
- People with albinism have an increased risk of skin cancer

## Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA)

- The most common type
- Autosomal recessive: the person inherits two copies of a mutated gene, one from each parent
- Results from a mutation in one of seven genes, labeled OCA1 to OCA7
- Causes decreased pigment in the skin, hair, and eyes, as well as vision problems
- The amount of pigment varies by type, and the resulting color of skin, hair, and eyes varies by and within types

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Albinism | Vitiligo |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | Inherited | Most probably autoimmune |
| Melanocytes | Normal number | Destroyed |
| Defect | Little or no melanin made | Melanocytes lost |
| Pattern | Skin, hair, and eyes | Irregular patches |

> In albinism, melanocyte number is normal but reduced tyrosinase activity or transport gives little or no melanin, and OCA is autosomal recessive.

Library: Vitiligo vs albinism vs melasma
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Clinical photo of both hands of a person with dark skin, showing irregular sharply defined depigmented white patches on the fingers and hands from vitiligo](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-vitiligo-hands.jpg)

![Clinical photo of a cheek with blotchy brown hyperpigmented patches from melasma](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-melasma-cheek.jpg)

## Key findings

These are the three skin pigment disorders in this lecture, and each one affects melanocytes or melanin differently.

| Disorder | Pigment change | Melanocytes | Cause |
|---|---|---|---|
| Albinism | Little or no melanin | Normal number | Inherited; reduced tyrosinase activity or transport |
| Vitiligo | Patches of complete depigmentation | Destroyed | Most probably autoimmune |
| Melasma | Acquired hyperpigmentation | Overproducing melanin | Hormones and UV, among others |

## Vitiligo

- Irregular patches of complete depigmentation
- Caused by destruction of melanocytes, most probably autoimmune

## Melasma (chloasma)

- Acquired hyperpigmentation, from overproduction of melanin by melanocytes
- Can be associated with pregnancy, the "mask of pregnancy"
- Etiologic factors include genetic influences, UV radiation, pregnancy, hormonal therapies, cosmetics, phototoxic drugs, and antiseizure medications
- The female sex hormones estrogen and progesterone stimulate melanocytes to produce more melanin when the skin is exposed to the sun

> Vitiligo destroys melanocytes, albinism keeps normal melanocytes that make little melanin, and melasma is melanocyte overproduction driven by hormones and sun.

Library: Bullous pemphigoid: hemidesmosome autoantibodies
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![Two black and white skin sections: A shows the epidermis lifted off below with a double arrow across the gap, and B shows intact skin with layers labeled SC, GR, SP, BL, and DR](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-bullous-pemphigoid-split-vs-normal.jpg)

![Clinical photo of large fluid-filled blisters on red skin, circled, beside an H&E section with an oval marking the separation of the epidermis from the dermis](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-bullous-pemphigoid-blisters-and-he.jpg)

## Key findings

- A rare skin condition causing large, fluid-filled blisters (bullae)
- Blisters develop on skin that often flexes, such as the lower abdomen, upper thighs, or armpits
- Most common in older adults; a chronic, generally benign disease
- A basal layer disease: a hemidesmosome defect in keratinocytes
- Separation of the epidermis from the sub-epidermal structure, causing detachment of the entire epidermis

## Mechanism

1. IgG (with or without IgE) autoantibodies and activated T lymphocytes attack the basement membrane of the epidermis.
2. The target is BP180 (type XVII collagen), or less frequently BP230 (a plakin), proteins associated with hemidesmosomes.
3. Hemidesmosomes normally make basal keratinocytes stick to the dermis to make a waterproof seal.
4. Autoantibody binding and T cell cytokines lead to complement activation, recruitment of neutrophils, and release of proteolytic enzymes.
5. These destroy the hemidesmosomes and cause subepidermal blisters.

> Bullous pemphigoid is autoimmunity against hemidesmosome proteins (BP180, type XVII collagen), giving subepidermal blisters, mostly in older adults.

Library: Pemphigus vulgaris: desmoglein autoantibodies
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Integument

![H&E of pemphigus vulgaris skin showing a blister cavity, with a sheet of epidermis lifted away from the cells below, above the pink dermis](library/images/msk-week-13/integ-pemphigus-vulgaris-he.jpg)

## Key findings

- A desmosome defect in keratinocytes
- Caused by autoantibodies against keratinocyte desmosome proteins, the desmogleins
- Circulating IgG autoantibodies bind intercellular adhesion molecules
- The result is acantholysis: loss of keratinocyte to keratinocyte adhesion

## Background

- Desmosomes in the stratum spinosum bind keratinocytes tightly together and anchor keratin filaments for mechanical resilience
- Desmogleins and desmocollin are the cadherin family proteins of the desmosome
- Desmosomes serve as attachment sites for keratin filaments, so losing them loosens keratinocytes from one another

Pemphigus vulgaris and bullous pemphigoid both come from autoantibodies against keratinocyte adhesion structures, and the difference is which junction is targeted. The lecture leaves their full H&E appearance to Dr. Davis's dermatology lecture.

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Pemphigus vulgaris | Bullous pemphigoid |
|---|---|---|
| Junction attacked | Desmosome | Hemidesmosome |
| Target | Desmogleins | BP180 (type XVII collagen), BP230 |
| Antibody | IgG | IgG with or without IgE |
| Adhesion lost | Keratinocyte to keratinocyte (acantholysis) | Epidermis to basement membrane |
| Blister level | Between keratinocytes | Subepidermal |

> Pemphigus vulgaris is IgG autoimmunity against desmogleins, causing acantholysis, a loss of keratinocyte to keratinocyte adhesion.

Library: Macule vs patch
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Clinical photo of the leg with a small oval hypopigmented macule, labeled ash leaf macule of tuberous sclerosis](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-macule-ash-leaf-tuberous-sclerosis.jpg)

![Clinical photo of the back of a hand with large depigmented patches of vitiligo, labeled depigmented](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-patch-vitiligo-hand.jpg)

## Identify it

- Flat: a change in color with no elevation
- Macule: flat discoloration 1 cm or smaller
- Patch: flat discoloration larger than 1 cm

## Key features

Primary lesions describe the basic morphology of an individual lesion, and the lecture calls them the key to the diagnosis. The macule and the patch are the two flat primary lesions, and size is the only thing that separates them. The lecture's two examples are both light lesions, one hypopigmented and one depigmented.

| Lesion | Elevation | Size | Lecture example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Macule | Flat | 1 cm or less | Ash leaf macule of tuberous sclerosis (hypopigmented) |
| Patch | Flat | More than 1 cm | Vitiligo (depigmented) |

- The ash leaf macule of tuberous sclerosis is described as hypopigmented
- Vitiligo is the lecture's patch example and is described as depigmented
- The same 1 cm cutoff separates the raised primary lesions (papule vs plaque)
- Purpura follows the same flat lesion vocabulary: a petechia is a macule and an ecchymosis is a patch

> A flat discoloration is a macule when it's 1 cm or smaller and a patch when it's larger than 1 cm.

Library: Papule vs plaque
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Clinical photo of a small raised skin-colored to pink cerebriform papule, labeled intradermal nevus](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-papule-intradermal-nevus.jpg)

![Clinical photos of two plaques: a brown stuck-on appearing seborrheic keratosis and a well-demarcated scaly psoriasis vulgaris plaque](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-plaques-seborrheic-keratosis-psoriasis.jpg)

## Identify it

- Papule: raised, 1 cm or smaller
- Plaque: flat-topped elevation larger than 1 cm

## Key features

The papule and plaque are the raised primary lesions. They use the same 1 cm cutoff as the flat lesions (macule and patch), so a student can sort any lesion by two questions: is it flat or raised, and is it bigger than 1 cm?

| Lesion | Elevation | Size | Lecture example | Descriptor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Papule | Raised | 1 cm or less | Intradermal nevus | Cerebriform |
| Plaque | Flat-topped elevation | More than 1 cm | Seborrheic keratosis | Stuck-on appearing |
| Plaque | Flat-topped elevation | More than 1 cm | Psoriasis vulgaris | Well-demarcated |

- The intradermal nevus is the lecture's papule example, with a cerebriform surface
- Seborrheic keratosis is a stuck-on appearing plaque
- Psoriasis vulgaris forms well-demarcated plaques, and the same disease shows white, micaceous scale on the scalp
- A wheal is a special raised lesion: an edematous papule or plaque

> A raised lesion is a papule at 1 cm or less and a plaque (flat-topped elevation) when larger than 1 cm.

Library: Wheals and urticaria (hives)
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Schematic skin block labeled wheal, showing a pale raised swelling from fluid in the dermis](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-wheal-diagram-dermal-edema.jpg)

![Clinical photo of urticaria, with scattered pink raised wheals on the skin](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-wheal-urticaria-hives.jpg)

## Identify it

- An edematous papule or plaque
- Pink, raised lesions that come and go
- In urticaria (hives), each individual lesion lasts less than 24 hours

## Key features

A wheal is a primary lesion defined by edema, which the lecture defines as infiltration of the dermis with fluid. The defining behavior is speed: the edema enters and exits quickly, so a single wheal is gone within a day even if new ones keep appearing.

- Wheal = edematous papule or plaque
- Edema = fluid infiltrating the dermis
- Urticaria (hives) is the lecture's wheal example
- Individual urticarial lesion: under 24 hours

## Look-alikes

| Term | What it is | Feel or timing | Lecture example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wheal | Dermal edema | Enters and exits quickly | Urticaria |
| Induration | Firm dermal edema | Firm to touch | Cellulitis |
| Urticarial plaque | Seen with an autoimmune blistering disease | Occurs alongside subepidermal bullae | Bullous pemphigoid |

> An individual urticarial wheal lasts less than 24 hours because the dermal edema enters and exits quickly.

Library: Vesicle vs bulla
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Schematic skin block showing fluid-filled blisters of two sizes, labeled vesicle (small) and bulla (large)](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-vesicle-bulla-diagram.jpg)

![Two clinical photos of herpes simplex: grouped clear vesicles near the lip (new) and grouped cloudy vesicles on the cheek below the eye (old), both on an erythematous base](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-vesicles-herpes-simplex-new-old.jpg)

## Identify it

- Blister: a fluid-filled raised lesion
- Bulla: larger than 1 cm
- Vesicle: 1 cm or smaller

## Key features

Vesicles and bullae are both blisters, and size is what separates them (bulla > 1 cm ≥ vesicle). The lecture uses herpes simplex as its vesicle example: grouped vesicles on an erythematous base. The vesicles change with age, so new lesions are clear and old lesions are cloudy.

- Herpes simplex: grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
- New herpes vesicles are clear, and old ones are cloudy
- Herpes vesicles are intraepidermal, so they're fragile and readily rupture, ooze, and crust
- Vesicle and bulla describe size only; the level of the split (intraepidermal or subepidermal) decides whether a blister is fragile or tense

## Look-alikes

| Lesion | Grouping | Lecture note |
|---|---|---|
| Herpes simplex vesicles | Grouped on an erythematous base | New clear, old cloudy; fragile |
| Dermatitis herpetiformis vesicles | Somewhat grouped, "herpes-like" | Severely itchy, so rarely intact |
| Diabetic bulla | Single large blister | Tense, without erythema |

> A bulla is a blister larger than 1 cm; a vesicle is 1 cm or smaller.

Library: Intraepidermal vs subepidermal blisters
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Clinical photo of the top of a foot with a single large tense bulla and no surrounding redness, a diabetic bulla](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-bulla-diabetic-tense.jpg)

## Identify it

- Fragile blister that breaks easily, leaving ooze, crust, and erosions: think intraepidermal
- Tense blister that resists rupture: think subepidermal

## Key features

The level of the split predicts how a blister behaves. The lecture describes intraepidermal vesicles as fragile: they readily rupture, ooze, and crust. A subepidermal bulla is tense and resists rupture. The diabetic bulla is the lecture's example of a tense blister without erythema.

| Level | Blister feel | Lecture examples |
|---|---|---|
| Intraepidermal | Fragile; ruptures, oozes, crusts | Herpes simplex, pemphigus vulgaris |
| Subepidermal | Tense; resists rupture | Diabetic bulla, epidermolysis bullosa, bullous pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis |

- Pemphigus vulgaris has intraepidermal vesicles and bullae, and its slides label the lesions fragile, with erosions and crusts
- Bullous pemphigoid has tense subepidermal bullae, and the Nikolsky sign is negative
- Epidermolysis bullosa forms subepidermal, non-inflammatory blisters
- In dermatitis herpetiformis, multiloculated microabscesses become a subepidermal blister

> Intraepidermal blisters are fragile (rupture, ooze, crust), while subepidermal blisters are tense and resist rupture.

Library: Pustules: acne vs tinea capitis
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Clinical photos of pustules: small raised pustules along the mandible in acne vulgaris, and pustules on the occipital scalp in tinea capitis](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-pustules-acne-tinea-capitis.jpg)

## Identify it

- Small, circumscribed, raised lesion
- Contains leukocytes and fluid

## Key features

A pustule is a primary lesion. Where a vesicle holds fluid, a pustule holds leukocytes and fluid. The lecture pairs two pustular diseases and ties each to a location.

| Disease | Location shown | Lecture prompt |
|---|---|---|
| Acne vulgaris | Along the mandible | Pustules among other acne lesions |
| Tinea capitis | Occipital scalp | Any palpable lymph nodes? |

- Acne vulgaris pustules are shown along the mandible
- Tinea capitis pustules are shown on the occipital scalp
- The tinea capitis slide asks "Any palpable lymph nodes?"
- The primary lesion of acne is the closed comedo, not the pustule

## Look-alikes

| Lesion | Contents | Lecture example |
|---|---|---|
| Vesicle | Blister fluid; 1 cm or smaller | Herpes simplex (new clear, old cloudy) |
| Pustule | Leukocytes and fluid | Acne vulgaris, tinea capitis |
| Cyst | Fluid or debris inside an epithelial lining | Epidermal inclusion cyst (keratin-filled) |

> A pustule is a small, circumscribed, raised lesion that contains leukocytes and fluid.

Library: Nodule vs cyst
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Clinical photos of two nodules: a rock-hard calcinosis cutis nodule with a crusted center over the elbow, and a red tender erythema nodosum nodule on the leg](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-nodules-calcinosis-cutis-erythema-nodosum.jpg)

![Schematic skin block labeled cyst, filled, showing a round sac in the dermis under a dome-shaped elevation](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-cyst-diagram.jpg)

![Clinical photo of the lower face with a dome-shaped swelling over the cheek, an epidermal inclusion cyst](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-cyst-epidermal-inclusion-face.jpg)

## Identify it

- Nodule: firm, solid, deep
- Cyst: sac-like nodule with an epithelial lining, containing fluid or debris

## Key features

The nodule is a deep primary lesion, and the lecture contrasts two by feel: calcinosis cutis is rock hard and erythema nodosum is tender. A cyst is a special kind of nodule because it has an epithelial lining around its contents. The lecture's example is the epidermal inclusion cyst, which is keratin-filled, and the slide stresses that these are not sebaceous cysts.

| Lesion | Feel or contents | Lecture example |
|---|---|---|
| Nodule | Rock hard | Calcinosis cutis |
| Nodule | Tender | Erythema nodosum |
| Cyst | Keratin-filled sac with epithelial lining | Epidermal inclusion cyst |

When you evaluate a cyst, the lecture lists the questions to ask:

1. Single vs multiple?
2. Fixed vs mobile?
3. Tender vs non-tender?
4. Inflamed vs non-inflamed?
5. Growing vs stable in size?

> An epidermal inclusion cyst is keratin-filled, so the lecture says it isn't a sebaceous cyst.

Library: Scale: psoriasis vs seborrheic dermatitis
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Clinical photos of scale: white micaceous scale at the occipital scalp hairline in psoriasis, and yellow greasy scale on an infant's scalp (cradle cap) in seborrheic dermatitis](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-scale-psoriasis-seborrheic-dermatitis.jpg)

## Identify it

- Flakes on the skin surface from built-up stratum corneum
- Color and texture point to the disease: white and micaceous vs yellow and greasy

## Key features

Scale is a secondary lesion. The lecture frames secondary lesions as changes that come with time and manipulation (a clock and picking fingers on the opening slide), layered on top of the primary lesion. Scale is defined as an abnormal accumulation of stratum corneum.

| Disease | Scale | Location shown |
|---|---|---|
| Psoriasis | White, micaceous | Occipital scalp |
| Seborrheic dermatitis | Yellow, greasy | Infant scalp ("cradle cap") |

- Psoriasis scale is white and micaceous, shown at the occipital scalp
- Seborrheic dermatitis scale is yellow and greasy, and in infants it's called cradle cap
- Psoriasis vulgaris plaques are well-demarcated, and the lecture uses them as a plaque example too

> Scale is an abnormal accumulation of stratum corneum: white and micaceous in psoriasis, yellow and greasy in seborrheic dermatitis.

Library: Crust: impetigo vs hemorrhagic crust
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Clinical photos of crust: honey-colored crust around the nostril in impetigo, and dark hemorrhagic crust on the lips in Stevens-Johnson syndrome](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-crust-impetigo-hemorrhagic.jpg)

## Identify it

- Dried material sitting on the skin surface (a scab)
- Honey-colored crust vs dark, bloody (hemorrhagic) crust

## Key features

Crust is a secondary lesion. Serum, blood, or exudate oozes onto the surface, and that ooze dries to form a crust, which the lecture equates with a scab. The color of the crust reflects what dried.

| Crust type | Appearance | Lecture example |
|---|---|---|
| Honey-comb colored | Golden, honey-colored crust | Impetigo |
| Hemorrhagic | Dark red to black, bloody crust | Stevens-Johnson syndrome |

- Impetigo shows the classic honey-colored crust, here around the nostril
- Stevens-Johnson syndrome shows hemorrhagic crust on the lips
- Fragile intraepidermal blisters (herpes simplex) readily rupture, ooze, and crust
- Pemphigus vulgaris lesions progress from vesicle and bulla to erosion and crust

> Crust forms when oozing serum, blood, or exudate dries; impetigo gives a honey-colored crust.

Library: Atrophy: discoid lupus and morphea
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Schematic skin block labeled atrophy, showing a smooth depression of the surface with the epidermis still intact](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-atrophy-diagram.jpg)

![Clinical photo of discoid lupus around the ear, with erythematous, dyspigmented atrophic plaques](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-atrophy-discoid-lupus.jpg)

![Clinical photo of the forehead with a linear, bound-down depression, labeled en coup de sabre (morphea)](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-atrophy-morphea-en-coup-de-sabre.jpg)

## Identify it

- A depressed area with the epidermis still intact
- Discoid lupus: erythema and dyspigmentation
- En coup de sabre (morphea): linear and bound down

## Key features

Atrophy is a secondary lesion defined as underlying tissue loss beneath an intact epidermis. The tissue lost can be epidermal, dermal, or subcutis. Because the surface stays intact, atrophy differs from an erosion or ulcer, where the epidermis itself is gone.

| Disease | Clinical clue | Location shown |
|---|---|---|
| Discoid lupus | Erythema, dyspigmentation | Around the ear |
| En coup de sabre (morphea) | Linear, bound down | Forehead |

- Atrophy can involve loss of epidermis, dermis, or subcutis
- Discoid lupus atrophy comes with erythema and dyspigmentation
- En coup de sabre is a linear, bound-down form of morphea

## Look-alikes

| Lesion | Epidermis | Depth of loss |
|---|---|---|
| Atrophy | Intact | Epidermal, dermal, or subcutis |
| Erosion | Focally lost | Above the dermoepidermal junction |
| Ulcer | Lost | Dermis, with or without subcutis |

> Atrophy is tissue loss under an intact epidermis.

Library: Fissure vs erosion vs ulcer
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Schematic skin block with three labeled defects: a fissure (narrow linear crack into the dermis), an erosion (shallow loss of epidermis), and an ulcer (deep crater through the dermis)](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-fissure-erosion-ulcer-diagram.jpg)

![Clinical photo of both hands with cracked, fissured skin over the fingers, labeled irritant contact dermatitis](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-fissures-irritant-contact-dermatitis.jpg)

![Clinical photos labeled focal loss of epidermis above the dermoepidermal junction (erosions on the hands in porphyria cutanea tarda) and loss of dermis plus or minus subcutis that heals with scarring (venous stasis ulceration on the lower leg)](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-erosion-pct-ulcer-venous-stasis.jpg)

## Identify it

- Fissure: linear crack
- Erosion: shallow, focal loss of the surface
- Ulcer: deeper crater with tissue loss below the surface

## Key features

These three secondary lesions are sorted by shape and depth. The key landmark is the dermoepidermal junction: an erosion stays above it, while a fissure and an ulcer reach into the dermis.

| Lesion | Definition | Depth | Lecture example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fissure | Linear crack | Extends into the dermis | Irritant contact dermatitis |
| Erosion | Focal loss of epidermis | Above the dermoepidermal junction | Porphyria cutanea tarda |
| Ulcer | Loss of dermis, with or without subcutis | Dermis and possibly subcutis; heals with scarring | Venous stasis ulceration |

- Fissures are linear cracks that extend into the dermis, shown on the hands in irritant contact dermatitis
- Erosions are focal loss of epidermis above the dermoepidermal junction, shown in porphyria cutanea tarda
- Ulcers lose dermis (with or without subcutis) and heal with scarring, shown in venous stasis ulceration
- Pemphigus vulgaris and bullous pemphigoid both leave erosions after blisters break

> An erosion is focal epidermal loss above the dermoepidermal junction; an ulcer loses dermis and heals with scarring.

Library: Lichenification and excoriation
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Schematic skin block labeled lichenification, showing a thickened epidermis with exaggerated skin lines, with clip art of a back scratcher and scratching fingers](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-lichenification-diagram.jpg)

![Clinical photo of a child's arms and trunk with scratched, eczematous skin in atopic dermatitis](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-excoriation-atopic-dermatitis.jpg)

![Clinical photo labeled lichen simplex chronicus, a red scaly thickened plaque with two circled punctate excoriations](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-excoriation-lichen-simplex-chronicus.jpg)

## Identify it

- Lichenification: thickened epidermis with accentuated skin lines
- Excoriation: linear or punctate marks of trauma from scratching

## Key features

Both are secondary lesions caused by the patient's own manipulation of the skin. Lichenification develops with chronic rubbing and scratching, which thickens the epidermis until the normal skin lines stand out. Excoriation is the direct injury from scratching, seen as linear or punctate trauma.

| Lesion | Definition | Cause | Lecture example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lichenification | Thickened epidermis, accentuated skin lines | Chronic rubbing, scratching | Diagram with back scratcher |
| Excoriation | Linear or punctate trauma | Scratching | Atopic dermatitis, lichen simplex chronicus |

- Scratching leads to excoriation
- Chronic rubbing and scratching lead to lichenification
- Atopic dermatitis and lichen simplex chronicus are the lecture's excoriation examples
- Dermatitis herpetiformis is so itchy that scratching leaves vesicles rarely intact

> Lichenification is a thickened epidermis with accentuated skin lines from chronic rubbing and scratching.

Library: Erythema vs purpura
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Clinical photos of erythema: pink erythema on the cheek in rosacea, and lilac or purplish erythema in a lichen planus plaque](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-erythema-rosacea-lichen-planus.jpg)

![Clinical photos of purpura: tiny red petechiae around the mouth (macule: petechia) and a larger purple-yellow bruise on a limb (patch: ecchymosis)](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-purpura-petechiae-ecchymosis.jpg)

## Identify it

- Erythema: redness from blood inside dilated vessels
- Purpura: bleeding into the skin, so the blood is outside the vessels

## Key features
