The lecture says erythema is "not a color." It reflects vascular dilatation, and its shade varies with the disease. Purpura is different in mechanism because it is bleeding into the skin, and it's named with the flat lesion vocabulary.

| Finding | Mechanism | Forms | Lecture example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Erythema | Vascular dilatation | Pink | Rosacea |
| Erythema | Vascular dilatation | Lilac or purplish | Lichen planus |
| Purpura | Bleeding into the skin | Petechia (macule) | Petechiae around the mouth |
| Purpura | Bleeding into the skin | Ecchymosis (patch) | Bruise on a limb |

- A petechia is a purpuric macule, and an ecchymosis is a purpuric patch
- Plurals: petechiae and ecchymoses
- Diascopy separates the two: erythema blanches under a glass slide and purpura doesn't

> Erythema is vascular dilatation (blood in the vessel), while purpura is bleeding into the skin.

Library: Diascopy: blanching vs non-blanching lesions
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Clinical photos labeled glass slide: a small red circled lesion on the nose, then the same area pressed with a glass slide and blanched](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-diascopy-glass-slide.jpg)

![Clinical photos of a venous lake: a dark blue-purple papule on the ear, then the same ear compressed with a glass slide](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-venous-lake-diascopy.jpg)

![Magnified photos of a juvenile xanthogranuloma: a pink dome-shaped papule, and a second view in which the papule looks yellow](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-juvenile-xanthogranuloma.jpg)

## Identify it

- Diascopy: press a glass slide on the lesion to compress its blood vessels
- Blanches (turns pale): blood is inside the vessel
- Doesn't blanch: blood is outside the vessel (purpura)

## Key features

Diascopy answers the question "Where is the blood?" The glass slide compresses the blood vessels. If the blood is in the vessel, the lesion blanches and turns pale. If the blood is out of the vessel, the lesion doesn't blanch, and that's purpura.

| Result | Where the blood is | Lesions |
|---|---|---|
| Blanches | In the vessel | Erythema, telangiectasia |
| Doesn't blanch | Out of the vessel | Purpura (petechia, ecchymosis), vasculitis |

- Spider angioma: an arteriole, and it pulsates
- The lecture then shows a venous lake on the ear before and under a glass slide
- It also shows a juvenile xanthogranuloma, a pink papule that looks yellow in the second view (the slide title highlights "Xantho" in yellow)

> Blood inside a vessel blanches under diascopy (erythema, telangiectasia); blood outside a vessel doesn't (purpura, vasculitis).

Library: Open vs closed comedones
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Schematic skin block labeled comedo, showing plugged follicular openings, some closed and some open at the surface](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-comedo-diagram.jpg)

![Clinical photos of comedones: small comedones on the skin in acne vulgaris, and open comedones on sun-damaged skin beside the eye](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-comedones-acne-sun-damage.jpg)

## Identify it

- Closed comedo: white head
- Open comedo: black head

## Key features

The comedo is one of the lecture's special lesions. Comedones come in two forms, and the closed comedo is singled out as the primary lesion of acne.

| Comedo | Common name | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Closed | White head | Primary lesion of acne |
| Open | Black head | Shown in acne and in sun-damaged skin |

- Closed comedo = white head, and it's the primary lesion of acne
- Open comedo = black head
- The plural is comedones
- The lecture shows comedones in two settings: acne vulgaris and sun-damage
- Acne vulgaris also forms pustules, shown along the mandible

The lecture groups the comedo with its other special lesions: telangiectasia, scar, and induration. In acne, the comedo is the starting lesion, and the lecture's acne photos also show pustules along the mandible.

> The closed comedo (white head) is the primary lesion of acne; the open comedo is the black head.

Library: Telangiectasia: rosacea vs dermatomyositis
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Clinical photos of telangiectasia: a circled area of fine dilated vessels on the cheek in rosacea, and circled dilated vessels at the nail fold (periungual) in dermatomyositis](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-telangiectasia-rosacea-dermatomyositis.jpg)

## Identify it

- Fine, visible dilated superficial blood vessels
- Location points to the disease: cheek vs periungual (around the nail)

## Key features

Telangiectasia is a special lesion defined as a dilated superficial blood vessel. The lecture teaches it by location, pairing each site with a disease.

| Location | Disease |
|---|---|
| Cheek | Rosacea |
| Periungual | Dermatomyositis |

- Cheek telangiectasia is shown in rosacea
- Periungual telangiectasia is shown in dermatomyositis
- Because the blood stays inside the vessel, telangiectasia blanches with diascopy
- Rosacea also shows pink erythema from vascular dilatation
- A spider angioma differs because it's an arteriole and it pulsates

## Look-alikes

| Finding | What it is | Diascopy |
|---|---|---|
| Telangiectasia | Dilated superficial blood vessel | Blanches |
| Erythema | Vascular dilatation | Blanches |
| Spider angioma | Arteriole; pulsates | Not stated |
| Purpura | Bleeding into the skin | Doesn't blanch |

> Periungual telangiectasia points to dermatomyositis, while cheek telangiectasia is shown in rosacea.

Library: Scar vs keloid
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Clinical photos of a cicatrix: a circled linear surgical scar in front of the ear, and a keloid, a raised mass on the earlobe](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-scar-linear-surgical-keloid.jpg)

## Identify it

- Scar: permanent fibrotic change in the skin
- Keloid: a scar that's larger than the original wound

## Key features

A scar forms when damage extends into the dermis, and it's permanent fibrotic change. Cicatrix is the term for the scar of a healed wound. The lecture contrasts a linear surgical scar, which stays within the wound line, with a keloid, which grows beyond it.

| Term | Definition | Lecture example |
|---|---|---|
| Scar | Permanent fibrotic change; damage extends to dermis | Linear surgical scar |
| Cicatrix | Scar of a healed wound | Linear surgical scar |
| Keloid | Larger than the original wound | Earlobe keloid |

- Damage has to reach the dermis to scar
- Ulcers lose dermis, and the lecture says they heal with scarring
- Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa is named for its scarring
- Discoid lupus and morphea cause atrophy (tissue loss under an intact epidermis), which is a different secondary lesion

> A keloid is a scar that's larger than the original wound.

Library: Induration and cellulitis
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Schematic skin block labeled induration, showing a firm, thickened dermis](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-induration-diagram.jpg)

![Clinical photo of cellulitis on a limb, with a red, swollen area and small crusted erosions](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-cellulitis-induration.jpg)

## Identify it

- Firm swelling of the skin on palpation
- In cellulitis, the involved skin feels indurated

## Key features

Induration is a special lesion defined as firm dermal edema. The lecture's example is cellulitis, a soft tissue infection, which feels indurated.

- Induration = firm dermal edema
- Cellulitis = soft tissue infection that feels indurated

## Look-alikes

| Term | Definition | Behavior | Lecture example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Induration | Firm dermal edema | Firm to palpation | Cellulitis |
| Wheal | Edematous papule or plaque (fluid in the dermis) | Enters and exits quickly | Urticaria |
| Nodule | Firm, solid, deep | Can be rock hard or tender | Calcinosis cutis, erythema nodosum |

Induration and the wheal both involve edema in the dermis. The wheal of urticaria comes and goes within 24 hours, while induration is the firm edema you feel in an infection such as cellulitis.

> Induration is firm dermal edema, and cellulitis feels indurated.

Library: Mechanobullous vs autoimmune blistering diseases
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

## Key features

Vesiculobullous diseases are the blistering diseases. The lecture splits them into two groups by whether inflammation is part of the process.

| Group | Inflammation | Cause | Lecture examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mechanobullous | Non-inflammatory | Defective epidermal-dermal attachment; mechanical shearing | Epidermolysis bullosa (simplex, junctional, dystrophic) |
| Autoimmune | Inflammatory | Autoantibodies (antibodies against self) | Pemphigus, bullous pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis |

## Mechanobullous

- The mechanobullous disorder in the lecture is epidermolysis bullosa (EB)
- EB is a defect at the epidermal-dermal junction
- Blisters are subepidermal with no inflammation, and they come from mechanical shearing

## Autoimmune

- Pemphigus
- Bullous pemphigoid
- Dermatitis herpetiformis
- Acquired epidermolysis bullosa is on the list but the lecture doesn't discuss it

The autoimmune group is confirmed with skin biopsy for routine histology, biopsy of normal-appearing perilesional skin for direct immunofluorescence, and serum tests (indirect immunofluorescence and antigen-specific ELISA).

> Mechanobullous diseases (epidermolysis bullosa) are non-inflammatory, while autoimmune blistering diseases are inflammatory and driven by autoantibodies.

Library: Epidermolysis bullosa overview
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Labeled diagram of the epidermal-dermal junction, from basal keratinocyte and keratin intermediate filaments through hemidesmosome, plasma membrane, lamina lucida with anchoring filaments, lamina densa, and the sublamina densa region with anchoring fibrils, microfibrils, micro-thread-like fibers, interstitial collagens, and anchoring plaques; the junction is circled](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-dej-diagram-eb-split.jpg)

![Histology section of epidermolysis bullosa showing the epidermis separated from the dermis by a clear subepidermal blister cavity, with no inflammatory infiltrate](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-eb-histo-subepidermal-noninflammatory.jpg)

## Identify it

- Vesicles or bullae from minor mechanical trauma
- Histology: a subepidermal blister with no inflammation

## Key features

Epidermolysis bullosa (EB) is the lecture's mechanobullous disorder. The problem is defective epidermal-dermal attachment, so the skin separates at the junction with shearing. Because the cause is structural rather than immune, the blister is non-inflammatory.

- Defective epidermal-dermal attachment
- Subepidermal blisters
- No inflammation
- Three basic types: simplex, junctional, dystrophic

## Structures at the junction

The diagram shows the layers where the EB defects sit, from top to bottom:

1. Basal keratinocyte with keratin intermediate filaments
2. Hemidesmosome and plasma membrane
3. Lamina lucida with anchoring filaments
4. Lamina densa
5. Sublamina densa region with anchoring fibrils, microfibrils, micro-thread-like fibers, interstitial collagens, and anchoring plaques

The three types are named for where the defect sits: keratins 5 and 14 (simplex), laminin 332 (junctional), and collagen VII (dystrophic).

> Epidermolysis bullosa is a mechanobullous disease of defective epidermal-dermal attachment that gives subepidermal blisters without inflammation.

Library: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Epidermal-dermal junction diagram with an arrow pointing to the keratin intermediate filaments in the basal keratinocyte, above the hemidesmosome](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-ebs-diagram-keratin-defect.jpg)

![Clinical photos of epidermolysis bullosa simplex: the sole of an infant's foot and a child's hands with small blisters and red erosions on the fingers](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-ebs-foot-hands.jpg)

## Identify it

- Blisters and erosions on the feet and hands in the lecture's photos
- Classic trigger: marching

## Key features

Epidermolysis bullosa simplex is the type with the keratin defect. On the lecture's diagram, the arrow points to the keratin intermediate filaments in the basal keratinocyte, which sit above the hemidesmosome.

- Inheritance: autosomal dominant (mostly)
- Defect: keratins 5 and 14
- Classic trigger: marching (the slide shows soldiers and a marching band)
- Location of the defect on the diagram: keratin intermediate filaments of the basal keratinocyte

## Look-alikes

| EB type | Inheritance | Defect |
|---|---|---|
| Simplex | Autosomal dominant (mostly) | Keratins 5 and 14 |
| Junctional | Autosomal recessive | Laminin 332 |
| Dystrophic | Autosomal dominant or recessive | Collagen VII |

The friction trigger fits the general EB picture: no inflammation, and blisters form from mechanical shearing, so management centers on avoiding trauma.

> Epidermolysis bullosa simplex is mostly autosomal dominant, comes from defects in keratins 5 and 14, and is classically triggered by marching.

Library: Junctional epidermolysis bullosa
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Epidermal-dermal junction diagram with an arrow pointing to the anchoring filaments in the lamina lucida, between the hemidesmosome and the lamina densa](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-jeb-diagram-lamina-lucida-defect.jpg)

![Clinical photos of junctional epidermolysis bullosa on day 1: a newborn's hand and foot with raw red erosions](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-jeb-day1.jpg)

![Clinical photo of junctional epidermolysis bullosa on day 2: a newborn with large raw red areas where the epidermis has sheared off around the mouth and hand](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-jeb-day2-shearing.jpg)

## Identify it

- Newborn with erosions from day 1
- By day 2 the epidermis shears off, leaving large raw areas

## Key features

On the diagram, the arrow points to the anchoring filaments in the lamina lucida, the layer between the hemidesmosome and the lamina densa.

- Inheritance: autosomal recessive
- Defect: laminin 332
- Prognosis: typical early death
- Location of the defect on the diagram: anchoring filaments in the lamina lucida

The day 1 and day 2 photos show how fast the skin fails. Erosions are present on the first day, and by the second day the epidermis shears off.

| EB type | Inheritance | Defect | Course |
|---|---|---|---|
| Simplex | Autosomal dominant (mostly) | Keratins 5 and 14 | Triggered by friction (marching) |
| Junctional | Autosomal recessive | Laminin 332 | Typical early death |
| Dystrophic | Autosomal dominant or recessive | Collagen VII | Scarring; squamous cell carcinoma risk |

> Junctional epidermolysis bullosa is autosomal recessive, comes from a laminin 332 defect, and typically causes early death.

Library: Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Epidermal-dermal junction diagram with an arrow pointing to the anchoring fibrils in the sublamina densa region, below the lamina densa](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-deb-diagram-anchoring-fibril-defect.jpg)

![Clinical photos of dominant dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa: hands and knees with erosions, crusts, and scars](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-deb-dominant-hands-knees.jpg)

![Clinical photos of recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa: fused, scarred hands (mitten deformity) and a scarred, deformed foot (sock deformity)](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-deb-recessive-mitten-sock.jpg)

## Identify it

- Blisters that heal with scarring
- Recessive form: mitten and sock deformities of the hands and feet

## Key features

Dystrophic EB is named for its scarring. On the diagram, the arrow points to the anchoring fibrils in the sublamina densa region, the deepest level of the three EB defects.

- Inheritance: autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive
- Defect: collagen VII
- Scarring is what "dystrophic" refers to
- Location of the defect on the diagram: anchoring fibrils below the lamina densa

| Form | Clinical picture in the lecture |
|---|---|
| Dominant | Erosions, crusts, and scars on the hands and knees |
| Recessive | Mitten and sock deformities |

## Complications

- Dystrophic EB carries a risk of squamous cell carcinoma (SCCa)
- In recessive dystrophic EB, the lecture ranks SCCa above infection as a cause of death

> Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa comes from a collagen VII defect, scars, and in its recessive form causes mitten and sock deformities and death from squamous cell carcinoma more than infection.

Library: Epidermolysis bullosa types and management
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

## Key features

All three types of epidermolysis bullosa share defective epidermal-dermal attachment, subepidermal blisters, and no inflammation. They differ in inheritance, the protein that's defective, and the outcome.

| Type | Inheritance | Defect | Defect on the diagram | Hallmark |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Simplex | Autosomal dominant (mostly) | Keratins 5 and 14 | Keratin intermediate filaments of the basal keratinocyte | Classic trigger: marching |
| Junctional | Autosomal recessive | Laminin 332 | Anchoring filaments in the lamina lucida | Typical early death |
| Dystrophic | Autosomal dominant or recessive | Collagen VII | Anchoring fibrils in the sublamina densa region | Scarring; mitten and sock deformities (recessive) |

## Treatment

Because the blisters come from mechanical shearing rather than inflammation, care focuses on protecting the skin.

- Avoid trauma
- Wound dressings
- Watch for infection, since the risk is increased
- In dystrophic EB, watch for squamous cell carcinoma (SCCa)

## Associations

- Dystrophic EB: squamous cell carcinoma
- Recessive dystrophic EB: SCCa is a more common cause of death than infection
- Junctional EB: typical early death

> In epidermolysis bullosa there's no inflammation and blisters come from mechanical shearing, so management is avoiding trauma, wound dressings, and watching for infection and (in dystrophic EB) squamous cell carcinoma.

Library: Diagnostic tests for autoimmune blistering diseases
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

## Key features

The autoimmune blistering diseases (pemphigus, bullous pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis) are caused by autoantibodies, antibodies against self. Diagnosis uses two different biopsies and serum testing, and the biopsy site depends on the test.

| Test | Sample | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| Routine histology | Skin biopsy of lesional skin | Histology, such as the level of split |
| Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) | Skin biopsy of normal-appearing perilesional skin | Autoantibody bound in the patient's skin |
| Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) | Serum | Circulating autoantibodies |
| Antigen-specific ELISA | Serum | Antibodies to a specific antigen |

- Biopsy the lesion itself for routine histology
- Biopsy normal-appearing skin next to the lesion (perilesional) for DIF
- Use serum for IIF and ELISA to detect circulating antibodies

## How the lecture uses each test

- Pemphigus: DIF shows a "chicken wire" pattern from antidesmoglein antibodies; IIF and ELISA test for Dsg 3 and Dsg 1 antibodies
- Bullous pemphigoid: DIF shows autoantibodies to the bullous pemphigoid antigens in hemidesmosomes; IIF and ELISA test for BPAg1 and BPAg2 antibodies
- Dermatitis herpetiformis: DIF shows granular deposits of IgA at the tips of the dermal papillae

> Direct immunofluorescence is done on a biopsy of normal-appearing perilesional skin, while routine histology is done on lesional skin.

Library: Pemphigus vulgaris: clinical features and treatment
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Clinical photo of pemphigus vulgaris of the lips, with raw red erosions and dark crusts](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-pv-lips.jpg)

![Clinical photos of pemphigus vulgaris on the skin, labeled vesicle and bulla and erosion and crust, with circled small vesicles and a fragile label](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-pv-vesicle-bulla-erosion-crust.jpg)

## Identify it

- Mucocutaneous disease, typically beginning with oral lesions
- Lips with raw erosions and crusts
- Fragile vesicles and bullae that break into erosions and crusts
- Cutaneous lesions on the scalp, face, and creases

## Level of split and immunofluorescence

- Intraepidermal vesicles and bullae, so the blisters are fragile
- Autoantibodies to desmoglein 3 (Dsg 3)
- Oral disease tracks with Dsg 3, while cutaneous disease involves Dsg 1 and Dsg 3
- DIF shows a "chicken wire" pattern

## Associations

- Age: 5th to 6th decades
- Typically begins with oral lesions

## Treatment

The lecture calls for "big time" immunosuppression:

- Prednisone
- Azathioprine
- Mycophenolate mofetil
- Rituximab (anti-CD20 antibody), which is FDA approved; CD20 is a pan-B-cell antigenic marker

> Pemphigus vulgaris is an intraepidermal blistering disease from antibodies to desmoglein 3 that typically begins with oral lesions and needs heavy immunosuppression, including rituximab.

Library: Pemphigus foliaceus vs pemphigus vulgaris
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

## Key features

The lecture presents pemphigus foliaceus as a contrast to pemphigus vulgaris. The difference comes down to which desmoglein the antibodies target, and that decides whether the mouth is involved.

- Pemphigus foliaceus: antibodies target only Dsg 1
- No mucosal involvement
- Superficial "cornflake" peeling

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Pemphigus vulgaris | Pemphigus foliaceus |
|---|---|---|
| Antibody target | Dsg 3 (oral); Dsg 1 and Dsg 3 (skin) | Dsg 1 only |
| Mucosa | Typically begins with oral lesions | No mucosal involvement |
| Skin lesions | Fragile intraepidermal vesicles and bullae, erosions, crusts | Superficial "cornflake" peeling |
| Skin sites | Scalp, face, creases | Not stated |

The pattern links antigen to site. In pemphigus vulgaris, oral lesions go with Dsg 3, and the skin lesions involve both Dsg 1 and Dsg 3. Pemphigus foliaceus has antibodies against Dsg 1 alone, and it spares the mucosa.

- Both forms are pemphigus, and the lecture's pemphigus DIF shows a "chicken wire" pattern from antidesmoglein antibodies
- IIF and ELISA test for Dsg 3 and Dsg 1 antibodies

> Pemphigus foliaceus targets only Dsg 1, so it has no mucosal involvement and shows superficial "cornflake" peeling.

Library: Pemphigus vulgaris: acantholysis and Nikolsky sign
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![H&E sections of pemphigus vulgaris showing an intraepidermal split with loose rounded keratinocytes in the cavity (one circled), a higher power view of basal cells left standing on the basement membrane, and a photo of a row of tombstones as the visual analogy](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-pv-acantholysis-tombstones.jpg)

![Histology of a large intraepidermal blister with a cartoon finger pressing from the side, illustrating the Nikolsky sign](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-pv-nikolsky-sign.jpg)

## Identify it

- Histology: an intraepidermal split with loose, separated keratinocytes floating in the cavity
- A single row of basal cells left on the floor of the blister, like tombstones
- Clinically, sideways pressure spreads the blister

## Key features

Acantholysis is loss of keratinocyte cell-to-cell adhesion. Pemphigus vulgaris has autoantibodies to desmoglein 3 and intraepidermal blisters, and on histology the keratinocytes come apart from each other within the epidermis. The basal cells stay attached to the basement membrane, and the lecture calls them "tombstones."

- Acantholysis = loss of keratinocyte cell-to-cell adhesion
- "Tombstones" = basal cells that remain attached to the basement membrane
- The split is intraepidermal, so the blisters are fragile

## Nikolsky sign

The Nikolsky sign is lateral pressure extending the blister. The lecture shows it in the pemphigus section, and it's negative in bullous pemphigoid.

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Pemphigus vulgaris | Bullous pemphigoid |
|---|---|---|
| Split | Intraepidermal with acantholysis | Subepidermal |
| Blister | Fragile | Tense |
| Nikolsky sign | Shown (lateral pressure extends the blister) | Negative |

> Acantholysis (loss of keratinocyte cell-to-cell adhesion) leaves basal cells attached to the basement membrane as "tombstones" in pemphigus vulgaris.

Library: Pemphigus chicken wire immunofluorescence
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Direct immunofluorescence of pemphigus showing green fluorescence outlining each keratinocyte in a net-like chicken wire pattern, with arrows labeled antidesmoglein antibodies](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-pv-dif-chicken-wire.jpg)

## Identify it

- Green fluorescence outlining the individual keratinocytes throughout the epidermis
- A net-like pattern that the lecture calls "chicken wire"

## Level of split and immunofluorescence

Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) in pemphigus shows antidesmoglein antibodies in a net-like "chicken wire" pattern within the epidermis. This fits the intraepidermal split and the acantholysis seen on routine histology.

- DIF pattern: "chicken wire"
- Antibody: antidesmoglein
- DIF sample: normal-appearing perilesional skin

## Other confirmatory tests

- Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) on serum
- ELISA testing for Dsg 3 and Dsg 1 antibodies

## Look-alikes

| Disease | DIF pattern in the lecture | Antigen |
|---|---|---|
| Pemphigus | "Chicken wire" around keratinocytes | Desmoglein (Dsg 3, Dsg 1) |
| Bullous pemphigoid | Fluorescence along the epidermal-dermal junction | BPAg1, BPAg2 in hemidesmosomes |
| Dermatitis herpetiformis | Granular IgA at the tips of dermal papillae | Epidermal transglutaminase (TG3) |

> Pemphigus direct immunofluorescence shows a "chicken wire" pattern from antidesmoglein antibodies.

Library: Bullous pemphigoid: clinical features and treatment
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Clinical photos of bullous pemphigoid showing tense, fluid-filled and hemorrhagic bullae on red skin of the limb](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-bp-tense-blisters.jpg)

![Clinical photo of the trunk and inner arms in bullous pemphigoid, with sharply demarcated red erosions concentrated in the flexures](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-bp-flexural-erosions.jpg)

## Identify it

- Tense bullae, along with urticarial plaques
- Sharply demarcated erosions after blisters break
- Flexures: flexor forearms, axillae, and groin
- Nikolsky sign: negative
- Chief complaint is itch, often before blisters develop

## Level of split and immunofluorescence

- Subepidermal bullae, which is why they're tense
- IgG antibodies to basement membrane antigens, the hemidesmosomal proteins BPAg1 and BPAg2

## Associations

- Elderly patients
- Rarely involves mucosa
- Itch often comes before the blisters

## Treatment

- Topical or systemic corticosteroids (prednisone)
- Steroid sparing agents
- Dupilumab
- Rituximab

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Bullous pemphigoid | Pemphigus vulgaris |
|---|---|---|
| Age | Elderly | 5th to 6th decades |
| Mucosa | Rarely | Typically begins with oral lesions |
| Blister | Tense, subepidermal | Fragile, intraepidermal |
| Nikolsky | Negative | Lateral pressure extends the blister |

> Bullous pemphigoid gives tense subepidermal bullae in the flexures of elderly patients, rarely involves mucosa, and has a negative Nikolsky sign.

Library: Bullous pemphigoid: histology and immunofluorescence
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![H&E section of bullous pemphigoid showing the whole epidermis lifted off the dermis by a subepidermal blister](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-bp-histo-subepidermal-blister.jpg)

![H&E section of bullous pemphigoid at higher power with many eosinophils in the dermis and at the epidermal-dermal junction](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-bp-histo-eosinophils.jpg)

![Direct immunofluorescence of bullous pemphigoid with a continuous green band following the epidermal-dermal junction, labeled autoantibodies to bullous pemphigoid antigens in hemidesmosomes](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-bp-dif-basement-membrane.jpg)

## Identify it

- Histology: the full epidermis forms the roof of a subepidermal blister
- Eosinophils in the infiltrate
- DIF: fluorescence along the epidermal-dermal junction

## Level of split and immunofluorescence

The split in bullous pemphigoid is subepidermal, which is why the blisters are tense. The autoantibodies are IgG against the bullous pemphigoid antigens in hemidesmosomes (BPAg1 and BPAg2), so on direct immunofluorescence the signal follows the junction instead of outlining each keratinocyte.

- Level of split: subepidermal
- Antibody: IgG to BPAg1 and BPAg2 (hemidesmosomal proteins)
- DIF: autoantibodies to bullous pemphigoid antigens in hemidesmosomes
- Other confirmatory tests: indirect immunofluorescence and ELISA for BPAg1/BPAg2 antibodies

## Key features

The lecture links the eosinophils to the main symptom: eosinophils make it itchy. The chief complaint is itch, often before the patient develops blisters.

| Finding | Bullous pemphigoid | Dermatitis herpetiformis |
|---|---|---|
| Split | Subepidermal | Subepidermal |
| Key cells | Eosinophils | Neutrophils (with eosinophils and fibrin) |
| DIF | Along the junction, to hemidesmosomal antigens | Granular IgA at dermal papillary tips |

> Bullous pemphigoid shows a subepidermal blister with eosinophils (which cause itch), and DIF shows autoantibodies to the bullous pemphigoid antigens in hemidesmosomes.

Library: Dermatitis herpetiformis: clinical features and treatment
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Clinical photo of dermatitis herpetiformis with somewhat grouped vesicles, crusts, and red papules on two adjacent skin surfaces (site not labeled on the slide)](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-dh-grouped-vesicles.jpg)

![Clinical photos of dermatitis herpetiformis on the elbows, with scratched papules and crusts and one circled lesion, labeled itch, scratch: vesicles rarely intact](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-dh-elbows-excoriated.jpg)

## Identify it

- Somewhat grouped, "herpes-like" vesicles
- Elbows and knees
- Severely pruritic, so scratching leaves vesicles rarely intact
- Chronic, relapsing course

## Level of split and immunofluorescence

- Subepidermal blister
- Autoantigen: epidermal transglutaminase (TG3)
- DIF: granular deposits of IgA at the tips of the dermal papillae

## Associations

- Gluten-sensitive enteropathy
- Genetic predisposition: HLA-B8

## Treatment

- Dapsone, which is thought to inhibit neutrophil migration and function
- Gluten-free diet

The dapsone mechanism ties to the histology, where neutrophils collect at the tips of the dermal papillae.

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Dermatitis herpetiformis | Herpes simplex |
|---|---|---|
| Grouping | Somewhat grouped, "herpes-like" | Grouped on an erythematous base |
| Level | Subepidermal | Intraepidermal (fragile) |
| Clue | Severe itch; elbows and knees | New vesicles clear, old cloudy |

> Dermatitis herpetiformis is an intensely itchy blistering disease of the elbows and knees associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy, treated with dapsone and a gluten-free diet.

Library: Dermatitis herpetiformis: histology and IgA immunofluorescence
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![H&E section of dermatitis herpetiformis with a circled collection of neutrophils at the tip of a dermal papilla](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-dh-histo-neutrophils-papillary-tips.jpg)

![H&E sections of dermatitis herpetiformis labeled microabscesses at the tips of the dermal papillae (one circled) and subepidermal vesicles](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-dh-histo-microabscess-subepidermal-vesicle.jpg)

![Direct immunofluorescence of dermatitis herpetiformis showing granular bright green IgA deposits clustered in the tip of a dermal papilla](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-dh-dif-granular-iga.jpg)

## Identify it

- Neutrophils collected at the tips of the dermal papillae
- Small pockets (microabscesses) at the papillary tips that merge into a subepidermal blister
- DIF: granular IgA at the papillary tips

## Key features

The lecture describes the histology as a sequence. Neutrophils, eosinophils, and fibrin accumulate at the tips of the dermal papillae, forming microabscesses. When several of these microabscesses join (multiloculated), they make a subepidermal blister.

1. Accumulation of neutrophils, eosinophils, and fibrin
2. Collections at the tips of dermal papillae become "microabscesses"
3. Multiloculated microabscesses become a subepidermal blister

## Level of split and immunofluorescence

- Level of split: subepidermal
- DIF: granular deposits of IgA at the tips of the dermal papillae
- Autoantigen: epidermal transglutaminase (TG3)

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Dermatitis herpetiformis | Bullous pemphigoid | Pemphigus |
|---|---|---|---|
| Split | Subepidermal | Subepidermal | Intraepidermal |
| Main cells | Neutrophils | Eosinophils | Acantholytic keratinocytes |
| DIF | Granular IgA at papillary tips | Along the junction (hemidesmosome antigens) | "Chicken wire" |

> Dermatitis herpetiformis shows neutrophilic microabscesses at the tips of the dermal papillae and granular IgA deposits there on direct immunofluorescence.

Library: Pemphigus vs bullous pemphigoid vs dermatitis herpetiformis
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

## Key features

The three autoimmune blistering diseases in the lecture are told apart by the level of the split, the target antigen, the immunofluorescence pattern, and who gets them. Every row below comes from the lecture's slides.

| Feature | Pemphigus vulgaris | Bullous pemphigoid | Dermatitis herpetiformis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Level of split | Intraepidermal | Subepidermal | Subepidermal |
| Blister | Fragile; erosions and crusts | Tense; urticarial plaques | Grouped "herpes-like" vesicles, rarely intact |
| Antigen | Desmoglein 3 (and Dsg 1 in skin) | BPAg1, BPAg2 (hemidesmosomes) | Epidermal transglutaminase (TG3) |
| DIF | "Chicken wire" | Along the junction | Granular IgA at papillary tips |

| Feature | Pemphigus vulgaris | Bullous pemphigoid | Dermatitis herpetiformis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Patient | 5th to 6th decades | Elderly | Not stated |
| Sites | Mouth first; scalp, face, creases | Flexor forearms, axillae, groin | Elbows and knees |
| Mucosa | Typically begins orally | Rarely | Not stated |
| Nikolsky | Lateral pressure extends the blister | Negative | Not stated |
| Treatment | Prednisone, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab | Corticosteroids, steroid sparing agents, dupilumab, rituximab | Dapsone, gluten-free diet |

## Associations and clues

- Pemphigus vulgaris: acantholysis with basal "tombstones"
- Bullous pemphigoid: eosinophils, and itch often comes before the blisters
- Dermatitis herpetiformis: HLA-B8, gluten-sensitive enteropathy, neutrophilic microabscesses

> Pemphigus vulgaris is the intraepidermal one (desmoglein, chicken wire DIF); bullous pemphigoid and dermatitis herpetiformis are subepidermal, separated by IgG to hemidesmosomes vs granular IgA at the papillary tips.

Library: Direct vs indirect immunofluorescence
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Introduction to Dermatology and Vesiculobullous Diseases

![Diagram of direct immunofluorescence: the patient's autoantibody bound to self antigen in a biopsy of normal-appearing perilesional skin, detected by fluorescein-labeled anti-immunoglobulin antibody](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-dif-diagram.jpg)

![Diagram of indirect immunofluorescence: autoantibody from the patient's serum bound to antigen on a non-patient substrate (example monkey esophagus), detected by fluorescein-labeled anti-immunoglobulin antibody](library/images/msk-week-13/vbd-iif-diagram.jpg)

## Key features

Both tests use a fluorescein-labeled anti-immunoglobulin antibody and a fluorescence microscope. The difference is where the patient's autoantibody is and what tissue holds the antigen.

| Feature | Direct (DIF) | Indirect (IIF) |
|---|---|---|
| Patient sample | Skin biopsy | Serum |
| Tissue with the antigen | Patient's normal-appearing perilesional skin | Non-patient substrate (e.g., monkey esophagus) |
| What it detects | Autoantibody already bound in the skin | Circulating autoantibodies in the serum |
| Label | Fluorescein-labeled anti-immunoglobulin | Fluorescein-labeled anti-immunoglobulin |

## Steps for IIF

1. Use a substrate that contains the specific antigen, such as monkey esophagus
2. Add the patient's serum, and the autoantibody binds to the antigen
3. Add fluorescein-labeled anti-immunoglobulin antibody
4. View with a fluorescence microscope

## DIF in one line

DIF is done on the patient's skin biopsy, and fluorescein-labeled antibodies bind to the autoantibody that's already attached to self antigen in the skin.

> Direct immunofluorescence finds autoantibody bound in the patient's skin; indirect immunofluorescence finds circulating autoantibody in the patient's serum using a substrate such as monkey esophagus.

Library: Acne vulgaris: presentation and diagnosis
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photo of a forehead covered with many small skin-colored comedones and a few red papules, acne vulgaris](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-acne-vulgaris-forehead-comedones-papules.jpg)

## Identify it

- Comedones must be present to make the diagnosis
- Papules and pustules are often present too
- Face, chest, and back
- Common during the teenage years, 20s, and 30s

## Key features

- Very common: adolescents more than adults, with an incidence of up to 85%
- Significant psychological impact, including depression and poor self-image
- Long-term sequelae are postinflammatory hyperpigmentation and permanent scarring
- Effective treatments are available, and the choice depends on the severity and the category of lesions

## Severity categories

The lecture sorts acne into four categories, from mildest to most severe. Each one has its own page with its treatment.

| Category | Lesions |
|---|---|
| Comedonal | Comedones; the mildest form |
| Mild inflammatory | Papules and pustules with comedones, none to few deep nodules |
| Moderate inflammatory | Tender nodules plus comedones, papules, and pustules |
| Nodulocystic | Many deep-seated nodules and cysts plus inflammatory papules and pustules |

> Acne vulgaris is diagnosed by the presence of comedones, often with papules and pustules.

Library: Acne pathogenesis: comedo to nodule
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Diagram of the pathogenesis of acne in four stages (early comedo, later comedo shown closed and open, inflammatory papule/pustule, nodule/cyst), labeled epidermis, sebaceous lobule, and follicular epithelium, with a key for corneocytes, sebum, and P. acnes](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-acne-pathogenesis-comedo-to-nodule.jpg)

## Early comedo

- Hyperkeratosis and increased corneocyte cohesiveness in the upper sebaceous follicle lead to microcomedo formation
- Androgens stimulate sebum production

## Later comedo

- Shed keratin and sebum accumulate
- Whorled lamellar concretions form
- The comedo may be closed or open

| Comedo | Description |
|---|---|
| Closed | No obvious follicular opening |
| Open | Dilated follicular opening; the keratin plug darkens from oxidized lipids and melanin |

## Inflammatory papule or pustule

- *Propionibacterium acnes* proliferates and upregulates innate immune responses (for example, through TLRs)
- Mild inflammation, mainly neutrophils, increases when the comedo wall ruptures
- The sebaceous lobule regresses

## Nodule or cyst

- Marked inflammation, mainly T cells
- May lead to scarring

> Inflammation in acne papules and pustules is mainly neutrophils, while nodules and cysts show marked inflammation that's mainly T cells.

Library: Comedonal acne
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photo of a forehead with many closed and open comedones and a few small papules, comedonal acne](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-comedonal-acne-forehead.jpg)

## Identify it

- Comedones on the face
- The mildest form of acne

## Treatment

First-line treatment is a **topical retinoid**, a vitamin A analog.

| Drug | Mechanism of action |
|---|---|
| Tretinoin | Normalizes follicular keratinization |
| Tazarotene | Normalizes follicular keratinization |
| Adapalene | Normalizes follicular keratinization |

- Normalized keratinization means less follicular plugging and less comedone formation
- Retinoids take at least 6 weeks to be effective
- This fits the first step of acne pathogenesis, where hyperkeratosis and sticky corneocytes in the upper follicle form the microcomedo

> First-line treatment for comedonal acne is a topical retinoid (tretinoin, tazarotene, adapalene), which normalizes follicular keratinization and takes at least 6 weeks to work.

Library: Mild inflammatory acne
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photo of a cheek and chin below the lower lip with red papules, pustules, and comedones, mild inflammatory acne](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-mild-inflammatory-acne-cheek.jpg)

## Identify it

- Papules and pustules with comedones
- None to few deep nodules

## Treatment

| Drug | Type | Mechanism of action |
|---|---|---|
| Tretinoin, adapalene | Topical retinoid | Normalizes follicular keratinization |
| Clindamycin, erythromycin | Topical antibiotic | Kills acne-causing bacteria (*Propionibacterium acnes*) |
| Benzoyl peroxide face wash (4-6%) | Topical wash | Kills acne-causing bacteria (*Propionibacterium acnes*) |

The step up from comedonal acne is adding something that kills *P. acnes* (a topical antibiotic or benzoyl peroxide) to the retinoid. In the pathogenesis diagram, *P. acnes* proliferation is what drives the inflammatory papule and pustule stage.

> Mild inflammatory acne adds a topical antibiotic (clindamycin, erythromycin) or benzoyl peroxide, which kill *Propionibacterium acnes*, to a topical retinoid.

Library: Moderate inflammatory acne and hormonal treatment
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photo of the side of a face with scattered red papules and tender nodules on the cheek and jaw, moderate inflammatory acne](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-moderate-inflammatory-acne-cheek.jpg)

## Identify it

- Tender nodules along with comedones, papules, and pustules
- In females, flares may precede the menstrual cycle and favor the chin and jawline

![Clinical photo of the cheek and chin beside the lips with inflamed papules and small nodules, hormonal pattern of moderate acne in a female](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-hormonal-acne-chin-jawline.jpg)

## Treatment

- Tretinoin
- Benzoyl peroxide face wash
- Oral antibiotics: doxycycline 100 mg BID

## Added options in females

- Oral contraceptive pills
- Spironolactone, a K+ sparing diuretic and antihypertensive
- Spironolactone is also an anti-androgen that alters sebum production in response to hormones
- Spironolactone has similar efficacy to oral antibiotics

Moderate acne is where oral antibiotics enter the plan. For a female whose acne tracks with her cycle along the chin and jawline, oral contraceptive pills and spironolactone are extra choices, and spironolactone works about as well as oral antibiotics.

> In females with moderate inflammatory acne, spironolactone (an anti-androgen that alters sebum production) has similar efficacy to oral antibiotics.

Library: Nodulocystic acne
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Two clinical photos of cheeks with many deep nodules, cysts, and inflamed papules and pustules, nodulocystic acne](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-nodulocystic-acne-cheek-two-patients.jpg)

## Identify it

- Many deep-seated nodules and cysts
- Inflammatory papules and pustules alongside them
- Leads to scarring if untreated

## Treatment

Antibiotics with topical treatments can be considered, but many patients require **isotretinoin**.

| Isotretinoin feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Drug class | Oral retinoid |
| Major risk | Severe teratogen |
| Prescribing | Monthly prescription registered with the iPledge monitoring program |
| Mechanism | Induces sebocyte apoptosis |
| Result | Normalized keratinization and decreased *P. acnes* |

Because nodulocystic acne scars, treatment shouldn't be delayed. The lecture stresses that scarring is difficult to treat and easier to prevent with early isotretinoin.

> Many patients with nodulocystic acne need isotretinoin, an oral retinoid and severe teratogen that requires monthly iPledge registration.

Library: Isotretinoin for acne
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Two profile photos of a patient with the eyes blocked out, shown on the isotretinoin slide: on the left many inflamed papules, nodules, and dark spots on the cheek and jaw, and on the right much clearer skin](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-isotretinoin-before-after.jpg)

## Mechanism

- Oral retinoid
- Induces sebocyte apoptosis, which leads to normalized keratinization and decreased *P. acnes*

## Course and monitoring

- 6 to 8 month treatment course
- Weight-based dosing to reach a goal dose
- Monthly prescription through the iPledge monitoring program
- Labs: LFTs, lipids, and a monthly pregnancy test

## Side effects

- Dryness of skin and mucous membranes
- Increased sun sensitivity
- Inflammatory bowel disease
- Hair loss
- Joint pain
- Depression
- LFT and triglyceride elevations
- **Severe birth defects**

## Role

Isotretinoin is highly effective. Many nodulocystic acne patients need it, and starting it early is the easier way to deal with scarring, since established scars are difficult to treat. When used properly, it's a safe and highly effective medication.

> Isotretinoin causes severe birth defects, so it requires iPledge registration and a monthly pregnancy test, plus LFT and lipid monitoring.

Library: Acne treatment by severity
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

## Treatment ladder

Acne treatment depends on the severity and the category of lesions. Therapy is added as lesions get deeper and more inflamed.

| Category | Lesions | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Comedonal | Comedones (mildest) | Topical retinoid: tretinoin, tazarotene, adapalene |
| Mild inflammatory | Papules/pustules with comedones, few or no nodules | Tretinoin or adapalene; topical clindamycin or erythromycin; benzoyl peroxide wash |
| Moderate inflammatory | Tender nodules, comedones, papules, pustules | Tretinoin; benzoyl peroxide wash; oral doxycycline 100 mg BID |
| Moderate, female | Flares before menses on chin and jawline | Add oral contraceptive pills or spironolactone |
| Nodulocystic | Many deep nodules and cysts | Antibiotics with topicals; many need isotretinoin |

## Mechanisms of action

| Drug | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Topical retinoids | Normalize follicular keratinization, less plugging and comedone formation |
| Topical antibiotics, benzoyl peroxide | Kill *Propionibacterium acnes* |
| Spironolactone | Anti-androgen; alters sebum production in response to hormones |
| Isotretinoin | Induces sebocyte apoptosis; normalizes keratinization and decreases *P. acnes* |

## Timing

- Topical retinoids take at least 6 weeks to work
- Isotretinoin needs a 6 to 8 month course

> Acne treatment is chosen by severity: topical retinoid for comedonal, add antibacterials for inflammatory, oral antibiotics for moderate, and isotretinoin for many nodulocystic patients.

Library: Acne sequelae: scarring and hyperpigmentation
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photo of the lower face with many small depressed acne scars on both cheeks](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-acne-scarring-cheeks.jpg)

## Scarring

- Permanent
- Difficult to treat
- Easier to prevent with early initiation of isotretinoin
- When used properly, isotretinoin is safe and highly effective

![Clinical photo of a cheek in darker skin with many dark brown to purple spots where acne lesions healed, postinflammatory hyperpigmentation](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-acne-postinflammatory-hyperpigmentation.jpg)

## Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation

- Common with all acne types
- Worse in darker skin types
- Worsened by picking and popping lesions

## Treating the hyperpigmentation

- Tincture of time, since it can take months to fade
- Prevention of new acne lesions
- Sunscreen

## Look-alikes

| Sequela | Permanent? | Approach |
|---|---|---|
| Scarring | Yes | Hard to treat; prevent with early isotretinoin |
| Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation | No, fades over months | Time, preventing new lesions, sunscreen |

> Acne scarring is permanent and best prevented with early isotretinoin, while postinflammatory hyperpigmentation fades with time and is worse in darker skin.

Library: Rosacea pathophysiology and subtypes
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photo of the central face with redness of the nose and cheeks and scattered red papules, rosacea](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-rosacea-central-face.jpg)

## Pathophysiology

Rosacea is an inflammatory disorder due to immune and neurovascular dysregulation, with a possible role for an exaggerated immune reaction to demodex. A genetic predisposition plus triggers (alcohol, sun, spicy foods) lead to two problems.

| Dysregulation | Result |
|---|---|
| Neurovascular dysregulation | Flushing, sensitivity |
| Abnormal innate immune response | Inflammatory papules and pustules, no comedones |

## Four subtypes

| Subtype | Key findings |
|---|---|
| Erythematotelangiectatic | Facial redness, telangiectasias, burning, flushing |
| Papulopustular | Erythematous papules and pustules on the central face over background erythema |
| Phymatous | Papulopustular plus sebaceous gland hypertrophy and fibrosis; men, nose |
| Ocular | Blepharitis with eyelid swelling, conjunctival injection, dry eyes |

## Triggers to avoid

- Alcohol
- Sun
- Spicy foods

> Rosacea has inflammatory papules and pustules but no comedones, which separates it from acne vulgaris.

Library: Erythematotelangiectatic rosacea
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photo of the nose, cheeks, and mouth with diffuse facial redness and fine visible vessels, erythematotelangiectatic rosacea](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-erythematotelangiectatic-rosacea.jpg)

## Identify it

- Facial redness
- Telangiectasias
- Skin sensitivity with burning and flushing

## Pathophysiology

This subtype reflects the neurovascular side of rosacea, where neurovascular dysregulation causes flushing and sensitivity.

## Treatment

| Treatment | Purpose or mechanism |
|---|---|
| Avoid triggers | Alcohol, sun, spicy foods |
| Sunscreen | Sun is a trigger |
| Gentle skin care | Skin is sensitive (burning, flushing) |
| Pulse dye laser | Procedural option |
| Beta blockers | For flushing |
| Topical alpha2 agonist (brimonidine) | Blood vessel constriction |

> Brimonidine, a topical alpha2 agonist, treats erythematotelangiectatic rosacea by constricting blood vessels, and beta blockers help flushing.

Library: Papulopustular rosacea
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photo of the central face with many red papules and pustules on a background of redness over the nose, cheeks, and chin, papulopustular rosacea](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-papulopustular-rosacea.jpg)

## Identify it

- Erythematous papules and pustules
- Typically on the central face
- Background of erythema
- No comedones

## Treatment

| Treatment | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Sunscreen, gentle skin care | Supportive |
| Avoid triggers | Alcohol, sun, spicy foods |
| Topical metronidazole | Anti-inflammatory rather than antimicrobial |
| Topical ivermectin | Kills demodex mites on the skin |
| Low-dose doxycycline | Anti-inflammatory dose |

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Acne vulgaris | Papulopustular rosacea |
|---|---|---|
| Comedones | Present, needed for diagnosis | Absent |
| Distribution | Face, chest, back | Central face |
| Background | No background redness described | Background of erythema |
| Doxycycline | Oral antibiotic, 100 mg BID | Low dose, anti-inflammatory |
| Topical agents | Retinoids, antibiotics, benzoyl peroxide | Metronidazole, ivermectin |

> Topical metronidazole works in papulopustular rosacea as an anti-inflammatory rather than an antimicrobial, and topical ivermectin kills demodex mites.

Library: Phymatous rosacea
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photo of a man's nose and cheek with a markedly enlarged, thickened, bumpy nose and red papules on the cheek, phymatous rosacea](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-phymatous-rosacea-nose.jpg)

## Identify it

- Papulopustular rosacea plus sebaceous gland hypertrophy and fibrosis
- Most common in men, on the nose
- Can result in disfigurement

## Pathophysiology

Sebaceous glands undergo hypertrophy and fibrosis in response to chronic, longstanding inflammation. That's why it builds on papulopustular rosacea instead of appearing on its own.

## Treatment

| Treatment | Type |
|---|---|
| Surgical excision | Procedural |
| Ablative laser treatments | Procedural |

> Phymatous rosacea is sebaceous gland hypertrophy and fibrosis from chronic inflammation, most commonly on the nose in men, and it's treated with surgical excision or ablative laser.

Library: Ocular rosacea
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Three photos of ocular rosacea: (A) an eye with a red, swollen lid margin and red conjunctiva, (B) a nearly closed eye with eyelid changes, and (C) both eyes with red, inflamed eyelid margins and conjunctival injection](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-ocular-rosacea-eyelids.jpg)

## Identify it

- Blepharitis with eyelid swelling
- Conjunctival injection
- Dry eyes and frequent blinking
- Often seen together with other rosacea subtypes

## Treatment

| Treatment | Notes |
|---|---|
| Artificial tears | For dry eyes |
| Low-dose doxycycline | Same anti-inflammatory dosing used in papulopustular rosacea |

> Ocular rosacea is blepharitis with eyelid swelling and conjunctival injection, treated with artificial tears and low-dose doxycycline.

Library: Hidradenitis suppurativa
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photo of an axilla with linear, scarred sinus tracts and a few inflamed nodules, hidradenitis suppurativa](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-hidradenitis-axilla-sinus-tracts-scars.jpg)

## Identify it

- Also known as acne inversa
- Inflamed nodules and sterile abscesses, then draining sinus tracts and scarring
- Intertriginous sites with apocrine glands: axilla, inframammary region, groin, buttocks

![Clinical photo of the buttocks and upper thigh with inflamed nodules, draining lesions, and scarring, hidradenitis suppurativa](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-hidradenitis-buttocks.jpg)

## Pathophysiology

1. Unknown trigger
2. Occlusion of pilosebaceous units in skin with apocrine glands
3. Inflammation of apocrine glands
4. Inflamed nodules and sterile abscesses
5. Draining sinus tracts and scarring

## Who gets it

- Starts at or soon after puberty
- Females more than males, African Americans more than Caucasians
- Obesity and tobacco use are risk factors

## Course

- Chronic and progressive, and difficult to treat
- Physical and emotional sequelae: painful, disfiguring, malodorous
- Early treatment minimizes complications
- Divided into Hurley stages by severity, and treatment for all stages includes weight loss and smoking cessation

> Hidradenitis suppurativa starts with occlusion of pilosebaceous units in apocrine gland skin (axilla, inframammary, groin, buttocks) and progresses to sterile abscesses, sinus tracts, and scarring.

Library: Hurley staging and treatment of hidradenitis suppurativa
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Hurley stage I hidradenitis suppurativa: axilla with a few red inflammatory nodules and no sinus tracts or scars](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-hidradenitis-hurley-stage-1-axilla.jpg)

![Hurley stage II hidradenitis suppurativa: two photos of axillae with inflamed nodules, abscesses, and a few sinus tracts and scars](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-hidradenitis-hurley-stage-2.jpg)

![Hurley stage III hidradenitis suppurativa: an axilla with extensive interconnected sinus tracts, crusting, and scarring, and a groin and buttock region with widespread nodules and scarring](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-hidradenitis-hurley-stage-3.jpg)

## Hurley stages

| Stage | Lesions | Sinus tracts and scars |
|---|---|---|
| I | Inflammatory nodules, sterile abscesses | None |
| II | Inflammatory nodules, sterile abscesses | Few |
| III | Nodules and abscesses, often covering the entire region | Multiple, interconnected |

## Treatment by stage

| Stage | Treatment |
|---|---|
| All stages | Weight loss, smoking cessation |
| I | Topical antibiotics, antiseptic washes, intralesional steroids |
| I | Oral antibiotics (rifampin + clindamycin, doxycycline) for anti-inflammatory effects |
| II | Oral antibiotics |
| II | Spironolactone or finasteride (anti-androgen effects) |
| II | Adalimumab (TNF-alpha inhibitor); surgical excision |
| III | Biologics: adalimumab, infliximab, secukinumab |
| III | Surgical excision |

The stage III biologics are anti-inflammatory monoclonal antibodies against TNF-alpha or IL-17. Surgical excision is an option from stage II on, and biologics become the main medical therapy in stage III, when sinus tracts are multiple and interconnected.

> Hurley stage depends on sinus tracts and scars: none in stage I, few in stage II, and multiple interconnected tracts in stage III.

Library: Hyperhidrosis: primary vs. secondary
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photo of the sole and toes of a foot with shiny, moist skin from excessive sweating (panel A), hyperhidrosis](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-hyperhidrosis-sole-of-foot.jpg)

## Identify it

- Excessive sweating
- Primary disease favors the palms, soles, and axillae

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Primary | Secondary |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | No underlying disease | Underlying disease, medication, etc. |
| Family history | 80% have one | Not a feature listed |
| Sites | Palms, soles, axillae | Not specified |

## Secondary causes

- Febrile illness
- Hyperthyroidism
- Lymphoma or other cancer
- Medications: amphetamines, insulin, sulfonylureas, SSRIs, opioids

The first question with a sweaty patient is whether there's something driving it. If there's no apparent secondary cause and the sweating is focal, the next step is checking the diagnostic criteria for primary hyperhidrosis.

> Primary hyperhidrosis has no underlying disease, a family history in 80%, and affects the palms, soles, and axillae; secondary hyperhidrosis comes from illness (fever, hyperthyroidism, lymphoma) or drugs.

Library: Primary hyperhidrosis diagnostic criteria
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Table titled Criteria for the Diagnosis of Primary Hyperhidrosis listing focal visible excess sweating, present at least 6 months, no apparent secondary causes, and at least two supporting features](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-primary-hyperhidrosis-criteria-table.jpg)

![Clinical photo of both palms glistening with sweat, primary hyperhidrosis](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-primary-hyperhidrosis-palms.jpg)

## Criteria

1. Focal, visible excess sweating
2. Present for at least 6 months
3. No apparent secondary causes
4. At least two of the supporting features below

## Supporting features

- Bilateral and symmetric
- Impairs activities of daily life
- At least one episode per week
- Age of onset under 25 years
- Positive family history
- Stops during sleep

## Identify it

- Palms, soles, and axillae
- Visible sweat, as on the glistening palms in the photo

> Primary hyperhidrosis needs focal, visible sweating for at least 6 months with no secondary cause, plus at least two features such as bilateral symmetry, onset before 25, family history, or stopping during sleep.

Library: Primary hyperhidrosis treatment
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

## Treatment

| Treatment | Mechanism of action | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Topical aluminum chloride 12-20% (DrySol) | Physically occludes eccrine sweat glands | Topical |
| Glycopyrrolate, oxybutynin | Block muscarinic receptors on eccrine sweat glands | Topical or oral anticholinergics |
| Botulinum toxin injections | Blocks acetylcholine release | Repeat every 6-9 months |

## How they fit together

- Aluminum chloride works by plugging the eccrine glands physically
- Anticholinergics and botulinum toxin both act on cholinergic signaling to eccrine sweat glands, one by blocking the muscarinic receptor and the other by blocking acetylcholine release
- Botulinum toxin isn't permanent, so it requires repeated treatments every 6 to 9 months

> Primary hyperhidrosis is treated with topical aluminum chloride (occludes eccrine glands), anticholinergics like glycopyrrolate and oxybutynin (block muscarinic receptors), or botulinum toxin (blocks acetylcholine release, repeated every 6 to 9 months).

Library: Vitiligo
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photos of vitiligo: sharply bordered white depigmented patches on both knees, and white patches on the backs of two hands](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-vitiligo-knees-hands.jpg)

## Identify it

- Depigmentation of the skin (white patches)
- Commonly on the hands and feet
- Commonly on perioral and periocular skin

## Pathophysiology

Autoimmunity targets melanocytes, so the skin loses its pigment.

## Associations

Vitiligo is associated with other autoimmune diseases:

- Alopecia areata
- Autoimmune hypothyroidism
- Graves disease

## Treatment

- Topical steroids
- Narrowband UVB
- Ruxolitinib

> Vitiligo is depigmentation from autoimmunity targeting melanocytes, and it's associated with alopecia areata, autoimmune hypothyroidism, and Graves disease.

Library: Pityriasis alba
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photo of a child's lower face with pale, hypopigmented patches on the cheeks around the mouth, pityriasis alba](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-pityriasis-alba-face.jpg)

## Identify it

- Hypopigmented, round patches with slight scale
- On the face of young children
- May worsen in the summer

## Key features

- Typically in children with atopic dermatitis, and it may represent a mild variant of it
- The lecture lists it among hypopigmented rashes as atopic dermatitis (pityriasis alba)
- Benign, and it resolves with age

## Treatment

| Treatment | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Moisturizers | Help the dry appearance |
| 1% hydrocortisone | Helps the dry appearance |

Because it's benign and resolves with age, treatment is aimed at the dry look of the patches. For how it compares with the other hypopigmented rashes, see the look-alikes table on the tinea versicolor page.

> Pityriasis alba is hypopigmented, slightly scaly round patches on the face of young children with atopic dermatitis; it's benign and resolves with age.

Library: Tinea versicolor
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photo of the upper back with many pale, hypopigmented patches that merge across the skin, tinea versicolor](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-tinea-versicolor-back.jpg)

![Close clinical photo of a tanned shoulder with many small round hypopigmented patches, some merging, tinea versicolor](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-tinea-versicolor-shoulder.jpg)

## Identify it

- Hypopigmented patches, most commonly on the chest and back
- Often in teenagers and young adults
- Appearance worsens in the summer

## Pathophysiology

A common cutaneous reaction caused by overgrowth of *Malassezia* yeast. The yeast decreases melanin synthesis and tanning of the underlying skin, so the patches stand out more in summer.

## Treatment

- Topical azoles
- Fluconazole
- Over-the-counter dandruff shampoo

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Pityriasis alba | Tinea versicolor | Vitiligo |
|---|---|---|---|
| Color | Hypopigmented, slight scale | Hypopigmented | Depigmented |
| Sites | Face | Chest and back | Hands, feet, perioral, periocular |
| Patients | Young children | Teens, young adults | Not specified |
| Cause | May be a mild variant of atopic dermatitis | *Malassezia* yeast overgrowth | Autoimmunity against melanocytes |
| Treatment | Moisturizers, 1% hydrocortisone | Azoles, dandruff shampoo | Topical steroids, NB-UVB, ruxolitinib |

> Tinea versicolor is *Malassezia* yeast overgrowth that decreases melanin synthesis, giving hypopigmented patches on the chest and back that worsen in summer.

Library: Hair loss disorders compared
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

## Disorders of hair

The lecture's list of hair disorders:

- Androgenic alopecia
- Tinea capitis
- Telogen effluvium
- Drug-induced hair loss
- Deficiency-induced hair loss

Alopecia areata is covered in detail as well. Hair loss can have a profound emotional and psychological impact on patients.

## Look-alikes

| Disorder | Pattern | Cause | Course or treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alopecia areata | Circular, smooth patches; no erythema or scale | T cell autoimmune destruction of follicles | Often self-resolves in 6 months; steroids |
| Tinea capitis | Mimics alopecia areata, with scaling and itching | Dermatophyte infection of hair follicles | Oral antifungals for 4-8 weeks |
| Telogen effluvium | Diffuse, sudden loss | Faster hair cycling after illness, pregnancy, surgery, stress | Self-resolves in 6-12 months |
| Androgenic alopecia | Men: frontal and vertex; women: wider part | Androgens miniaturize follicles | Minoxidil, anti-androgens |

## Sorting clues

- Patchy loss with smooth skin and no symptoms points to alopecia areata
- Patchy loss with scale and itch points to tinea capitis
- Diffuse sudden shedding after a stressful event points to telogen effluvium
- A progressive pattern (frontal and vertex in men, widening part in women) points to androgenic alopecia

> Alopecia areata and tinea capitis both cause patchy hair loss, but tinea capitis has scaling and itching while alopecia areata is smooth and asymptomatic.

Library: Alopecia areata
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Two clinical photos of alopecia areata: a round, smooth bald patch on the back of the scalp, and a round patch of hair loss being held open in dark curly hair](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-alopecia-areata-scalp-patches.jpg)

## Identify it

- Circular areas of hair loss
- Smooth skin, with no erythema or scaling
- Asymptomatic
- Common, non-scarring alopecia

## Pathophysiology

T cell mediated autoimmune destruction of hair follicles.

## Who gets it

- Occurs in all ages and races
- Often a positive family history
- Often affects children and young adults

## Variants

![Clinical photo of a scalp with complete hair loss (panel C), from the alopecia areata variants slide](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-alopecia-totalis-scalp.jpg)

| Variant | Hair lost |
|---|---|
| Alopecia totalis | All scalp hair |
| Alopecia universalis | All body hair |

![Three clinical photos from the alopecia areata variants slide: patchy hair loss in a beard, loss of eyebrow hair, and extensive scalp hair loss with a few remaining tufts](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-alopecia-areata-beard-eyebrow-scalp.jpg)

## Associations

- Atopy (allergies, asthma, atopic dermatitis)
- Hashimoto's thyroiditis
- Vitiligo

> Alopecia areata is a non-scarring, T cell mediated autoimmune destruction of hair follicles that causes smooth, circular, asymptomatic patches of hair loss.

Library: Alopecia areata treatment and prognosis
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

## Treatment by extent

| Extent | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Localized | Topical corticosteroids |
| Localized | Intralesional corticosteroids |
| Localized | Topical calcineurin inhibitors |
| Widespread or rapidly progressive | Oral steroids |
| Widespread or rapidly progressive | Tofacitinib (JAK/STAT inhibitor) |

The systemic options are immunosuppressants that decrease T cell function. That matches the disease mechanism, since alopecia areata is T cell mediated autoimmune destruction of hair follicles.

## Prognosis

- Usually self-resolves within 6 months
- Localized disease often responds well to treatment
- May periodically recur
- More extensive hair loss is treatment resistant

## Putting it together

Localized disease is treated locally and often responds well. Widespread or rapidly progressive loss gets systemic immunosuppression, and more extensive hair loss is the form most likely to resist treatment.

> Localized alopecia areata is treated with topical or intralesional corticosteroids or topical calcineurin inhibitors, while widespread disease gets oral steroids or tofacitinib (a JAK/STAT inhibitor).

Library: Tinea capitis
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Clinical photo of the scalp with an area of thinned hair and white scale, tinea capitis](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-tinea-capitis-scalp-scale.jpg)

## Identify it

- Dermatophyte fungal infection of hair follicles
- Can mimic alopecia areata
- Differences from alopecia areata include scaling and itching

## Diagnosis

- Scraping and microscopic examination of scale
- Fungal culture

![Light micrograph of a positive scale scraping after applying potassium hydroxide (KOH), showing long, branching fungal hyphae](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-tinea-capitis-koh-hyphae.jpg)

## Treatment

| Drug | Duration |
|---|---|
| Terbinafine | 4-8 weeks |
| Griseofulvin | 4-8 weeks |
| Fluconazole | 4-8 weeks |

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Tinea capitis | Alopecia areata |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | Dermatophyte infection | T cell autoimmune |
| Scale | Present | None |
| Itching | Present | Asymptomatic |
| Treatment | Oral antifungals | Corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors |

> Tinea capitis mimics alopecia areata but has scaling and itching; confirm it with a KOH scraping or fungal culture and treat with oral antifungals for 4 to 8 weeks.

Library: Telogen effluvium
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

## Identify it

- Diffuse, sudden hair loss
- Follows illness, hospitalization, pregnancy, surgery, or other stressful events

## Pathophysiology

Telogen effluvium is caused by more rapid cycling of hair and increased shedding. In normal conditions, about 100 hairs a day are lost.

| Hair cycle phase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Anagen | Growth |
| Catagen | Regression |
| Telogen | Rest |

## Course

- Self-resolves in 6 to 12 months
- No specific treatment is given in the lecture

## Look-alikes

| Feature | Telogen effluvium | Alopecia areata |
|---|---|---|
| Pattern | Diffuse | Circular patches |
| Course | Resolves in 6-12 months | Often resolves within 6 months, may recur |

> Telogen effluvium is diffuse, sudden shedding after illness, pregnancy, surgery, or stress from faster hair cycling, and it self-resolves in 6 to 12 months.

Library: Androgenic alopecia
Folder: MSK / Week 13 / Spectrum of Acneiform Disorders, Pigmentation, and Hair

![Drawing of male pattern baldness progressing from a full hairline to frontal recession and then loss at the vertex and crown](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-androgenic-alopecia-male-pattern.jpg)

![Four photos of the top of the scalp viewed from above showing progressive widening of the central part line, the pattern seen in women with androgenic alopecia](library/images/msk-week-13/derm-androgenic-alopecia-part-widening.jpg)

## Identify it

- Male and female pattern baldness
- Often familial
- Men present with loss of the frontal scalp and vertex
- Women present with widening of the part line

## Pathophysiology

Circulating androgen hormones (testosterone) lead to progressive miniaturization of hair follicles.

## Treatment

| Treatment | Mechanism of action |
|---|---|
| Topical minoxidil | Increases blood circulation to hair follicles to prevent miniaturization |
| Finasteride | Anti-androgen; decreases androgen stimulation of follicles |
| Spironolactone | Anti-androgen; decreases androgen stimulation of follicles |
| Dutasteride | Anti-androgen; decreases androgen stimulation of follicles |

Spironolactone and finasteride show up elsewhere in this lecture for the same anti-androgen reason: spironolactone for hormonal acne in females, and both for Hurley stage II hidradenitis suppurativa.

> Androgenic alopecia comes from androgens causing progressive miniaturization of hair follicles; men lose the frontal scalp and vertex, and women get a widening part line.

Library: Regions and fascial compartments of the upper limb
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Right anterior oblique view of the upper limb with the fascia color coded into an anterior (flexor) fascial compartment and a posterior (extensor) fascial compartment, with three inferior cross section views taken through the arm, the forearm, and the hand](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s05.jpg)

## Identify it

- Arm: the segment between the shoulder and the elbow
- Forearm: the segment between the elbow and the wrist
- On the cross sections, the anterior (flexor) compartment is the lighter fascial band and the posterior (extensor) compartment is the darker one

## Key features

Both the arm and the forearm are divided into an anterior and a posterior compartment, and the naming works the same way in each.

| Segment | Anterior compartment | Posterior compartment |
|---|---|---|
| Arm | Flexor muscles | Extensor muscles |
| Forearm | Flexor muscles | Extensor muscles |

The pectoral region itself is loosely defined as the external aspect of the anterior superior thoracic wall, and it helps anchor the upper limb to the trunk. It has two compartments of its own. The superficial compartment holds skin, superficial fascia, and the breasts, and the deep compartment holds the muscles and their associated structures.

> Anterior compartments of both the arm and the forearm contain flexors, and posterior compartments contain extensors.

Library: Sternum and the sternal angle of Louis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the sternum labeled manubrium, body, sternal angle of Louis, and xiphoid process, with the costal cartilages of the ribs attaching along its margins](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s09.jpg)

## Identify it

- Manubrium: the superior portion, with the palpable jugular notch on its superior border
- Body: the flat, elongated middle portion
- Sternal angle (of Louis): the somewhat palpable projection at the fusion of the manubrium and body
- Xiphoid process: the smaller inferior portion

## Key features

| Part | Articulates with |
|---|---|
| Manubrium | Clavicle and the costal cartilages of the 1st pair of ribs |
| Sternal angle | 2nd pair of ribs |
| Body | Costal cartilages of ribs 2 to 7 |

The sternal angle sits at the level of the T4/T5 intervertebral disc. It matters clinically because the 2nd pair of ribs articulates there, which makes it the starting point for counting ribs, and because several internal landmarks sit at the same level, including the arch of the aorta and the bifurcation of the trachea.

> The sternal angle of Louis marks the T4/T5 IV disc and the articulation of the 2nd rib, which is how you start counting ribs.

Library: Ribs of the pectoral region
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the thoracic cage with the ribs labeled, showing the costal cartilages joining the upper ribs directly to the sternum](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s13.jpg)

## Identify it

- Twelve pairs of ribs, each connected to the sternum by a flexible costal cartilage
- Ribs 1 to 7 attach directly to the sternum, which makes them the true ribs

## Key features

- The ribs provide attachment sites for the muscles of the pectoral region
- Pectoralis major takes origin from the upper 6 costal cartilages, pectoralis minor from ribs 3 to 5 near their costal cartilages, subclavius from the 1st rib, and serratus anterior from the lateral surfaces of ribs 1 to 8

> Ribs 1 to 7 attach directly to the sternum and are therefore the true ribs.

Library: Clavicle: articulations and functions
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the shoulder girdle with the clavicle labeled along with the sternoclavicular joint medially and the acromioclavicular joint laterally](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s12.jpg)

## Identify it

- The clavicle, or collarbone, runs between the manubrium of the sternum and the acromion of the scapula
- Sternoclavicular joint at its medial end
- Acromioclavicular joint at its lateral end
- The bone is palpable along its entire length

## Key features

- Attaches the upper limb to the trunk as part of the shoulder girdle at the sternoclavicular joint
- Articulates with the scapula at the acromioclavicular joint
- Protects the underlying neurovascular structures that supply the upper limb
- Transmits force from the upper limb to the axial skeleton

Because the clavicle lies directly over the vessels and nerves heading into the limb, a clavicular fracture puts those structures at risk, which is also why subclavius is described as giving them minor protection.

> The sternoclavicular joint is where the clavicle attaches the upper limb to the axial skeleton.

Library: Scapula: coracoid process, acromion, and glenoid fossa
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the scapula and proximal humerus labeled acromion process, coracoid process, acromioclavicular joint, and glenohumeral joint](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s11.jpg)

## Identify it

- Coracoid process: hook-like process on the anterior superolateral edge of the scapula, from the Latin for crow's beak
- Acromion: the most lateral portion of the scapula, extending anteriorly from the spine of the scapula, from the Greek for point of the shoulder
- Glenoid fossa: shallow cavity on the lateral border
- Acromioclavicular joint between the clavicle and the acromion
- Glenohumeral joint between the glenoid fossa and the head of the humerus

## Key features
