- The scapula is a triangular, flat bone
- It serves as a stable platform for the muscles that move the upper extremity
- The coracoid process is a site of muscle and ligament attachment
- The glenoid fossa is shallow, which is part of why the glenohumeral joint trades stability for mobility

> The scapula articulates with the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint and with the humerus at the glenohumeral joint.

Library: Proximal humerus: tubercles and the intertubercular groove
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

## Identify it

- Head of the humerus: articulates with the glenoid fossa of the scapula at the glenohumeral joint
- Greater tubercle: prominence on the superior posterior portion of the humerus
- Lesser tubercle: prominence on the superior anterior portion of the humerus
- Intertubercular groove: the groove running between the greater and lesser tubercles

## Key features

The humerus is the long bone of the arm, extending from the shoulder to the elbow. Three of the pectoral region muscles sort themselves out along these landmarks, so the tubercles are worth keeping straight. Pectoralis major attaches to the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove, and subscapularis attaches to the lesser tubercle.

| Landmark | Position |
|---|---|
| Greater tubercle | Superior and posterior |
| Lesser tubercle | Superior and anterior |
| Intertubercular groove | Between the two tubercles |

> The greater tubercle is the superior posterior prominence and the lesser tubercle is the superior anterior one, with the intertubercular groove between them.

Library: Breast: composition, location, and the axillary tail of Spence
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Sagittal section through the female breast and anterior thoracic wall, with the ribs and the axillary tail labeled and the gland sitting superficial to pectoralis major](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s17.jpg)

## Identify it

- Breast tissue lying within the skin and subcutaneous tissue, superficial to pectoralis major
- Axillary tail (of Spence): mammary gland tissue extending along the inferior border of pectoralis major into the axilla

## Key features

The breast consists of mammary glands, supporting fibrous connective tissue, and fat. The mammary glands themselves are modified sweat glands on the slide and modified apocrine sweat glands in the notes, and they are a series of ducts and secretory lobules that produce and secrete milk immediately after pregnancy.

Breasts are present in both males and females but become more prominent in females after puberty, and the glandular system rarely develops in males.

| Dimension | Extent |
|---|---|
| Vertical | 2nd to 6th ribs |
| Transverse | Lateral edge of the sternum to the midaxillary line |

Size is highly variable between individuals, so the rib and midaxillary landmarks matter more than any measurement.

> The axillary tail of Spence is mammary tissue running along the inferior border of pectoralis major into the axilla, which is why breast tissue can be found in the armpit.

Library: Retromammary space
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Sagittal section through the breast showing the layer of connective tissue separating the gland from the deep fascia overlying the underlying muscles](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s18.jpg)

## Identify it

- A layer of loose connective tissue between the breast and the deep fascia overlying pectoralis major and serratus anterior

## Key features

- The space allows the breast some degree of movement over the chest wall
- It is a potential site for the placement of breast implants

Because the plane is loose connective tissue rather than a firm attachment, the breast normally glides on the chest wall. Loss of that mobility is one of the things a clinician notices when tumor fibrosis tethers the gland down.

> The retromammary space is the loose connective tissue plane between the breast and the deep fascia over pectoralis major, and it is where implants are placed.

Library: Internal structure of the breast: lobules, ducts, and suspensory ligaments
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Sagittal section of the breast labeled lobules, lactiferous ducts, lactiferous sinus, and nipple, with the glandular tissue arranged radially toward the nipple](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s19.jpg)

## Identify it

- Lobules: the milk producing glands, 15 to 20 of them, aligned radially
- Lactiferous ducts: drain the lobules toward the nipple
- Lactiferous sinuses: dilations of the ducts just proximal to their opening in the nipple
- Suspensory ligaments (of Cooper): dense connective tissue bands running from the glands to the dermis

## Key features

Each lobule holds many smaller sacs called alveoli that produce milk, and the alveoli sit in clusters that the notes compare to bunches of grapes. Secretions from each glandular lobule drain into lactiferous ducts, which dilate into lactiferous sinuses just before opening at the nipple.

The suspensory ligaments of Cooper firmly attach the mammary glands to the dermis of the overlying skin. They separate and support the glandular lobes and lobules, and they are most clearly defined in the superior aspect of the breast.

> Cooper's ligaments anchor the glandular tissue to the dermis, which is why fibrosis around a tumor pulls on them and dimples the skin.

Library: Nipple and areola
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the breast surface with the nipple and the surrounding circular pigmented areola labeled](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s20.jpg)

## Identify it

- Nipple: sits at the center of the areola and contains the lactiferous duct and sinus openings
- Areola: the circular pigmented area surrounding the nipple

## Key features

- The nipple is usually located around the level of the 4th intercostal space in women who have borne no children (nulliparous)
- It is the landmark for the T4 dermatome and is supplied by the 4th intercostal nerve
- The areola contains areolar sebaceous glands that secrete an oily substance to lubricate the nipple and prevent chafing during nursing

> The nipple sits at the 4th intercostal space in nulliparous women and marks the T4 dermatome.

Library: Arterial supply and venous drainage of the breast
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the thorax labeled subclavian artery, axillary artery, internal thoracic artery, and lateral thoracic artery, showing the vessels converging on the breast](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s21.jpg)

## Identify it

- Internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery: a branch of the subclavian artery descending beside the sternum
- Lateral thoracic artery: a branch of the axillary artery running down the lateral chest wall

## Key features

| Region of the breast | Arterial source | Parent vessel |
|---|---|---|
| Medial aspect | Perforating branches of the internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery | Subclavian artery |
| Lateral aspect | Lateral thoracic artery | Axillary artery |
| Whole breast | Branches of the 2nd to 6th anterior and posterior intercostal arteries | Intercostal supply |

Venous drainage is primarily by the axillary, internal thoracic, and intercostal veins, so the veins follow the same three routes the arteries do.

> Medial breast is supplied by the internal thoracic artery off the subclavian, and lateral breast by the lateral thoracic artery off the axillary.

Library: Innervation of the breast and the T4 dermatome
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the thoracic wall showing the intercostal nerves giving off anterior and lateral cutaneous branches to the skin of the breast, with the nipple marked at the T4 level](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s22.jpg)

## Identify it

- Anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves reaching the skin of the breast
- The nipple as the surface landmark of the T4 dermatome

## Key features

These branches carry both sensory and sympathetic innervation to the skin of the breast. The lecture gives two slightly different ranges for which intercostal nerves are involved, so keep both in mind.

| Source | Intercostal nerves named |
|---|---|
| Slide | Anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th to 6th |
| Typed notes | Anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 2nd to 6th |

Both agree on the nipple. The nipple is supplied by the 4th intercostal nerve and is located at the T4 dermatome.

> The nipple is supplied by the 4th intercostal nerve and marks the T4 dermatome.

Library: Lymphatic drainage of the breast
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the breast and chest wall labeled parasternal lymph nodes, axillary lymph nodes, and an arrow directed to abdominal lymph nodes](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s23.jpg)

## Identify it

- Axillary lymph nodes, located near the lateral border of pectoralis major
- Parasternal lymph nodes, located near the internal thoracic artery
- The inferior route passing deeply toward abdominal lymph nodes

## Key features

Lymph passes from the nipple, areola, and glandular tissue into the subareolar lymphatic plexus first, and from there it takes one of three routes.

| Region drained | Destination |
|---|---|
| Most of the breast, more than 75 percent, especially the lateral quadrants | Axillary lymph nodes |
| Medial quadrants | Parasternal lymph nodes, or the opposite breast |
| Inferior quadrants | Abdominal lymph nodes |

Lymph from the axillary nodes is drained by the subclavian lymphatic trunk. On the right side it enters the venous system via the right lymphatic duct, and on the left it returns via the thoracic duct.

This pathway is clinically important because breast carcinomas tend to spread by metastasizing through the lymphatic vessels.

> More than 75 percent of breast lymph, especially from the lateral quadrants, drains to the axillary nodes near the lateral border of pectoralis major.

Library: Sentinel lymph node biopsy and axillary lymph node dissection
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

## Key features

A sentinel node is the first lymph node or nodes to which cancer cells are likely to spread from a primary tumor. A sentinel node biopsy is the surgical procedure used to find out whether cancer has spread beyond the primary tumor into the lymphatic system, and it is commonly used in evaluating breast cancer.

To identify the sentinel node, the surgeon injects a radioactive substance, blue dye, or both near the tumor. The surgeon then uses a probe to find the node containing the radioactive substance, or looks for the node stained with dye, and removes it to check for cancer cells.

## Clinical note

Axillary lymph node dissection is the removal of lymph nodes and lymphatic channels in the axillary region when surgeons are staging the cancer, and the axilla is often treated with radiation as adjuvant therapy. Surgical or radiation damage to the lymphatic channels in the axilla can interfere with lymphatic drainage from the arm on that side, and the result is lymphedema, swelling from accumulated lymph fluid, in the upper extremity.

> Damage to axillary lymphatics from dissection or radiation causes lymphedema of the upper limb on that side.

Library: Signs of breast cancer and their anatomical basis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

## Key features

Breast cancer may arise from any of the breast tissue components in both male and female patients. One in eight women in the United States will develop breast cancer in her lifetime, and it is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in women.

| Sign | Anatomical basis |
|---|---|
| Abnormal contours or dimpling | Cancerous invasion of glandular tissue and fibrosis that shortens or places traction on the suspensory ligaments |
| Nipple retraction | Pressure on the lactiferous ducts |
| Peau d'orange | Blocked lymphatics producing a pitted, orange peel appearance with skin thickening and dimpling |

Other signs include breast masses, swelling of all or part of the breast, swollen lymph nodes, nipple discharge, and breast or nipple pain.

Because breast carcinomas tend to metastasize via the lymphatics, the nodal routes matter as much as the local findings.

> Skin dimpling comes from traction on Cooper's suspensory ligaments, nipple retraction from pressure on the lactiferous ducts, and peau d'orange from blocked lymphatics.

Library: Mastectomy and breast reconstruction
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

## Key features

Mastectomy is the complete removal of the tissue of the breast. It is one option for the surgical treatment of breast cancer and the only surgical option for breast cancer risk reduction.

| Procedure | What is removed |
|---|---|
| Total (simple) mastectomy | All breast tissue including the nipple, the areola, and most of the overlying skin, leaving the pectoral muscles beneath |
| Modified radical mastectomy | All breast tissue and some axillary lymph nodes |
| Radical mastectomy | All breast tissue, axillary lymph nodes, and the pectoral muscles under the breast |

There are two main types of breast reconstruction, implant reconstruction and tissue (flap) reconstruction, the latter using a muscle such as latissimus dorsi. Sometimes the implant and flap procedures are used together to rebuild a breast.

> A total (simple) mastectomy spares the pectoral muscles, a modified radical adds axillary nodes, and a radical mastectomy takes the pectoral muscles as well.

Library: Pectoralis major
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the chest wall with pectoralis major in place and its tendon labeled at the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove of the humerus](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s26.jpg)

## Attachments

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Proximal attachment | Clavicular head from the medial half of the clavicle, sternocostal head from the sternum and the upper 6 costal cartilages |
| Distal attachment | Lateral lip of the intertubercular groove of the humerus |
| Actions | Adducts and medially rotates the humerus, draws the scapula anteroinferiorly, flexes the humerus (clavicular head) |
| Innervation | Lateral and medial pectoral nerves |

## Key features

- Superficial, fan shaped muscle that forms most of the anterior axillary fold
- Separated from the deltoid by a groove called the deltopectoral groove, which carries the cephalic vein
- Forms the anterior wall of the axilla along with pectoralis minor

The slide lists the actions as adduction, medial rotation, and flexion of the arm, and the notes table adds drawing the scapula anteroinferiorly to that list.

> Pectoralis major inserts on the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove and is supplied by both the lateral and the medial pectoral nerves.

Library: Pectoralis minor
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the chest wall with pectoralis major reflected to show the triangular pectoralis minor running from the upper ribs to the coracoid process of the scapula](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s27.jpg)

## Attachments

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Superior attachment | Coracoid process of the scapula |
| Inferior attachment | 3rd to 5th ribs close to the costal cartilage |
| Action | Stabilizes the scapula by drawing it anteroinferiorly against the thoracic wall |
| Innervation | Medial pectoral nerve |

## Key features

- Triangular muscle lying deep to pectoralis major
- The medial pectoral nerve pierces pectoralis minor before going on to innervate pectoralis major
- It is an important clinical landmark used to locate and subdivide the axillary vessels that run deep to it
- Contributes to the anterior wall of the axilla

> Pectoralis minor is the landmark that divides the axillary artery into its three parts, and the medial pectoral nerve pierces it on the way to pectoralis major.

Library: Subclavius
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the shoulder girdle with the small subclavius muscle running from the 1st rib to the inferior surface of the middle third of the clavicle](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s28.jpg)

## Attachments

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Proximal attachment | 1st rib |
| Distal attachment | Inferior side of the middle third of the clavicle |
| Action | Anchors and depresses the clavicle |
| Innervation | Nerve to subclavius |

## Key features

- Small muscle sitting inferior to the clavicle
- Provides minor protection to the underlying neurovascular structures, for example in cases of clavicular fracture or other trauma
- The nerve to subclavius, also called the subclavian nerve, comes off the superior trunk of the brachial plexus and carries C5 and C6 fibers

> Subclavius runs from the 1st rib to the middle third of the clavicle and is supplied by the nerve to subclavius off the superior trunk.

Library: Serratus anterior
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Sagittal and axial views of the thoracic wall with serratus anterior wrapping from the lateral surfaces of the ribs to the medial border of the scapula and the long thoracic nerve labeled on its superficial surface](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s29.jpg)

## Attachments

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Anterior attachment | Lateral surfaces of ribs 1 to 8 |
| Posterior attachment | Anterior surface of the medial border of the scapula |
| Actions | Protracts the scapula, holds it against the thoracic wall, and rotates the scapula upwards so the arm can be raised over 90 degrees |
| Innervation | Long thoracic nerve |

## Key features

- Forms the medial wall of the axilla
- The upward rotation it produces is what lets abduction continue past 90 degrees, so a weak serratus anterior limits overhead reach
- The long thoracic nerve runs on the superficial surface of the muscle, which is unusual and leaves it exposed

> Serratus anterior forms the medial wall of the axilla and rotates the scapula upward to allow the arm to be raised above 90 degrees.

Library: Long thoracic nerve injury and winged scapula
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Posterior view of the trunk with the long thoracic nerve and serratus anterior muscle labeled, beside a photograph of a patient whose medial scapular border protrudes off the back](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s30.jpg)

## Identify it

- Winged scapula: the medial border and inferior angle of the scapula pull away from the thoracic wall and protrude off the back

## Key features

The long thoracic nerve is unique because it innervates serratus anterior on the muscle's superficial side, which leaves it exposed and vulnerable to injury. The lecture lists knife fights, gunshot wounds, and mastectomy surgery as mechanisms.

Damage to the nerve weakens or paralyzes serratus anterior. The medial border of the scapula moves laterally, is no longer held against the ribcage, and protrudes off the back. Serratus anterior weakness also impairs upward rotation of the scapula, so the patient cannot raise the arm fully overhead.

## Testing

To test for a long thoracic nerve injury, the patient is asked to place both palms against a wall and push. If serratus anterior is weakened or paralyzed, the medial border of the scapula becomes abnormally prominent.

The lecture gives the root value with a mnemonic, worded slightly differently in the two sources. The slide says "C5, 6, 7 earns you wings to heaven" and the notes say "C5, C6, and C7 keep your wings from heaven." Either way the nerve is C5, C6, and C7.

> The long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) runs on the superficial surface of serratus anterior, so injury to it produces a winged scapula.

Library: Subscapularis in the posterior axillary wall
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the scapula with the subscapularis muscle labeled filling the subscapular fossa and running laterally toward the lesser tubercle of the humerus](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s31.jpg)

## Attachments

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Proximal attachment | Subscapular fossa |
| Distal attachment | Lesser tubercle of the humerus |
| Action | Medially rotates the arm |
| Innervation | Upper and lower subscapular nerves |

## Key features

- Forms the posterior wall of the axilla, where the notes list it alongside the scapula, teres major, and latissimus dorsi
- The upper subscapular nerve supplies subscapularis alone, while the lower subscapular nerve supplies subscapularis and teres major
- Both subscapular nerves come off the posterior cord of the brachial plexus

> Subscapularis runs from the subscapular fossa to the lesser tubercle, medially rotates the arm, and is supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves.

Library: Boundaries of the axilla
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Axial view through the shoulder labeled subscapularis muscle, serratus anterior, pectoralis major muscle, and pectoralis minor muscle around the axillary space, with a sagittal section and a skeletal diagram of the pyramidal shape](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s34.jpg)

## Identify it

- A pyramidal shaped space between the thorax and the arm

## Key features

| Border | Formed by |
|---|---|
| Apex | Clavicle, 1st rib, and the superior border of the scapula |
| Base | Skin, subcutaneous tissue, and axillary fascia |
| Anterior wall | Pectoralis major and pectoralis minor |
| Medial wall | Serratus anterior and the thoracic wall (ribs 1 to 4 and intercostal muscles) |
| Posterior wall | Scapula, subscapularis, teres major, and latissimus dorsi |
| Lateral wall | Narrow wall at the intertubercular groove of the humerus |

The apex forms the cervico-axillary canal, a passageway between the neck and the axilla, and the base forms the axillary fossa, which is the armpit itself.

The slide gives a shorter version of this list with the anterior wall as pectoralis minor and major, the medial wall as serratus anterior, and the posterior wall as subscapularis. The notes expand each wall as shown in the table above.

> The axilla's apex is bounded by the clavicle, 1st rib, and superior border of the scapula, and forms the cervico-axillary canal between the neck and the axilla.

Library: Contents of the axilla
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Axial view through the shoulder showing the axillary vessels and nerves surrounded by fat within the pyramidal axillary space bounded by subscapularis, serratus anterior, and the pectoral muscles](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s34.jpg)

## Key features

- Axillary artery and its branches, the main artery supplying the upper limb
- Axillary vein and its tributaries, the main vein draining the upper limb
- Brachial plexus, specifically the cords and branches, which form the peripheral nerves of the upper limb
- Axillary lymph nodes, which filter lymph draining from the upper limb and the pectoral region
- Axillary fat

The axilla provides a passageway for neurovascular structures travelling to and from the upper limb, and it is protected by the adducted upper limb.

Note that the roots, trunks, and divisions of the brachial plexus are in the neck, and only the cords and branches are in the axilla.

> The axilla contains the axillary artery and vein, the cords and branches of the brachial plexus, the axillary lymph nodes, and fat.

Library: Axillary artery: course and three parts
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the thorax and upper limb labeled subclavian artery, axillary artery, and brachial artery, showing the vessel changing names along its course](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s36.jpg)

## Identify it

- The axillary artery begins at the lateral border of the 1st rib as the continuation of the subclavian artery
- It ends at the inferior border of teres major, where it continues as the brachial artery

## Key features

On the right, the subclavian artery arises from the brachiocephalic trunk. On the left, it branches directly from the arch of the aorta. The full proximal sequence on the slide runs arch of the aorta, brachiocephalic trunk, subclavian artery, axillary artery, brachial artery.

The axillary artery is enclosed in the axillary sheath, a fibrous layer that covers the artery and the three cords of the brachial plexus that surround it.

| Part | Position relative to pectoralis minor | Number of branches |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | Proximal | 1 |
| 2nd | Deep to the muscle | 2 |
| 3rd | Distal | 3 |

Pectoralis minor is the landmark that divides the artery into its three parts, and the number of branches conveniently matches the part number.

> The axillary artery runs from the lateral border of the 1st rib to the inferior border of teres major, and pectoralis minor divides it into three parts with one, two, and three branches.

Library: First part of the axillary artery: superior thoracic artery
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the axilla with the superior thoracic artery labeled arising from the axillary artery proximal to pectoralis minor](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s37.jpg)

## Identify it

- The first part lies proximal to pectoralis minor
- Its single branch is the superior thoracic artery

## Key features

- The superior thoracic artery is a small vessel
- It supplies the 1st and 2nd intercostal spaces

One branch for the first part is the easiest of the three to remember, and the superior thoracic artery is the only branch arising before pectoralis minor crosses the vessel.

> The first part of the axillary artery lies proximal to pectoralis minor and gives off only the superior thoracic artery, which supplies the 1st and 2nd intercostal spaces.

Library: Second part of the axillary artery: thoracoacromial trunk and lateral thoracic artery
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the axilla with the thoracoacromial trunk labeled along with its clavicular, acromial, deltoid, and pectoral branches, and the lateral thoracic artery descending along the chest wall](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s39.jpg)

## Identify it

- The second part lies deep to pectoralis minor and has two branches
- Thoracoacromial trunk, which fans out into four named branches
- Lateral thoracic artery, descending along the lateral margin of pectoralis minor

## Key features

The thoracoacromial trunk divides into four branches that supply the structures they are named for.

| Branch | Supplies |
|---|---|
| Acromial | Acromion |
| Clavicular | Clavicle |
| Pectoral | Pectoralis major and minor |
| Deltoid | Deltoid muscle |

The lateral thoracic artery courses inferiorly along the lateral margin of pectoralis minor and supplies lateral structures of the thorax, including serratus anterior, the pectoral muscles, and subscapularis, as well as the lateral breast. It usually runs with the long thoracic nerve on the superficial surface of serratus anterior, which means the nerve and the artery are at risk together.

> The lateral thoracic artery runs with the long thoracic nerve on the superficial surface of serratus anterior and supplies the lateral breast.

Library: Third part of the axillary artery: subscapular and humeral circumflex arteries
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the axilla labeled subscapular artery, circumflex scapular artery, thoracodorsal artery, anterior circumflex humeral artery, and posterior circumflex humeral artery](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s40.jpg)

## Identify it

- The third part lies distal to pectoralis minor and has three branches
- Subscapular artery, which the notes call a large but short branch
- Anterior humeral circumflex artery
- Posterior humeral circumflex artery

## Key features

The subscapular artery descends and splits into two.

| Branch of the subscapular artery | Course and supply |
|---|---|
| Circumflex scapular artery | Courses around the lateral border of the scapula and supplies muscles on the posterior aspect of the scapula; takes part in the arterial anastomoses around the scapula |
| Thoracodorsal artery | Continues inferiorly with the thoracodorsal nerve to supply latissimus dorsi; also takes part in the scapular anastomoses |

The two humeral circumflex arteries encircle the humerus and anastomose with each other lateral to it, and both supply the glenohumeral joint and the surrounding muscles.

| Vessel | Course | Relative size |
|---|---|---|
| Anterior humeral circumflex | Passes anteriorly around the surgical neck of the humerus | Usually the smaller |
| Posterior humeral circumflex | Passes medially through the posterior wall of the axilla via the quadrangular space with the axillary nerve | Usually the larger |

The lecture adds a warning worth keeping: the arterial system is quite variable, so expect variations in body donors and in future patients. You always name an artery for where it goes, not where it came from.

> The posterior humeral circumflex artery travels through the quadrangular space with the axillary nerve and is usually the larger of the two circumflex vessels.

Library: Axillary vein and the axillary sheath
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the axilla labeled axillary vein, axillary artery, brachial vein, and basilic vein, with the vein lying anterior to the artery](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s41.jpg)

## Identify it

- The axillary vein lies anterior to the axillary artery, within the axillary sheath
- It is formed by the union of the brachial and basilic veins in the arm

## Key features

- The vein continues as the subclavian vein at the lateral border of the 1st rib, which is the same landmark where the subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery
- Its tributaries usually correspond to the branches of the axillary artery
- The cephalic vein is a tributary that empties into it directly, below the clavicle
- The axillary sheath is a fibrous layer covering the axillary artery and the three cords of the brachial plexus that surround it

> The axillary vein lies anterior to the axillary artery and becomes the subclavian vein at the lateral border of the 1st rib.

Library: Basilic vein
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the upper limb with the basilic vein labeled running up the medial side of the forearm and arm](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s42.jpg)

## Identify it

- A superficial vein of the arm and forearm
- Runs medially up the limb

## Key features

- Joins the brachial vein to form the axillary vein
- Being superficial, it lies in the subcutaneous tissue rather than travelling with an artery

The basilic vein and the cephalic vein are the two superficial veins of the limb that this lecture names, and the easy way to keep them apart is that the basilic runs medially and the cephalic runs laterally in the deltopectoral groove.

> The basilic vein runs medially and joins the brachial vein to form the axillary vein.

Library: Cephalic vein and the deltopectoral groove
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the shoulder labeled deltoid muscle, pectoralis major muscle, and cephalic vein, with the vein running in the groove between the two muscles](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s43.jpg)

## Identify it

- A superficial vein of the arm and forearm, with no accompanying artery
- Runs in the deltopectoral groove, the groove between the deltoid and pectoralis major

## Key features

- The vein runs from the lateral border of the wrist, up the forearm and arm, to terminate in the axillary vein
- The slide says it empties into the axillary vein near the clavicle, and the notes say it empties directly into the axillary vein below the clavicle
- It is the landmark that defines the deltopectoral groove, which is why the groove is a reliable surface landmark for finding the vein

> The cephalic vein runs in the deltopectoral groove between the deltoid and pectoralis major and empties into the axillary vein near the clavicle.

Library: Brachial plexus: overall organization
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the brachial plexus with its five stages labeled roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and branches](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s48.jpg)

## Identify it

- Roots, then trunks, then divisions, then cords, then branches, running from the neck into the axilla

## Key features

- A network of nerves derived from the anterior rami of the C5 to T1 spinal nerves that gives rise to the peripheral nerves of the upper limb and shoulder
- Conveys motor, sensory, and sympathetic innervation to the upper limb
- Surrounds the axillary artery in the axilla

The five stages are remembered with the mnemonic Real Truckers Drink Cold Beer, for Roots, Trunks, Divisions, Cords, Branches.

Location matters for localizing an injury. The roots, trunks, and divisions are in the neck, and the cords and branches are in the axilla.

> The brachial plexus comes from the anterior rami of C5 to T1 and runs roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches (Real Truckers Drink Cold Beer).

Library: Roots of the brachial plexus: dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the brachial plexus with the C5 to T1 roots labeled and the dorsal scapular nerve and long thoracic nerve coming off them](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s50.jpg)

## Identify it

- Five roots, the anterior rami of the C5 to T1 spinal nerves
- Dorsal scapular nerve leaving the C5 root
- Long thoracic nerve formed from C5, C6, and C7

## Key features

The roots are located in the neck, lateral to the vertebral column, and they pass between the anterior and middle scalene muscles along with the subclavian artery.

| Nerve off the roots | Root value | Muscles supplied |
|---|---|---|
| Dorsal scapular nerve | C5 | Levator scapulae, rhomboid major, rhomboid minor |
| Long thoracic nerve | C5, C6, C7 | Serratus anterior |

These are the only two nerves that come directly off the roots, and both supply muscles that position the scapula, which is why both show up as scapular problems when injured.

> Only two nerves arise directly from the roots: the dorsal scapular nerve from C5 and the long thoracic nerve from C5, C6, and C7.

Library: Trunks of the brachial plexus: suprascapular nerve and nerve to subclavius
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the brachial plexus with the superior, middle, and inferior trunks shown and the suprascapular nerve and nerve to subclavius labeled coming off the superior trunk](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s52.jpg)

## Identify it

- Superior (upper) trunk: union of the C5 and C6 roots
- Middle trunk: continuation of the C7 root
- Inferior (lower) trunk: union of the C8 and T1 roots

## Key features

All three trunks are located in the neck. Only the superior trunk gives off named nerves at this level.

| Nerve off the trunks | Root value | Supplies |
|---|---|---|
| Suprascapular nerve | C5, C6 | Supraspinatus and infraspinatus |
| Nerve to subclavius | C5, C6 | Subclavius |

The nerve to subclavius is also called the subclavian nerve. Both of these branches carry C5 and C6 fibers, which is why both are affected in an upper plexus injury.

> Both nerves that come off the trunks, the suprascapular nerve and the nerve to subclavius, arise from the superior trunk and carry C5 and C6.

Library: Divisions of the brachial plexus
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the brachial plexus with the anterior divisions and posterior divisions labeled where the three trunks split](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s53.jpg)

## Identify it

- Each of the three trunks splits into an anterior and a posterior division, for six divisions in total
- The divisions are located in the neck

## Key features

- Nerves arising from the anterior divisions generally supply the flexor (anterior) compartments of the upper extremity
- Nerves arising from the posterior divisions generally supply the extensor (posterior) compartments of the upper extremity
- No named nerves come off the divisions themselves

This is the step that sorts the plexus by function rather than by level, and it is why every nerve from the posterior cord ends up supplying extensors.

> Anterior divisions go on to supply flexor compartments and posterior divisions supply extensor compartments, which is why the posterior cord supplies all the extensors.

Library: Cords of the brachial plexus and their relation to the axillary artery
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the axilla with the medial cord and lateral cord labeled where they lie alongside the axillary artery](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s55.jpg)

## Identify it

- Lateral cord, lying lateral to the second part of the axillary artery
- Medial cord, lying medial to the second part of the axillary artery
- Posterior cord, lying posterior to the second part of the axillary artery

## Key features

| Cord | Formed from | Position |
|---|---|---|
| Lateral | Anterior divisions of the superior and middle trunks | Lateral to the 2nd part of the axillary artery |
| Medial | Continuation of the anterior division of the inferior trunk | Medial to the 2nd part of the axillary artery |
| Posterior | Union of all three posterior divisions | Posterior to the 2nd part of the axillary artery |

The cords are named according to their position in relation to the axillary artery, not according to which trunks feed them. The cords form within the axilla, and the axillary sheath wraps the artery together with all three of them.

> The cords are named for where they sit relative to the second part of the axillary artery, and the second part is the one deep to pectoralis minor.

Library: Branches of the lateral and medial cords
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the axilla with the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm and medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm labeled arising from the medial cord, along with the lateral and medial pectoral nerves](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s57.jpg)

## Key features

| Nerve | Cord | Root value | Supplies |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lateral pectoral nerve | Lateral | C5, C6, C7 | Motor to pectoralis major |
| Lateral root of the median nerve | Lateral | Not stated | Joins the medial root to form the median nerve |
| Medial pectoral nerve | Medial | C8, T1 | Motor to pectoralis major and pectoralis minor |
| Medial cutaneous nerve of the arm | Medial | T1 | Sensory from the skin of the medial arm |
| Medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm | Medial | C8, T1 | Sensory from the skin of the medial forearm |
| Medial root of the median nerve | Medial | Not stated | Joins the lateral root to form the median nerve |

The medial cutaneous nerve of the arm is also called the medial brachial cutaneous nerve, and the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm is also called the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve.

The medial pectoral nerve pierces pectoralis minor before travelling on to pectoralis major, so it supplies both pectoral muscles while the lateral pectoral nerve supplies only pectoralis major.

> The medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1) supplies both pectoralis major and minor and pierces pectoralis minor on the way, while the lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6, C7) supplies pectoralis major only.

Library: Branches of the posterior cord
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the axilla with the upper subscapular nerve, thoracodorsal nerve, and lower subscapular nerve labeled arising from the posterior cord](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s58.jpg)

## Key features

| Nerve | Root value | Supplies |
|---|---|---|
| Upper subscapular nerve | C5, C6 | Subscapularis |
| Thoracodorsal nerve | C6, C7, C8 | Latissimus dorsi |
| Lower subscapular nerve | C5, C6 | Subscapularis and teres major |

The thoracodorsal nerve is also called the middle subscapular nerve, which keeps all three in the same upper, middle, lower sequence.

The thoracodorsal nerve runs with the thoracodorsal artery, a branch of the subscapular artery, to reach latissimus dorsi, so the nerve and its artery travel together.

The posterior cord also gives rise to two terminal branches, the axillary nerve and the radial nerve.

> The lower subscapular nerve supplies both subscapularis and teres major, while the upper subscapular nerve supplies subscapularis alone.

Library: Terminal branches: musculocutaneous, median, and ulnar nerves
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the brachial plexus with the musculocutaneous nerve, median nerve, and ulnar nerve labeled as terminal branches arising from the cords](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s59.jpg)

## Key features

| Nerve | Root value | Motor | Sensory | Landmark |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Musculocutaneous | C5 to C7 | Anterior arm muscles (biceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialis) | Lateral aspect of the forearm, via the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm | Pierces coracobrachialis |
| Median | C5 to T1 | Most flexors of the forearm, thenar muscles, and the 2 lateral lumbricals | Skin of the lateral palm and the lateral 3 and a half digits on the palmar surface | None stated |
| Ulnar | C8, T1 | 1 and a half flexors of the forearm (flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum profundus) and most intrinsic hand muscles | Skin of the medial hand and the medial 1 and a half digits | None stated |

The slide describes all three as supplying the anterior compartment, the musculocutaneous to the anterior arm and the median and ulnar to the anterior forearm and hand, which fits the rule that anterior divisions supply flexors.

> The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis and supplies the three anterior arm muscles, while the median and ulnar nerves pass through the arm without branching to reach the forearm and hand.

Library: Terminal branches: axillary and radial nerves
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

![Anterior view of the brachial plexus with the axillary nerve and radial nerve labeled as terminal branches of the posterior cord](library/images/msk-week-14/pect-s60.jpg)

## Key features

| Nerve | Root value | Motor | Sensory |
|---|---|---|---|
| Axillary | C5, C6 | Deltoid and teres minor | Skin of the superior lateral aspect of the shoulder, overlying the deltoid |
| Radial | C5 to T1 | Posterior compartment of the arm (triceps brachii, anconeus) and posterior compartment of the forearm, primarily the extensors of the wrist and fingers | Posterior aspect of the arm and forearm and the posterolateral aspect of the hand |

Both come off the posterior cord, which is formed from all three posterior divisions. The lecture's general rule is that nerves arising from the posterior divisions supply the extensor compartments, but note that the axillary nerve's own targets as the lecture lists them are deltoid and teres minor, which are not extensor compartment muscles.

The axillary nerve passes through the quadrangular space with the posterior humeral circumflex artery, which is why both are at risk in the same injuries.

> The axillary nerve is C5 and C6 to deltoid and teres minor with sensation over the deltoid, and the radial nerve is C5 to T1 to triceps brachii, anconeus, and the posterior forearm extensors.

Library: Erb palsy
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

## Key features

Erb palsy, also called Erb-Duchenne palsy, is an upper brachial plexus injury affecting the C5 and C6 roots. It usually results from an excessive increase in the angle between the neck and the shoulder, for example when someone is thrown from a horse or a motorcycle, or during a difficult vaginal delivery. The mechanism stretches or ruptures the superior parts of the plexus, or avulses the roots from the spinal cord.

| What is affected | Detail |
|---|---|
| Nerves | Peripheral nerves derived from C5 and C6: musculocutaneous, axillary, suprascapular, and nerve to subclavius |
| Muscles | Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subclavius, biceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialis, deltoid, teres minor |
| Motor functions | Abduction at the shoulder, lateral rotation of the arm, supination of the forearm, flexion at the shoulder |
| Sensory functions | Sensation over the lateral aspect of the upper limb (C5 and C6 dermatomes) |

## Clinical note

The affected limb hangs limply and is medially rotated by the unopposed action of pectoralis major. The forearm is pronated because biceps brachii is lost, and the wrist is weakly flexed because the normal tone of the wrist flexors outweighs the weakened extensors. That posture is known as the waiter's tip position and is characteristic of Erb palsy.

> Erb palsy is a C5 and C6 injury producing the waiter's tip position: the limb hangs medially rotated, the forearm is pronated, and the wrist is weakly flexed.

Library: Klumpke palsy
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Pectoral Region and Axilla

## Key features

Klumpke palsy is a lower brachial plexus injury affecting the C8 and T1 roots. It is much less common than an upper plexus injury. It happens when the upper limb is suddenly pulled superiorly, for example when a person grasps something to break a fall or when a baby's upper limb is pulled excessively during delivery. These events injure the inferior trunk of the plexus and may avulse the spinal nerve roots from the spinal cord.

| What is affected | Detail |
|---|---|
| Nerves | Peripheral nerves derived from the T1 root are most affected: the ulnar and median nerves |
| Muscles | The intrinsic hand muscles |
| Sensory functions | Sensation along the medial side of the upper limb (C8 and T1 dermatomes) |

## Clinical note

The primary feature is a clawed hand. The lumbrical muscles normally flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints. When they are paralyzed, the fingers become extended at the MCP joints and flexed at the IP joints, which produces the clawed appearance.

> Klumpke palsy is a C8 and T1 injury producing a clawed hand, because paralyzed lumbricals leave the MCP joints extended and the IP joints flexed.

Library: Proximal humerus landmarks of the arm
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Humerus in anterior and posterior views labeled head of humerus, anatomical neck, surgical neck, greater tubercle, lesser tubercle, and intertubercular sulcus](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s05.jpg)

## Identify it

- Head: the rounded proximal end of the bone
- Anatomical neck: the line immediately distal to the head, separating the head from the tubercles, marked by a dashed line on the posterior view
- Surgical neck: the narrowed region distal to both tubercles, marked by a second dashed line
- Greater tubercle: the larger prominence, labeled on the lateral side in the anterior view
- Lesser tubercle: the smaller prominence, labeled on the medial side in the anterior view
- Intertubercular sulcus (bicipital groove): the vertical furrow running between the two tubercles

## Key features

The lecture splits the proximal humerus into the head, the two necks, the two tubercles, and the groove between the tubercles. The anatomical neck and the surgical neck are different structures at different levels, and the figure shows that by marking them with two separate dashed lines.

The intertubercular sulcus goes by two names in this lecture, intertubercular sulcus and bicipital groove, and both are used again in the biceps material.

> The anatomical neck sits just distal to the head and separates the head from the tubercles, while the surgical neck is the narrower region distal to both tubercles.

Library: Humeral shaft: deltoid tuberosity and radial groove
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Humerus in anterior and posterior views with the deltoid tuberosity labeled on the shaft in the anterior view and the radial groove labeled on the posterior view](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s05.jpg)

## Identify it

- Shaft (diaphysis): the long tubular portion between the proximal and distal ends
- Deltoid tuberosity: the roughened elevation on the shaft, labeled on the anterior view
- Radial (spiral) groove: the oblique furrow crossing the shaft, labeled on the posterior view

## Key features

The lecture lists only two named features on the shaft itself, and they sit on opposite surfaces. The deltoid tuberosity is the one you find from the front, and the radial groove is the one you find from the back.

The radial groove is also called the spiral groove, and it matters later in the lecture because the radial nerve and the profunda brachii artery run in it once they enter the posterior compartment.

> The radial groove is a posterior feature of the humeral shaft, and it carries the radial nerve and the profunda brachii artery.

Library: Distal humerus: condyle, epicondyles, and fossae
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Distal humerus in anterior and posterior views labeled condyle, capitulum, trochlea, medial epicondyle, lateral epicondyle, radial fossa, coronoid fossa, olecranon fossa, and ulnar groove](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s05.jpg)

## Identify it

- Condyle: the articular region at the distal end, bracketed in the anterior view, made of the capitulum and the trochlea
- Capitulum: the rounded lateral part of the condyle
- Trochlea: the spool-shaped medial part of the condyle
- Lateral epicondyle: the non-articular prominence lateral to the capitulum
- Medial epicondyle: the non-articular prominence medial to the trochlea
- Radial fossa: the depression above the capitulum on the anterior surface
- Coronoid fossa: the depression above the trochlea on the anterior surface
- Olecranon fossa: the large depression on the posterior surface
- Ulnar groove: the furrow behind the medial epicondyle on the posterior view

## Key features

| Feature | Surface | Position in the figure |
|---|---|---|
| Radial fossa | Anterior | Above the capitulum |
| Coronoid fossa | Anterior | Above the trochlea |
| Olecranon fossa | Posterior | Above the trochlea, posteriorly |
| Ulnar groove | Posterior | Behind the medial epicondyle |

The two epicondyles are landmarks you can feel, and the lecture uses them again for the superior boundary of the cubital fossa and for the course of the ulnar nerve and the ulnar collateral arteries.

> Of the three distal fossae, the radial and coronoid fossae are anterior and the olecranon fossa is posterior.

Library: Proximal radius: head, neck, and radial tuberosity
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Proximal radius and ulna in anterior and posterior views with head of radius, neck of radius, and radial tuberosity labeled](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s06.jpg)

## Identify it

- Head of radius: the disc-shaped proximal end
- Neck of radius: the narrowed segment immediately distal to the head
- Radial tuberosity: the roughened prominence distal to the neck, on the medial side of the bone

## Key features

The lecture names only three features on the proximal radius, and they run in sequence from proximal to distal: head, then neck, then tuberosity.

The radial tuberosity is the distal attachment of biceps brachii, which is why the biceps can supinate the forearm as well as flex it.

> The radial tuberosity is the distal attachment of biceps brachii.

Library: Proximal ulna: olecranon, trochlear notch, and coronoid process
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Proximal radius and ulna in anterior and posterior views with olecranon process, trochlear notch, coronoid process, radial notch, and ulnar tuberosity labeled](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s06.jpg)

## Identify it

- Olecranon process: the large hook at the very top of the ulna, prominent on the posterior view
- Trochlear notch: the C-shaped concavity on the anterior aspect between the olecranon and the coronoid process
- Coronoid process: the forward projecting lip at the lower end of the trochlear notch
- Radial notch: the small facet on the lateral side of the coronoid process that faces the head of the radius
- Ulnar tuberosity: the roughening just distal to the coronoid process

## Key features

The olecranon and the coronoid process are the two ends of the trochlear notch, and together they grip the trochlea of the humerus. The radial notch sits off to the side of that grip and faces the radial head instead.

The coronoid process and the ulnar tuberosity are the distal attachments of brachialis, and the olecranon is the landmark the ulnar nerve passes medial to at the elbow.

> The trochlear notch is bounded above by the olecranon process and below by the coronoid process.

Library: Fascial compartments of the arm: brachial fascia and intermuscular septa
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Cross section of the arm labeled brachial fascia boundary, lateral intermuscular septum of the arm, medial intermuscular septum of the arm, humerus, brachialis, biceps brachii long and short heads, and triceps brachii long, lateral, and medial heads](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s08.jpg)

## Identify it

- Brachial fascia: the continuous sleeve of deep fascia wrapping the whole arm
- Lateral intermuscular septum: runs inward from the brachial fascia to the humerus on the lateral side
- Medial intermuscular septum: runs inward from the brachial fascia to the humerus on the medial side
- Anterior compartment: contains biceps brachii (long and short heads) and brachialis in the cross section
- Posterior compartment: contains the long, lateral, and medial heads of triceps brachii

## Key features

The brachial fascia surrounds the arm, and the two intermuscular septa run from that fascial sleeve to the humerus. Between them, the septa divide the arm into an anterior (flexor) compartment and a posterior (extensor) compartment, each with its own muscles and its own neurovasculature.

The lateral intermuscular septum runs between the insertion of the deltoid muscle and the lateral epicondyle of the humerus.

| Septum | What pierces it |
|---|---|
| Lateral intermuscular septum | Radial nerve, as it passes from the posterior compartment toward the lateral epicondyle |
| Medial intermuscular septum | Ulnar nerve, as it leaves the anterior compartment |

> The lateral intermuscular septum runs between the deltoid insertion and the lateral epicondyle, and the radial nerve pierces it while the ulnar nerve pierces the medial septum.

Library: Neurovasculature of the anterior compartment of the arm
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Cross section of the arm with the brachial artery, brachial vein, median nerve, musculocutaneous nerve, and ulnar nerve labeled on the medial side of the humerus](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s08.jpg)

## Identify it

- Brachial artery and brachial vein(s), grouped together on the medial side of the section
- Median nerve, next to the brachial artery
- Musculocutaneous nerve, out in the muscle between biceps brachii and brachialis rather than in the medial bundle
- Ulnar nerve, the most medial of the labeled nerves, close to the medial intermuscular septum

## Key features

Five structures are assigned to the anterior compartment in this lecture:

- Brachial artery
- Brachial vein(s)
- Median nerve
- Musculocutaneous nerve
- Ulnar nerve

The musculocutaneous nerve is the one that is actually supplying this compartment. The median and ulnar nerves pass through the arm without branching in it, and the ulnar nerve leaves the compartment partway down by piercing the medial intermuscular septum.

> The anterior compartment holds the brachial artery and veins, the median nerve, the musculocutaneous nerve, and the ulnar nerve.

Library: Neurovasculature of the posterior compartment of the arm
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Cross section of the arm with the radial nerve labeled next to the humerus on the lateral side, within the posterior compartment formed by the three heads of triceps brachii](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s08.jpg)

## Identify it

- Radial nerve, labeled against the humerus on the lateral side of the section
- Posterior compartment, bounded by the brachial fascia and the two intermuscular septa and filled by the three heads of triceps brachii

## Key features

The posterior compartment is supplied by one nerve and one artery:

- Radial nerve
- Profunda brachii artery, also called the deep brachial artery or the deep artery of the arm, with two named branches:
  - Middle collateral artery
  - Radial collateral artery

The radial nerve supplies all of the muscles of the posterior compartment in both the arm and the forearm, so a single nerve accounts for the whole extensor side of the limb below the shoulder.

> The posterior compartment of the arm is supplied by the radial nerve and the profunda brachii artery, whose branches are the middle collateral and radial collateral arteries.

Library: Anterior compartment muscle group: actions and innervation
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Slide listing the muscles, innervation, and actions of the anterior compartment of the arm beside a figure of the arm muscles](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s10.jpg)

## Key features

The anterior compartment of the arm holds three muscles:

- Biceps brachii, with a long head and a short head
- Brachialis
- Coracobrachialis

Innervation of the group comes from two nerves, the musculocutaneous nerve and the radial nerve. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies all three, and the radial nerve contribution goes to brachialis only.

The group produces three actions:

1. Flexion of the arm at the shoulder
2. Flexion of the forearm at the elbow
3. Supination

All three muscles cross at least one joint anteriorly, which is why every action of the group is a flexion or a supination rather than an extension.

> Three muscles (biceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialis) make up the anterior compartment, and the musculocutaneous nerve is the compartment's nerve.

Library: Biceps brachii
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Anterior view of the arm with the long head of biceps brachii, short head of biceps brachii, biceps brachii tendon, and bicipital aponeurosis labeled, beside a bone figure labeled supraglenoid tubercle and bicipital groove and a cadaver photo of the long head tendon](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s11.jpg)

## Attachments

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Proximal attachment, short head | Coracoid process of scapula |
| Proximal attachment, long head | Supraglenoid tubercle of scapula |
| Distal attachment | Radial tuberosity |
| Innervation | Musculocutaneous nerve |
| Actions | Supination of forearm at elbow, flexion of forearm at elbow |

## Identify it

- Long head: the more lateral of the two tendons superiorly, running down through the bicipital groove from the supraglenoid tubercle
- Short head: the more medial tendon, coming off the coracoid process
- Biceps brachii tendon: the single distal tendon heading for the radial tuberosity
- Bicipital aponeurosis: the flat sheet peeling off the distal tendon medially

## Key features

Both heads start on the scapula, so the muscle crosses the shoulder as well as the elbow. The long head is the one that takes the long route through the bicipital groove of the humerus, which is what exposes it to the wear described in the tendinopathy and rupture material.

Distally the muscle ends in two ways. The tendon proper goes to the radial tuberosity, and the bicipital aponeurosis spreads medially into the fascia of the forearm, where it forms part of the roof of the cubital fossa.

> The long head attaches to the supraglenoid tubercle and runs in the bicipital groove, while the short head attaches to the coracoid process, and both insert distally on the radial tuberosity.

Library: Bicipital myotatic reflex
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Slide describing the bicipital myotatic reflex with a photograph of the reflex being tested at the cubital fossa](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s12.jpg)

## Key features

The bicipital myotatic reflex is a deep tendon reflex, and the lecture gives a specific set-up for it:

1. The upper limb is relaxed
2. The limb is passively pronated
3. The elbow is partially extended
4. The thumb is placed firmly over the biceps brachii tendon at the cubital fossa

Striking the thumb stretches the biceps tendon, and the response tests the integrity of the musculocutaneous nerve and the C5 to C6 spinal cord levels. That makes the reflex a quick way to check both the nerve supplying the anterior compartment and the cord segments it comes from.

Placing the thumb over the tendon matters because the tendon lies in the cubital fossa, where it is the most lateral of the three TAN structures.

> The bicipital myotatic reflex tests the musculocutaneous nerve and the C5 to C6 spinal cord levels.

Library: Biceps tendinopathy
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Ultrasound images of the long head of the biceps brachii tendon in the bicipital groove between the lesser and greater tuberosities, with a second pair of images showing a thickened tendon sheath and Doppler color signal](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s13.jpg)

## Key features

Biceps tendinopathy presents as pain and tenderness in the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii. The lecture gives two findings:

- Anterior shoulder pain
- Point tenderness of the bicipital groove

The pain is felt at the shoulder even though the muscle belly is in the arm, because the affected part of the tendon is the segment running through the bicipital groove on the proximal humerus.

## Identify it

- Transverse ultrasound of the bicipital groove shows the long head tendon as a bright oval sitting between the lesser tuberosity on one side and the greater tuberosity on the other, with the subscapularis nearby
- In the tenosynovitis images the tendon looks inhomogeneous and the tendon sheath is thickened
- Doppler shows increased vascularity in the same area, reflecting inflammation

> Biceps tendinopathy involves the long head tendon in the bicipital groove and presents with anterior shoulder pain and point tenderness over the groove.

Library: Rupture of the long head of the biceps brachii tendon
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Clinical photograph of a flexed arm with the biceps muscle belly bunched distally, beside a bone figure of the scapula and proximal humerus](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s14.jpg)

## Key features

Rupture of the long head of the biceps brachii tendon is also called the Popeye deformity, after the way the detached muscle belly balls up in the arm.

It results from wear and tear of the tendon in the bicipital groove, following prolonged tendinitis, so the rupture is the end point of the same process described under biceps tendinopathy rather than a separate injury.

The tendon ruptures between the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula and the proximal part of the bicipital groove. That is exactly the stretch of tendon that has to turn a corner and run through the groove, which is why it is the segment that fails.

## Identify it

- The affected arm shows a rounded, distally displaced bulge of the biceps belly when the elbow is flexed

> The long head tendon ruptures between the supraglenoid tubercle and the proximal part of the bicipital groove, after prolonged tendinitis has worn it down in the groove.

Library: Brachialis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Anterior views of the arm with brachialis labeled, one view noting that it lies deep to biceps brachii](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s15.jpg)

## Attachments

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Proximal attachment | Distal half of humerus |
| Distal attachment | Coronoid process of ulna and ulnar tuberosity |
| Innervation | Musculocutaneous nerve and radial nerve |
| Action | Flexion of forearm at elbow |

## Key features

Brachialis is the one muscle of the anterior compartment with a dual nerve supply, taking both the musculocutaneous nerve and the radial nerve. That dual supply is the reason the compartment slide lists the radial nerve alongside the musculocutaneous nerve.

It is also the only one of the three anterior muscles that attaches to the ulna rather than the radius or the humerus, so it can flex the elbow but cannot supinate.

## Identify it

- Brachialis lies deep to biceps brachii and is uncovered when the biceps is reflected
- Its fibers run from the lower humerus straight down onto the proximal ulna

> Brachialis attaches to the coronoid process and ulnar tuberosity of the ulna and is innervated by both the musculocutaneous and radial nerves.

Library: Coracobrachialis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Anterior view of the arm with coracobrachialis labeled and the musculocutaneous nerve shown piercing coracobrachialis](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s16.jpg)

## Attachments

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Proximal attachment | Coracoid process of scapula |
| Distal attachment | Middle third of humeral diaphysis |
| Innervation | Musculocutaneous nerve |
| Actions | Flexion of arm at shoulder, adduction of arm at shoulder |

## Identify it

- Coracobrachialis runs from the coracoid process down to the middle of the humeral shaft, deep and medial to the short head of biceps brachii
- The musculocutaneous nerve is shown passing directly through the muscle belly

## Key features

Coracobrachialis is the only muscle of the anterior compartment that does not cross the elbow, so both of its actions are at the shoulder rather than the forearm.

It shares the coracoid process with the short head of biceps brachii, and it is the landmark for the musculocutaneous nerve, which pierces it on the way into the arm.

> The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis, and coracobrachialis acts only at the shoulder, flexing and adducting the arm.

Library: Musculocutaneous nerve in the arm
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Anterior view of the arm labeled lateral cord of brachial plexus, musculocutaneous nerve, and lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s18.jpg)

## Key features

The musculocutaneous nerve comes off the lateral cord of the brachial plexus, and the lecture traces it through the arm in four steps:

1. It pierces the coracobrachialis muscle
2. It travels between the biceps brachii and brachialis muscles
3. It supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment
4. It continues past the elbow as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, also called the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve

That terminal cutaneous branch innervates the skin of the lateral forearm, which is where the nerve gets the cutaneous half of its name.

## Identify it

- Look for the nerve emerging from the lateral cord and then disappearing into coracobrachialis
- Below that, it lies in the plane between biceps brachii and brachialis
- It reappears at the lateral side of the elbow as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm

> The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis, runs between biceps brachii and brachialis, and ends as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm supplying skin of the lateral forearm.

Library: Radial nerve in the arm
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Anterior view of the arm with the radial nerve highlighted in the radial groove with the profunda brachii artery, the lateral intermuscular septum of the arm, and the radial nerve again below the elbow](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s19.jpg)

## Key features

The radial nerve is the nerve of the posterior compartment, and the lecture follows it in four steps:

1. It enters the posterior compartment of the arm
2. It supplies all of the muscles of the posterior compartment, in both the arm and the forearm
3. It pierces the lateral intermuscular septum
4. It divides into deep and superficial branches

Piercing the lateral intermuscular septum is what brings the nerve back around to the front of the elbow, which is why it turns up again at the lateral edge of the cubital fossa.

## Identify it

- In the arm, the radial nerve is labeled alongside the profunda brachii artery in the radial groove of the humerus
- Distally it is found lateral to the brachialis and deep to the brachioradialis, before splitting into its two branches

> The radial nerve supplies every muscle of the posterior compartment of both the arm and the forearm, pierces the lateral intermuscular septum, and then divides into deep and superficial branches.

Library: Median and ulnar nerves in the arm
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Anterior view of the arm with the median nerve highlighted beside the brachial artery and the ulnar nerve highlighted passing the medial intermuscular septum toward the medial epicondyle of the humerus](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s19.jpg)

## Key features

Both of these nerves pass through the arm without supplying it. Neither one has any branches in the axilla or the arm.

| Nerve | Course in the arm |
|---|---|
| Median nerve | Travels with the brachial artery down to the cubital fossa |
| Ulnar nerve | Arises in the anterior compartment, pierces the medial intermuscular septum, then passes posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus and medial to the olecranon process of the ulna |

The ulnar nerve starts out anteriorly and then leaves, which is why it ends up behind the medial epicondyle where it can be struck directly. The median nerve stays with the artery the whole way, so it arrives in the cubital fossa as part of the TAN bundle.

## Identify it

- Median nerve: paired with the brachial artery along the medial side of the arm
- Ulnar nerve: more posterior and medial, crossing the medial intermuscular septum and then running behind the medial epicondyle

> Neither the median nor the ulnar nerve branches in the axilla or arm; the median travels with the brachial artery to the cubital fossa while the ulnar passes posterior to the medial epicondyle.

Library: Brachial artery
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Upper limb arterial figures labeled subclavian artery, brachiocephalic trunk, axillary artery, brachial artery, deep artery of the arm, radial collateral artery, middle collateral artery, superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries, radial artery, and ulnar artery](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s20.jpg)

## Key features

The brachial artery is the continuation of the axillary artery, and the name changes at the inferior border of the teres major muscle.

| Branch | Note |
|---|---|
| Profunda brachii artery | Also called the deep brachial artery or the deep artery of the arm; gives the radial collateral artery and the middle collateral artery |
| Superior ulnar collateral artery | Travels with the ulnar nerve, passes posterior to the medial epicondyle |
| Inferior ulnar collateral artery | Passes anterior to the medial epicondyle |
| Radial artery | Terminal branch |
| Ulnar artery | Terminal branch |

The artery ends by dividing into the radial and ulnar arteries, which are marked as its terminal branches. Everything in between, the profunda brachii and the two ulnar collaterals, feeds into the network of vessels around the elbow.

## Identify it

- Follow the vessel down from the axilla past teres major, where the label changes from axillary to brachial
- The profunda brachii leaves early and heads posteriorly toward the radial groove
- The two ulnar collaterals come off lower down, close to the medial epicondyle

> The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the inferior border of teres major, and the brachial artery ends by dividing into the radial and ulnar arteries.

Library: Ulnar collateral arteries and their relation to the medial epicondyle
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Arterial figure of the arm with the superior ulnar collateral artery and the inferior ulnar collateral artery labeled near the medial epicondyle of the humerus](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s20.jpg)

## Key features

Both ulnar collateral arteries come off the brachial artery and both head for the medial side of the elbow, but they pass the medial epicondyle on opposite sides.

| Artery | Relation to the medial epicondyle | Companion structure |
|---|---|---|
| Superior ulnar collateral artery | Posterior | Travels with the ulnar nerve |
| Inferior ulnar collateral artery | Anterior | None named in the lecture |

The superior ulnar collateral artery keeps company with the ulnar nerve, and the two of them take the same route behind the medial epicondyle. That pairing is the easiest way to remember which collateral is which, since the nerve is also posterior to the epicondyle.

> The superior ulnar collateral artery travels with the ulnar nerve posterior to the medial epicondyle, while the inferior ulnar collateral artery passes anterior to it.

Library: Elbow anastomosis and collateral circulation
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Anterior view of the arm and proximal forearm showing the brachial artery with the profunda brachii middle collateral and radial collateral branches, the superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries, and the recurrent radial, ulnar recurrent, and interosseous recurrent arteries, with color boxes pairing each collateral with a recurrent vessel](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s21.jpg)

## Key features

The elbow anastomosis is a network of arteries surrounding the elbow joint. It ensures continuous perfusion regardless of the position of the joint or if a main artery is compressed or blocked.

That is the point of collateral circulation at any joint. A joint has to bend, and bending can kink or compress the vessel running straight across it, so the blood supply is built with alternative routes around the joint rather than a single channel through it.

## Identify it

In the figure, the descending collateral branches from above are color matched to the ascending recurrent branches from below:

- Middle collateral branch of profunda brachii, matched with the recurrent interosseous artery
- Radial collateral branch of profunda brachii, matched with the recurrent radial artery
- Superior ulnar collateral artery, matched with the posterior ulnar recurrent artery
- Inferior ulnar collateral artery, matched with the anterior ulnar recurrent artery

> The elbow anastomosis keeps the forearm perfused no matter how the elbow is positioned or whether a main artery is compressed or blocked.

Library: Superficial veins of the arm
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Anterior view of the upper limb with the cephalic vein labeled laterally, the basilic vein labeled medially, and the median cubital vein labeled crossing between them at the elbow](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s22.jpg)

## Identify it

- Cephalic vein: the superficial vein running up the lateral side of the limb and over the front of the shoulder
- Basilic vein: the superficial vein running up the medial side of the limb
- Median cubital vein: the short oblique vein connecting the two at the front of the elbow

## Key features

The lecture names three superficial veins in the arm, the cephalic vein, the basilic vein, and the median cubital vein. They lie outside the brachial fascia, which is what makes them superficial and what makes them visible and accessible at the front of the elbow.

The median cubital vein is the crossing link between the lateral and medial channels, and it sits right over the cubital fossa.

> The three superficial veins of the arm are the cephalic (lateral), the basilic (medial), and the median cubital vein connecting them at the elbow.

Library: Deep veins of the arm
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Deep venous figure of the upper limb labeled axillary vein, basilic vein, brachial veins, radial veins, and ulnar veins](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s22.jpg)

## Key features

The deep veins of the arm are the brachial vein or veins, and the lecture gives three facts about them:

1. They accompany the brachial artery
2. They are formed by the union of the radial and ulnar veins
3. They merge with the basilic vein to form the axillary vein

The sequence runs the opposite direction from the arteries. The radial and ulnar veins come together to make the brachial veins, the brachial veins pick up the basilic vein, and the result is the axillary vein.

## Identify it

- In the figure the brachial veins are the paired deep channels flanking the position of the brachial artery
- Trace them up and they join the basilic vein, and the single channel above that junction is labeled axillary vein

> The brachial veins are formed by the union of the radial and ulnar veins and merge with the basilic vein to form the axillary vein.

Library: Boundaries of the cubital fossa
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Anterior view of the elbow and proximal forearm with brachioradialis labeled laterally and pronator teres labeled medially, and a dashed triangle outlining the cubital fossa](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s24.jpg)

## Key features

The cubital fossa is a triangle at the front of the elbow, and the lecture gives five boundaries:

| Boundary | Structure |
|---|---|
| Superior | Imaginary line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles of the humerus |
| Medial | Pronator teres muscle |
| Lateral | Brachioradialis muscle |
| Deep (floor) | Brachialis and supinator muscles |
| Superficial (roof) | Brachial and antebrachial fascia, bicipital aponeurosis |

The superior boundary is the only one that is not a real structure. It is a line drawn between two palpable bony points, which is what makes the epicondyles useful landmarks for finding the fossa on a patient.

The bicipital aponeurosis in the roof comes off the biceps tendon, so the same muscle contributes to both the roof of the fossa and its contents.

## Identify it

- The two muscles forming the sides converge toward the apex of the triangle, brachioradialis on the lateral side and pronator teres on the medial side
- The dashed outline in the figure runs along the epicondylar line above and down both muscle borders

> The cubital fossa is bounded laterally by brachioradialis, medially by pronator teres, superiorly by a line between the epicondyles, with brachialis and supinator as the floor.

Library: Contents of the cubital fossa
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Anterior Arm and Cubital Fossa

![Two anterior views of the right cubital fossa labeled tendon of biceps brachii, brachial artery and veins, median nerve, radial nerve, and superficial and deep branches of the radial nerve, with a cadaver photograph of the same region](library/images/msk-week-14/aarm-s25.jpg)

## Key features

The contents of the cubital fossa are remembered as TAN, running from lateral to medial:

1. **T**endon of biceps brachii muscle
2. Brachial **a**rtery
3. Media**n** nerve

The radial nerve is also in the region, at the lateral edge, where it has already divided into its superficial and deep branches.

Order matters here. The tendon is the most lateral of the three, the artery sits next to it, and the median nerve is the most medial. That is also why the thumb goes on the tendon for the bicipital myotatic reflex and why the brachial pulse is felt just medial to the tendon.

## Identify it
