- Tendon of biceps brachii: the cord running down the middle of the fossa toward the radial tuberosity, with the bicipital aponeurosis spreading medially from it
- Brachial artery and veins: immediately medial to the tendon
- Median nerve: medial to the artery
- Radial nerve: at the lateral margin, splitting into superficial and deep branches

> From lateral to medial the cubital fossa contains the tendon of biceps brachii, the brachial artery, and the median nerve (TAN), with the radial nerve and its two branches at the lateral edge.

Library: Purpose of the shoulder complex
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Lecture slide titled Shoulder Complex asking what the purpose of the shoulder complex is, listing a mobile yet strong base for the hand and transmission of loads to the axial skeleton, then listing mobility and stability as what is required](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s03.jpg)

## Key features

The shoulder complex exists to do two jobs at once. It gives the hand a very mobile but still strong base to work from, which is what lets the hand carry out both its gross and its skilled functions, and it transmits loads from the upper extremity back to the axial skeleton.

Meeting both demands requires two properties that normally trade off against each other:

- Mobility
- Stability

The rest of the lecture is organized around where each of those comes from. Mobility comes largely from the glenohumeral joint and from the scapula moving on the thorax, and stability comes from the ligaments at the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints, the glenoid labrum and capsule, and the rotator cuff acting as a dynamic stabilizer.

> The shoulder complex has to provide mobility and stability at the same time, because it serves as a strong but mobile base for the hand and transmits load from the limb to the axial skeleton.

Library: Clavicle in the shoulder complex
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Anterior view illustration of the clavicle showing its S shape, with the sternal end medially and the acromial end laterally](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s05.jpg)

## Identify it

- S-shaped bone running between the sternum and the acromion
- Visible and palpable along its entire length, which is unusual for a long bone
- Sternal end is the medial end, acromial end is the lateral end

## Key features

The clavicle is what connects the upper limb to the trunk. It does that through a joint at each end:

| End | Joint | Articulates with |
|---|---|---|
| Sternal (medial) | Sternoclavicular | Manubrium of the sternum |
| Acromial (lateral) | Acromioclavicular | Acromion of the scapula |

Because the whole bone is subcutaneous, a deformity after a fracture is usually obvious on inspection and palpation rather than needing imaging to detect.

> The clavicle connects the upper limb to the trunk, articulating medially with the manubrium at the sternoclavicular joint and laterally with the acromion at the acromioclavicular joint.

Library: Clavicle fracture
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Radiograph of a fractured clavicle beside text describing the mechanism and the resulting shoulder drop, with before and after photographs of a patient's shoulder contour](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s09.jpg)

## Key features

The clavicle is commonly fractured. Two mechanisms are given: an indirect force transmitted up the limb from a fall on an outstretched hand, and a direct fall onto the shoulder itself.

The lecture describes the usual site two slightly different ways. The slide says the fracture is most common at the middle third of the bone, and the typed notes say the weakest part of the clavicle is the junction of its middle and lateral thirds.

## Why the shoulder drops

After the fracture the two fragments are pulled in different directions:

- The medial fragment is elevated by the sternocleidomastoid
- The lateral fragment cannot be held up by the trapezius against the weight of the upper extremity, so the shoulder drops
- The lateral fragment may also be pulled medially by the muscles that adduct the arm at the shoulder joint

> A fractured clavicle drops the shoulder because trapezius can no longer hold the lateral fragment up against the weight of the limb, while sternocleidomastoid elevates the medial fragment.

Library: Scapula: landmarks of the shoulder
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Numbered scapula figure with the acromion process, suprascapular notch, coracoid process, glenoid fossa, supraglenoid tubercle, infraglenoid tubercle, subscapular fossa, spine of scapula, supraspinous fossa, infraspinous fossa, and spinoglenoid notch labeled, shown with a sagittal view](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s06.jpg)

## Identify it

1. Acromion process
2. Suprascapular notch
3. Coracoid process
4. Glenoid fossa
5. Supraglenoid tubercle
6. Infraglenoid tubercle
7. Subscapular fossa
8. Spine of scapula
9. Supraspinous fossa
10. Infraspinous fossa

The spinoglenoid notch is also labeled, between the spine and the glenoid.

## Key features

The scapula is a triangular flat bone overlying ribs 2 to 7 on the posterolateral surface of the thorax, with medial, lateral and superior borders and superior and inferior angles. The spine divides the posterior surface into the smaller supraspinous fossa above and the larger infraspinous fossa below.

| Landmark | What attaches there |
|---|---|
| Subscapular fossa (anterior, costal surface) | Subscapularis |
| Supraspinous fossa | Supraspinatus |
| Infraspinous fossa | Infraspinatus |
| Supraglenoid tubercle | Long head of biceps brachii |
| Infraglenoid tubercle | Long head of triceps brachii |
| Coracoid process | Pectoralis minor, short head of biceps brachii, coracobrachialis |

The suprascapular notch is an indentation on the superior border that is converted into a foramen by the superior transverse scapular ligament. The glenoid fossa is the shallow fossa that takes the head of the humerus.

> The supraglenoid tubercle gives origin to the long head of biceps brachii and the infraglenoid tubercle to the long head of triceps brachii.

Library: Humerus and ulna landmarks for the shoulder and posterior arm
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Numbered anterior and posterior views of the humerus with the head, greater tubercle, lesser tubercle, intertubercular groove, anatomical neck, surgical neck, deltoid tuberosity, radial or spiral groove and olecranon fossa labeled, alongside the olecranon of the ulna](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s07.jpg)

## Identify it

Humerus:

1. Head of humerus
2. Greater tubercle
3. Lesser tubercle
4. Intertubercular groove
5. Anatomical neck
6. Surgical neck
7. Deltoid tuberosity
8. Radial (spiral) groove
9. Olecranon fossa

Ulna:

10. Olecranon

## Key features

| Landmark | Where it is | What attaches or runs there |
|---|---|---|
| Head | Proximal ball-shaped end | Articulates with the glenoid cavity |
| Greater tubercle | Superior posterior | Insertion of supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor |
| Lesser tubercle | Superior anterior | Insertion of subscapularis |
| Intertubercular (bicipital) groove | Between the tubercles | Long head of biceps tendon runs through it, latissimus dorsi inserts on its floor |
| Anatomical neck | Between head and tubercles | Separates the head from the tubercles |
| Surgical neck | Narrow part distal to the tubercles | Common fracture site |
| Deltoid tuberosity | Lateral shaft | Deltoid |
| Radial (spiral) groove | Posterior shaft | Radial nerve and deep brachial artery |
| Olecranon fossa | Distal posterior humerus | Receives the olecranon of the ulna |

The olecranon itself is the thick curved eminence on the posterior aspect of the proximal ulna, and it is the insertion site for triceps brachii and anconeus.

Note that the typed notes describe the radial groove as carrying "radial and deep brachial arteries," which does not match the rest of the lecture. Everywhere else, including both fracture slides and the posterior arm section, the structures in the groove are the radial nerve and the deep brachial artery.

> The greater tubercle takes supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor, the lesser tubercle takes subscapularis, and the radial groove on the posterior shaft carries the radial nerve and deep brachial artery.

Library: Shoulder radiograph: identifying structures
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Plain anteroposterior radiograph of a right shoulder with colored arrows and dashed outlines marking the coracoid process of the scapula, acromion of the scapula, clavicle, head of humerus, greater tubercle, lesser tubercle, surgical neck and glenoid fossa](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s08.jpg)

## Identify it

On the plain film the lecture labels:

- Clavicle, running medially off the top of the image
- Acromion of the scapula, overlying the superolateral humeral head
- Coracoid process of the scapula, projecting anteriorly medial to the acromion
- Head of the humerus, sitting against the glenoid
- Greater tubercle on the lateral side of the proximal humerus
- Lesser tubercle medial to the greater tubercle
- Surgical neck, the narrowed segment just distal to the tubercles
- Glenoid fossa, outlined where the scapula meets the humeral head

## Key features

One of the lecture objectives is identifying shoulder structures on X-ray, MRI and CT, so the same landmarks learned on the dry bone need to be recognizable on a film. The surgical neck is worth finding deliberately, because it is the common fracture site and the slides that follow use plain films of exactly this region.

> On an AP shoulder film the surgical neck is the narrowed segment immediately distal to the greater and lesser tubercles, and it is the site to check on any proximal humerus film.

Library: Sternoclavicular joint: type and articulation
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Illustration of the sternoclavicular joint showing the medial end of the clavicle meeting the manubrium and first rib, with the opposing curvatures of the clavicular and manubrial surfaces indicated](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s12.jpg)

## Key features

The sternoclavicular joint is a saddle joint. The typed notes add that although it is structurally a saddle synovial joint, it functions as a ball and socket joint and is multiaxial. It is the only articulation joining the upper extremity to the axial skeleton.

The slide gives the articulation as the medial end of the clavicle with the manubrium and the 1st rib. The typed notes give it as the proximal end of the clavicle, the manubrium of the sternum, and the 1st costal cartilage.

## Reciprocal surfaces

| Surface | Vertically (longitudinal axis) | Anteroposteriorly (transverse axis) |
|---|---|---|
| Medial end of clavicle | Convex | Concave |
| Manubrium | Concave | Convex |

Each surface is the mirror of the other, which is what makes it a saddle joint.

## Movements

The joint allows anteroposterior motion (protraction and retraction), superoinferior motion (elevation and depression), and circumduction.

> The sternoclavicular joint is the only joint connecting the upper limb to the axial skeleton, and it is a saddle synovial joint that functions as a multiaxial ball and socket.

Library: Sternoclavicular joint: ligaments and articular disc
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Illustration of the sternoclavicular joints with the interclavicular, sternoclavicular and costoclavicular ligaments labeled and the fibrocartilaginous articular disc shown dividing the joint cavity](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s13.jpg)

## Identify it

- Interclavicular ligament, running between the two clavicles
- Sternoclavicular ligament, thickening the capsule anteriorly and posteriorly
- Costoclavicular ligament, running from the first rib and its cartilage up to the clavicle
- Articular disc, sitting inside the joint space

## Key features

The slide describes each ligament by the translation it resists:

| Ligament | Resists |
|---|---|
| Interclavicular | Inferior translation |
| Sternoclavicular | Anterior and posterior translation |
| Costoclavicular | Superior translation |

Collectively they restrain lateral and superior displacement of the clavicle.

The typed notes describe the same ligaments by where they sit rather than by what they resist, calling the interclavicular ligament a superior support, the costoclavicular ligament an inferior anchor that limits elevation of the pectoral girdle, and the anterior and posterior sternoclavicular ligaments thickenings of the joint capsule. The two descriptions are compatible (a ligament sitting superiorly is what resists the clavicle dropping inferiorly), but the wording runs in opposite directions, so read the slide version as what the ligament prevents and the notes version as where the ligament lies.

## Articular disc

- Fibrocartilaginous
- Separates the joint into two cavities
- Increases congruency between the two reciprocally curved surfaces
- Absorbs shock
- The notes add that it prevents medial dislocation

> The costoclavicular ligament resists superior translation and limits elevation of the pectoral girdle, while the interclavicular ligament resists inferior translation.

Library: Sternoclavicular joint dislocation
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Illustration of the sternoclavicular ligaments beside images of anterior and posterior sternoclavicular joint dislocations](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s14.jpg)

## Key features

Dislocation here is rare, because the surrounding ligaments are strong enough that the clavicle usually fractures before the joint gives way. An avulsion fracture of the proximal end of the clavicle may happen instead.

The lecture separates two degrees of injury by how many of the two ligaments have torn:

| Injury | Ligaments torn |
|---|---|
| Subluxation | One of the two (sternoclavicular or costoclavicular) |
| Dislocation | Both |

Displacement is shown in two directions, anterior and posterior.

> Sternoclavicular dislocation is rare because the ligaments are so strong that the clavicle usually fractures first, and it takes tearing both the sternoclavicular and costoclavicular ligaments to dislocate the joint.

Library: Acromioclavicular joint: type and articulation
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Illustration of the acromioclavicular joint showing the lateral end of the clavicle meeting the acromion with planar articular surfaces](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s15.jpg)

## Key features

The acromioclavicular joint is a plane type of synovial joint and is uniaxial. It is the articulation between the lateral (acromial) end of the clavicle and the acromion of the scapula, and both surfaces are planar.

Its movement is described as the acromion of the scapula rotating on the acromial end of the clavicle.

## Articular disc

A complete articular disc is present in roughly 10 percent of adults. The lecture is specific that this is not an anomaly but an indication of degeneration. The typed notes describe the disc, when present, as wedge-shaped.

> A complete articular disc in the acromioclavicular joint shows up in about 10 percent of adults and signals degeneration rather than a normal variant.

Library: Acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Illustration of the acromioclavicular region with the acromioclavicular ligament over the joint and the coracoclavicular ligament running from the coracoid process to the clavicle, its conoid and trapezoid parts labeled](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s16.jpg)

## Identify it

- Acromioclavicular ligament, crossing the joint itself with superior and inferior parts, reinforced by the attachments of deltoid and trapezius
- Coracoclavicular ligament, running vertically from the coracoid process up to the clavicle, well away from the joint line
- Conoid part, the medial component, vertically oriented, shaped like an inverted triangle
- Trapezoid part, the lateral component, horizontally oriented

## Key features

The coracoclavicular ligament is the primary stabilizer of the acromioclavicular joint. The typed notes describe it as a pair of strong bands anchoring the clavicle to the coracoid process, conferring a great deal of stability and strength, and enabling the scapula and free limb to be passively suspended from the strut-like clavicle. The acromioclavicular ligament itself strengthens the joint superiorly.

That division matters clinically, because which of the two ligaments has torn is what separates an acromioclavicular subluxation from a dislocation.

> The coracoclavicular ligament, not the acromioclavicular ligament, is the primary stabilizer of the acromioclavicular joint, and it has a medial conoid part and a lateral trapezoid part.

Library: Acromioclavicular sprain and shoulder separation
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Illustration comparing a normal acromioclavicular joint with injured joints showing progressive superior displacement of the clavicle, annotated with the word gravity](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s17.jpg)

## Key features

An acromioclavicular sprain is also called a shoulder separation, and it results from either direct or indirect force on the joint. The lecture distinguishes two grades by which ligament fails:

| Injury | Mechanism | Ligaments ruptured |
|---|---|---|
| Subluxation | Upward force along the humerus | Acromioclavicular ligament |
| Dislocation (more severe) | Blunt force trauma to the tip of the shoulder | Acromioclavicular and the strong coracoclavicular |

Once the coracoclavicular ligament goes, the clavicle is no longer anchored to the coracoid and the weight of the limb pulls the scapula down. The patient presents with the clavicle displaced superiorly and the acromion more prominent on palpation. The slide makes the point with one word, gravity, since the clavicle is not actually riding up so much as the limb is dropping away from it.

> A shoulder separation becomes a dislocation rather than a subluxation when the coracoclavicular ligament ruptures along with the acromioclavicular ligament.

Library: Glenohumeral joint: type and articulation
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Illustration of the glenohumeral joint showing the humeral head against the shallow ovoid glenoid fossa of the scapula](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s18.jpg)

## Key features

The glenohumeral joint is a ball and socket synovial joint and is multiaxial. It is the articulation between the glenoid fossa of the scapula and the head of the humerus, and the lecture's summary of it is that it produces great mobility and poor stability.

The geometry explains why:

- The glenoid fossa is a shallow ovoid
- Only about 30 percent of the humeral head is in contact with the glenoid at any given position

The typed notes list four things that enhance mobility, which are poor articular congruency, several bursae, a high degree of articular cartilage, and a lax joint capsule. Stability has to be supplied separately, by the fibrocartilaginous glenoid labrum that increases the fit and deepens the socket, by the musculotendinous rotator cuff, and by ligamentous support.

> Only about 30 percent of the humeral head contacts the shallow glenoid fossa at any one time, which is why the lecture sums the joint up as great mobility and poor stability.

Library: Glenoid labrum
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Frontal view section through the glenohumeral joint labeled fibrous capsule, glenoid labrum, articular cartilage, axillary pouch, transverse ligament cut, synovial sheath for biceps tendon and biceps brachii tendon long head, above a sagittal reflected view labeling the acromion, subacromial space, coracoacromial ligament, coracoid process, biceps brachii tendon long head, glenoid labrum and inferior capsule](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s20.jpg)

## Identify it

- The labrum is the rim running around the edge of the glenoid in both views
- In the frontal section it appears as a wedge at the superior and inferior margins of the glenoid, with the axillary pouch hanging below
- The long head of biceps tendon can be traced from the superior labrum out through its synovial sheath

## Key features

- Fibrocartilaginous rim
- Deepens the socket by 50 percent
- The long head of biceps brachii tendon is a partial extension of the superior labrum
- Mobile and meniscoid superiorly, but rounder, smaller and more firmly attached inferiorly

The difference between the superior and inferior labrum is worth holding onto. The superior part is loosely attached and continuous with the biceps tendon, and the inferior part is firmly anchored, which is why the labrum behaves differently at the top and bottom of the socket.

> The glenoid labrum deepens the socket by 50 percent, and the long head of biceps brachii tendon is a partial extension of its superior part.

Library: Fibrous capsule of the glenohumeral joint
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Anterior and posterior view illustrations of the glenohumeral joint capsule attaching around the rim of the glenoid fossa and onto the humerus](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s21.jpg)

## Identify it

- The capsule attaches medially to the rim of the glenoid fossa
- Laterally it attaches to the anatomical neck of the humerus
- Inferiorly the humeral attachment sits lower, out toward the surgical neck

## Key features

- The capsule is twice the size of the humeral head
- That slack allows translational movements, with 2 to 2.5 cm of distraction

The redundancy of the capsule is what permits the humeral head to translate rather than simply spin, and the inferior attachment reaching down toward the surgical neck is what creates the axillary pouch seen on the labrum figure. It is also why the capsule is weakest anteroinferiorly, which matters for the direction most dislocations take.

> The glenohumeral capsule is twice the size of the humeral head and allows 2 to 2.5 cm of distraction, attaching to the anatomical neck except inferiorly where it reaches toward the surgical neck.

Library: Glenohumeral and coracohumeral ligaments
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Illustration of the anterior glenohumeral joint with the superior, middle and inferior glenohumeral ligaments labeled as capsular thickenings, the inferior one showing its anterior band, axillary pouch and posterior band](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s22.jpg)

## Identify it

- Superior glenohumeral ligament
- Middle glenohumeral ligament
- Inferior glenohumeral ligament, with an anterior band, an axillary pouch, and a posterior band

## Key features

The glenohumeral ligaments are thickenings of the joint capsule rather than separate structures. The slide describes them as reinforcement of the anterior and inferior joint capsule, and the typed notes describe them as strengthening the anterior aspect of the capsule.

Two other ligaments belong with them:

| Ligament | Course | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Coracohumeral | Base of the coracoid process to the anterior aspect of the greater tubercle | Strengthens the capsule superiorly |
| Transverse humeral | Greater tubercle to lesser tubercle, over the intertubercular groove | Provides passage for the long head of biceps brachii tendon |

> The glenohumeral ligaments are capsular thickenings reinforcing the anterior and inferior capsule, while the coracohumeral ligament strengthens it superiorly.

Library: Coracoacromial arch
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Illustration of the coracoacromial arch formed by the acromion, the coracoacromial ligament and the distal tip of the coracoid process, spanning above the humeral head](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s23.jpg)

## Identify it

The arch is made of three things in continuity above the humeral head:

- Acromion
- Coracoacromial ligament
- Coracoid process, at its distal tip

## Key features

The typed notes describe the coracoacromial ligament as a protective structure spanning from the acromion to the coracoid process, with the inferior aspect of those bony structures plus the ligament together termed the coracoacromial arch. Its function is to prevent superior displacement of the humeral head.

That roof is also what makes dislocation go the direction it does. The arch is strong superiorly, the capsule is weak anteroinferiorly, so the head leaves the socket anteriorly rather than upward.

> The coracoacromial arch (acromion, coracoacromial ligament, and distal coracoid) prevents superior displacement of the humeral head.

Library: Subacromial space and bursa
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Superior, sagittal, frontal cross-section and superolateral view illustrations of the shoulder labeling the subacromial bursa, subdeltoid bursa, supraspinatus and tendon, deltoid, capsular ligament, synovial membrane, glenoid labrum and axillary pouch](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s24.jpg)

## Identify it

- The subacromial space is the gap between the coracoacromial arch above and the humeral head below
- The subacromial bursa sits in that gap, continuous laterally with the subdeltoid part beneath the deltoid
- The supraspinatus tendon runs through the space to reach the greater tubercle

## Key features

- About 1 cm between the arch and the humeral head
- Contents are the supraspinatus tendon and muscle, the subacromial/subdeltoid bursa, the biceps brachii long head tendon, and the superior fibrous capsule
- The bursae are direct extensions of the synovial membrane of the glenohumeral joint
- They function to reduce friction

A space only about a centimeter deep, with a tendon and a bursa both running through it under a bony roof, is the anatomical setup for impingement when anything in it swells or the head rides up.

> The subacromial space is only about 1 cm deep and contains the supraspinatus tendon, the subacromial/subdeltoid bursa, the long head of biceps tendon, and the superior fibrous capsule.

Library: Glenohumeral dislocation
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Illustration of an anteriorly dislocated glenohumeral joint with the humeral head displaced off the glenoid fossa](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s25.jpg)

## Key features

The glenohumeral joint is the most frequently dislocated joint in the body, and 90 percent of dislocations are anterior.

The reason is structural. The coracoacromial arch is strong superiorly, and the joint capsule is weak anteroinferiorly, so the head takes the path of least resistance.

## What is at risk

The slide lists the axillary nerve and artery as at risk. The typed notes name the axillary nerve as the structure at risk during a typical dislocation. Neurovascular integrity should be documented both before and after reduction, which protects the patient and makes clear whether a deficit was caused by the injury or by the reduction.

> Ninety percent of glenohumeral dislocations are anterior, because the coracoacromial arch is strong superiorly while the capsule is weak anteroinferiorly, and the axillary nerve is the structure at risk.

Library: Scapulothoracic interface
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Illustration of the scapula lying against the posterior thoracic wall, labeled as the scapulothoracic interface](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s26.jpg)

## Key features

The scapulothoracic interface is not a true anatomic joint. There are no articulating bone surfaces meeting each other and no joint capsule, which is why the typed notes put the word joint in quotation marks and describe it as the scapula moving against the thorax.

Movement of the scapula here is entirely dependent on movement at the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints. The scapula is tethered to the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint, and the clavicle is tethered to the sternum at the sternoclavicular joint, so the scapula cannot move on the thorax unless those two joints move.

> The scapulothoracic interface is not a true joint, and scapular movement there depends entirely on motion at the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints.

Library: Shoulder girdle muscles and movers of the humerus
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Slide listing shoulder girdle muscles in one column and movers of the humerus in another, divided into thoracohumeral, scapulohumeral and other extrinsic groups](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s28.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture splits the muscles acting on the shoulder complex by what they move. Shoulder girdle muscles position the scapula and clavicle, and movers of the humerus act on the humerus itself.

| Group | Muscles |
|---|---|
| Shoulder girdle | Subclavius, pectoralis minor, serratus anterior, trapezius, levator scapulae, rhomboid major, rhomboid minor |
| Thoracohumeral | Pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi |
| Scapulohumeral | Deltoid, teres major, coracobrachialis, rotator cuff |
| Other extrinsic | Biceps brachii, triceps brachii |

The typed notes define the scapulohumeral group more precisely as short muscles passing from the scapula to the humerus that act on the glenohumeral joint, which is also why they are called the intrinsic shoulder muscles.

> Thoracohumeral muscles run from the trunk to the humerus (pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi), while scapulohumeral muscles run from the scapula to the humerus (deltoid, teres major, coracobrachialis, and the rotator cuff).

Library: Deltoid
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Anterior and posterior view illustrations of the shoulder with the deltoid shown in three parts relative to trapezius, pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi, and the deltoid tuberosity marked on the humerus](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s29.jpg)

## Attachments and innervation

| | |
|---|---|
| Proximal attachment | Anterior part: lateral third of the clavicle. Middle part: acromion process. Posterior part: spine of the scapula |
| Distal attachment | Deltoid tuberosity of the humerus |
| Innervation | Axillary nerve, C5 and C6 |

## Actions by part

| Part | Action |
|---|---|
| Anterior | Assists in flexion and medial rotation of the arm |
| Middle | Abduction of the arm |
| Posterior | Assists in extension and lateral rotation of the arm |

The three parts take origin from three different points spread across the front, side and back of the shoulder girdle, and that spread is exactly why one muscle can flex, abduct and extend depending on which fibers are active.

## Clinical note

When the axillary nerve is severely damaged the deltoid atrophies and the rounded contour of the shoulder disappears. The shoulder looks flattened, there is a slight hollow inferior to the acromion, and sensation can be lost over the deltoid area.

> Deltoid is innervated by the axillary nerve, so axillary nerve injury flattens the shoulder contour, leaves a hollow below the acromion, and costs sensation over the deltoid.

Library: Teres major
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Anterior and posterior view illustrations showing teres major running from the inferior angle of the scapula to the humerus, with its C5 and C6 root values noted](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s30.jpg)

## Attachments and innervation

| | |
|---|---|
| Proximal attachment | Inferior angle of the scapula |
| Distal attachment | Medial lip of the intertubercular groove |
| Action | Adduction and medial rotation of the arm |
| Innervation | Lower subscapular nerve, C5 and C6 |

## Key features

Teres major is a scapulohumeral muscle but it is not part of the rotator cuff, and its insertion is the giveaway. The cuff muscles reach the greater or lesser tubercle, while teres major goes to the medial lip of the intertubercular groove, which is why it adducts and medially rotates rather than stabilizing the joint.

It is also a border structure. Teres major forms the lower border of both the quadrangular space and the triangular interval, and the inferior border of teres major is where the axillary artery becomes the brachial artery and where the deep brachial artery branches off.

> Teres major inserts on the medial lip of the intertubercular groove, adducts and medially rotates the arm, and is supplied by the lower subscapular nerve.

Library: Rotator cuff: the SITS muscles
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Illustration of the four rotator cuff muscles on the scapula and humerus with the SITS grouping listed](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s31.jpg)

## Identify it

SITS:

- **S**upraspinatus
- **I**nfraspinatus
- **T**eres minor
- **S**ubscapularis

## Key features

The tendons of supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis blend with the capsule of the shoulder joint to form the musculotendinous rotator cuff. The cuff protects and strengthens the joint and helps stabilize the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity.

Three of the four reach the greater tubercle and only subscapularis reaches the lesser tubercle, which is also the reason three of them rotate the humerus laterally or abduct it while subscapularis rotates it medially.

| Muscle | Tubercle | Facet |
|---|---|---|
| Supraspinatus | Greater | Superior |
| Infraspinatus | Greater | Middle |
| Teres minor | Greater | Inferior |
| Subscapularis | Lesser | |

> The rotator cuff tendons blend with the joint capsule, and three of the four (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor) take the superior, middle and inferior facets of the greater tubercle while subscapularis takes the lesser tubercle.

Library: Supraspinatus
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Superior and posterior view illustrations of supraspinatus running from the supraspinous fossa under the acromion to the greater tubercle, with the superior transverse scapular ligament, suprascapular notch and deltoid labeled](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s32.jpg)

## Attachments and innervation

| | |
|---|---|
| Proximal attachment | Supraspinous fossa of the scapula |
| Distal attachment | Superior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus |
| Action | Abduction of the arm |
| Innervation | Suprascapular nerve, C5 and C6 |

## Key features

Supraspinatus is the only rotator cuff muscle that abducts rather than rotates, and its tendon has to pass through the subacromial space under the coracoacromial arch to reach the greater tubercle. That route is what makes it the cuff muscle most often torn and the one involved in impingement.

> Supraspinatus runs from the supraspinous fossa to the superior facet of the greater tubercle, abducts the arm, and is supplied by the suprascapular nerve.

Library: Infraspinatus
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Posterior view illustrations of infraspinatus filling the infraspinous fossa and running to the greater tubercle, with the superior transverse scapular ligament, suprascapular notch and deltoid labeled](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s33.jpg)

## Attachments and innervation

| | |
|---|---|
| Proximal attachment | Infraspinous fossa of the scapula |
| Distal attachment | Middle facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus |
| Action | Lateral rotation of the arm |
| Innervation | Suprascapular nerve, C5 and C6 |

## Key features

Infraspinatus shares its nerve with supraspinatus, so a single suprascapular nerve lesion costs both abduction and lateral rotation. The two muscles sit on either side of the spine of the scapula, supraspinatus in the smaller fossa above and infraspinatus in the larger fossa below, and their tendons reach adjacent facets on the greater tubercle.

> Infraspinatus laterally rotates the arm from the infraspinous fossa to the middle facet of the greater tubercle, and like supraspinatus it is supplied by the suprascapular nerve.

Library: Teres minor
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Posterior view illustrations of teres minor running from the lateral border of the scapula to the greater tubercle beside the deltoid](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s34.jpg)

## Attachments and innervation

| | |
|---|---|
| Proximal attachment | Middle part of the lateral border of the scapula |
| Distal attachment | Inferior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus |
| Action | Lateral rotation of the arm |
| Innervation | Axillary nerve, C5 and C6 |

Note that the slide labels both of these as "Proximal Attachment," which is a slide typo. The typed notes table lists the middle part of the lateral border of the scapula as the proximal attachment and the inferior facet of the greater tubercle as the distal attachment.

## Key features

Teres minor is the odd one out in the cuff for its nerve supply. The other three are supplied by the suprascapular nerve or the subscapular nerves, while teres minor shares the axillary nerve with deltoid. It laterally rotates the arm, the same action as infraspinatus, but it does so on a different nerve.

> Teres minor is the rotator cuff muscle supplied by the axillary nerve, and it laterally rotates the arm from the lateral border of the scapula to the inferior facet of the greater tubercle.

Library: Subscapularis as a rotator cuff muscle
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Anterior view illustration of the right shoulder showing subscapularis on the costal surface of the scapula running to the lesser tubercle, with the upper and lower subscapular nerves and deltoid labeled](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s35.jpg)

## Attachments and innervation

| | |
|---|---|
| Proximal attachment | Subscapular fossa |
| Distal attachment | Lesser tubercle of the humerus |
| Innervation | Upper subscapular nerve and lower subscapular nerve, C5 and C6 |

## Action

The slide gives the action as medial rotation of the arm. The typed notes table gives it as medially rotates and adducts the humerus, so the notes add adduction.

## Key features

Subscapularis is the only rotator cuff muscle on the anterior (costal) surface of the scapula, the only one reaching the lesser tubercle, and the only one that rotates the humerus medially. It is also the only cuff muscle with two nerves, since both the upper and lower subscapular nerves supply it. Both of those nerves come off the posterior cord of the brachial plexus.

> Subscapularis is the only rotator cuff muscle on the anterior surface of the scapula, the only one inserting on the lesser tubercle, and the only medial rotator of the group.

Library: Functions of the rotator cuff
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Slide listing the SITS muscles alongside their roles as regulators of dynamic stability and controllers of arthrokinematics](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s36.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture gives the cuff two functional roles.

As regulators of dynamic stability, the cuff compensates for the lack of static stabilizers at a joint whose socket is shallow and whose capsule is lax. It does this dynamically, through isometric and isotonic (concentric and eccentric) muscle activity, which means the stabilizing force changes with the position and the load rather than being fixed.

As controllers of arthrokinematics, the cuff does three specific things:

- Compresses the humeral head into the glenoid fossa
- Keeps the humeral head down
- Rotates the humerus to clear the greater tubercle from contacting the acromion

That third point connects directly to impingement. If the cuff cannot rotate the humerus and depress the head, the greater tubercle runs into the acromion during elevation.

> The rotator cuff compresses the humeral head into the glenoid, keeps the head down, and rotates the humerus so the greater tubercle clears the acromion.

Library: Scapulohumeral rhythm
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Illustration of the shoulder in abduction showing glenohumeral motion and scapular rotation contributing to total abduction, annotated with the two to one ratio](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s38.jpg)

## Key features

Full abduction is not produced at the glenohumeral joint alone. The scapula has to rotate upward as the humerus elevates, and the lecture gives that relationship as a 2:1 ratio, noting it is highly variable.

The slide states it as: for every 3 degrees of complex abduction, 2 degrees occur at the glenohumeral joint and 1 degree at the scapulothoracic interface. That works out to 120 degrees of glenohumeral motion plus 60 degrees of scapular rotation equals 180 degrees of total abduction.

The typed notes state the same ratio from the other side, that for every 2 degrees of flexion or abduction at the glenohumeral joint the scapula must rotate 1 degree superiorly, and they add that the first 30 degrees is independent of the scapulohumeral rhythm.

## Joints involved

1. Glenohumeral
2. Acromioclavicular
3. Sternoclavicular
4. Scapulothoracic

## Muscles required

Upward rotation of the scapula requires the action of trapezius and serratus anterior. The notes frame the underlying principle as needing a stable origin for the muscles to work efficiently, which is what positioning the glenoid correctly accomplishes.

> Scapulohumeral rhythm is 2:1, so 180 degrees of abduction is 120 degrees of glenohumeral motion plus 60 degrees of scapular rotation, with the first 30 degrees independent of the rhythm.

Library: Rotator cuff injury and the deltoid force couple
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Coronal T1 and PD fat saturated MRI images of a right shoulder labeled supraspinatus and acromion, comparing a normal study with one showing injury](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s40.jpg)

## Key features

Rupture or tear of the supraspinatus tendon is the most common rotator cuff injury. The mechanism given is repetitive use of the upper limb above the horizontal plane, and the typed notes add that injury or disease damaging the cuff produces instability of the glenohumeral joint.

The functional consequence is specific. With a complete tear of supraspinatus, the patient loses the ability to abduct the upper limb at the glenohumeral joint, and clinically has difficulty initiating abduction of the arm.

## Why abduction fails

Abduction depends on a force couple between the deltoid and the rotator cuff. The lecture's account of the cuff's half of that couple is that it compresses the head into the glenoid fossa, keeps the humeral head down, and rotates to clear the greater tubercle from the acromion. When supraspinatus is torn the force couple is compromised and abduction is lost. The slide titled Disruption of RC/Deltoid Force Couple is a figure with no text, so the lecture doesn't spell out what the deltoid does on its own once the couple fails.

> A complete supraspinatus tear compromises the deltoid and rotator cuff force couple, so the patient cannot initiate abduction at the glenohumeral joint.

Library: Triceps brachii and anconeus
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Posterior view illustration of the three heads of triceps brachii converging on the olecranon, with the radial nerve and radial groove labeled and the C5 to T1 root values listed](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s43.jpg)

## Triceps brachii

| | |
|---|---|
| Proximal attachment | Long head: infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula. Lateral head: posterior aspect of the humerus, superior to the radial groove. Medial head: posterior aspect of the humerus, inferior to the radial groove |
| Distal attachment | Olecranon of the ulna |
| Innervation | Radial nerve, C5 to T1 |

The slide gives the action as extension of the arm and forearm plus adduction of the arm. The typed notes table gives it as extending the forearm, with the long head extending the shoulder joint and resisting dislocation of the humerus.

Only the long head crosses the shoulder, because only it originates on the scapula. That is why the long head acts on both joints and the other two heads act on the elbow alone.

## Anconeus

| | |
|---|---|
| Proximal attachment | Lateral epicondyle of the humerus |
| Distal attachment | Lateral side of the olecranon |
| Action | Stabilizes the elbow during extension |
| Innervation | Radial nerve |

## Key features

The radial groove separates the origins of the lateral and medial heads, with the lateral head above the groove and the medial head below it. The radial nerve and deep brachial artery run in that groove between the two heads.

> Only the long head of triceps crosses the shoulder, arising from the infraglenoid tubercle, and the lateral head arises above the radial groove while the medial head arises below it.

Library: Suprascapular nerve and the superior transverse scapular ligament
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Posterior view illustration of the suprascapular region with the suprascapular nerve passing beneath the superior transverse scapular ligament and the suprascapular artery passing above it](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s45.jpg)

## Identify it

- The suprascapular notch on the superior border of the scapula
- The superior transverse scapular ligament bridging across the notch and closing it into a foramen
- The suprascapular nerve passing under the ligament
- The suprascapular artery passing over the ligament

## Key features

The suprascapular nerve arises from the superior trunk of the brachial plexus and runs deep to the transverse scapular ligament. It innervates supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and the glenohumeral joint.

The relationship at the notch is the memorable part, and the lecture gives it as a mnemonic:

> Army (artery) over the bridge, Navy (nerve) under the bridge.

Library: Axillary and subscapular nerves at the shoulder
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Anterior view illustration of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus giving off the upper subscapular, lower subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial nerves, with teres major, subscapularis and latissimus dorsi labeled](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s47.jpg)

## Identify it

All of these come off the posterior cord:

| Nerve | Supplies |
|---|---|
| Upper subscapular | Subscapularis |
| Lower subscapular | Teres major and subscapularis |
| Thoracodorsal | Latissimus dorsi |
| Axillary | Deltoid, teres minor, the glenohumeral joint, and skin over the deltoid |
| Radial | Continues on into the posterior arm |

## Key features

The posterior cord supplies the shoulder muscles that rotate the humerus medially (subscapularis, teres major) along with the two muscles supplied by the axillary nerve (deltoid, teres minor). The axillary nerve is a terminal branch of the posterior cord and is the only one of this group carrying cutaneous sensation, over the deltoid.

Subscapularis is worth noting again here, since it is supplied by both the upper and the lower subscapular nerves, while teres major takes only the lower subscapular nerve.

> Every nerve supplying the posterior shoulder muscles (upper subscapular, lower subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial) comes off the posterior cord of the brachial plexus.

Library: Radial nerve in the radial groove
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Posterior view illustration of the radial nerve wrapping around the posterior aspect of the humeral shaft within the radial groove](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s48.jpg)

## Identify it

- The radial nerve crossing the back of the humeral shaft at an angle
- The radial groove, the shallow oblique channel on the posterior humerus it travels in
- The nerve lying between the lateral and medial heads of triceps

## Key features

The radial nerve is a terminal branch of the brachial plexus that passes around the posterior aspect of the humeral shaft in the radial groove, running there with the deep brachial artery between the lateral and medial heads of triceps brachii. It supplies the posterior compartment of the arm.

Distally it pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to course anterior to the lateral epicondyle, where it splits into superficial and deep branches.

Its course directly against the bone is why a transverse fracture of the humeral shaft puts it at risk.

> The radial nerve runs in the radial groove directly against the posterior humeral shaft with the deep brachial artery, then pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to reach the front of the lateral epicondyle.

Library: Cutaneous innervation of the shoulder and posterior arm
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Anterior and posterior view diagrams of the upper limb with cutaneous territories shaded and labeled for the axillary nerve and the radial nerve](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s49.jpg)

## Identify it

- Axillary nerve territory over the deltoid region of the shoulder
- Radial nerve territory down the posterior arm and forearm

## Key features

The axillary nerve carries sensation from the skin over the superior lateral aspect of the shoulder, the area overlying the deltoid. The radial nerve gives cutaneous branches that supply sensory innervation to the posterior arm, and its territory continues down the posterior forearm.

These two territories are how a motor finding gets confirmed on exam. A patient with a surgical neck fracture who cannot abduct should also be checked for sensory loss over the deltoid, and a patient with a mid-shaft fracture and wrist drop should be checked over the posterior arm and forearm.

> Sensation over the deltoid is axillary nerve territory, and sensation over the posterior arm and forearm is radial nerve territory.

Library: Suprascapular, dorsal scapular, and thoracoacromial arteries
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Anterior and posterior view illustrations showing the subclavian artery giving the thyrocervical trunk, suprascapular artery and dorsal scapular artery, with the suprascapular artery passing above the superior transverse scapular ligament](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s50.jpg)

## Identify it

- Subclavian artery, the parent vessel on the anterior view
- Thyrocervical trunk arising from it
- Suprascapular artery running laterally and posteriorly toward the scapula
- Dorsal scapular artery running down along the medial border of the scapula
- Superior transverse scapular ligament, with the artery passing superior to it

## Key features

| Artery | Origin | Course |
|---|---|---|
| Suprascapular | Subclavian artery, or the thyrocervical trunk | Passes posteriorly with the suprascapular nerve, running superior to the superior transverse scapular ligament, to supply the posterior shoulder |
| Dorsal scapular | Subclavian | Runs along the scapula to contribute to the posterior scapular supply |
| Thoracoacromial | Second part of the axillary artery | Divides into clavicular, acromial, deltoid and pectoral branches |

The thoracoacromial branches are shown numbered on the following slide as clavicular, acromial, deltoid and pectoral, and they supply the clavicle, acromion, deltoid, and pectoral muscles respectively.

> The suprascapular artery passes above the superior transverse scapular ligament while the suprascapular nerve passes below it, and the thoracoacromial artery comes off the second part of the axillary artery with clavicular, acromial, deltoid and pectoral branches.

Library: Subscapular and circumflex humeral arteries at the shoulder
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Anterior view illustration of the axillary artery giving off the numbered subscapular artery with its circumflex scapular branch, the anterior circumflex humeral artery and the posterior circumflex humeral artery](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s52.jpg)

## Identify it

1. Subscapular artery, with the circumflex scapular artery branching from it
2. Anterior circumflex humeral artery
3. Posterior circumflex humeral artery

## Key features

| Artery | Origin | Course and space |
|---|---|---|
| Subscapular | Third part of the axillary artery | Short trunk dividing into the thoracodorsal and circumflex scapular arteries |
| Circumflex scapular | Subscapular artery | Curves around the lateral border of the scapula, deep to teres minor and infraspinatus, to anastomose with the suprascapular artery. Found in the triangular space |
| Posterior circumflex humeral | Third part of the axillary artery | Runs with the axillary nerve to supply the shoulder, proximal humerus and deltoid. Found in the quadrangular space |
| Anterior circumflex humeral | Third part of the axillary artery | Passes anteriorly around the proximal humerus |

Pairing each vessel with its space is the efficient way to hold this. The circumflex scapular artery travels alone through the triangular space, and the posterior circumflex humeral artery travels with the axillary nerve through the quadrangular space.

> The circumflex scapular artery passes through the triangular space, and the posterior circumflex humeral artery passes through the quadrangular space with the axillary nerve.

Library: Scapular arterial anastomoses and collateral circulation
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Anterior and posterior view illustrations of the scapular region with colored overlays marking the posterior circumflex humeral artery and acromial branch of the thoracoacromial artery anteriorly and the dorsal scapular, suprascapular and circumflex scapular arteries posteriorly](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s53.jpg)

## Identify it

Anterior view:

- Posterior circumflex humeral artery
- Acromial branch of the thoracoacromial artery

Posterior view:

- Dorsal scapular artery
- Suprascapular artery
- Circumflex scapular artery

## Key features

Anastomoses are communications between arteries that allow for collateral circulation. Three arteries anastomose on the posterior surface of the scapula: the dorsal scapular, suprascapular and circumflex scapular.

The clinical importance shows up when ligation of a lacerated subclavian or axillary artery is necessary, or when there is vascular stenosis of the axillary artery. The suprascapular and circumflex scapular arteries can provide collateral flow between the subclavian and axillary arteries if the first or second parts of the axillary artery are ligated, because the suprascapular comes off the subclavian side and the circumflex scapular comes off the axillary side below the ligature.

Timing determines whether this works. Slow occlusion of an artery often allows sufficient collateral circulation to develop and prevents ischemia, while sudden occlusion does not allow enough time, and ischemia of the upper limb results.

> The dorsal scapular, suprascapular and circumflex scapular arteries anastomose on the posterior scapula, and the suprascapular and circumflex scapular route can carry collateral flow if the first or second part of the axillary artery is ligated.

Library: Deep brachial artery in the posterior arm
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Anterior and posterior view illustrations tracing the axillary artery changing name to the brachial artery and giving off the deep brachial artery, which runs in the radial groove of the humerus](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s54.jpg)

## Identify it

- Axillary artery, which changes name to the brachial artery
- Brachial artery, which gives the branch below
- Deep brachial artery, running in the radial groove of the humerus

## Key features

The deep brachial artery arises as a branch of the brachial artery inferior to teres major. It wraps around the humerus to enter the posterior compartment, where it runs with the radial nerve in the radial groove between the lateral and medial heads of triceps brachii.

Its distal continuation is the radial collateral artery, which anastomoses with the radial recurrent branch of the radial artery. That connection is part of the collateral network around the elbow.

The name sequence is worth keeping straight. The subclavian becomes the axillary at the lateral border of the first rib, the axillary becomes the brachial at the inferior border of teres major, and the deep brachial comes off the brachial just below that same landmark.

> The deep brachial artery branches from the brachial artery just inferior to teres major and runs with the radial nerve in the radial groove between the lateral and medial heads of triceps.

Library: Quadrangular space
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Posterior view illustration of the shoulder and proximal arm with colored outlines marking the quadrangular space, triangular space and triangular interval between the teres muscles, the long head of triceps and the humerus](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s55.jpg)

## Identify it

The slide lists the borders as the long head of triceps brachii, teres minor, the humerus, and teres major. The typed notes give the same four borders with their positions specified:

| Border | Structure |
|---|---|
| Upper | Teres minor |
| Medial | Long head of triceps brachii |
| Lateral | Surgical neck of the humerus |
| Lower | Teres major |

The only difference between the two is that the notes specify the lateral border as the surgical neck of the humerus rather than the humerus generally.

## Contents

- Axillary nerve
- Posterior circumflex humeral artery

## Key features

The contents explain a clinical pattern seen elsewhere in the lecture. The axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery travel together through this space right against the surgical neck, which is why a surgical neck fracture threatens both of them at once.

> The quadrangular space transmits the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery, bounded laterally by the surgical neck of the humerus.

Library: Triangular space and triangular interval
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Posterior view illustration of the shoulder and proximal arm with colored outlines marking the quadrangular space, triangular space and triangular interval between the teres muscles, the long head of triceps and the humerus](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s55.jpg)

## Triangular space

| | |
|---|---|
| Borders | Long head of triceps brachii, teres major, teres minor |
| Contents | Circumflex scapular artery |

## Triangular interval

| | |
|---|---|
| Borders | Long head of triceps brachii, teres major, humerus |
| Contents | Deep brachial artery, radial nerve |

The triangular interval appears only on the slides. The typed notes cover the quadrangular space and the triangular space but do not include the triangular interval, so take the slide as the source for it.

## Telling the three apart

All three spaces share the long head of triceps brachii as a border, and the distinguishing border is what to key on:

| Space | Distinguishing border | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| Quadrangular | Teres minor above and teres major below, humerus laterally | Axillary nerve, posterior circumflex humeral artery |
| Triangular | Teres minor and teres major, no humerus | Circumflex scapular artery |
| Triangular interval | Teres major and the humerus, no teres minor | Deep brachial artery, radial nerve |

> The triangular space contains only the circumflex scapular artery, while the triangular interval contains the deep brachial artery and radial nerve.

Library: Humeral shaft fracture: structures at risk
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Radiograph of a right humerus showing a transverse fracture of the shaft, beside text asking which vessels and nerves are at risk](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s56.jpg)

## Key features

A transverse fracture of the humeral shaft is most commonly caused by a direct blow to the arm.

The structures at risk are the ones running in the radial groove against the posterior surface of the shaft:

- Radial nerve
- Deep brachial artery

Because the radial nerve supplies the posterior compartment of the forearm, including the wrist and finger extensors, an injury here threatens extension at the wrist in addition to sensation over the posterior arm and forearm.

> A transverse mid-shaft humeral fracture puts the radial nerve and deep brachial artery at risk, because both run in the radial groove against the posterior shaft.

Library: Surgical neck fracture: structures at risk
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

![Radiograph of a right shoulder showing a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus, beside text asking which vessels and nerves are at risk](library/images/msk-week-14/shld-s57.jpg)

## Key features

Fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus is most common in elderly patients with a history of osteoporosis.

The structures at risk are the two that pass through the quadrangular space against the surgical neck:

- Axillary nerve
- Posterior circumflex humeral artery

Losing the axillary nerve costs deltoid and teres minor, so the patient loses abduction at the shoulder and has sensory loss over the deltoid. With time the deltoid atrophies and the rounded shoulder contour flattens.

Pairing the two fracture sites is the efficient way to keep them apart. The surgical neck takes the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery, and the shaft takes the radial nerve and deep brachial artery.

> A surgical neck fracture puts the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery at risk, because both run through the quadrangular space against the surgical neck.

The lecture names Hilton's Law twice, in learning objective 5 and in the innervation line for the glenohumeral joint, but it never states what the law says. What the lecture does give is the list below, introduced as following Hilton's Law, and that list is the testable part. Any definition of the law you find elsewhere is outside material for this exam.

## Nerves supplying the glenohumeral joint

> The lecture names Hilton's Law without defining it, and lists the glenohumeral joint's innervation as the suprascapular, axillary, lateral and medial pectoral, musculocutaneous, upper and lower subscapular, thoracodorsal, and radial nerves.

Library: Adhesive capsulitis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Shoulder and Posterior Arm

## Key features

Adhesive capsulitis is also called frozen shoulder. It is caused when adhesive fibrosis and scarring thicken and tighten the glenohumeral joint capsule.

## Presentation

- Pain
- Stiffness
- Difficulty abducting the arm

## Risk factors

- Medical conditions that prevent moving the arm
- Injuries to the glenohumeral joint region
- Having diabetes

> Adhesive capsulitis is adhesive fibrosis and scarring that thickens and tightens the glenohumeral joint capsule, and it presents with pain, stiffness, and difficulty abducting the arm.

Library: Papulosquamous morphology: papule, scale, and sharp margins
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Title slide defining the papulosquamous group by its three morphologic features](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s02.jpg)

## Identify it

- A papule or a plaque, so the lesion is raised rather than flat
- Scale sitting on the surface
- Well-defined margins, so you can trace where the lesion stops

## Key features

The lecture opens with the group name rather than a disease, and the name is the description. "Papulo" is the raised part and "squamous" is the scale, so a papulosquamous eruption is a red, scaly rash made of raised lesions with borders you can see.

Those three features are what let you sort a rash into this group before you name the disease. The diseases covered under it here are psoriasis, pityriasis rosea, lichen planus, seborrheic dermatitis, tinea, secondary syphilis, and mycosis fungoides.

Margins matter because they separate this group from eczema, which the companion lecture describes as having poorly defined margins.

> Papulosquamous means a raised lesion (papule or plaque) with scale and well-defined margins.

Library: Psoriasis vulgaris: epidemiology and the IL-23 to IL-17 axis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

## Key features

Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory disorder. The lecture gives the immunology in one line: IL-23 and IL-12 drive IL-17 producing T cells, and the psoriatic cytokines are IL-17, TNF alpha, and interferon gamma. Those four targets are the reason the biologic agents later in the lecture look the way they do.

| Feature | Lecture's figure |
|---|---|
| Prevalence | 2 to 4 percent of the worldwide population |
| Sex | Males equal females |
| Age | Two peaks, ages 20 to 30 and 50 to 60 |
| Cause | Genetic predisposition plus a triggering event |

The two age peaks are worth holding onto, because a papulosquamous eruption starting in the twenties and one starting in the fifties can both be psoriasis.

> Psoriasis is driven by IL-23 and IL-12 stimulating IL-17 producing T cells, with IL-17, TNF alpha, and interferon gamma as the psoriatic cytokines.

Library: Psoriasis: plaque morphology and favored sites
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Slide listing the morphology and favored sites of psoriasis beside a clinical photograph](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s05.jpg)

## Identify it

- Well-demarcated lesions
- Erythematous papules and plaques
- Silvery white scale on the surface

## Key features

The lecture lists the favored sites as a set, and they come up again and again in the slides that follow.

- Extensors, meaning elbows and knees
- Low back, gluteal cleft, and umbilicus
- Scalp and nails
- Genitalia

Extensor involvement is the distribution students usually know, but the lecture spends most of its photographs on the others, because those are the ones that get missed. A scaly plaque in the gluteal cleft or the umbilicus is psoriasis until proven otherwise.

> Psoriasis is a well-demarcated erythematous plaque with silvery white scale, favoring extensors, low back, gluteal cleft, umbilicus, scalp, nails, and genitalia.

Library: Psoriasis of the low back and gluteal cleft
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Two clinical photographs showing psoriasis of the low back and of the gluteal cleft](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s07.jpg)

## Identify it

- Low back: scaly erythematous plaques sitting above the belt line
- Gluteal cleft: scaly plaques running down the cleft itself

## Key features

Both sites belong to the lecture's "favorite locations" list. They are easy to miss because neither is exposed during a routine examination, and a patient who comes in about their elbows may never mention them.

The gluteal cleft in particular is a site the lecture returns to under inverse psoriasis, where the lesions in creases lose their scale and look shiny and red instead.

> The low back and gluteal cleft are favored psoriasis sites that are only found if you look for them.

Library: Psoriasis of the umbilicus and genitalia
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Two clinical photographs showing psoriasis of the umbilicus and of the genitalia](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s08.jpg)

## Identify it

- Umbilicus: a red plaque in and around the navel
- Genitalia: erythematous plaques on genital skin

## Key features

The umbilicus and the genitalia round out the lecture's favored sites. Genital psoriasis matters clinically out of proportion to its size, because patients rarely volunteer it and it responds to treatment chosen for thin skin rather than the superpotent steroids used on knees and elbows.

> Psoriasis favors the umbilicus and the genitalia, two sites patients seldom report on their own.

Library: Psoriasis of the occipital scalp
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photographs of scaly psoriatic plaques at the occipital scalp and posterior hairline](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s09.jpg)

## Identify it

- Thick scaly plaques in the hair-bearing scalp
- Lesions extending to the posterior hairline, where they become visible

## Key features

The occipital scalp gets its own slide because it is where scalp psoriasis is most often found and most often confused with seborrheic dermatitis. The lecture separates the two later: psoriasis gives silvery white scale with sharp borders, while seborrheic dermatitis gives greasy scale in a different distribution (eyebrows, nasolabial folds, and the scalp more diffusely).

> Scalp psoriasis favors the occipital region, and the plaque edge is sharply defined rather than fading out.

Library: Psoriatic nail pitting and onycholysis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Two clinical photographs of psoriatic nails, one showing pitting and one showing onycholysis](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s10.jpg)

## Identify it

- Pitting: small punched out depressions in the surface of the nail plate
- Onycholysis: the distal nail plate lifted off the nail bed, leaving a scalloped edge

## Key features

The lecture's note on onycholysis is worth copying out: the distal nail plate is scalloped and lifted off the nail bed. That scalloped border is what separates it from a nail that is simply broken or trimmed short.

The reason the slide pairs nail disease with arthritis is that nail involvement carries an increased risk for psoriatic arthritis. Finding pits during a skin examination is a reason to ask about joints.

> Psoriatic nail disease, including pitting and onycholysis, carries an increased risk for psoriatic arthritis.

Library: Subungual hyperkeratosis and oil spots in psoriatic nails
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Two clinical photographs of psoriatic nails showing subungual hyperkeratosis and oil spots](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s11.jpg)

## Identify it

- Subungual hyperkeratosis: keratin debris piled up under the distal nail, lifting it
- Oil spots: yellow-brown patches under the nail plate, as though oil had been dropped beneath it

## Key features

These are the second pair of psoriatic nail findings, and together with pitting and onycholysis they make four. Oil spots are the one with the most descriptive name, and the colour (yellow to brown, translucent) is the point.

> Pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, and oil spots are the four psoriatic nail findings in this lecture.

Library: Psoriatic arthritis and its link to nail disease
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photograph of hands with psoriatic arthritis](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s12.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture gives one number for psoriatic arthritis: it affects about 20 percent of patients with psoriasis. The preceding slide adds that psoriatic nail disease raises the risk.

That pairing is the testable relationship. Nail changes in a patient with skin psoriasis are not just cosmetic, they flag the group more likely to develop joint disease, and methotrexate appears later in the lecture specifically as the systemic agent chosen when psoriatic arthritis is present.

> About 20 percent of patients with psoriasis develop psoriatic arthritis, and nail disease marks increased risk.

Library: Clinical diagnosis of psoriasis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Slide of psoriasis photographs under the heading that diagnosis is usually clinical](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s13.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture states plainly that the diagnosis of psoriasis is usually clinical. Biopsy exists and the histology is distinctive, but the typical patient is diagnosed by the look of the plaque, its scale, and its distribution.

That matters for how the rest of the lecture is built. The histopathology slides that follow are there so you recognise the microscopic picture when a biopsy is done, not because a biopsy is routine.

> Psoriasis is diagnosed clinically in most patients rather than by biopsy.

Library: Psoriasis histopathology
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Micrograph of psoriasis showing hyperkeratosis with parakeratosis and regular acanthosis](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s15.jpg)

## Identify it

- Hyperkeratosis with parakeratosis, meaning retained nuclei in a thickened stratum corneum
- Regular epidermal acanthosis, with rete ridges extended to an even depth
- Decreased granular layer
- Epidermal thinning over the tips of the dermal papillae
- Dilated vessels within the dermal papillae

## Key features

The lecture lists six microscopic features, and Munro microabscesses (neutrophils in the stratum corneum) is the sixth, covered on its own page.

The word doing the work in "regular acanthosis" is regular. The rete ridges are elongated to a similar depth across the lesion, which gives psoriasis its even, comb-like profile at low power.

The last two features, thinning over the papillary tips and dilated papillary vessels, are not just descriptive. They are the anatomic reason the Auspitz sign exists.

> Psoriasis shows hyperkeratosis with parakeratosis, regular acanthosis, a decreased granular layer, thinning over the dermal papillary tips, and dilated papillary vessels.

Library: Munro microabscesses
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Micrograph showing neutrophils collected within the stratum corneum](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s16.jpg)

## Identify it

- Collections of neutrophils sitting inside the stratum corneum
- Found in the parakeratotic scale rather than the dermis

## Key features

A Munro microabscess is neutrophils in the stratum corneum, and that location is the whole definition. Inflammatory cells have travelled all the way up through the epidermis to sit in the scale.

It is one of the six histopathologic features of psoriasis the lecture lists, and the one most likely to be asked by name.

> A Munro microabscess is a collection of neutrophils within the stratum corneum.

Library: Auspitz sign and its histologic basis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photograph showing pinpoint bleeding after psoriatic scale was removed](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s17.jpg)

![Micrograph showing suprapapillary plate thinning with elongated tortuous capillaries in the dermal papillae](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s18.jpg)

## Identify it

- Clinically: pinpoint bleeding when the scale is lifted off a plaque
- Microscopically: suprapapillary plate thinning, with elongated and tortuous capillaries in the papillae beneath

## Key features

The Auspitz sign is pinpoint bleeding when scale is removed, and the lecture puts the explanation on the very next slide rather than leaving it as a trick of the bedside. The epidermis over the tips of the dermal papillae is thinned (the suprapapillary plate), and the capillaries in those papillae are elongated and tortuous. Strip the scale and you take the thin roof off vessels that are sitting right at the surface, so each papilla bleeds as a separate point.

That is why the bleeding is pinpoint rather than a sheet. Each point is one dermal papilla.

> Auspitz sign is pinpoint bleeding on removing scale, caused by thinning of the epidermis over dilated, tortuous capillaries in the dermal papillae.

Library: Koebner phenomenon in psoriasis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photographs showing psoriatic lesions arising along sites of trauma](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s19.jpg)

## Identify it

- New lesions appearing exactly where the skin was injured
- An arrangement that follows the injury rather than the disease's usual distribution

## What the photographs on this slide show

The slide states only that lesions develop at sites of trauma and leaves the rest to its two pictures, neither of which is captioned. On the left, scaly erythematous lesions run in a single straight line down the limb, with separate round plaques beside it for comparison. On the right, scaly erythematous change sits within and along the edges of a tattooed design, taking its shape.

Read those two as descriptions of the photographs rather than as triggers the lecture names, since the deck gives no caption for either and lists no specific causes of trauma.

## Key features

The Koebner phenomenon is the development of lesions at sites of trauma. The arrangement is what gives it away, since a lesion laid out in a line or a shape is following the injury rather than the distribution the disease would otherwise take.

The lecture shows it twice, once in psoriasis and later in lichen planus, which is the point worth remembering: koebnerization is shared by both, so the arrangement tells you the process rather than the disease.

> Koebner phenomenon is new lesions developing at sites of trauma, and it occurs in both psoriasis and lichen planus.

Library: Guttate psoriasis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photograph of guttate psoriasis beside the slide's diagnostic questions](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s20.jpg)

## Identify it

- Crops of small papules rather than a few large plaques
- Erythema present
- Scale present

## Key features

The lecture teaches this one as a worked example, walking through the questions you would ask at the bedside. The primary lesion is a papule, there is erythema, there is scale, so it is papulosquamous. The history that settles it is streptococcal pharyngitis.

That sequence (morphology, then erythema, then scale, then the trigger) is the lecture's method for any red scaly rash, and guttate psoriasis is where it demonstrates it.

> Guttate psoriasis is crops of small scaly papules, classically following streptococcal pharyngitis.

Library: Inverse (intertriginous) psoriasis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photographs of psoriasis in the body creases](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s22.jpg)

## Identify it

- Lesions sitting in the creases: inguinal folds, axillae, gluteal cleft, umbilicus, popliteal creases
- Red and well-demarcated, but without the silvery scale seen on extensor plaques

## Key features

Inverse psoriasis is named for its distribution. Ordinary psoriasis favors extensor surfaces, and this variant does the opposite by occupying flexural, intertriginous skin.

The scale is the thing that changes. Creases are moist and rub against themselves, so the silvery scale that defines psoriasis elsewhere is worn away, leaving shiny red plaques that can be mistaken for a fungal or bacterial intertrigo.

> Inverse psoriasis occupies the creases and loses its scale, so it presents as shiny, well-demarcated red plaques in flexural skin.

Library: Pustular and erythrodermic psoriasis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photographs of pustular psoriasis and erythrodermic psoriasis side by side](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s23.jpg)

## Identify it

- Pustular: pustules studding an erythematous base
- Erythrodermic: generalized erythema with sheets of scale over most of the body surface

## Key features

The lecture labels these two the life threatening varieties of psoriasis, which is why they sit apart from the rest.

The trigger to remember is on the same slide: the most common one is withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids. That connects directly to the treatment slides, where the lecture tells you to avoid oral corticosteroids in psoriasis. Giving them sets up the rebound that produces these forms.

> Pustular and erythrodermic psoriasis are the life threatening variants, and the most common trigger is withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids.

Library: Topical treatment of psoriasis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

## Key features

The lecture organises topical therapy by mechanism rather than by brand.

| Agent | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Salicylic acid | Keratolytic |
| Tar | Decreases keratinocyte proliferation |
| Calcipotriene (vitamin D analog) | Binds the vitamin D receptor, decreasing proliferation and promoting differentiation of keratinocytes |
