| Tazarotene (vitamin A analog, a retinoid) | Down-regulates keratinocyte differentiation, proliferation, and inflammation |
| Topical corticosteroids | Anti-inflammatory |

The slide ends with an instruction in its own line: avoid oral corticosteroids. The reason sits two slides earlier, since withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids is the most common trigger of pustular and erythrodermic psoriasis.

> Calcipotriene binds the vitamin D receptor to decrease keratinocyte proliferation and promote differentiation, and oral corticosteroids are avoided in psoriasis.

Library: Phototherapy, systemic agents, and biologics in psoriasis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

## Key features

When topicals are not enough, the lecture moves to light and then to systemic drugs.

Ultraviolet light therapy comes first, either ultraviolet B or PUVA, which is psoralen plus ultraviolet A.

| Systemic agent | Lecture's note | Toxicity |
|---|---|---|
| Methotrexate | For psoriatic arthritis | Liver and bone marrow |
| Acitretin (oral retinoid) | For pustular disease | Teratogenic |
| Cyclosporine | Severe disease, inexpensive | Nephrotoxic |
| Apremilast | Oral PDE4 inhibitor | GI upset, depression |

Biologic agents are monoclonal antibodies or fusion proteins with highly specific targets, and the targets are the cytokines from the pathogenesis slide: TNF alpha, IL-17, IL-12/23, and IL-23 inhibitors.

Pairing each drug with its own toxicity is the way this slide is usually tested, since the four systemic agents have four different organs at risk.

> Biologics in psoriasis target TNF alpha, IL-17, IL-12/23, and IL-23, the same cytokines named in the pathogenesis.

Library: Pityriasis rosea
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photograph of pityriasis rosea with a herald patch and smaller oval lesions](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s27.jpg)

## Identify it

- A single larger lesion, the herald patch, appearing first
- Multiple smaller lesions following it
- A collarette of scale at the edge of each lesion, with the free edge pointing inward
- Lesions aligned along skin lines, giving the fir tree pattern on the back

## Key features

| Feature | Lecture's detail |
|---|---|
| Age | 10 to 35 |
| Itch | May or may not be present |
| Cause | Possibly viral, human herpesvirus 7 or 6 |
| Therapy | Strong topical corticosteroid, valacyclovir, ultraviolet light |

The herald patch is the diagnostic handle, because it appears days to weeks before the rest and is often larger, so a patient may describe one spot that came first.

The fir tree pattern comes from the lesions following the lines of skin cleavage, which on the back run obliquely downward from the midline.

> Pityriasis rosea begins with a herald patch, then smaller lesions with a collarette of scale following skin lines in a fir tree pattern.

Library: Lichen planus: the five Ps
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photograph of lichen planus papules beside the slide's list of the five Ps](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s30.jpg)

## Identify it

- Pruritic
- Pink, and more specifically purple or violaceous
- Planar, meaning flat-topped
- Polygonal, with angular rather than round borders
- Papules

## Key features

Lichen planus is a mucocutaneous condition of unknown etiology, so both skin and mucosa are involved and no cause is given.

Two further points from the lecture sit outside the five Ps. It heals with marked hyperpigmentation, which the slide emphasises twice ("heals dark, dark"), and there is a higher incidence in hepatitis C.

Treatment is topical or oral corticosteroids.

> Lichen planus is pruritic, purple, planar, polygonal papules, and it heals with marked hyperpigmentation.

Library: Wickham's striae
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photograph showing lacy white lines over a violaceous plaque](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s31.jpg)

## Identify it

- Fine white lines in a reticulated, lacy network
- Lying on the surface of a violaceous lichen planus lesion

## Key features

Wickham's striae are the reticulated white lines seen on lichen planus lesions, and the pattern is the point. A net or lace of white over purple is close to specific for this disease among the papulosquamous group.

The same reticulated lines appear on mucosa, which the lecture covers on the next slide.

> Wickham's striae are reticulated, lacy white lines on the surface of lichen planus lesions.

Library: Oral and genital lichen planus
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photograph of reticulated white lines on mucosal surfaces](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s32.jpg)

## Identify it

- The same reticulated white lines seen on skin, now on oral or genital mucosa
- Occasional ulceration within the involved mucosa

## Key features

Lichen planus is defined in this lecture as a mucocutaneous condition, and this slide is where the mucosal half is shown. The pattern transfers unchanged, so the lacy reticulated lines look the same inside the mouth as they do on a wrist.

The lecture flags occasional ulceration, set off with asterisks on the slide, because an ulcerated mucosal lesion is the one that causes symptoms and prompts biopsy.

> Lichen planus involves mucosa as well as skin, with the same reticulated white lines and occasional ulceration.

Library: Koebnerization in lichen planus
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photograph of linear lichen planus papules along a site of trauma](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s33.jpg)

## Identify it

- New lichen planus lesions at a site of trauma
- Papules arranged in a line, following where the skin was scratched

## Key features

This is the second appearance of the Koebner phenomenon in the lecture, after psoriasis. The definition does not change, which is the useful part: new lesions develop at sites of trauma.

What changes is what the lesions look like once they get there. In psoriasis the line is made of scaly plaques, and in lichen planus it is made of violaceous flat-topped papules.

> Lichen planus koebnerizes, producing violaceous flat-topped papules in a line at the site of trauma.

Library: Lichen planus histology: interface dermatitis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Micrographs of lichen planus showing a band-like infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction and basal vacuolization](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s34.jpg)

## Identify it

- Inflammation so dense at the dermoepidermal junction that the junction itself is obscured
- Basal cell vacuolization
- Pigment incontinence, meaning melanin dropped into the dermis

## Key features

Interface dermatitis is the pattern name, and the interface being damaged is the epidermal-dermal junction. The infiltrate sits right at that line and hides it.

The clinical consequence is on the slide in bold: interface dermatitis heals dark. Basal cells are where melanin is held, so when they are vacuolized and damaged, pigment falls into the dermis where macrophages take it up and it stays. That is the mechanism behind the marked hyperpigmentation listed among lichen planus's clinical features.

> Interface dermatitis obscures the dermoepidermal junction and causes pigment incontinence, which is why lichen planus heals dark.

Library: Seborrheic dermatitis: distribution, course, and treatment
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Slide listing the features and distribution of seborrheic dermatitis](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s35.jpg)

## Identify it

- Erythematous patches carrying greasy scale rather than dry silvery scale
- In older children and adults: scalp, eyebrows, and nasolabial folds, occasionally the mid chest
- In infants: the scalp, where it is called cradle cap

## Key features

The organism is a lipophilic yeast, Malassezia, and the treatment follows from it. Ketoconazole is the antifungal named, and the other shampoos listed are zinc, selenium sulfide, and tar.

Two associations are worth carrying: seborrheic dermatitis is more common and more severe in AIDS and in neurologic diseases, so unusually extensive disease is a reason to think about both.

The lecture also notes that it flares with stress, showing the same patient on a good day and a bad day to make the point that this is a chronic relapsing condition rather than something cured.

> Seborrheic dermatitis gives greasy scale on the scalp, eyebrows, and nasolabial folds, is driven by the lipophilic yeast Malassezia, and is treated with ketoconazole.

Library: Cradle cap in infants
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photograph of greasy adherent scale on an infant's scalp](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s36.jpg)

## Identify it

- Greasy, yellowish, adherent scale on the scalp of an infant
- Scale sits on erythematous skin underneath

## Key features

Cradle cap is seborrheic dermatitis in infants, and the lecture gives it its own slide because the age changes both the name and the site. In infants the scalp is the typical location, while in older children and adults the eyebrows and nasolabial folds are involved as well.

> Cradle cap is infantile seborrheic dermatitis, presenting as greasy adherent scalp scale.

Library: Tinea as a papulosquamous mimic
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photographs of annular tinea lesions and a KOH preparation](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s39.jpg)

![Clinical photograph of a single annular plaque with a raised scaly rim](library/images/msk-week-14/questions/q-papu-060.jpg)

## Identify it

- An annular plaque with a scaly, advancing border and relative central clearing
- A rim that is raised and more inflamed than the skin it encircles, so the edge stands out from the center
- Scale taken from that border, examined as a KOH preparation, showing branching hyphae

## Key features

The lecture lists tinea under "other papulosquamous diseases" and names it as a dermatophyte fungal infection. It belongs in this group because it is red and scaly with a defined edge, which is exactly the papulosquamous description.

The reason it earns a slide of its own is that it is the mimic you can confirm or exclude in the clinic. Scraping the scale and looking at it with KOH gives hyphae, which no other disease on this list produces.

> Tinea is a dermatophyte infection that mimics other papulosquamous diseases and is confirmed by finding hyphae on a KOH preparation of scale.

Library: Secondary syphilis as a papulosquamous mimic
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Slide comparing plantar psoriasis with the plantar, palmar, and scalp findings of secondary syphilis](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s40.jpg)

## Identify it

- Coppery macules and papules on the palms and soles
- Patchy "moth eaten" alopecia of the scalp

## Key features

The lecture places secondary syphilis directly beside psoriasis under the heading of papulosquamous differential diagnoses, and the comparison is the lesson. Both can present with scaly lesions on the sole, so site alone does not separate them.

Two features point toward syphilis. The eruption involves palms as well as soles, and the scalp shows moth eaten alopecia, a patchy hair loss named for the irregular motheaten outline it leaves.

> Secondary syphilis mimics psoriasis but involves the palms and soles and produces moth eaten alopecia.

Library: Mycosis fungoides: cutaneous T cell lymphoma
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Clinical photographs of mycosis fungoides lesions](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s41.jpg)

## Key features

Mycosis fungoides is the cutaneous T cell lymphoma the lecture includes among the papulosquamous diseases. The name is misleading, since it has nothing to do with fungus, and the disease is a lymphoma of T cells in the skin.

It is listed here because its early lesions are red and scaly and look like the benign diseases around it, which is the reason it is included at the end of a lecture about red, scaly rashes. A scaly eruption that does not behave like psoriasis or eczema and does not respond to treatment is the setting where it needs to be considered.

> Mycosis fungoides is a cutaneous T cell lymphoma whose early lesions look like an ordinary red, scaly rash.

Library: Mycosis fungoides: patch, plaque, nodular, and erythrodermic stages
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Papulosquamous Diseases

![Four clinical photographs showing mycosis fungoides in its patch, plaque, nodular, and erythrodermic forms](library/images/msk-week-14/papu-s42.jpg)

## Identify it

| Form | What you see |
|---|---|
| Patch | Flat, subtly erythematous areas with fine scale |
| Plaque | Raised, well-demarcated erythematous plaques |
| Nodular | Firm raised nodules, here on the face |
| Erythrodermic | Generalized erythema with scale over most of the body |

## Key features

The lecture presents the four forms on one slide so they can be compared directly. Reading them in order (patch, then plaque, then nodular) follows the lesion from flat to raised to tumor.

Erythrodermic disease sits apart from that sequence, because generalized erythema is how several conditions in this lecture end. Erythrodermic psoriasis appeared earlier as a life threatening variant, so erythroderma on its own does not name the disease and the history is what separates them.

> Mycosis fungoides presents as patch, plaque, nodular, and erythrodermic forms.

Library: Eczema: defining features and spongiosis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide listing the defining features of eczema](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s02.jpg)

## Identify it

- Inflammatory and very common
- Itchy, which the lecture flags twice because pruritus is the constant
- Margins are poorly defined, which is what separates eczema from the sharply bordered papulosquamous diseases
- The lecture adds its own caveat, "but not always", so poorly defined margins are the rule rather than an absolute

## Key features

Eczema has many etiologies rather than one, and the word itself is Greek. The lecture builds it from two images, something boiling out and something effervescing, which is the sense the term carries.

The unifying microscopic change behind all of it is spongiosis, intercellular edema that pushes keratinocytes apart. The lecture makes that stick with the sponge comparison, and spongiosis is the feature every form of eczema shares no matter which trigger produced it.

> Eczema is itchy, poorly marginated inflammation whose shared microscopic change is spongiosis, intercellular edema separating keratinocytes.

Library: The three stages of eczema
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide showing acute, subacute and chronic eczema side by side](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s05.jpg)

## Identify it

- Acute: vesicles and weeping, the lecture's one word is ooze
- Subacute: drying lesions with crust
- Chronic: thickened skin with accentuated skin lines, which is lichenification

## Key features

| Stage | Hallmark | What you see |
|---|---|---|
| Acute | Ooze | Vesicles, moist weeping surface |
| Subacute | Crust | Erythema drying into crust and scale |
| Chronic | Lichenification | Thickened plaque with exaggerated skin markings |

These are stages of one process rather than three diseases, so the same patient moves along the sequence as the lesion ages or as scratching continues. The lecture ties lichenification specifically to the itch and the rubbing that follows it.

> Ooze is acute, crust is subacute, and lichenification is chronic.

Library: Acute spongiotic dermatitis histopathology
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Micrograph of acute spongiotic dermatitis showing epidermal spongiosis and vesicles](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s07.jpg)

## Identify it

- Normal stratum corneum, because the process is too new to have changed it
- No acanthosis
- Epidermal spongiosis
- An intraepidermal vesicle
- Papillary dermal edema

## Key features

The stratum corneum being normal is the detail that dates the lesion. Acute disease has not yet had time to alter keratinization, so hyperkeratosis and acanthosis are both absent, and what you see instead is fluid: spongiosis between keratinocytes, a vesicle where that fluid has pooled, and edema in the papillary dermis.

> Acute spongiotic dermatitis has a normal stratum corneum and no acanthosis, with spongiosis, an intraepidermal vesicle, and papillary dermal edema.

Library: Chronic eczematous dermatitis histopathology
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Micrograph of chronic eczematous dermatitis showing hyperkeratosis and acanthosis](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s09.jpg)

## Identify it

- Hyperkeratosis
- Acanthosis
- Mild spongiosis only
- No vesicles
- Thickened collagen with vertical streaking

## Key features

Chronic disease is the mirror image of acute disease on the slide. Where the acute lesion had a normal corneum, no acanthosis and obvious vesicles, the chronic lesion has a thickened corneum, a thickened epidermis, and spongiosis that has faded to a trace with no vesicle left.

The vertical streaking of thickened collagen in the papillary dermis is the microscopic footprint of rubbing. The lecture spells out the sequence: itch leads to scratching and rubbing, which leads to lichenification.

> Chronic eczematous dermatitis shows hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and only mild spongiosis with no vesicles, plus vertically streaked thickened collagen.

Library: Allergic contact eczema: the type IV mechanism
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide describing allergic contact eczema as a type IV hypersensitivity reaction](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s11.jpg)

## Key features

Allergic contact eczema is an immune reaction, specifically a type IV hypersensitivity reaction. It happens in a sensitized individual, meaning someone who has met the antigen before, and memory T cells recognize the antigen on re-exposure and produce the eczema.

That requirement for prior sensitization is what separates allergic from irritant contact eczema, the two halves of contact eczema the lecture sets against each other. Irritant disease needs no immune memory at all.

> Allergic contact eczema is a type IV hypersensitivity in a sensitized person, with memory T cells recognizing the antigen on re-exposure.

Library: Poison ivy contact dermatitis and rebound
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Clinical photograph of poison ivy showing linear vesicles](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s12.jpg)

## Identify it

- Acute spongiotic dermatitis with vesicles
- Lesions laid down in streaks and lines, which is where the plant brushed the skin

## Key features

The lecture's practical points about the resin matter more than the rash. Blister fluid is not contagious, but the resin is, and it travels on fingernails, tools, pet fur and clothing. The lecture's one-line advice is not to play with it.

Treatment is a superpotent topical steroid. Oral steroids are rarely needed, and when they are used the course runs three weeks. A course shorter than that produces rebound poison ivy, the lesion flaring again as the inadequate course wears off.

The lecture also asks which fruit skin cross-reacts, and the answer is mango.

## Therapy

| Situation | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Typical case | Superpotent topical corticosteroid |
| Severe, rarely | Oral corticosteroid for three weeks |
| Course too short | Rebound flare |

> Blister fluid is not contagious but the resin is, and an oral steroid course shorter than three weeks produces rebound poison ivy.

Library: Airborne contact dermatitis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Clinical photograph of airborne contact dermatitis on the face](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s15.jpg)

## Identify it

- Eczema on skin that is exposed to the air rather than on skin that touched anything
- The face, including the eyelids, takes the brunt

## Key features

Airborne contact dermatitis is the pattern that gives away the route of exposure. The allergen arrives through the air, so the rash maps onto uncovered skin and reaches sheltered sites like the eyelids that a hand-carried allergen would usually spare.

> Airborne contact dermatitis follows exposed skin, especially the face and eyelids, rather than the pattern of direct contact.

Library: Nickel allergic contact dermatitis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Clinical photograph of nickel allergic contact dermatitis](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s18.jpg)

## Identify it

- Eczema that reproduces the shape and site of a metal object
- Earlobes under earrings, the periumbilical skin under a snap or belt buckle, the temples under eyeglass frames

## Key features

Nickel affects about 10 percent of women. The lecture's sources are jewelry, eyeglass frames, snaps, buckles and tools, and the distribution of the rash points straight back to whichever one is responsible.

There is no treatment that removes the allergy, so the solution is avoidance. The lecture's substitutes are stainless steel and gold.

> Nickel sensitivity affects about 10 percent of women, the rash mirrors the metal object touching the skin, and the answer is avoidance using stainless steel or gold.

Library: Patch testing for allergic contact dermatitis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide showing patch testing on the back with positive reactions](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s20.jpg)

## Identify it

- A gridded array of test sites marked out on the back
- Positive sites show as discrete inflamed squares where the allergen sat

## Key features

Patch testing is how allergic contact dermatitis gets its answer when the history does not supply one. The lecture names preservatives and fragrances as the common allergens it turns up.

The panel is read twice rather than once, and the timing is on its own page.

> Patch testing identifies the allergen in allergic contact dermatitis, and preservatives and fragrances are the common offenders.

Library: Topical corticosteroid potency: molecule and vehicle
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide explaining that steroid potency depends on molecule and vehicle](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s22.jpg)

## Key features

Potency is set by two things, and concentration is not one of them.

The molecule decides first. The lecture's demonstration is that 0.05 percent clobetasol is vastly stronger than 2.5 percent hydrocortisone, so a bigger percentage on the label can still be the weaker drug.

The vehicle decides second, in a fixed order:

| Vehicle | Relative strength |
|---|---|
| Ointment | Strongest |
| Cream | |
| Lotion | |
| Solution | Weakest |

## The worked example on the chart

The potency chart on the next slide proves the vehicle rule with a single drug. Mometasone furoate 0.1 percent appears twice, circled both times. As Elocon Ointment it sits in class 2, and as Elocon Cream it sits in class 4. Same molecule, same concentration, two classes apart on vehicle alone.

The chart repeats the pattern with other drugs. Triamcinolone acetonide 0.1 percent is class 4 as Kenalog Ointment and class 5 as Kenalog Lotion, and fluocinolone acetonide 0.025 percent is class 4 as Synalar Ointment and class 5 as Synalar Cream.

> Potency comes from the molecule and the vehicle, not the concentration, and mometasone furoate 0.1 percent is class 2 as an ointment and class 4 as a cream.

Library: Choosing a topical steroid by body site
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide matching steroid strength to body site](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s23.jpg)

## Key features

| Potency | Example | Where it goes |
|---|---|---|
| Super high, class I | Clobetasol | Thick skin (palms, soles), thick or severe lesions such as poison ivy or psoriasis on the knees |
| Medium to high, class IV | Triamcinolone | Trunk, extremities, atopic eczema |
| Low, class VI or VII | Hydrocortisone | Face, groin, skin folds, children |

## More to consider

Compliance is part of the choice. The lecture's line is that if the patient does not like the greasy stuff, they will not use it.

Site dictates the form as much as the strength. The scalp takes a solution, shampoo or foam for easy application. A hairy chest does better with a gel or lotion than a cream or ointment. Creases take a low strength lotion or gel, because adding a cream adds moisture to a site where moisture may be the problem in the first place, and because stretch marks are a real risk there.

> Match strength to skin thickness: superpotent on palms and soles, mid potency on trunk and extremities, low potency on face, groin, folds and children.

Library: Topical steroid atrophy and striae
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide comparing new erythematous striae with old silvery striae](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s26.jpg)

## Identify it

- New striae are erythematous, red to violaceous
- Old striae are silvery white and atrophic
- Both run as linear bands in the direction of skin tension

## Key features

The lecture is blunt about this: striae are not reversible, and patients should be educated that they are permanent. That makes the age of the striae a one-way clock rather than a sign of improvement.

Prevention is the only lever. Use potent topical steroids appropriately, and do not use them too long. The lecture's dosing instruction is two weeks as needed for flares.

## Quantity is part of the prescription

The atrophy slide makes a second point through a picture rather than words. Beside the striae it shows a 454 gram jar of triamcinolone acetonide 0.1 percent with a large red X through it and the weight circled. A jar that size invites months of unsupervised use over large areas, which is how patients arrive with the atrophy and striae on the same slide. The amount dispensed is as much a part of safe prescribing as the potency and the duration.

> Striae from topical steroids are permanent, the limit is two weeks as needed for flares, and the slide crosses out the 454 gram jar because quantity dispensed drives the same risk.

Library: Perioral dermatitis and tinea incognito from topical steroids
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide showing perioral dermatitis and tinea incognito as steroid side effects](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s27.jpg)

## Identify it

- Perioral dermatitis: papules clustered around the mouth
- Tinea incognito: a fungal infection whose usual appearance has been blunted by steroid, often in a crease or the groin

## Key features

Both are side effects of topical corticosteroids rather than new diseases. Tinea incognito is the more dangerous idea for an exam, because treating a fungal infection with a steroid changes how it looks and the diagnosis gets missed.

Topical corticosteroids are absorbed, so the risk is not limited to the skin. The lecture notes they can cause adrenal suppression.

> Topical steroids can produce perioral dermatitis and tinea incognito locally, and because they are absorbed they can cause adrenal suppression.

Library: Irritant contact eczema and dishpan hands
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Clinical photograph of irritant hand dermatitis](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s29.jpg)

## Identify it

- Dry, fissured, erythematous skin on the hands
- No vesicles of the allergic kind, and the damage follows exposure rather than sensitization

## Key features

Irritant contact eczema has no immune problem behind it. The mechanism is damage to the skin barrier by acid, solvent or detergent, which is why anyone exposed enough will get it and prior sensitization is irrelevant.

The lecture's two named examples are dishpan hands and diaper rash, and it adds too much hand sanitizer as a modern cause of the same thing.

Treatment repairs and protects the barrier: gentle cleansers, moisturizers, barrier creams, and topical steroids.

> Irritant contact eczema is barrier damage from acids, solvents and detergents with no immune mechanism, treated with gentle cleansers, moisturizers, barrier creams and topical steroids.

Library: Irritant diaper dermatitis and lip licker's dermatitis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Clinical photograph of irritant diaper dermatitis](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s30.jpg)

## Identify it

- Diaper dermatitis sits on the skin the soiled diaper touches
- Lip licker's dermatitis draws a ring around the mouth, out to wherever the tongue reaches

## Key features

Both are irritant rather than allergic, and both name their own cause. The lecture's instruction for the diaper is simply that a messy diaper needs changed, and for the lips that saliva is an irritant.

The ring shape of lip licker's dermatitis is the useful sign, because it maps the reach of the tongue rather than the border of anything applied to the skin.

> Diaper dermatitis and lip licker's dermatitis are both irritant reactions, one to a soiled diaper and one to saliva.

Library: Atopic eczema: features and triggers
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide introducing atopic eczema as the itch that rashes](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s32.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture calls atopic eczema the itch that rashes, which puts the pruritus first and the rash second as its consequence.

It travels with asthma, allergies and what patients call sensitive skin. Triggers are temperature and humidity, meaning extremes of either.

The itch costs sleep, the patient is restless and scratches, and the lecture closes the loop explicitly: stress leads to scratching which makes it worse.

> Atopic eczema is the itch that rashes, associated with asthma and allergies, and triggered by extremes of temperature and humidity.

Library: Atopic eczema distribution by age
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide showing atopic eczema in the popliteal and antecubital fossae](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s34.jpg)

## Identify it

- Infants and young children: the face
- Older children and adults: the creases, meaning the popliteal fossae and the antecubital fossae
- Long-standing disease in a crease becomes lichenified

## Key features

Distribution is the most useful single discriminator in this lecture, because it separates atopic eczema from contact and stasis disease without any history at all. A flexural rash in an older child or adult is atopic until proven otherwise, and a facial rash in an infant is the same disease at a younger age.

> Atopic eczema sits on the face in infants and young children and moves to the antecubital and popliteal creases in older children and adults.

Library: Other atopic findings: hyperlinear palms and infraorbital pleats
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide showing hyperlinear palms and infraorbital pleats](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s36.jpg)

## Identify it

- Hyperlinear palms: exaggerated creases across the palm
- Infraorbital pleats: extra folds under the lower eyelids

## Key features

These are supporting signs rather than the rash itself, and they are useful precisely because they sit away from the active eczema. Finding them on a patient whose creases are inflamed moves the diagnosis toward atopic disease.

The lecture adds the management detail that goes with the itch: trim the nails, and give sedating antihistamines at bedtime, because the damage comes from scratching during restless sleep.

> Hyperlinear palms and infraorbital pleats are atopic stigmata found away from the active rash.

Library: Atopic eczema therapy: basic and biologic
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide listing basic atopic therapy](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s38.jpg)

## Basic therapy

- Avoid triggers, meaning extremes of temperature and humidity
- Gentle cleansers and soap substitutes
- Moisturizers, in the order ointments then creams then lotions
- Topical steroids, favoring low potency over high potency
- Topical immunomodulators, the calcineurin inhibitors pimecrolimus cream and tacrolimus ointment

## Biologic therapy

| Agent | Target |
|---|---|
| Dupilumab | IL4 and IL13, which are over-expressed and promote the Th2 inflammatory response |
| Tralokinumab | IL13 |
| Nemolizumab | The IL31 receptor |

Patients on these avoid live vaccines. The risks the lecture lists are non-infectious conjunctivitis and herpes reactivation.

Janus kinase inhibitors come as both topical and oral forms and limit inflammatory cytokine production. Their risks are infection, malignancy, cardiovascular events and thromboses.

> Dupilumab blocks IL4 and IL13, tralokinumab blocks IL13, and nemolizumab targets the IL31 receptor, and patients on them avoid live vaccines.

Library: Secondary infection of eczema
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide comparing impetiginized eczema with eczema herpeticum](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s40.jpg)

## Identify it

- Impetiginized eczema from Staphylococcus aureus: crusted and tender
- Eczema herpeticum from herpes simplex: grouped lesions

## Key features

| Infection | Organism | The sign the lecture gives |
|---|---|---|
| Impetiginized eczema | Staphylococcus aureus | Tender |
| Eczema herpeticum | Herpes simplex | Grouped |

Secondary infection is common rather than rare in eczema, so a flare that changes character deserves a look for one of these two. Grouped lesions are the tell for herpes, and that distinction is the point of the slide.

> Staphylococcus aureus gives tender impetiginized eczema and herpes simplex gives grouped eczema herpeticum.

Library: Dyshidrotic eczema
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Clinical photograph of dyshidrotic eczema with deep seated vesicles](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s42.jpg)

## Identify it

- Deep seated vesicles the lecture compares to tapioca pudding
- Sides of the fingers first, more often than the toes
- Can spread onto the palms and soles

## Key features

Dyshidrotic eczema is hand and foot eczema, and the vesicles sitting deep rather than on the surface are what make it recognizable. Treatment is a strong topical corticosteroid together with gentle skin care.

> Dyshidrotic eczema produces deep seated tapioca-like vesicles on the sides of the fingers, more often than the toes.

Library: Nummular eczema
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Clinical photograph of coin shaped nummular eczema lesions](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s44.jpg)

## Identify it

- Coin shaped lesions, which is what nummular means
- Subacute, so crusted rather than weeping or lichenified
- Arms and legs

## Key features

The shape is the diagnosis here. Round, discrete, coin-sized plaques on the limbs separate nummular eczema from the flexural pattern of atopic disease and from the streaks of contact disease. Treatment is a superpotent topical steroid.

> Nummular eczema is subacute, coin shaped, sits on the arms and legs, and takes a superpotent topical steroid.

Library: Stasis dermatitis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Clinical photograph of stasis dermatitis on the lower leg](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s46.jpg)

## Identify it

- Lower legs, with swelling
- Erythema and scaling
- Brown discoloration
- Ulceration in advanced disease

## Key features

Stasis dermatitis sits on top of venous insufficiency, so the edema is part of the diagnosis rather than a complication of it. The brown discoloration is what separates it from the other eczemas on the leg.

There is a second trap here. Stasis dermatitis carries an increased risk of allergic contact dermatitis, and the lecture names triple antibiotic ointment, specifically its neomycin, as the offender. Patients treat the leg, become sensitized, and arrive with two diseases.

Medications can drive the edema that feeds the whole process. The lecture names calcium channel blockers, gabapentin and pregabalin.

> Stasis dermatitis is venous insufficiency with edema, erythema, scale and brown discoloration, and it carries an increased risk of allergic contact dermatitis to neomycin.

Library: Asteatotic eczema and eczema craquele
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Clinical photograph of eczema craquele with cracked plate-like scale](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s50.jpg)

## Identify it

- Red and scaly skin broken into plates by shallow fissures
- The lecture's two comparisons are cracked porcelain and a dried up river bed

## Key features

Asteatotic eczema goes by dry skin or xerotic eczema. It belongs to older individuals, swimmers and winter, and it is driven by over-bathing and harsh soaps or cleansers. The lecture also lists cholesterol lowering agents as a cause.

The named pattern, eczema craquele, is the cracked appearance itself, and it is the reason this one is recognizable on sight.

> Asteatotic eczema is dry skin in older people, swimmers and winter, worsened by over-bathing, harsh soaps and cholesterol lowering agents, and it cracks into the plates of eczema craquele.

Library: Habit eczemas: lichen simplex chronicus and prurigo nodularis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide comparing lichen simplex chronicus with prurigo nodularis](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s52.jpg)

## Identify it

- Lichen simplex chronicus comes from constant scratching and leaves a thickened lichenified plaque
- Prurigo nodularis comes from constant picking and leaves discrete firm nodules

## Key features

| Habit | Result | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Constant scratching | Lichen simplex chronicus | Superpotent topical corticosteroid |
| Constant picking | Prurigo nodularis | Intralesional corticosteroids, ultraviolet light therapy, nemolizumab or dupilumab |

Prurigo nodularis carries an association the lecture singles out, which is renal failure.

The lecture's advice to family and friends is to tell the patient to stop scratching, picking and fussing, which makes the point that the behavior maintains the disease.

> Scratching produces lichen simplex chronicus and picking produces prurigo nodularis, and prurigo nodularis carries a risk of renal failure.

Library: Topical corticosteroid potency classes and their members
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide showing the seven class topical corticosteroid potency chart](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s21.jpg)

## Identify it

- Seven numbered classes, class 1 at the top and class 7 at the bottom
- Each row gives a generic name with its concentration beside examples of branded products
- The cartoon down the left side runs from a figure flexing to a figure flattened under a barbell, which is the direction of falling potency

## The classes

| Class | Label | Members the chart lists |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Super potent | 0.05% clobetasol propionate (Clobex, Olux-E, Temovate E), 0.05% halobetasol propionate (Ultravate Cream), 0.1% fluocinonide (Vanos Cream) |
| 2 | Potent | 0.05% diflorasone diacetate, 0.1% mometasone furoate (Elocon Ointment), 0.1% halcinonide, 0.25% desoximetasone (Topicort) |
| 3 | Upper mid-strength | 0.05% fluocinonide (Lidex-E Cream), 0.05% desoximetasone (Topicort LP Cream) |
| 4 | Mid-strength | 0.1% clocortolone pivalate (Cloderm), 0.1% mometasone furoate (Elocon Cream), 0.1% triamcinolone acetonide (Kenalog Ointment), 0.1% betamethasone valerate (Valisone Ointment), 0.025% fluocinolone acetonide (Synalar Ointment) |
| 5 | Lower mid-strength | 0.05% fluticasone propionate (Cutivate), 0.1% prednicarbate (Dermatop), 0.1% hydrocortisone probutate (Pandel), 0.1% triamcinolone acetonide (Kenalog Lotion), 0.025% fluocinolone acetonide (Synalar Cream) |
| 6 | Mild | 0.05% alclometasone dipropionate (Aclovate), 0.05% desonide (Verdeso Foam, Desonate Gel), 0.025% triamcinolone acetonide, 0.1% hydrocortisone butyrate (Locoid), 0.01% fluocinolone acetonide |
| 7 | Least potent | 2% and 2.5% hydrocortisone (Nutracort Lotion, Synacort Cream), 0.5 to 1% hydrocortisone (Cortaid and many other over-the-counter products) |

## Reading the chart against the two rules

The chart is the evidence for both potency rules at once. Clobetasol at 0.05 percent sits in class 1 while hydrocortisone at 2 to 2.5 percent sits in class 7, so the weaker drug carries the larger number on the label, which is the molecule rule.

Mometasone furoate 0.1 percent appears twice and is circled both times, as Elocon Ointment in class 2 and Elocon Cream in class 4. Nothing changes but the vehicle, and the agent moves two classes.

Class 7 is also where the over-the-counter products live, which is worth knowing when a patient says they already tried hydrocortisone.

> The chart runs from class 1 super potent (clobetasol 0.05%) to class 7 least potent (hydrocortisone 0.5 to 2.5%), and over-the-counter hydrocortisone sits in class 7.

Library: Allergic contact eczema: common offenders
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide showing three over the counter products as common contact allergens](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s19.jpg)

## Identify it

The slide names no agent in text. The three offenders are shown as photographs of the products themselves:

- Neomycin first aid antibiotic ointment
- Extra strength anti-itch cream 2 percent, whose active ingredient is diphenhydramine hydrochloride
- White petrolatum, sold as 100 percent pure petroleum jelly

## Key features

What these three share is that patients reach for all of them to treat irritated skin, so the agent causing the eczema is the one being used as the remedy. A rash that spreads or worsens under self-treatment should raise this possibility rather than prompting more of the same.

Two of them are counterintuitive. Topical diphenhydramine is sold to relieve itch, and petrolatum is the bland emollient usually treated as inert, yet both appear here as common sensitizers.

Neomycin connects to the stasis material, where the lecture names the neomycin in triple antibiotic ointment as the reason stasis dermatitis so often acquires a second, allergic disease on top of the first.

> Neomycin, topical diphenhydramine 2 percent, and white petrolatum are the common offenders, and all three are products patients apply to soothe skin that is already inflamed.

Library: Stasis eczema therapy
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide showing stasis eczema therapy as leg elevation and compression stockings](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s47.jpg)

## Identify it

The treatment is carried entirely by photographs rather than text:

- Two women sitting on a couch with their legs hanging down, the posture to avoid
- A leg raised on a wedge pillow
- Compression stockings, shown worn and as a range of colors and lengths

## Key features

Every image points at the same target, which is the edema. Stasis dermatitis follows venous insufficiency, so therapy works on the venous return rather than on the skin: keep the legs from hanging dependent for long stretches, elevate them, and use compression.

The one line of text on the slide adds the drugs that work against you by causing edema.

| Medication | Why it matters here |
|---|---|
| Calcium channel blockers | Cause edema |
| Gabapentin | Causes edema |
| Pregabalin | Causes edema |

Reviewing the medication list is part of treating the leg, because a drug driving the swelling will undo elevation and compression.

> Stasis eczema therapy is elevation, compression and avoiding prolonged dependent sitting, and calcium channel blockers, gabapentin and pregabalin can cause the edema that drives it.

Library: Patch test reading at 48 and 96 hours
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / The Spectrum of Eczema

![Lecture slide showing a patch test panel photographed at two time points with an arrow between them](library/images/msk-week-14/ecz-s20.jpg)

## Identify it

- The slide is a before and after pair with a red arrow running between them
- The left panel is labeled 48 hours and the right panel 96 hours
- The same column of test sites appears in both, with the reactions clearer at the later reading

## Key features

The panel is read twice. A single reading at 48 hours would catch the reactions already present but would miss anything still developing, and the second reading at 96 hours is there to pick those up.

The schedule follows from the mechanism. Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV hypersensitivity, which is cell mediated and takes days to express itself, so the readings are spaced in days. An immediate IgE mediated test would be read in minutes, and that contrast is the quickest way to remember why patch testing waits.

This timing exists on the slide only as two numbers set into the figure, so it is easy to miss when working from a text transcript of the deck.

> Patch tests are read at 48 hours and again at 96 hours, because a delayed cell mediated reaction can still be developing at the first reading.

Library: Normal skin layers and adnexal structures
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Diagram of normal skin labeled epidermis, papillary dermis, reticular dermis, sebaceous gland, hair follicle, sweat gland and subcutis](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s03.jpg)

## Identify it

- Epidermis, the thin surface layer
- Papillary dermis immediately beneath it
- Reticular dermis, the thicker layer below that
- Subcutis at the base
- Three adnexal structures sit within the dermis: sebaceous gland, hair follicle and sweat gland

## Key features

The lecture opens with this orientation slide because every neoplasm that follows is named for the layer or the structure it comes from. Epithelial lesions arise from the epidermis, melanocytic lesions from melanocytes in the basal layer, mesenchymal lesions from the dermis and subcutis, and adnexal neoplasms from the three adnexal structures listed above.

> Skin is organized as epidermis, papillary dermis, reticular dermis and subcutis, with sebaceous glands, hair follicles and sweat glands as the adnexa.

Library: Seborrheic keratosis: clinical features
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photographs of pigmented stuck-on plaques](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s07.jpg)

## Identify it

- A sharply bordered plaque that looks stuck onto the skin surface
- Often pigmented, from tan through dark brown to nearly black
- Frequently multiple, especially over the trunk

## Key features

- Benign
- Very common
- Middle-aged and older adults
- Arises spontaneously
- Often pigmented
- Can resemble malignant melanoma
- Rarely part of a paraneoplastic syndrome

The resemblance to melanoma is the clinically important point, because a heavily pigmented seborrheic keratosis and a melanoma can look alike to the naked eye.

> Seborrheic keratosis is a benign pigmented lesion of middle-aged and older adults that can resemble malignant melanoma.

Library: Seborrheic keratosis: histopathology
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Low power H and E micrograph of an exophytic epidermal lesion with horn pseudocysts](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s09.jpg)

## Identify it

- An epidermal lesion that sits above the plane of the surrounding skin (exophytic)
- Sharply demarcated from adjacent normal epidermis
- Round keratin-filled spaces within the thickened epidermis (pseudocysts)

## Key features

| Feature | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| Epidermal lesion | Confined to the epidermis |
| Exophytic | Grows outward above the skin surface |
| Well demarcated | Abrupt edges against normal epidermis |
| Acanthosis | Thickened epidermis |
| Cytologically bland | No atypia in the cells |
| Hyperkeratosis with pseudocysts | Surface keratin plus keratin-filled pseudocysts inside the lesion |
| Variable melanin pigmentation | Explains why some are dark and some are not |

Cytologic blandness is what separates this from the malignant epithelial lesions later in the lecture. The cells are increased in number but normal in appearance.

> A seborrheic keratosis is an exophytic, well demarcated, cytologically bland epidermal proliferation with hyperkeratosis and keratin pseudocysts.

Library: Hair follicle anatomy behind the follicular cysts
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Labeled diagram and micrographs of a hair follicle showing infundibulum, isthmus, suprabulbar area and bulb](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s13.jpg)

## Identify it

Four levels, numbered from the surface down:

1. Infundibulum
2. Isthmus
3. Suprabulbar area
4. Bulb

## Key features

Two of those levels matter for the cysts that follow, and they differ in a way you can see on a slide.

| Level | Keratinization | Keratin produced |
|---|---|---|
| Infundibulum | Like epidermis, has a granular layer | Loose, lamellar keratin |
| Isthmus | No granular layer | Dense, pilar keratin |

That single distinction (granular layer present or absent) is what tells the two follicular cysts apart under the microscope.

> The infundibulum keratinizes like epidermis with a granular layer and loose lamellar keratin, while the isthmus has no granular layer and makes dense pilar keratin.

Library: Epidermal inclusion cyst (follicular infundibular cyst)
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Micrograph of a cyst lined by epithelium with a granular layer containing loose lamellar keratin](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s16.jpg)

## Identify it

- A cyst lined by epithelium that keratinizes like epidermis
- A granular layer is present in the lining
- The contents are loose, lamellar keratin

## Key features

- Derived from the hair follicle infundibulum
- Exceedingly common
- Occurs anywhere, at any age

The lecture gives this lesion several names that all mean the same thing: epidermal inclusion cyst, abbreviated EIC, epidermoid cyst, and the older clinical term "sebaceous cyst."

> An epidermal inclusion cyst comes from the follicular infundibulum, so its lining has a granular layer and it contains loose lamellar keratin.

Library: Pilar cyst (follicular isthmic cyst)
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Micrograph of a cyst lined by epithelium lacking a granular layer and filled with dense keratin](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s17.jpg)

## Identify it

- A cyst whose lining abruptly makes keratin without forming a granular layer
- Dense, compact keratin filling the cavity

## Key features

- Derived from the hair follicle isthmus
- Also common
- Usually on the scalp
- Usually in adults

The alternative name is trichilemmal cyst.

> A pilar cyst comes from the follicular isthmus, has no granular layer in its lining, contains dense pilar keratin, and is usually a scalp lesion in an adult.

Library: Verruca: cause and subtypes
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Slide listing the verruca subtypes](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s19.jpg)

## Key features

- Very common
- Any age, especially children and adolescents
- Caused by human papillomaviruses (HPV)
- Usually self limited, regressing over months to years

## Subtypes

| Name | Common name |
|---|---|
| Verruca vulgaris | Common wart |
| Verruca plana | Flat wart |
| Verruca plantaris | Plantar wart |
| Verruca palmaris | Palm wart |
| Condyloma acuminatum | Venereal or genital wart |

The subtypes are named for where the wart sits rather than for different viruses.

> Verrucae are HPV-induced, usually self limited over months to years, and their subtypes are named by site, from verruca vulgaris to condyloma acuminatum.

Library: Verruca vulgaris: clinical and histologic features
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Micrograph of a wart showing hyperkeratosis and papillomatosis with koilocytes](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s21.jpg)

## Identify it

- Thickened surface keratin (hyperkeratosis)
- The epidermis thrown into finger-like projections (papillomatosis, also described as papillary epidermal hyperplasia)
- Cells with a clear halo around the nucleus (koilocytosis, a halo-like cytoplasmic vacuolization)

## Key features

Koilocytosis is the viral cytopathic change and is the feature that identifies the lesion as HPV related rather than simply a thickened epidermis. The architectural change (papillomatosis) and the surface change (hyperkeratosis) go with it.

> Verruca vulgaris shows hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis and koilocytosis, the last being the halo-like cytoplasmic vacuolization caused by HPV.

Library: Acrochordon (skin tag)
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photograph of pedunculated papules on the neck beside a micrograph of a polypoid lesion](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s23.jpg)

## Identify it

- Soft papules hanging from a narrow stalk, usually at the neck or other flexural sites
- Microscopically a polypoid projection covered by otherwise normal appearing skin

## Key features

- Benign outgrowth of otherwise normal appearing skin
- Pathology: polypoid, normal skin, with or without inflammation

This is the one lesion in the epithelial group with no distinctive cytology at all. The diagnosis rests on architecture, a polyp of normal skin.

> An acrochordon is a benign polypoid outgrowth of otherwise normal appearing skin, with no distinctive cellular change.

Library: Actinic keratosis: clinical features and treatment
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photographs of gritty scaly lesions on sun-damaged skin](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s25.jpg)

## Identify it

- Rough, scaly, poorly marginated lesions on chronically sun-exposed skin
- Typically multiple, on a background of actinic damage
- Favoured sites are the face, hands and arms

## Key features

- Dysplastic, and therefore premalignant rather than benign or malignant
- Adults
- Fairer skin types
- Caused by ultraviolet radiation
- Sun exposed areas, especially face, hands and arms
- Excessive keratin production
- Has the potential to progress to squamous cell carcinoma
- May also regress or remain stable

## Treatment

| Approach | What it is |
|---|---|
| Individual lesion | Cryotherapy |
| Field treatment | Topical chemotherapy with 5-fluorouracil (Efudex) |

Field treatment exists because these lesions come in crops across a whole sun-damaged area rather than singly.

> Actinic keratosis is a UV-induced dysplastic (premalignant) lesion that may progress to squamous cell carcinoma, regress, or stay stable, and is treated lesion by lesion with cryotherapy or across a field with topical 5-fluorouracil.

Library: Actinic keratosis: histopathology
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Micrograph showing parakeratosis above an epidermis with basal layer atypia](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s28.jpg)

## Identify it

- Thickened surface keratin in which nuclei are retained (hyperkeratosis with parakeratosis)
- Atypical keratinocytes concentrated in the lower epidermis

## Key features

- Hyperkeratosis with parakeratosis
- Epidermal cytologic atypia, predominantly in the basal layer

The word "predominantly" is doing the work here. The atypia is real but it is bottom-heavy and does not fill the epidermis, which is exactly what separates this lesion from squamous cell carcinoma in situ.

> Actinic keratosis shows hyperkeratosis with parakeratosis and cytologic atypia that is predominantly basal, not full thickness.

Library: Squamous cell carcinoma in situ
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Micrograph of an acanthotic epidermis with atypia through its full thickness](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s30.jpg)

## Identify it

- Atypical keratinocytes occupying the full thickness of the epidermis
- The basal layer and basement membrane remain intact, with no invasion into the dermis
- The epidermis is often thickened

## Key features

- In situ means non-invasive
- Full thickness dysplasia involving the epidermis
- Basal layer and basement membrane intact, so there is no invasion
- Often a thickened, acanthotic epidermis
- Parakeratosis and hyperkeratosis are common
- Can arise as progression from an actinic keratosis or can appear de novo

> Squamous cell carcinoma in situ is full thickness epidermal dysplasia with an intact basement membrane and no invasion, and it may arise from an actinic keratosis or de novo.

Library: Invasive squamous cell carcinoma: risk factors and behavior
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photographs of ulcerated and keratotic tumours on sun-exposed skin](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s32.jpg)

## Identify it

- A firm keratotic or ulcerated nodule on chronically sun-exposed skin
- Commonly on the face, ear, lip, scalp or forearm

## Key features

- Affects the same patient population as actinic keratosis
- Caused by UV radiation
- Very high incidence with immunosuppression, especially solid organ transplant, and the risk is proportional to the patient's risk before they became immunosuppressed
- Invades into the dermis
- Usually produces keratin
- The second most common malignancy in the USA

The immunosuppression point is worth holding onto, because it changes who gets screened and how aggressively.

> Invasive squamous cell carcinoma arises in the same UV-damaged population as actinic keratosis, invades the dermis, usually makes keratin, and is markedly more common after solid organ transplantation.

Library: Invasive squamous cell carcinoma: histopathology
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Micrograph of nests of squamous cells with keratin pearls extending into the dermis](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s36.jpg)

## Identify it

- Irregular nests and tongues of squamous epithelium below the level of the epidermis, so the tumour is invading the dermis
- Keratin formed within the tumour nests, often as concentric pearls

## Key features

The two features the lecture labels on this image are keratin and invasion into the dermis. Those are also the two features that separate invasive disease from carcinoma in situ, where the basement membrane is intact.

> Invasive squamous cell carcinoma is recognized by tumour that has breached into the dermis and by the keratin it produces.

Library: Basal cell carcinoma: incidence and behavior
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photographs of pearly telangiectatic papules on the face](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s37.jpg)

## Identify it

- A pearly papule or nodule, often with surface telangiectasia
- Frequently on the nose, eyelid, cheek or other sun-exposed facial site
- May ulcerate centrally

## Key features

- The most common skin cancer, and the highest incidence cancer in the USA by a wide margin
- Caused by UV radiation
- Locally aggressive, but typically slow growing
- Essentially never metastasizes, with near zero mortality
- Occurs at sun exposed sites
- Has aggressive and non-aggressive growth patterns, and which one it is determines how it is removed (excision versus destruction)
- Derived from basal layer cells, with the lecture raising the open question of epidermis versus hair follicle origin

The combination of highest incidence and near zero mortality is the thing to keep straight. It is extremely common and locally destructive without being a killer.

> Basal cell carcinoma is the most common cancer in the USA, is locally aggressive but essentially never metastasizes, and its growth pattern decides whether it is excised or destroyed.

Library: Basal cell carcinoma: pathologic features
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Micrograph of a basaloid dermal nest showing peripheral palisading and retraction from the surrounding stroma](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s40.jpg)

## Identify it

- Nests of small, dark blue cells sitting in the dermis
- The outermost cells of each nest lined up like a picket fence (peripheral palisading)
- A clear white space separating tumour from stroma (stromal retraction)
- Grey-blue mucin in or around the nests

## Key features

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| Basaloid cells | High nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, small and blue |
| Dermal tumour | Sits in the dermis, usually at least focally attached to the epidermis |
| Peripheral palisading | Outer cells of the nest lining up like a picket fence |
| Stromal retraction | Separation of cells from stroma creating white space |
| Mucin | Present in the tumour stroma |

> Basal cell carcinoma is a dermal tumour of small blue basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, stromal retraction and mucin, usually attached to the epidermis somewhere along its length.

Library: Basal cell carcinoma subtypes and why they matter
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Micrographs of the nodular, superficial, infiltrative and micronodular growth patterns](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s41.jpg)

## Identify it

- Nodular: large, rounded, well circumscribed dermal nests
- Superficial: small buds hanging from the undersurface of the epidermis
- Infiltrative and morpheaform: thin, angulated strands threading through a fibrotic stroma
- Micronodular: many small nests scattered through the dermis

## Key features

| Growth pattern | Group |
|---|---|
| Nodular type | Non-aggressive |
| Superficial type | Non-aggressive |
| Infiltrative and/or morpheaform types | Aggressive |
| Micronodular type | Aggressive |

The split matters because the lecture ties it directly to management: the growth pattern determines the type of removal, excision versus destruction.

> Nodular and superficial basal cell carcinomas are the non-aggressive patterns, while infiltrative, morpheaform and micronodular are the aggressive ones, and that distinction drives how the tumour is removed.

Library: Basal cell carcinoma versus squamous cell carcinoma on histology
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Side by side micrographs contrasting a blue basaloid tumour with a pink keratinizing tumour](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s42.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture reduces this to a colour contrast you can use at scanning power.

| | Basal cell carcinoma | Squamous cell carcinoma |
|---|---|---|
| Cells | Basaloid, high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, so blue | Abundant cytoplasm, low nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, so pink |
| Characteristic material | Mucin, greyish-blue | Keratin, pink |
| Stromal retraction | Present | Not a feature |

> At low power a basal cell carcinoma reads blue because of its high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio and mucin, while a squamous cell carcinoma reads pink because of abundant cytoplasm and keratin.

Library: Merkel cell carcinoma
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Micrograph of sheets of small round blue cells with finely stippled chromatin](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s43.jpg)

## Identify it

- Sheets of small round blue cells filling the dermis
- Neuroendocrine nuclear detail, described as salt and pepper chromatin
- Clinically a pink or purple nodule

## Key features

- A primary cutaneous neuroendocrine carcinoma
- Relatively rare
- Most are caused by sun damage in combination with Merkel cell polyomavirus, though not all are virus associated
- Aggressive, and frequently metastasizes
- Arises from Merkel cells, which are native neuroendocrine cells normally located in the basal layer
- Many different growth patterns

This is the one epithelial malignancy in the lecture that behaves badly. Basal cell carcinoma essentially never metastasizes, and Merkel cell carcinoma frequently does.

> Merkel cell carcinoma is a rare, aggressive, frequently metastasizing neuroendocrine carcinoma of small round blue cells with salt and pepper chromatin, usually linked to sun damage plus Merkel cell polyomavirus.

Library: Benign melanocytic nevi: the variants
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Slide listing the benign melanocytic nevus variants](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s47.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture organizes benign nevi into one ordinary group and five named variants.

| Group | Members |
|---|---|
| Ordinary, also called banal | Junctional, compound, intradermal |
| Named variants | Congenital, Spitz, blue, halo, dysplastic |

Everything that follows in the melanocytic section is one of these, and then melanoma.

> Benign melanocytic nevi divide into the ordinary or banal group (junctional, compound, intradermal) and the named variants: congenital, Spitz, blue, halo and dysplastic.

Library: Ordinary nevi: junctional, compound, and intradermal
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Three micrographs showing melanocytic nests at the junction only, at the junction and in the dermis, and in the dermis only](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s49.jpg)

## Identify it

The three ordinary nevi differ only in where the nests sit.

| Nevus | Where the nests are | Lecture's shorthand |
|---|---|---|
| Junctional | At the dermoepidermal junction | All epidermal |
| Compound | At the junction and in the dermis | Mixed |
| Intradermal | In the dermis only | All dermal |

## Key features

This is a pure architecture distinction. The cells themselves are the same bland melanocytes in all three; only their location changes. Reading the slide means finding the junction and asking whether nests are above it, below it, or both.

> Junctional nevi are all epidermal, compound nevi are mixed, and intradermal nevi are all dermal, which is a difference of location rather than of cell type.

Library: Congenital nevus
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photograph of a large pigmented patch beside a micrograph of nevus cells extending deep into the dermis](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s50.jpg)

## Identify it

- Clinically a large pigmented patch, frequently hairy
- Microscopically nevus cells reaching deep into the dermis
- Nevus cells growing around adnexal structures and blood vessels

## Key features

- Cells are similar to those of a compound or intradermal nevus
- Deep dermal involvement
- Growth around adnexa and blood vessels
- Frequently hairy clinically
- Increased risk of melanoma in the large variants

The cells are ordinary. What marks the lesion as congenital is how deep it goes and how it wraps around the structures already in the dermis.

> A congenital nevus has ordinary nevus cells but extends deep into the dermis and grows around adnexa and vessels, and the large variants carry an increased melanoma risk.

Library: Spitz nevus
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photograph of a pink dome-shaped papule beside a micrograph of large epithelioid and spindle cells](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s52.jpg)

## Identify it

- Clinically a pink to brown papule
- Microscopically large plump (epithelioid) cells and fusiform (spindle) cells

## Key features

- Occurs in children and young adults
- Pink to brown papule
- Microscopically may be confused for melanoma
- Large plump epithelioid and fusiform spindle cells

The diagnostic trap is explicit in the lecture: this benign lesion can be mistaken for melanoma under the microscope, which is why the patient's age matters.

> A Spitz nevus is a pink to brown papule of children and young adults made of large epithelioid and spindle cells, and it can be microscopically confused for melanoma.

Library: Blue nevus
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photograph of a blue-grey macule beside a micrograph of pigmented dendritic spindle cells in the dermis](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s53.jpg)

## Identify it

- Clinically a blue-grey lesion
- Microscopically heavily pigmented, elongated dendritic and spindle shaped cells lying in the dermis
- No nests

## Key features

- Heavily pigmented
- Dendritic and spindle cells
- Located in the dermis
- Lacks a nested pattern

The absence of nests is the point of contrast with the ordinary nevi, which are defined by their nests.

> A blue nevus is a heavily pigmented dermal proliferation of dendritic and spindle cells that lacks the nested pattern of ordinary nevi.

Library: Halo nevus
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photograph of a central papule ringed by pale skin beside a micrograph of a nevus infiltrated by lymphocytes](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s54.jpg)

## Identify it

- Clinically a nevus surrounded by a ring of depigmented skin
- Microscopically a dense lymphocytic infiltrate running through and destroying the nevus cells

## Key features

- Depigmented zone, the halo
- Lymphocytic infiltration destroying nevus cells
- The clinical halo does not always correlate with the lymphocytic response

That last caveat is worth remembering: you can find the infiltrate without a visible halo, and the reverse.

> A halo nevus is a nevus being destroyed by a lymphocytic infiltrate, with a surrounding depigmented zone that does not always correlate with the microscopic response.

Library: Dysplastic nevus: naming, syndrome, and clinical features
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photographs of irregular variegated macules and a back covered with numerous nevi](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s56.jpg)

## Identify it

- Usually larger than 5 mm across
- Variable pigmentation within a single lesion
- Irregular borders
- Flat to only slightly raised
- Often numerous

## Key features

The lecture gives this lesion four names: dysplastic nevus, nevus with architectural disorder and cytologic atypia, atypical nevus, and Clark's nevus.

- Can be familial, as dysplastic nevus syndrome
- That syndrome is autosomal dominant
- It carries a higher risk of melanoma
- Lesions occur on sun-exposed and non-exposed areas alike

The distribution matters. Unlike actinic keratosis and the keratinocyte cancers, these are not confined to sun-exposed skin.

> A dysplastic nevus is usually over 5 mm with variable pigmentation and irregular borders, occurs on exposed and unexposed skin, and in its autosomal dominant familial form carries a higher melanoma risk.

Library: Dysplastic nevus: histologic criteria
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Micrograph showing adjacent rete ridges bridged by melanocytic nests with fibrosis beneath](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s57.jpg)

## Identify it

- Adjacent rete ridges joined by melanocytic nests (fusion of rete, also called bridging)
- Layered fibrosis in the papillary dermis beneath the lesion (lamellar dermal fibrosis)
- Scattered rather than uniform nuclear abnormality

## Key features

| Category | Findings |
|---|---|
| Architectural disorder | Fusion of rete, lamellar dermal fibrosis |
| Random cytologic atypia | Irregular nuclear contours, hyperchromasia |

The word "random" is deliberate. The atypia is scattered rather than uniform, which distinguishes it from the consistent atypia of melanoma.

> A dysplastic nevus shows architectural disorder (fusion of rete and lamellar dermal fibrosis) together with random cytologic atypia.

Library: Melanoma: origin and risk factors
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photograph of a large asymmetric multicoloured lesion](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s58.jpg)

## Key features

- A malignant neoplasm of melanocytes
- Can arise de novo or from other nevus types, and de novo is probably the most common
- Incidence is increasing in the US, with the rate depending on the melanoma subtype
- Most are cured by surgical excision
- Can metastasize to almost any body site

## Risk factors

- Chronic sun exposure and sun burns
- Skin type, with red hair and fair skin carrying far higher risk than skin of colour
- Hereditary factors, through germline mutations

The de novo point runs against the common assumption that melanomas grow out of existing moles. Most do not.

> Melanoma is a malignant melanocytic neoplasm that most often arises de novo rather than from an existing nevus, is usually cured by excision, and can metastasize almost anywhere.

Library: Melanoma subtypes: the longtime paradigm and the 2018 WHO classification
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Slide showing the 2018 WHO melanoma classification organized by cumulative solar damage](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s60.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture presents two ways of carving melanoma up.

The longtime paradigm, by growth pattern:

- Superficial spreading melanoma
- Nodular melanoma
- Lentigo maligna melanoma
- Acral lentiginous melanoma
- Others, including mucosal, uveal and spitzoid

The 2018 WHO classification, organized instead around cumulative solar damage (CSD), which the slide defines as cumulative solar damage or chronic sun damage. It sorts melanoma into three groups and nine numbered pathways.

| Group | Pathway | Entity |
|---|---|---|
| A. Associated with CSD | I | Superficial spreading melanoma, low-CSD melanoma |
| A. Associated with CSD | II | Lentigo maligna melanoma, high-CSD melanoma |
| A. Associated with CSD | III | Desmoplastic melanoma |
| B. Not consistently associated with CSD | IV | Spitz melanomas |
| B. Not consistently associated with CSD | V | Acral melanoma |
| B. Not consistently associated with CSD | VI | Mucosal melanomas |
| B. Not consistently associated with CSD | VII | Melanomas arising in congenital nevi |
| B. Not consistently associated with CSD | VIII | Melanomas arising in blue nevi |
| B. Not consistently associated with CSD | IX | Uveal melanoma, which the source notes is not considered further |
| C. | | Nodular melanoma, which may occur in any or most of the pathways |

Group A is the sun-driven half and contains only three pathways. Everything else, including the two that arise within a pre-existing nevus, sits in group B because its occurrence does not track with sun exposure.

> The 2018 WHO classification puts superficial spreading, lentigo maligna and desmoplastic melanoma in the CSD-associated group, Spitz, acral, mucosal, congenital nevus, blue nevus and uveal melanoma in the group not consistently associated with CSD, and nodular melanoma in a category of its own that may occur across most pathways.

Library: Melanoma: the clinical ABCDEs
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photographs of asymmetric pigmented lesions with irregular notched borders](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s61.jpg)

## Identify it

| Letter | Feature | What to look for |
|---|---|---|
| A | Asymmetry | One half does not look like the other |
| B | Border irregular | Scalloped, notched, discontinuous |
| C | Colour variable | Multiple shades ranging from white to tan to red to brown to black |
| D | Diameter | Usually greater than 6 mm |
| E | Enlargement | Increase, usually gradual, in size and elevation |

## Key features

The lecture lists these in alphabetical order rather than in order of importance, which is worth noting so you do not read the sequence as a ranking.

> The clinical ABCDEs of melanoma are asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variability, diameter usually over 6 mm, and enlargement in size and elevation.

Library: Melanoma: histologic features
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Slide listing the architectural and cytological features of melanoma](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s62.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture splits the microscopic findings into architecture and cytology.

### Architectural

- Asymmetry
- Poor circumscription
- Epidermal findings: variable size and shape of nests, confluent growth, solitary epidermal melanocytes, haphazard arrangement, and pagetoid (upward) spread
- Dermal findings: lack of maturation and dispersion, stromal desmoplasia and fibrosis

### Cytological

- Nuclear pleomorphism
- Nucleolar variability
- Mitoses, both superficial and deep, and sometimes atypical

Pagetoid spread, meaning melanocytes climbing upward through the epidermis rather than staying at the junction, is the architectural finding that appears again under superficial spreading melanoma.

> Melanoma is recognized architecturally by asymmetry, poor circumscription, pagetoid upward spread and lack of dermal maturation, and cytologically by nuclear pleomorphism, nucleolar variability and mitoses at depth.

Library: Superficial spreading melanoma and low cumulative solar damage
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Micrograph showing melanocytes scattered upward through the full thickness of the epidermis](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s63.jpg)

## Identify it

- Melanocytes scattered upward through the epidermis, well above the junction (pagetoid spread)

## Key features

- Carries BRAF mutations
- Shows pagetoid spread
- Occurs on the trunk and extremities
- Affects younger patients
- Sits in the low CSD group of the WHO classification

> Superficial spreading melanoma is the low cumulative solar damage, BRAF mutated subtype of younger patients, arising on trunk and extremities and showing pagetoid spread.

Library: Lentigo maligna melanoma and high cumulative solar damage
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Slide describing lentigo maligna melanoma on sun-damaged head and neck skin](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s64.jpg)

## Key features

- Arises in more heavily sun-damaged skin
- Often head and neck
- Older patients
- Shows confluent growth of single melanocytes along the basal layer
- Has a prolonged in situ or radial growth course, which can run many years to decades before dermal invasion

The contrast with superficial spreading melanoma is almost point for point: older rather than younger, head and neck rather than trunk and extremities, growth along the basal layer rather than upward through the epidermis, and high rather than low cumulative solar damage.

> Lentigo maligna melanoma is the high cumulative solar damage subtype of older patients on head and neck skin, growing as confluent single melanocytes along the basal layer for years to decades before invading.

Library: Acral lentiginous melanoma
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photographs of pigmented lesions on the sole and heel](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s65.jpg)

## Identify it

- A pigmented lesion on palmar, plantar or subungual skin

## Key features

- Involves palmar, plantar or subungual skin
- Incidence is fairly stable across all skin types
- Its incidence follows rather than relates to UV exposure and cumulative solar damage
- It is the most common subtype in skin of colour populations

The reason it is the most common subtype in skin of colour is not that it occurs more often there, but that the UV-driven subtypes occur less often, so this UV-independent one makes up a larger share.

> Acral lentiginous melanoma arises on palmar, plantar and subungual skin, has an incidence that is stable across skin types and independent of UV exposure, and is therefore the most common subtype in skin of colour populations.

Library: Melanoma prognosis: Breslow thickness
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Micrograph of a melanoma with the depth of dermal invasion shown](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s66.jpg)

## Key features

Depth of invasion, measured as Breslow thickness, is the single most important prognostic factor.

- Highly predictive of survival
- Measured as the distance from the uppermost nucleated cell in the epidermis to the deepest cell that is clearly identifiable as a melanoma cell
- True for all subtypes

## Other prognostic factors

- Ulceration, which is also important and increases the substage
- Dermal mitoses
- Lymphovascular invasion
- Tumour infiltrating lymphocytes
- Microsatellites

> Breslow thickness, measured from the uppermost nucleated epidermal cell to the deepest identifiable melanoma cell, is the most important prognostic factor in melanoma and applies to every subtype.

Library: Melanoma staging: AJCC T categories
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Table of melanoma T categories listing thickness and ulceration status for each](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s67.jpg)

## Identify it
