The table has three columns: the T category, the Breslow thickness that defines it, and the ulceration status.

## Key features

| T category | Thickness | Ulceration |
|---|---|---|
| Tis (melanoma in situ) | Not applicable | Not applicable |
| T1 | 1.0 mm or less | Unknown or unspecified |
| T1a | Less than 0.8 mm | Without ulceration |
| T1b | Less than 0.8 mm | With ulceration |
| T1b | 0.8 to 1.0 mm | With or without ulceration |
| T2 | Over 1.0 to 2.0 mm | Unknown or unspecified |
| T2a | Over 1.0 to 2.0 mm | Without ulceration |
| T2b | Over 1.0 to 2.0 mm | With ulceration |
| T3 | Over 2.0 to 4.0 mm | Unknown or unspecified |
| T3a | Over 2.0 to 4.0 mm | Without ulceration |
| T3b | Over 2.0 to 4.0 mm | With ulceration |
| T4 | Over 4.0 mm | Unknown or unspecified |
| T4a | Over 4.0 mm | Without ulceration |
| T4b | Over 4.0 mm | With ulceration |

## How to read it

There are four thickness cutoffs to hold: 0.8 mm, 1.0 mm, 2.0 mm and 4.0 mm. The number after the T comes from thickness alone, so 1.0 mm or less is T1, over 1.0 up to 2.0 mm is T2, over 2.0 up to 4.0 mm is T3, and anything over 4.0 mm is T4.

The a and b suffixes come from ulceration, with a meaning without ulceration and b meaning with ulceration. That holds cleanly for T2, T3 and T4.

T1 is the exception worth memorizing. A melanoma under 0.8 mm is T1a without ulceration and T1b with it, but a melanoma from 0.8 to 1.0 mm is T1b with or without ulceration. So within T1 the suffix depends on thickness as well as ulceration, and 0.8 mm is the extra cutoff that exists nowhere else in the table.

Melanoma in situ is Tis, and both the thickness and ulceration columns read not applicable because there is no invasion to measure.

> Thickness sets the T number at cutoffs of 1.0, 2.0 and 4.0 mm, ulceration sets a versus b, and the one exception is that a 0.8 to 1.0 mm melanoma is T1b whether or not it is ulcerated.

Library: Mesenchymal and soft tissue neoplasms of skin: the categories
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Slide listing the mesenchymal and soft tissue neoplasm categories](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s69.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture sorts these by the tissue they come from, and then says there are countless others.

| Category | Examples given |
|---|---|
| Adipocytic | Lipoma, spindle cell / pleomorphic lipoma, liposarcoma and variants |
| Fibrohistiocytic | Dermatofibroma, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) |
| Neural | Neurofibroma, plexiform neurofibroma, granular cell tumour |
| Vascular | Hemangioma with many variants, Kaposi sarcoma, angiosarcoma |
| Muscle | Leiomyoma, leiomyosarcoma |
| Unknown or undifferentiated | Atypical fibroxanthoma (AFX), pleomorphic dermal sarcoma |

Of this list the lecture then develops only three in detail: dermatofibroma, neurofibroma and hemangioma.

> Cutaneous mesenchymal neoplasms are grouped as adipocytic, fibrohistiocytic, neural, vascular, muscle, and undifferentiated, and the lecture develops dermatofibroma, neurofibroma and hemangioma from that list.

Library: Dermatofibroma
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photograph of a firm brown papule and the dimple produced by lateral compression](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s71.jpg)

## Identify it

- A firm papule or nodule, tan to brown
- Squeezing the skin from the sides pulls the lesion inward instead of pushing it up, producing the dimple sign
- Microscopically a spindle cell proliferation in the dermis with collagen trapped at the edges

## Key features

- Very common
- Leg is the most common site
- Firm papule or nodule, tan to brown
- Variably cellular proliferation of spindle cells in the dermis
- Peripheral collagen trapping
- Possibly an exaggerated healing response

> A dermatofibroma is a firm tan to brown papule, most often on the leg, made of dermal spindle cells that trap collagen at the periphery, and it dimples inward on lateral compression.

Library: Neurofibroma
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photograph of numerous soft skin-coloured papules beside a micrograph of wavy spindle cells](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s73.jpg)

## Identify it

- A soft, skin coloured papule, often many of them
- Microscopically bland pink spindled cells with wavy nuclei in a pale pink stroma

## Key features

- Very common
- Most are sporadic
- Numerous lesions are associated with neurofibromatosis
- Benign behaviour
- Rare subtypes can progress to malignancy, usually in NF1 patients, specifically the diffuse type and the plexiform type

The number of lesions is the clinical signal. One is usually sporadic, many suggest neurofibromatosis.

> A neurofibroma is a soft skin-coloured papule of bland wavy spindle cells, usually sporadic and benign, but numerous lesions suggest neurofibromatosis and the diffuse and plexiform subtypes can progress to malignancy in NF1.

Library: Hemangioma and its clinical variants
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Clinical photographs of several vascular lesions beside micrographs of lobular vascular proliferations](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s76.jpg)

## Identify it

- Clinically red to blue papules or nodules
- Microscopically lobules of capillaries filled with red cells

## Key features

- Very common
- Grossly red to blue
- Presents as papules or nodules
- Has many clinical variants

## Variants named in the lecture

- Congenital hemangioma
- Pyogenic granuloma, also called lobular capillary hemangioma
- Cherry hemangioma
- Infantile hemangioma

> Hemangiomas are very common red to blue vascular papules and nodules with many variants, including congenital, infantile, cherry, and pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary hemangioma).

Library: Adnexal neoplasms: scope and the few worth knowing
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Cutaneous Neoplasms

![Slide listing the three adnexal neoplasms worth recognizing](library/images/msk-week-14/neo-s83.jpg)

## Key features

Adnexal neoplasms arise from the three adnexal structures: hair follicles, sweat glands and sebaceous glands. The lecture lists dozens of them and then tells you explicitly not to learn the details.

- Relatively uncommon to rare
- Know that they exist
- Do not worry about the details
- In general most are benign, and the malignant versions are exceptionally rare

## The three it says you may actually see

| Neoplasm | What to know |
|---|---|
| Pilomatricoma | Benign, almost always on the head and neck in children |
| Syringoma | Benign, usually tiny papules around the eyes |
| Sebaceous tumours | Can be sporadic, head and neck, elderly |

Sebaceous tumours carry one association worth keeping. They are linked to Muir-Torre syndrome, a variant of Lynch syndrome caused by germline mutations in the microsatellite instability genes MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2. The lecture says to test for it when sebaceous tumours are multiple, occur off the head and neck, or occur at a younger age (under 65).

> Adnexal neoplasms are mostly benign and not worth memorizing in detail, but sebaceous tumours should prompt testing for Muir-Torre syndrome when they are multiple, off the head and neck, or in a patient under 65.

Library: Non-bullous impetigo: presentation and causes
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing non-bullous impetigo with thick honey-colored crusts on the face, alongside the causative organisms and treatment](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s02.jpg)

## Identify it

- Thick, honey-colored crusts
- Irregular margins
- Usually on exposed skin, often the face

## Key features

The name comes from the Latin *impetere*, meaning to attack. Most cases are caused by *Staphylococcus aureus*, some by *Streptococcus pyogenes*, and some by both organisms together.

It's common wherever socioeconomic conditions are poor, and poor hygiene is a contributing factor. The lecture also notes an association with scabies (*Sarcoptes*), where the excoriated burrows give bacteria a way in.

> Non-bullous impetigo is the honey-crusted one, and *S. aureus* is the most common cause, with *S. pyogenes* or both organisms also possible.

Library: Non-bullous impetigo: treatment
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing the topical and systemic treatment of non-bullous impetigo split by number of lesions and by MSSA or MRSA](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s02.jpg)

## Key features

Treatment splits on how many lesions there are.

| Extent | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Few lesions | Mupirocin, retapamulin, or fusidic acid, all protein synthesis inhibitors |
| Many lesions | Culture first, then treat systemically |

For the systemic route the choice follows the culture:

- MSSA: amoxicillin/clavulanate or a first generation cephalosporin
- MRSA: clindamycin or TMP/SMX

Whatever else is done, the crusts are soaked or scrubbed away with a soft brush.

> Few lesions get a topical protein synthesis inhibitor, many lesions get cultured and treated systemically with the MSSA or MRSA regimen.

Library: Bullous impetigo: presentation and mechanism
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing bullous impetigo with flaccid bullae and denuded skin, with the toxin mechanism below](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s03.jpg)

## Identify it

- Flaccid bullae that rupture to leave moist denuded areas
- No honey-colored crust, which is what separates it from the non-bullous form
- 90 percent of cases are in infants and children

## Key features

The cause is *S. aureus*, specifically phage group II, type 71. It produces exfoliating toxins A, B and D, and those toxins cleave desmoglein-1. Cleaving desmoglein-1 means keratinocytes lose their adhesion to each other, so the epidermis splits and a blister forms.

On biopsy the split sits high in the epidermis with neutrophils collecting in the blister cavity, which is what the slide labels as loss of keratinocyte adhesion.

> Bullous impetigo is *S. aureus* phage group II type 71 making exfoliating toxins that cleave desmoglein-1, and unlike the non-bullous form it has no honey crust.

Library: Bullous impetigo: treatment
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing the parenteral and oral treatment of bullous impetigo split by MSSA and MRSA](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s03.jpg)

## Key features

The slide gives two treatment columns, one parenteral and one oral, each split by whether the organism is methicillin sensitive or resistant.

| | MSSA | MRSA |
|---|---|---|
| Parenteral | Nafcillin, ampicillin/sulbactam, clindamycin | Ceftaroline, vancomycin |
| Oral | Dicloxacillin | Doxycycline, TMP/SMX, clindamycin |

Clindamycin shows up on both the MSSA and the MRSA side, which is worth remembering when a single agent has to cover both possibilities.

> Bullous impetigo is treated by route and by resistance: nafcillin or dicloxacillin for MSSA, and vancomycin, ceftaroline, doxycycline, TMP/SMX or clindamycin for MRSA.

Library: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing a child with widespread superficial epidermal detachment and sheeting of skin](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s04.jpg)

## Identify it

- Widespread superficial exfoliation, with the epithelium detaching and shedding in sheets
- Mucosa is spared

## Key features

Also called Ritter's disease. Exfoliative toxins A and B, produced by about 5 percent of *S. aureus* strains, digest the adhesive protein holding keratinocytes together, so adhesion falls and the epidermis separates.

What makes this different from bullous impetigo is where the toxin acts. In SSSS a remote colonization or infection disseminates the toxin hematogenously, so exfoliation appears far from the site of infection and covers a wide area. Sparing of the mucosa is a defining feature.

> SSSS is toxin spread through the bloodstream from a remote staph infection, producing widespread epidermal detachment that spares the mucosa.

Library: Exfoliative toxins and loss of keratinocyte adhesion
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing staphylococcal exfoliative toxin causing epithelium to detach and shed, with widespread exfoliation sparing the mucosa](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s04.jpg)

## Key features

Two conditions in this lecture share one mechanism, and the difference between them is how far the toxin travels.

| | Bullous impetigo | Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome |
|---|---|---|
| Toxins | Exfoliating toxins A, B, D | Exfoliative toxins A and B |
| Strain | Phage group II, type 71 | About 5 percent of strains |
| Target | Cleaves desmoglein-1 | Digests adhesive protein |
| Spread | Local, at the site of infection | Hematogenous from a remote site |
| Extent | Localized bullae | Widespread exfoliation, mucosa spared |

> Both bullous impetigo and SSSS come from staphylococcal exfoliative toxin attacking keratinocyte adhesion, but only SSSS spreads the toxin through the blood to produce widespread disease.

Library: Ecthyma
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing ecthyma with punched-out crusted ulcers surrounded by edema](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s05.jpg)

## Identify it

- Circular, punched-out ulcers with crust
- Surrounding edema
- Begins as vesicles at the site of insect bites or trauma, which rupture to form the ulcers

## Key features

The name comes from the Greek *ekthuma*, to break out in a rush. The organisms are *S. pyogenes* (the lecture marks this one as the main cause) and *S. aureus*, or both together.

The feature that separates ecthyma from impetigo is depth. Ecthyma goes deeper, and because it does, it heals with scars.

## Treatment

- Frequent warm soaks to remove crusts
- Few lesions: mupirocin
- Many lesions: amoxicillin/clavulanate, dicloxacillin, or clindamycin if MRSA is a concern

> Ecthyma is deeper than impetigo, which is why it scars, and it starts as vesicles at bite or trauma sites that rupture into circular ulcers.

Library: Erysipelas: presentation and predisposing conditions
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing erysipelas as a well-demarcated erythematous plaque on the lower leg with peau d'orange surface change](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s06.jpg)

## Identify it

- Well-demarcated, raised, erythematous plaque, often with bleb formation
- Peau d'orange surface, the dimpled orange-peel look
- Lower extremities in 85 percent of cases
- Often recurrent

## Key features

The name is Greek, from *erythros* (red) plus *pella* (skin). It's an epidermal infection, which is why the border is so sharply defined. Fever and chills are common.

Predisposing conditions are obesity, venous insufficiency, lymphedema, and intravenous drug use.

> Erysipelas is the sharply demarcated, peau d'orange plaque of the lower leg, and the sharp border reflects its epidermal depth.

Library: Erysipelas: organism and treatment
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing erysipelas with its Gram stains and the penicillin G and vancomycin options](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s06.jpg)

## Key features

*Streptococcus pyogenes* is the cause, and penicillin G is the treatment.

There's one exception the lecture singles out. Facial erysipelas can be caused by *S. aureus*, which is rare, and that case is treated with vancomycin rather than penicillin.

| Site | Usual organism | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Lower extremity (85 percent) | *S. pyogenes* | Penicillin G |
| Face | *S. aureus*, rarely | Vancomycin |

> Erysipelas is a penicillin G disease because it's *S. pyogenes*, except on the face, where rare *S. aureus* cases call for vancomycin.

Library: Lymphangitis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing lymphangitis as a red streak running proximally up the forearm with tender lymphadenopathy](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s07.jpg)

## Identify it

- A red streak running proximally from the site of infection
- Tender lymphadenopathy at the draining nodes
- Fever, chills and malaise

## Key features

*Streptococcus pyogenes* is the usual organism. Blood cultures are part of the workup, because the infection is tracking through lymphatics and can seed the bloodstream.

## Empirical treatment by severity

| Severity | Agent |
|---|---|
| Mildly ill | Penicillin V |
| Moderately ill | Ceftriaxone |
| Severely ill | Vancomycin or ceftaroline |

> The red streak with tender nodes is lymphangitis, usually *S. pyogenes*, and empirical therapy escalates from penicillin V to ceftriaxone to vancomycin or ceftaroline with severity.

Library: Furuncles and carbuncles
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing furuncles and carbuncles as tender fluctuant nodules containing pus](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s08.jpg)

## Identify it

- Tender, fluctuant nodule containing pus
- Fever, chills and systemic toxicity may or may not be present
- A carbuncle is the larger coalescing version, often on the posterior neck

## Key features

*S. aureus* is the cause and the majority are MRSA, which drives the antibiotic choice.

The lecture flags a mimic worth knowing: patients often present convinced they have a brown recluse spider bite, when what they actually have is a staphylococcal abscess.

## Treatment

- Warm soaks, then incision and drainage, which is the core of treatment
- Mildly ill: doxycycline, TMP/SMX, or clindamycin
- Moderately to severely ill: vancomycin or ceftaroline

> Furuncles and carbuncles are mostly MRSA, they're treated primarily by incision and drainage, and they're the lesion commonly mistaken for a brown recluse bite.

Library: Hidradenitis suppurativa: who gets it and what it looks like
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing hidradenitis suppurativa in the axilla with nodules, scarring and sinus tracts](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s09.jpg)

## Identify it

- Subcutaneous abscesses in apocrine-bearing skin, the axillae and groin above all
- Nodules, scarring and sinus tracts in established disease

## Key features

Women are affected far more often than men, and the lecture notes it's especially common in African-American women. Onset is at puberty.

The infection is mixed rather than caused by a single organism. The lecture frames it as dysbiosis, with Gram-positive aerobes and anaerobes together with Gram-negative anaerobes, and the flora differing from normal skin flora.

> Hidradenitis suppurativa starts at puberty, affects women far more than men, and is a mixed dysbiotic infection rather than a single-organism one.

Library: Hidradenitis suppurativa: follicular occlusion and the inflammatory cascade
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing the pathogenesis of hidradenitis suppurativa from follicular hyperkeratosis through rupture to chronic inflammation](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s10.jpg)

## Key features

The sequence the lecture gives runs in one direction, and each step causes the next.

1. Follicular hyperkeratosis
2. Hair follicle occlusion and hyperkeratosis
3. Accumulation of debris, including proteins, lipids, steroids and mixed flora
4. Dilation of the follicle and then rupture
5. Dysregulated immune response
6. Peri-folliculitis
7. Abscess, and with chronicity, scarring and sinus tracts

TNF alpha and IL-17A are increased, driven through the inflammasome. Those two cytokines are why a TNF alpha blocker works in severe disease.

Note that the problem starts in the follicle, not in the apocrine gland, even though the disease sits in apocrine-bearing skin.

> Hidradenitis suppurativa begins with follicular hyperkeratosis and occlusion, and the follicle's rupture is what triggers the inflammatory cascade that raises TNF alpha and IL-17A.

Library: Hidradenitis suppurativa: risk factors
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide listing obesity, smoking, familial tendency and skin dysbiosis as risk factors for hidradenitis suppurativa](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s11.jpg)

## Key features

- Obesity, which raises pro-inflammatory adipokines
- Smoking, where nicotine receptors in keratinocytes drive cell growth
- A familial tendency, possibly autosomal dominant, with loss-of-function mutations
- Skin dysbiosis and biofilm formation

Each of these connects back to the pathogenesis: adipokines and nicotine feed the inflammation and the hyperkeratosis, and dysbiosis supplies the mixed flora that accumulates behind the occluded follicle.

> The four risk factors are obesity, smoking, a familial tendency, and skin dysbiosis with biofilm formation.

Library: Hidradenitis suppurativa: stages I to III and their treatment
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing the three stages of hidradenitis suppurativa with their medical and surgical treatment](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s12.jpg)

## Identify it

- Stage I: nodules, with no scarring and no fistulae
- Stage II: recurrent abscesses and sinus tracts, with widely separated lesions
- Stage III: diffuse lesions with interconnected sinus tracts and abscesses

## Treatment by stage

| Stage | Medical | Surgical |
|---|---|---|
| I | Topical clindamycin twice daily or tetracycline twice daily for 12 weeks | Excision of localized or recurrent nodules or abscesses |
| II | Tetracycline twice daily for 12 weeks | Excision of sinus tracts |
| III | Clindamycin plus rifampin twice daily, or a TNF alpha blocker (adalimumab), for 12 weeks | Radical wide excision of apocrine sweat gland areas |

The medical course is 12 weeks at every stage. What changes with stage is the agent and how much tissue the surgery takes.

> Scarring and sinus tracts are what move a patient past stage I, and interconnection of those tracts is what defines stage III and brings in adalimumab and radical excision.

Library: Cellulitis: depth, organisms and empirical therapy
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing cellulitis with diffuse erythema and swelling, and the organisms and empirical treatment](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s14.jpg)

## Identify it

- Diffuse erythema and swelling with indistinct borders, unlike the sharp edge of erysipelas
- Infection reaching the deep dermis and fat

## Key features

| Organism | Setting | Empirical therapy |
|---|---|---|
| *S. pyogenes* | Most cases | Intravenous penicillin G |
| *S. aureus* | Penetrating trauma, paranasal infection | Vancomycin |

Supportive measures matter here: elevation to reduce edema, and moist heat for pain relief.

The depth is the point of comparison with erysipelas. Erysipelas is epidermal and sharply demarcated, cellulitis extends into the deep dermis and fat and has a vague border.

> Cellulitis is a deep dermis and fat infection, usually *S. pyogenes* treated with penicillin G, with *S. aureus* and vancomycin after penetrating trauma or paranasal infection.

Library: Cellulitis after injury in bodies of water
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing cellulitis following water exposure with the fresh water and salt water organisms and their treatment](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s15.jpg)

## Key features

Water exposure changes the organism, and which water it was changes it again.

| Water | Organism | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Fresh water | *Aeromonas hydrophila* | Fluoroquinolone |
| Salt water | *Vibrio vulnificus* | Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline |

Gram stain and cultures are taken in both cases.

The lecture attaches a particular patient to the salt water side: the patient with cirrhosis who presents with a septic picture. That combination of cirrhosis, salt water exposure and rapid sepsis is the classic *Vibrio vulnificus* setup.

> Fresh water points to *Aeromonas hydrophila* and a fluoroquinolone, salt water in a cirrhotic patient points to *Vibrio vulnificus* and ceftriaxone plus doxycycline.

Library: Pre-septal periorbital cellulitis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing pre-septal periorbital cellulitis in a toddler with eyelid swelling and erythema](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s17.jpg)

## Identify it

- Infection anterior to the orbital septum
- The eyes still move
- Not sight threatening and not life threatening

## Key features

It occurs mostly in infants and toddlers, and in adults it tends to follow an insect bite.

Organisms are *Haemophilus influenzae*, *S. aureus*, and *Streptococcus*. Treatment is vancomycin plus piperacillin/tazobactam.

The single most useful bedside discriminator is eye movement, because the orbital septum is what keeps the infection out of the orbit and away from the extraocular muscles.

> Pre-septal disease sits anterior to the orbital septum, so the eyes still move and neither sight nor life is threatened.

Library: Post-septal periorbital cellulitis
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing post-septal periorbital cellulitis with proptosis and orbital congestion](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s18.jpg)

## Identify it

- Infection posterior to the orbital septum
- Proptosis and orbital congestion
- The eyes don't move
- Life threatening and sight threatening

## Key features

The source is the paranasal sinuses, especially the ethmoid, which sits immediately medial to the orbit.

Organisms are *S. aureus*, *S. pyogenes* and *S. pneumoniae*. Treatment is vancomycin plus piperacillin/tazobactam, the same regimen as the pre-septal form, so the urgency rather than the drug is what changes.

> Post-septal disease gives proptosis and frozen eye movement, usually spreads from the ethmoid sinus, and threatens both sight and life.

Library: Periorbital cellulitis from Haemophilus influenzae
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing a child with marked periorbital swelling and violaceous discoloration from Haemophilus influenzae cellulitis](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s16.jpg)

## Identify it

- Marked periorbital swelling
- Violaceous or dusky discoloration of the involved lid and surrounding skin

## Key features

*Haemophilus influenzae* is one of the three organisms the lecture lists for pre-septal periorbital cellulitis, alongside *S. aureus* and *Streptococcus*, and it's the one it illustrates separately.

> *Haemophilus influenzae* periorbital cellulitis presents with swelling and a violaceous discoloration around the eye.

Library: Cellulitis mimics: gout and pyoderma gangrenosum
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide comparing gout and pyoderma gangrenosum as conditions that can be mistaken for cellulitis](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s19.jpg)

## Identify it

- Gout: hot, red, swollen joint, typically at the great toe, which can look like cellulitis of the forefoot
- Pyoderma gangrenosum: painful skin ulcers with undermined borders and surrounding erythema

## Key features

Pyoderma gangrenosum is a rare neutrophilic dermatosis. Its association worth remembering is with inflammatory bowel disease, so a chronic leg ulcer that hasn't responded to repeated antibiotic courses in a patient with Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis points here rather than to infection.

The undermined border is the physical sign that separates it from an infected ulcer.

> Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis producing painful ulcers with undermined borders, associated with inflammatory bowel disease and unresponsive to antibiotics.

Library: Cellulitis mimics: Sweet syndrome
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing Sweet syndrome with tender erythematous plaques on the face](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s20.jpg)

## Identify it

- Acute onset of tender plaques or nodules
- Fever

## Key features

The full name is acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, and it's rare. Beyond the skin lesions and fever it can bring arthralgia, ophthalmologic manifestations, headaches, and rarely oral or genital lesions.

Its associations are with cancer, autoimmune disorders, and gastrointestinal infections.

Like pyoderma gangrenosum it's a neutrophilic dermatosis, which is why both sit on the cellulitis differential: they produce hot, tender, inflamed skin without an organism to treat.

> Sweet syndrome is acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, with abruptly appearing tender plaques and fever, associated with cancer, autoimmune disease and GI infections.

Library: Herpetic whitlow
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing herpetic whitlow with grouped vesicles on the distal finger around the nail](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s21.jpg)

## Identify it

- Grouped vesicles on the distal finger, clustered around the nail bed
- Pain, tenderness and paresthesias
- Recurrent, which is the feature that gives it away

## Key features

HSV 2 is the most common cause now. The history to look for is exposure to a person with HSV, which is why healthcare workers show up in these vignettes.

Treatment is valacyclovir.

Recurrence in the same digit is the discriminator against a staphylococcal paronychia, which doesn't recur at the same site in the same way.

> Recurrent grouped vesicles on one fingertip is herpetic whitlow, most often HSV 2 now, treated with valacyclovir.

Library: Necrotizing fasciitis type I
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing type I necrotizing fasciitis with extensive perineal necrosis and a Gram stain of mixed flora](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s22.jpg)

## Identify it

- Extensive necrosis, often of the abdomen or perineum
- Gram stain shows mixed flora

## Key features

Type I is a mixed infection, defined as one anaerobe (for example *Bacteroides*) together with one or more facultative anaerobes (for example *E. coli*).

It's most common in immunocompromised patients, with diabetes given as the example, and it often complicates abdominal or perineal surgery.

The mixed flora on Gram stain is the finding that assigns a case to type I rather than to the single-organism types.

> Type I necrotizing fasciitis is a mixed anaerobe plus facultative anaerobe infection of the immunocompromised, typically after abdominal or perineal surgery, with mixed flora on Gram stain.

Library: Fournier gangrene
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing Fournier gangrene with scrotal erythema, edema and necrosis](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s23.jpg)

## Identify it

- Erythema, edema and then necrosis of the scrotum and perineum

## Key features

Fournier gangrene is a variant of type I necrotizing fasciitis, so it carries the same mixed flora on Gram stain.

What defines it is the route of spread. It moves rapidly along Buck's fascia, the dartos, Colle's fascia and Scarpa's fascia, which is how an infection that starts in the perineum reaches the abdominal wall.

It complicates trauma, perirectal infections, and urethral rupture, especially in diabetics.

> Fournier gangrene is type I necrotizing fasciitis spreading through Buck's, dartos, Colle's and Scarpa's fascia, typically in a diabetic after perineal trauma, perirectal infection or urethral rupture.

Library: Necrotizing fasciitis type I: management
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing intraoperative wide debridement of necrotizing fasciitis](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s24.jpg)

## Key features

Three things happen, and the order matters.

1. Aerobic and anaerobic cultures are taken, from both the wound and the blood
2. Empirical antibiotics are chosen based on the Gram stain, then adjusted once culture results return
3. Emergency wide debridement

The slide shows the carbapenems with meropenem circled, so meropenem is the agent the lecture points to once the Gram stain shows mixed flora.

The debridement is the part that saves the patient. Antibiotics alone don't reach necrotic tissue with no blood supply, which is why the surgery is described as emergency and wide rather than conservative.

> Type I necrotizing fasciitis is managed by wound and blood cultures, Gram stain directed empirical antibiotics with meropenem, and emergency wide debridement.

Library: Necrotizing fasciitis type II
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing type II necrotizing fasciitis with dusky violaceous skin and bullae on the arm](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s25.jpg)

## Identify it

- Dusky violaceous skin with bullae over an extremity
- Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in chains

## Key features

Type II is *S. pyogenes*, a single organism rather than a mixture.

The patient profile is the opposite of type I. These are previously healthy persons, and the setting is a traumatic wound, typically of the extremities.

## Treatment

Penicillin G plus clindamycin, alongside surgical debridement. The lecture shows both drugs together with a plus sign rather than offering a choice between them.

> Type II necrotizing fasciitis is *S. pyogenes* in a previously healthy person after a traumatic wound to an extremity, treated with penicillin G plus clindamycin.

Library: Necrotizing fasciitis type III
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing type III necrotizing fasciitis with the two water-associated organisms and their treatment](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s27.jpg)

## Identify it

- Necrosis of a limb after water exposure
- Gram stain shows Gram-negative rods

## Key features

Type III covers the two water organisms, and each has its own regimen.

| Organism | Treatment |
|---|---|
| *Vibrio vulnificus* | Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline |
| *Aeromonas hydrophila* | Fluoroquinolone |

These are the same two organisms that cause the water-exposure cellulitis earlier in the lecture, which is worth noticing: the organism is determined by the exposure, and the depth of invasion determines whether it presents as cellulitis or as necrotizing fasciitis.

> Type III necrotizing fasciitis is *Vibrio vulnificus* or *Aeromonas hydrophila*, both Gram-negative rods, treated with ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or a fluoroquinolone respectively.

Library: Necrotizing fasciitis type IV
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing type IV necrotizing fasciitis with an extensive necrotic wound and a Gram stain of clustered cocci](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s28.jpg)

## Identify it

- Extensive necrotic wound
- Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in grape-like clusters

## Key features

Type IV is community-acquired MRSA.

Treatment is ceftaroline or vancomycin, the same two agents that cover MRSA elsewhere in this lecture, and clindamycin is added to whichever of those two is chosen. The slide sets it out as ceftaroline or vancomycin, plus clindamycin.

> Type IV necrotizing fasciitis is community-acquired MRSA, clusters on Gram stain, treated with ceftaroline or vancomycin plus clindamycin.

Library: Necrotizing fasciitis type V
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing type V necrotizing fasciitis with limb swelling and a Gram stain of Gram-negative rods](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s29.jpg)

## Identify it

- Dusky, swollen limb
- Gram stain shows plump Gram-negative rods

## Key features

Type V is *Klebsiella pneumoniae*.

The patient is immunocompromised, and the lecture gives diabetes and cirrhosis as the examples. That overlaps with type I's patient, so the Gram stain does the separating: mixed flora points to type I, pure Gram-negative rods point to type V.

## Treatment

Ertapenem. The slide shows the carbapenems with ertapenem circled, which is a different member of the class from the meropenem circled for type I.

> Type V necrotizing fasciitis is *Klebsiella pneumoniae* in an immunocompromised patient such as a diabetic or a cirrhotic, treated with ertapenem.

Library: The five types of necrotizing fasciitis compared
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

## Key features

| Type | Organism | Patient and setting | Gram stain | Treatment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | Mixed, one anaerobe plus one or more facultative anaerobes | Immunocompromised, abdominal or perineal surgery | Mixed flora | Meropenem, guided by the Gram stain |
| II | *S. pyogenes* | Previously healthy, traumatic wound of an extremity | Gram-positive cocci in chains | Penicillin G plus clindamycin |
| III | *Vibrio vulnificus* or *Aeromonas hydrophila* | Water exposure | Gram-negative rods | Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline, or a fluoroquinolone |
| IV | Community-acquired MRSA | Not specified in the lecture | Gram-positive cocci in clusters | Ceftaroline or vancomycin, plus clindamycin |
| V | *Klebsiella pneumoniae* | Immunocompromised, diabetes or cirrhosis | Gram-negative rods | Ertapenem |

Every type gets emergency wide debridement as well, since antibiotics can't reach tissue that has lost its blood supply.

The lecture labels the Gram stain on each type's own slide, which is where this column comes from. It narrows the possibilities rather than settling them on its own. Types I and V both occur in immunocompromised patients and are separated by the stain, while types III and V both show Gram-negative rods and are separated by the exposure history.

> Mixed flora points to type I, chains to type II and clusters to type IV, while Gram-negative rods leave types III and V to be told apart by whether there was water exposure.

Library: Gas gangrene: organism and predisposing factors
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing Clostridium perfringens as the cause of gas gangrene with a Gram stain of large Gram-positive rods](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s30.jpg)

## Identify it

- Gram stain shows large, boxcar-shaped Gram-positive rods

## Key features

*Clostridium perfringens* causes about 80 percent of cases.

The predisposing factors the lecture gives are trauma and surgery, which is consistent with an organism that needs devitalized, anaerobic tissue to grow in.

> Gas gangrene is *Clostridium perfringens* in 80 percent of cases, following trauma or surgery.

Library: Gas gangrene: clinical findings
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing gas gangrene findings with brick-red non-contracting muscle exposed at surgery](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s32.jpg)

## Identify it

- Brick-red muscle that doesn't contract
- Massive edema
- Hypotension, anxiety and fever

## Key features

The muscle findings are what the surgeon sees on opening the compartment, and the two of them together are diagnostic: the color change plus the loss of contraction on stimulation.

The massive edema isn't incidental. It compromises blood flow, which extends the anaerobic environment the organism needs and pushes the process further along.

Palpable crepitus from gas in the tissues, along with cutaneous anesthesia and skin that doesn't compress easily, is the bedside picture that should bring gas gangrene to mind in a patient who is febrile and toxic after a penetrating wound.

## Management

Penicillin G plus clindamycin, together with surgery. The lecture's management slide poses the drug choice as a question and answers it with the two structures side by side, and the accompanying photograph shows a closed amputation stump, which is how far the surgery sometimes has to go.

> Brick-red muscle that doesn't contract, with massive edema compromising blood flow, is the operative finding in gas gangrene, and it's managed with penicillin G plus clindamycin and surgery.

Library: Brown recluse envenomation
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

![Slide showing a brown recluse spider and the necrotic lesion with dry eschar that follows its bite](library/images/msk-week-14/ssti-s35.jpg)

## Identify it

- Pain increasing over a few hours
- A necrotic lesion forming, then a dry eschar at 24 to 48 hours

## Key features

The spider is *Loxosceles reclusa*. Its venom contains enzymes, and the lecture names sphingomyelinase as the one responsible for the tissue destruction.

## Treatment

- Pain control
- Elevation
- Cold packs
- Dapsone
- Antibiotics only if there's a secondary infection

That last point matters, because the lesion looks infected and isn't. The reverse error appears earlier in the lecture: patients who think they have a spider bite usually have a staphylococcal abscess, so the suspicion runs in both directions.

> Brown recluse venom contains sphingomyelinase, the bite progresses from hours of increasing pain to a dry eschar at 24 to 48 hours, and antibiotics are reserved for secondary infection.

Library: Urticaria: wheals and the under 24 hour rule
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Lecture slide defining urticaria, listing pruritic wheals, the evanescent nature of each lesion, and the mast cell mechanism](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s02.jpg)

## Identify it

- Pruritic wheals that are pink or pale flesh-colored
- Each individual lesion is evanescent, lasting less than 24 hours

## Key features

The defining feature of urticaria isn't the look of any one wheal, it's how long that wheal lasts. The lecture's rule is that an individual lesion resolves in under 24 hours, which is why the useful bedside maneuver is to circle a single wheal and come back to it. New lesions appear elsewhere while the circled one fades, so the eruption as a whole can persist for weeks even though no single lesion does.

> An individual urticarial wheal lasts less than 24 hours, and circling one lesion is how you prove it.

Library: Urticaria: annular and arcuate configurations
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Clinical photograph on a lecture slide showing ring-shaped and arc-shaped wheals, captioned as annular or arcuate urticaria](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s03.jpg)

## Identify it

- Wheals can take a ring shape (annular) or an incomplete arc (arcuate)
- Lesions expand outward and can run together into polycyclic shapes
- The circled lesion in the slide demonstrates the under 24 hour rule

## Key features

Configuration varies a great deal in urticaria, and the lecture's point is that an annular or arcuate shape doesn't take you away from the diagnosis. The shape is a distraction, and the time course is the test.

> Annular and arcuate shapes are still urticaria, because configuration doesn't change the under 24 hour rule.

Library: Urticaria: mast cell degranulation and the vascular sequence
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

## Key features

The lecture gives urticaria a single mechanical chain, and it's worth holding in that order because each step explains the next.

1. Mast cell degranulation
2. Release of histamine and heparin
3. Increased capillary permeability
4. Fluid extravasation into tissue

That last step is the wheal. Fluid has moved out of the vessels and into the dermis, which is also why the lesion can resolve so quickly once the mediator release stops, since the fluid simply reabsorbs.

> Urticaria is mast cell degranulation releasing histamine and heparin, which raises capillary permeability and drives fluid into the tissue.

Library: Urticaria histopathology: dermal edema separating collagen
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Micrograph on a lecture slide of urticaria showing dermal edema separating collagen bundles with a perivascular infiltrate](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s04.jpg)

## Identify it

- Dermal edema that pushes the collagen bundles apart from one another
- A perivascular infiltrate around the dermal vessels
- Neutrophils and eosinophils within that infiltrate

## Key features

The histology follows directly from the mechanism. Fluid driven out of permeable capillaries collects in the dermis, and under the microscope that fluid shows itself as widened clear spaces between collagen bundles that would normally sit tightly together. The epidermis is not the site of action here, which separates urticaria from the spongiotic and interface patterns elsewhere in this block.

> Urticaria is a dermal process: edema separates collagen bundles and a perivascular infiltrate containing neutrophils and eosinophils sits around the vessels.

Library: Acute, chronic, and physical urticaria
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Lecture slide listing the urticaria variants with their time cutoffs and triggers](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s05.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture sorts urticaria three ways, and the six week mark is the line between the first two.

| Variant | Definition | Triggers given |
|---|---|---|
| Acute | Less than 6 weeks | Drugs (penicillin, sulfa, aspirin, IV contrast); food (shellfish, nuts, strawberries); infections (strep) |
| Chronic | More than 6 weeks | Autoimmune, idiopathic |
| Physical | Provoked by a physical stimulus | Cold, solar, vibratory, exercise-induced |

Acute urticaria is where you go looking for an exposure, since that's the group with a named external trigger. Chronic urticaria mostly doesn't have one, and the lecture's two categories for it are autoimmune and idiopathic.

> Six weeks separates acute urticaria, which usually has an identifiable drug, food, or infectious trigger, from chronic urticaria, which is usually autoimmune or idiopathic.

Library: Urticaria treatment and anti-IgE biologics
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

## Key features

Treatment runs in three steps: avoidance of the trigger, long-acting antihistamines, and biologics.

The biologics named are omalizumab and ligelizumab. Both are IgG1 monoclonal antibodies, and both work on IgE rather than on the mast cell itself. They bind IgE and stop it from attaching to its high-affinity receptors on mast cells and basophils, so the cell never gets the signal to degranulate in the first place.

Holding that mechanism next to the one on the mast cell page is useful, because it shows the drug acting one step upstream of everything that produces the wheal.

> Omalizumab and ligelizumab are IgG1 monoclonal antibodies that bind IgE and block it from reaching its high-affinity receptors on mast cells and basophils.

Library: Time course of the three hypersensitivity mechanisms
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

## Key features

The lecture pairs each mechanism with the interval you'd expect between exposure and eruption, which makes the timing itself a diagnostic clue.

| Mechanism | Time course | Example given |
|---|---|---|
| IgE dependent | Minutes to 36 hours | Not specified |
| Direct action on mast cells or complement | Minutes to hours | Aspirin |
| Immune complex (serum sickness) | 4 to 12 days | Snake bite anti-venom |

The direct route matters clinically because it needs no prior sensitization, which is how a patient reacts to something on a first exposure. The immune complex route is the slow one, and a reaction arriving over a week after an exposure points there rather than at IgE.

> An eruption within minutes to hours fits IgE or direct mast cell activation, while one arriving 4 to 12 days later fits an immune complex (serum sickness) mechanism.

Library: Morbilliform drug reaction: macules and papules
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Clinical photographs on a lecture slide showing the macular and papular components of a morbilliform eruption, captioned as maculopapular](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s08.jpg)

## Identify it

- Blanchable macules, flat and discrete
- Papules, raised, mixed in among the macules
- Both components may run together into confluent areas

## Key features

Morbilliform and maculopapular describe the same eruption, and the word morbilliform means measles-like. The lesions are fixed rather than evanescent, which separates them from urticaria at the bedside even before you think about timing. The lecture's stated differential for this appearance is a viral exanthem.

Pathogenesis isn't entirely clear, though the lecture attributes it to T cell-mediated (type IV) immune reactions, and notes that virtually any drug can do it.

> Morbilliform means maculopapular and measles-like: blanchable macules and papules that are fixed rather than evanescent, and may become confluent.

Library: The well-appearing patient with a morbilliform eruption
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Clinical photograph on a lecture slide of a widespread morbilliform eruption in a patient captioned as not sick](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s09.jpg)

## Identify it

- Widespread eruption that can look alarming across the trunk
- The patient is comfortable and systemically well

## Key features

The lecture labels this slide "Not Sick" for a reason. A simple morbilliform drug reaction can cover a lot of skin while the patient remains perfectly well, and deaths from it are described as highly unlikely. That combination of extensive rash plus a well patient is the reassuring pattern.

The patients who look sick belong to a different diagnosis, which is where DRESS and the SJS/TEN group come in, so the systemic assessment is doing most of the triage work here rather than the extent of the rash.

> A simple morbilliform drug reaction can be extensive yet leave the patient systemically well, and deaths from it are highly unlikely.

Library: Morbilliform drug reaction: onset, duration, and rechallenge
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

## Key features

The behavior of a morbilliform reaction is less predictable than most students expect, and the lecture lists the ways it departs from the simple story.

- Onset is less than one week after starting the drug
- It lasts one to two weeks
- It can fade while the patient is still taking the drug
- It can appear shortly after the drug has been stopped
- It may not recur on re-challenge
- Rates are increased in the setting of viral infection, specifically mononucleosis and HIV

The one week onset is the number to anchor on, because the whole reason DRESS is dangerous is that it breaks this rule.

> A morbilliform drug reaction starts within one week of beginning the drug and lasts one to two weeks, and it can fade even while the drug is continued.

Library: Common drug offenders in hypersensitivity eruptions
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

## Key features

The lecture gives one short list of common offenders for morbilliform reactions.

- Penicillins
- Sulfonamides
- Phenytoin
- Carbamazepine
- Allopurinol

The same names keep reappearing as the lecture moves into the severe reactions, with anticonvulsants and sulfonamides driving DRESS, and sulfa antibiotics, seizure medications, NSAIDs and allopurinol driving SJS and TEN. Learning the list once pays off repeatedly.

> Penicillins, sulfonamides, phenytoin, carbamazepine, and allopurinol are the common offenders, and the anticonvulsants and sulfonamides on that list reappear as the drivers of DRESS and of SJS and TEN.

Library: DRESS: the late morbilliform eruption
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Lecture slide asking what begins as a simple maculopapular drug rash but appears late, 2 to 6 weeks after the culprit drug is started](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s12.jpg)

## Key features

DRESS stands for Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms, and the lecture introduces it by the way it imitates something harmless. It starts off looking like a simple maculopapular drug rash. What gives it away is when it arrives.

| Reaction | Interval from starting the drug |
|---|---|
| Simple morbilliform drug reaction | 1 to 2 weeks |
| DRESS | 2 to 6 weeks |

A morbilliform eruption appearing late, well past the window where you'd have stopped worrying, is the presentation the lecture wants recognized.

> A morbilliform eruption beginning 2 to 6 weeks after a drug was started is late for a simple drug rash and should raise DRESS.

Library: DRESS: mechanism and genetic risk
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

## Key features

DRESS is a T cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction, and the lecture lists three contributing factors that help explain why it strikes some patients and not others.

- HLA genetic risks
- A defect in drug detoxification
- Reactivation of HHV6 or another virus, which may occur

The drugs most associated with it are the anticonvulsants and the sulfonamides.

The viral reactivation point is worth noticing, because it means a drug reaction and a viral process can be running at once, which is part of why the illness drags on and why the diagnosis is difficult.

> DRESS is a T cell-mediated reaction with HLA genetic risk and impaired drug detoxification, classically from anticonvulsants or sulfonamides, and reactivation of HHV6 may occur.

Library: DRESS: facial edema, purpura, and systemic findings
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Clinical photographs on a lecture slide of a patient with facial swelling and of purpura on the forearms, captioned with fever, lymphadenopathy and abnormal labs](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s15.jpg)

## Identify it

- Facial edema, often striking enough to change the patient's appearance
- Purpura, which a simple morbilliform reaction does not produce
- Dermal edema underlying the swelling

## Key features

The lecture's blunt heading for these patients is that they look sick, which is the single most useful contrast with the well-appearing patient who has a simple morbilliform eruption.

Beyond the skin, the lecture lists fever, lymphadenopathy, and hepatitis, with eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes on the blood work. The eosinophilia is in the name of the syndrome.

> DRESS adds facial edema, purpura, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis, eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes to what otherwise looks like a morbilliform drug rash.

Library: DRESS: RegiSCAR scoring and treatment
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

## Key features

The lecture concedes that the diagnosis can be challenging, and points to the RegiSCAR scoring system as the structured way through it. Clinical and laboratory findings are each assigned points, and the total places a case into one of four categories: negative, possible, probable, or definitive.

Systemic corticosteroids are reserved for organ involvement. The lecture names the lung, the heart, acute kidney injury or failure, and a liver ALT transaminase greater than five times normal.

DRESS can be fatal, and the mechanism of death given is fulminant hepatitis with liver necrosis, which is why the transaminase threshold sits in the treatment criteria rather than only in the diagnostic ones.

> RegiSCAR scores clinical and lab findings into negative, possible, probable or definitive, and systemic corticosteroids are given for organ involvement including ALT greater than five times normal.

Library: Erythema multiforme: the three zone target
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Clinical photograph on a lecture slide of concentric target lesions, captioned as erythema multiforme targets](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s18.jpg)

## Identify it

- Targets built from three concentric zones
- Distribution is acral, on the distal extremities

## Key features

The three zone target is the lesion that defines erythema multiforme, and the acral distribution is the other half of the picture. Lesions concentrate on the distal extremities rather than appearing as a generalized trunk eruption, which is one of the features that separates EM from Stevens Johnson syndrome later in the lecture.

Note that the lecture repeatedly contrasts this true three zone target with the flat atypical targets of SJS, so it's worth fixing the real thing in mind first.

> Erythema multiforme is defined by three zone targets in an acral distribution on the distal extremities.

Library: Erythema multiforme minor versus major
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Clinical photographs on a lecture slide of acral targets with oral and genital mucosal involvement, captioned as erythema multiforme major with two or more mucosal sites](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s20.jpg)

## Identify it

- Minor: acral targets with one mucosal site
- Major: acral targets with two or more mucosal sites

## Key features

The split between minor and major is counted in mucosal sites, not in how much skin is involved. The lecture's slides make the count concrete, showing one mucosal site for minor and oral plus genital involvement for major.

The other thing the lecture insists on for EM major is the patient's condition. Its phrase is miserable, but not sick, and these patients are not usually hospitalized. That is the line that keeps EM major separate from SJS, where the patient genuinely is sick.

> Erythema multiforme minor has one mucosal site and major has two or more, and even EM major leaves the patient miserable but not sick and usually not hospitalized.

Library: Erythema multiforme: herpes simplex, MIRM, and RIME
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Lecture slide listing the features of erythema multiforme including its usual infectious trigger](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s17.jpg)

## Key features

Erythema multiforme usually follows an infection rather than a drug, and the trigger the lecture names is herpes simplex. That is the opposite emphasis from SJS and TEN, which are drug-induced, and it drives the treatment.

Two related named entities appear on the same slide:

- MIRM, Mycoplasma (pneumonia) Induced Rash and Mucositis
- RIME, Reactive Infectious Mucocutaneous Eruption

For treatment, when episodes are recurrent and related to HSV, the lecture's answer is suppressive oral antiviral therapy. You're preventing the trigger rather than treating the rash.

> Erythema multiforme usually has an infectious trigger, classically herpes simplex, and recurrent HSV-related episodes are managed with suppressive oral antiviral therapy.

Library: Stevens Johnson syndrome: flat atypical targets and purpuric blisters
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Clinical photograph on a lecture slide of widespread flat dusky macules over the trunk, captioned as atypical targets in Stevens Johnson syndrome](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s22.jpg)

## Identify it

- Flat atypical targets, lacking the three distinct concentric zones of true EM
- Generalized distribution rather than the acral one of erythema multiforme
- Blisters arising on purpuric macules
- Multiple mucosal sites

## Key features

Every morphologic feature here is a degraded version of erythema multiforme, which is what makes the pair confusable and what makes the contrast worth memorizing. The targets go flat and atypical, the distribution goes generalized, and the blisters sit on purpuric macules.

The decisive difference isn't morphologic at all. The lecture's one word description of the SJS patient is sick, against the miserable but not sick of EM major.

> Stevens Johnson syndrome shows flat atypical targets that are generalized rather than acral, with blisters on purpuric macules and multiple mucosal sites, in a patient who is sick.

Library: Stevens Johnson syndrome: mucosal sites and hemorrhagic crusted lips
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Clinical photographs on a lecture slide of thickly crusted hemorrhagic lips, captioned as the lips in Stevens Johnson syndrome](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s24.jpg)

## Identify it

- Thick hemorrhagic crust across the vermilion of the lips
- Involvement at more than one mucosal site

## Key features

The lecture gives the lips a slide of their own, titled simply "The Lips", and returns to the same finding again under TEN. Hemorrhagic crusted lips are the mucosal sign that travels with this whole severe end of the spectrum, and they are hard to miss on an exam photograph.

Multiple mucosal sites are part of the definition of SJS rather than an optional extra, which is worth separating from erythema multiforme where the mucosal count is what grades minor against major.

> Hemorrhagic crusted lips are the signature mucosal finding of Stevens Johnson syndrome, which involves multiple mucosal sites by definition.

Library: Drug triggers of Stevens Johnson syndrome
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

## Key features

Stevens Johnson syndrome is drug-induced, which is the cleanest single contrast with erythema multiforme and its infectious triggers. The lecture names four groups.

- Sulfa antibiotics
- Seizure medications
- NSAIDs
- Allopurinol

The same four reappear as the common offenders for toxic epidermal necrolysis, where the list is given as antibacterial sulfonamides, anticonvulsant agents, oxicam NSAIDs, and allopurinol. Treating SJS and TEN as one drug list is reasonable.

![Lecture slide posing a question about a patient with toxic epidermal necrolysis who filed a lawsuit, with one of the four possible claims marked by an arrow](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s35.jpg)

## Warning the patient before prescribing

The lecture closes this material with a case in which a patient who developed toxic epidermal necrolysis sued and was awarded a large sum of money. The claim that succeeded was not that his intensive care had been poor, and not that the drug had been given for an inappropriate indication. It was that he had never been told phenytoin could cause severe drug reactions.

Phenytoin sits on the common offender list beside carbamazepine, and anticonvulsants run through this entire lecture as triggers of DRESS, of Stevens Johnson syndrome, and of toxic epidermal necrolysis. The practical consequence is that starting an anticonvulsant carries a duty to warn the patient that a severe cutaneous reaction is possible, so that a developing rash is understood as a reason to seek help rather than something to sit out.

> Stevens Johnson syndrome is drug-induced, classically by sulfa antibiotics, seizure medications, NSAIDs or allopurinol, which is the reverse of the infectious trigger behind erythema multiforme.

Library: Toxic epidermal necrolysis and the body surface area thresholds
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Clinical photograph on a lecture slide of sheets of lost epidermis, captioned as SJS/TEN overlap with 10 to 30 percent epidermal loss](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s26.jpg)

## Identify it

- Acute epidermal necrosis with sheets of epidermis coming away
- Minimal dermal inflammation despite the dramatic surface
- Multiple mucosal sites
- A positive Nikolsky sign

## Key features

The three diagnoses in this group are separated by one number, the percentage of epidermal loss.

| Percentage of epidermal loss | Diagnosis |
|---|---|
| Less than 10 percent | SJS |
| 10 to 30 percent | SJS/TEN overlap |
| More than 30 percent | TEN |

Worth noticing that the thing being measured is epidermal loss, not redness, so the estimate is of skin that has detached or will detach, which is also why the Nikolsky sign matters for staging and not just for diagnosis.

> Epidermal loss under 10 percent is SJS, 10 to 30 percent is SJS/TEN overlap, and over 30 percent is toxic epidermal necrolysis.

Library: Toxic epidermal necrolysis: Nikolsky sign and the early course
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Clinical photograph on a lecture slide of gloved lateral traction shearing a sheet of epidermis off the skin, captioned as the Nikolsky sign on day 2](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s29.jpg)

## Identify it

- Day 1: a crop of fragile vesicles, all at the same stage of development
- Day 2: lateral traction shears the epidermis off, exposing red dermis
- Mucosal involvement, including the lips and tongue

## Key features

The lecture presents TEN as a two day sequence, and the pace is part of the diagnosis. On day one the blisters are fragile and uniform, all at the same stage of development, which separates them from eruptions that come in waves. By day two the epidermis has lost its attachment altogether, and sideways pressure on apparently intact skin slides it off. That is the Nikolsky sign.

> A positive Nikolsky sign means lateral traction shears the epidermis off intact-looking skin, and in TEN the day 1 vesicles are fragile and all at the same stage of development.

Library: Toxic epidermal necrolysis histopathology
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Micrographs on a lecture slide showing vacuolar change at the dermal epidermal junction and a subepidermal blister, captioned as interface vacuoles and necrotic keratinocytes](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s30.jpg)

## Identify it

- Interface vacuoles sitting at the dermal epidermal junction
- Necrotic keratinocytes scattered through the epidermis
- Basal cell damage
- A subepidermal blister, with the split beneath the whole epidermis

## Key features

The histology explains the clinical sign. Damage is concentrated at the basal layer and the interface, so the plane of separation forms underneath the entire epidermis rather than within it. A subepidermal split is exactly what allows a full sheet of epidermis to shear away under lateral traction.

The matching clinical description from the definition slide is acute epidermal necrosis with minimal dermal inflammation, and the micrographs bear that out: the action is at the junction, not deep in the dermis.

> TEN shows interface vacuoles, necrotic keratinocytes and basal cell damage producing a subepidermal blister, which is why whole sheets of epidermis detach.

Library: Toxic epidermal necrolysis: multisystem disease, sequelae, and care
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Clinical photograph on a lecture slide of extensive epidermal loss, captioned as TEN being a multisystem disease equivalent to a second degree burn](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s31.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture frames TEN as the equivalent of a second degree burn, and the systemic picture follows from that: high fever, hepatitis, CBC abnormalities, and mechanical ventilation in 10 to 20 percent of patients.

![Lecture slide listing the sequelae of toxic epidermal necrolysis alongside photographs of healed skin and mucosa](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s33.jpg)

Sequelae in survivors are extensive.

- Death in 30 percent
- Pigmentary disturbances
- Nail shedding
- Phimosis
- Esophageal strictures
- Persistent ocular lesions in 40 percent

Management follows the burn framing. Hospitalize and treat as a burn patient, but do not aggressively debride. Supportive care and an ophthalmology consult are specified, the latter because of that 40 percent figure for persistent eye disease. The lecture is explicit that there are no controlled treatment studies behind systemic steroids, cyclosporine, intravenous immunoglobulin, or TNF inhibitors.

Whatever else happens, the triggering drug must be avoided in future.

> TEN is managed like a second degree burn without aggressive debridement, carries 30 percent mortality and 40 percent persistent ocular lesions, and has no controlled treatment studies behind its systemic therapies.

Library: Fixed drug eruption: morphology and recurrence at the same site
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Clinical photographs on a lecture slide of a targetoid plaque with a bulla and of a dark plaque at a previously involved site, captioned as fixed drug eruption healing extremely dark](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s39.jpg)

## Identify it

- Round and sharply demarcated
- Erythematous and edematous while active, sometimes with a bulla
- Heals very dark
- On first exposure, one lesion or a few
- On later exposures, the old sites light up again and new ones are added

## Key features

The lecture introduces fixed drug eruption by asking what can imitate a single lesion of erythema multiforme, and the answer is this. A solitary targetoid plaque genuinely can pass for an EM target, so the distinguishing feature has to come from the history rather than from the lesion.

That feature is in the name. The eruption is fixed, meaning it returns to the same spot every time the drug is taken, and it leaves behind marked hyperpigmentation between episodes. A dark round patch that flares whenever a particular medication is used is the pattern.

> A fixed drug eruption recurs at the identical site on re-exposure and heals extremely dark, which is what separates it from the erythema multiforme lesion it can imitate.

Library: Fixed drug eruption: offenders and treatment
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Hypersensitivity Reactions to Drugs or Infections

![Clinical photographs on a lecture slide of discrete eroded lesions on the lips, captioned as fixed drug eruption](library/images/msk-week-14/hsr-s40.jpg)

## Key features

The offenders are a distinct list from the one behind morbilliform reactions and SJS.

- Sulfonamides
- Tetracyclines
- NSAIDs
- Barbiturates
- Carbamazepine
- Phenolphthalein in laxatives

The lecture adds a point that does a lot of diagnostic work: these are often drugs the patient does not take daily. The examples given are a pain or headache medication and a short course of an antibiotic. A patient asked what medications they take may not mention either, so the intermittent exposure has to be asked about directly, which is also why the lesions appear to come and go for no clear reason.

Treatment is to stop the offending drug and apply a superpotent topical corticosteroid.

> Fixed drug eruptions often follow drugs taken intermittently rather than daily, so the history has to ask about occasional pain medications and short antibiotic courses.

Library: Imaging modalities used in musculoskeletal evaluation
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide asking what an X-ray, an MRI and a CT scan are](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s04.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture opens by setting up three modalities and then works through them in order, so the whole deck hangs on telling them apart and knowing when each one earns its place.

| Modality | What it is | What it is best at |
|---|---|---|
| Radiograph (X-ray) | Electromagnetic radiation absorbed at different levels depending on the material | Fractures, foreign bodies, calcific tendinopathies |
| MRI | High powered magnets producing a 3D image from proton behavior | Soft tissue structures that plain films cannot show |
| CT | Many X-rays combined by computer into a rendering | Occult and complex fractures, bone obscured by soft tissue |

The organizing question for the whole lecture is not which modality is best in the abstract, it's which one answers the question you actually have about this patient.

> The deck frames all of musculoskeletal imaging around three modalities, radiograph, MRI and CT, and when each one is indicated.

Library: How an X-ray image is formed and what appears opaque or lucent
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide explaining X-ray absorption, bone appearing white, soft tissue appearing grey, and radio-opaque versus radio-lucent](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s05.jpg)

## Key features

An X-ray is electromagnetic radiation that is absorbed at varying levels depending on the material being imaged. The image is a map of how much got absorbed on the way through.

- Bone absorbs radiation well, so bone appears bright white
- Soft tissue does not absorb radiation well, so it appears in shades of grey

## Identify it

- Radio-opaque: absorbs radiation, shows up bright. Bone and metal behave this way
- Radio-lucent: lets radiation through, shows up darker

The lecture adds that some foreign bodies appear very well on X-ray, which is the whole reason foreign bodies are one of its three listed indications.

> Bone absorbs radiation and appears bright white on a radiograph, while soft tissue absorbs poorly and appears as shades of grey.

Library: When to order a radiograph
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide listing fractures, foreign bodies and calcific tendinopathies as X-ray indications, with example films](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s06.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture gives three indications and no more:

1. Fractures
2. Foreign bodies
3. Calcific tendinopathies

All three work for the same reason, which is that each one involves something dense enough to stand out against the tissue around it. A fracture line interrupts dense cortex, a metallic foreign body is more opaque than anything biological, and a calcific deposit is mineral sitting where soft tissue normally is.

> The deck's three stated indications for plain radiography are fractures, foreign bodies and calcific tendinopathies.

Library: The ABCDs approach to reading a radiograph
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide laying out the ABCDs approach of adequacy and alignment, bones, cartilage, disc or joint space, and soft tissue](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s07.jpg)

## Identify it

- **A** for adequacy and alignment
- **B** for bones
- **C** for cartilage
- **D** for disc or joint space
- **s** for soft tissue (effusion, soft tissue swelling, calcifications)

## Key features

The trailing letter is the one that gets lost. The slide lists cartilage and disc or joint space as two separate bullets, so C and D are different steps, and soft tissue is the lowercase s on the end of ABCDs rather than the D.

The point of a mnemonic here is coverage rather than cleverness. The lecture makes the same argument again later about MRI, that the more systematic you are while reading images, the less likely you are to miss something.

> The ABCDs run adequacy and alignment, bones, cartilage, disc or joint space, and soft tissue, so the D is the joint space and soft tissue is the trailing s.

Library: Adequacy and alignment on a radiograph
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide detailing the adequacy and alignment step of the ABCDs](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s07.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture splits the A into two separate questions that happen to start with the same letter.

- Adequacy: is the image showing what we want it to show? A film that misses the area of interest, or that is rotated or underpenetrated, cannot be read no matter how carefully you look
- Alignment: do the structures line up?

Adequacy comes first for a practical reason. If the answer is no, nothing downstream in the ABCDs is reliable, and the correct next step is a better film rather than a confident read of a bad one.

> Adequacy asks whether the image shows what you need it to show, and alignment asks whether the structures line up.

Library: Bones, cartilage and soft tissue on the ABCDs survey
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

## Key features

| Step | What the lecture says to check |
|---|---|
| Bones (B) | The cortex of the bone for abnormalities or fractures, then bone density for osteoporosis, osteopenia or even tumors |
| Cartilage (C) | Listed on its own, with no further detail given |
| Disc or joint space (D) | Listed as its own step, separate from cartilage |
| Soft tissue (the trailing s) | Effusion, soft tissue swelling, calcifications and similar findings |

Two different kinds of question live in the B step. Tracing the cortex is a search for a focal break, while judging density is a global impression of the bone as a whole, and a film can be abnormal on one and normal on the other.

The soft tissue step is easy to skip and often carries the only clue to an injury the bones do not show, which is the same reasoning that sends you to MRI later in the lecture.

> Under bones you check both the cortex for a break and the overall density for osteoporosis, osteopenia or tumor.

Library: Normal shoulder anatomy on imaging
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide showing a labeled AP shoulder radiograph with acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular distances, beside a labeled shoulder anatomy plate](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s08.jpg)

## Identify it

- Clavicle, acromion and the acromioclavicular joint across the top
- Coracoid process projecting anteriorly
- Humeral head seated against the glenoid fossa
- Acromioclavicular distance, given on the slide as less than 8 mm
- Coracoclavicular distance, given on the slide as less than 13 mm

## Key features

The anatomy plate beside the film adds the soft tissue that the radiograph cannot show, including the glenoid labrum, the supraspinatus tendon, and the long and short heads of the biceps tendon. Those are the structures that send you to MRI when the plain film looks normal.

The two measured distances matter because they are how you decide whether the acromioclavicular joint is simply visible or actually separated.

> The lecture gives a normal acromioclavicular distance of less than 8 mm and a normal coracoclavicular distance of less than 13 mm.

Library: Normal ankle and foot anatomy on radiographs
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide showing labeled ankle and foot radiographs beside a labeled illustration of the foot bones](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s09.jpg)

## Identify it

On the AP and mortise ankle film:

- Tibia and fibula above, with the medial and lateral malleoli
- The tibial plafond forming the roof of the joint
- The ankle joint space, which should be even across its width
- The talus below

On the lateral foot film:

- Talus and calcaneus
- The subtalar joint between them
- The transverse tarsal joint
- Navicular and cuboid moving forward, then the cuneiforms, metatarsals and phalanges

## Key features

The illustration beside the films names the same bones in three dimensions, which is the easier way to learn where the cuneiforms sit relative to the navicular and cuboid before trying to find them in a flat grey image.

> On the ankle film the mortise is formed by the tibial plafond with the medial and lateral malleoli, and the joint space should be even across its width.

Library: Normal knee anatomy on radiographs
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide showing paired lateral and AP knee radiographs](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s10.jpg)

## Identify it

- On the AP view, the femoral condyles above and the tibial plateau below, with the joint space between them and the fibular head lateral
- On the lateral view, the patella anterior to the distal femur, and the femoral condyles overlapping

## Key features

The knee is the joint the lecture returns to most often in its clinical scenarios, first for chronic degenerative pain in an older adult and then for an acute injury in a young athlete, so the normal appearance here is the baseline both of those are read against.

Judging the joint space is the D of the ABCDs applied to this joint, which is why the weightbearing views appear later in the views list.

> The AP knee shows the femoral condyles, the tibial plateau and the joint space between them, and the lateral shows the patella anterior to the distal femur.

Library: Normal wrist and carpal anatomy on imaging
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics
