![Slide showing a labeled dorsal view of the carpal bones beside wrist radiographs with each carpal bone labeled](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s11.jpg)

## Identify it

Carpal bones named on the slide include the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate and hamate, with the hook of the hamate and the pisiform marked separately.

The illustration also names the tendon grooves on the distal radius, for extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, extensor carpi ulnaris and extensor pollicis longus, along with the radial tuberosity and brachioradialis.

## Key features

The scaphoid is the one to fix in mind, because it is the bone behind the lecture's fall on an outstretched hand scenario and the reason that patient gets splinted and re-imaged rather than sent home on a normal film.

> The carpal bones named here include the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate and hamate, and the scaphoid is the one the deck's clinical scenario turns on.

Library: Describing a fracture: the four questions
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide listing the fracture description terms of which bone, where, what type and how aligned](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s12.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture reduces fracture description to four questions, asked in this order:

1. Which bone
2. Where is the fracture
3. What type of fracture
4. How is the fracture aligned

Everything in the terminology that follows is an answer to one of those four. Type covers the pattern of the break itself, such as transverse, oblique, spiral or comminuted, while alignment covers the relationship between the fragments, such as displacement, angulation and apposition.

Answering all four in order is what turns a radiograph into a description another clinician can act on without seeing the film.

> A fracture description answers four questions in order: which bone, where, what type, and how it is aligned.

Library: Open versus closed fractures
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide illustrating closed fracture beside open fracture from within and from without](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s14.jpg)

## Identify it

- Closed fracture: the overlying skin is intact
- Open fracture: the fracture communicates with the outside, either from within when a fragment pierces the skin from the inside, or from without when the injuring object breaks the skin on the way in

## Key features

This is the first distinction the terminology slide lists, and it is the one that changes urgency rather than vocabulary, because an open fracture is contaminated by definition.

> An open fracture communicates with the outside, either from within when a bone fragment pierces the skin or from without when the injuring object breaks it.

Library: Fracture displacement
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide comparing displaced and non displaced fractures](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s15.jpg)

## Identify it

- Non-displaced: normal alignment is preserved, the fragments sit where they belong
- Displaced: the fragments are pulled out of normal alignment

## Key features

Displacement describes the relationship between the distal and proximal bone fragments. The lecture gives one numeric threshold worth holding onto, which is that minimally displaced means 3 mm or less.

Note that displacement is about position, not about the number of pieces. A fracture can be comminuted and non-displaced, or simple and badly displaced.

> Displacement describes the distal fragment's relationship to the proximal one, and minimally displaced means 3 mm or less.

Library: Fracture angulation and apposition
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide illustrating displaced, angulated, shortened and rotated fracture alignment](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s16.jpg)

## Identify it

- Angulation: the fragments meet at an angle rather than in line
- Apposition: how much of the fracture surfaces are in contact, a type of displacement
- Shortening: overlap of the fragments so the bone is shorter than it was
- Rotation: one fragment turned about the long axis relative to the other

## Key features

The practical point the lecture makes about angulation is that you cannot judge it from one film. You need two views 90 degrees apart, because a fracture angulated purely in one plane can look perfectly aligned in the other.

The lecture also separates acceptable from unacceptable angulation, which is the judgment that decides whether a fracture needs reduction.

> Angulation needs two views 90 degrees apart to assess, because a fracture angulated in one plane can look aligned in the other.

Library: Comminuted, simple and segmental fractures
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide contrasting comminuted and simple fractures](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s17.jpg)

## Identify it

- Simple: one fracture line, two fragments
- Comminuted: the bone is broken into more than two pieces
- Segmental: the lecture's specific example, three fragments produced by two separate fracture lines

## Key features

Segmental is worth separating out because it is a particular kind of comminution, where two distinct breaks isolate a free segment of shaft between them rather than shattering one area.

> Comminuted means more than two fragments, and segmental is the specific pattern of three fragments created by two fracture lines.

Library: Avulsion fractures
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide illustrating an avulsion fracture with a tendon pulling a bone fragment away](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s18.jpg)

## Identify it

- A small fragment of bone pulled away from the main bone, sitting at a tendon or ligament attachment

## Key features

The lecture's definition is a tendon pulling a piece of bone off. The mechanism is traction rather than direct impact, which is why these turn up at attachment sites and why the fragment is typically small relative to the force involved.

Reading an avulsion correctly means recognizing that the soft tissue, not the bone, is the injured structure of interest.

> An avulsion fracture is a tendon pulling a piece of bone off its attachment, so the fragment marks the site of a soft tissue injury.

Library: Intra-articular fractures
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide comparing extra-articular and intra-articular fractures, each shown displaced and nondisplaced](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s19.jpg)

## Identify it

- Extra-articular: the fracture line stays outside the joint
- Intra-articular: the fracture extends into the joint line

## Key features

The lecture defines intra-articular simply as a fracture extending into the joint line, and the slide pairs each with a displaced and a nondisplaced version, which makes the point that articular involvement and displacement are two independent descriptors.

Articular involvement matters because the fracture now crosses a cartilage surface, so the alignment question becomes a question about the joint rather than just the bone.

> Intra-articular means the fracture line extends into the joint, which is independent of whether the fracture is displaced.

Library: Fracture patterns and additional fracture types
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide showing additional fracture types including pathologic, longitudinal, spiral, greenstick, simple, compound, oblique, comminuted and transverse](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s20.jpg)

## Identify it

| Pattern | What the lecture says about it |
|---|---|
| Transverse | Perpendicular to the bone |
| Oblique | Listed with no definition |
| Spiral | A result of twisting |
| Compression | Listed with no definition, immediately before impaction |
| Impaction fracture | Direct force down the length of the bone |
| Pathologic | Fracture at a site where the bone is weakened |

## Key features

Only four of these carry a definition on the slide. Transverse, spiral, impaction and pathologic each get a sub-bullet, while oblique and compression are listed as names only, so treat anything you have read elsewhere about them as outside this deck.

The slide adds longitudinal, greenstick and compound to the list without defining them further in the notes.

Spiral and pathologic are the two that carry information beyond the picture. A spiral fracture tells you the mechanism was torsion, and a pathologic fracture tells you to go looking for why the bone was weak, which loops back to the bone density check in the ABCDs.

> Transverse is perpendicular to the bone, spiral results from twisting, and pathologic means the bone was already weakened at that site.

Library: The importance of multiple views
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide making the point that a single view can be misleading](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s22.jpg)

## Key features

A radiograph flattens a three dimensional object into two dimensions, so a single projection can hide a finding entirely. The lecture already made this point about angulation, which needs two views 90 degrees apart, and the views slide generalizes it.

In practice this is why standard series exist rather than single films. The shoulder series, the wrist series and the ankle series each combine projections chosen so that what one view hides another shows.

> A single projection can hide a fracture or its angulation, which is why standard series combine views taken at different angles.

Library: Standard radiographic views by joint
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide listing standard radiographic views for the shoulder, wrist, knee and ankle](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s23.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture calls this slide Pandora's Box of radiology views, which is the right warning: the list is long, and the named views are specialty requests rather than things to memorize cold.

| Joint | Views listed |
|---|---|
| Shoulder | AP, lateral or scapular Y, modified trauma axial, Garth projection, Zanca, West Point view, Grashey |
| Wrist | PA, oblique, lateral, carpal tunnel view, clenched fist view |
| Knee | AP, lateral, merchant or sunrise, weightbearing, Rosenberg |
| Ankle | AP, mortise, lateral, AP stress view, horizontal beam lateral |

The patterns worth taking from the table are that every joint gets an AP and a lateral as its base, that the ankle adds the mortise view to open up the joint space, that the knee adds a sunrise view for the patellofemoral joint and weightbearing views for joint space, and that the wrist and shoulder have the longest lists because both are hard to see in two planes.

> Every joint's series starts with an AP and a lateral, and the extra views exist to show what those two hide, like the ankle mortise and the knee sunrise.

Library: How MRI produces an image and how to read it
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide explaining how MRI uses magnets and proton behavior to build a 3D image](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s25.jpg)

## Key features

MRI uses high powered magnets to produce a 3D image of the body, and the lecture's one line version is that it comes down to detecting change in the direction of the rotational axis of protons in living tissues.

The fuller mechanism as the deck gives it:

1. Protons align with the magnetic field
2. A radiofrequency current stimulates them, so they spin out of equilibrium
3. The current is removed
4. Sensors detect the energy released as the protons realign with the magnetic field

For reading, the lecture says to use the same systematic approach as with X-ray, and repeats that the more systematic you are, the less likely you are to miss something.

> MRI detects energy released as protons realign with the magnetic field after a radiofrequency current is removed, and it's read with the same systematic habit as a radiograph.

Library: T1 versus T2 weighted MRI
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide contrasting T1 weighted and T2 weighted MRI signal](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s26.jpg)

## Identify it

| Weighting | What it enhances | What is white |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | Signal of fatty tissue, suppresses the signal of water | Fat is white |
| T2 | Signal of water | Fat and water are both white |

## Key features

The practical consequence is that fluid is the thing that changes between them. Anything that collects water, such as an effusion, edema or a bone marrow stress response, looks bright on T2 and does not stand out on T1.

That is why the stress reaction case later in the lecture is made on the fluid sensitive sequence rather than on the T1.

> T1 makes fat white and suppresses water, while T2 makes both fat and water white, so fluid and edema stand out on T2.

Library: Indications and contraindications for MRI
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide listing when to order an MRI and when not to](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s27.jpg)

## Key features

When to order one, as the lecture frames it:

- MRI is excellent at evaluating the soft tissue structures that cannot be viewed on standard radiographs
- If you think there is an internal derangement of a soft tissue structure that plain films cannot image adequately, an MRI is warranted
- If you suspect a disorder of bone that X-ray cannot show, such as an occult scaphoid fracture or a stress reaction

When not to:

- As first-line imaging
- If the patient has implanted devices or metallic foreign bodies, including ICDs, cochlear implants, drug infusion pumps and piercings

The first contraindication is about sequencing rather than safety. MRI is the second study, ordered once a plain film has either answered the question or failed to.

> MRI is for soft tissue derangement and for bone disorders X-ray misses, but it is never the first-line study and is contraindicated with implanted devices or metallic foreign bodies.

Library: Normal MRI appearance of the shoulder
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Labeled coronal MRI of the shoulder](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s29.jpg)

## Identify it

Structures labeled across the deck's three shoulder planes include the acromioclavicular joint, acromion, clavicle, humeral head, glenoid, the inferior glenoid labrum and posterior labrum, the articular capsule, the subscapular muscle, deltoid, trapezius, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and teres major, the long head of biceps brachii in the bicipital groove, and the suprascapular and posterior circumflex humeral vessels.

## Key features

The coronal plane is where the supraspinatus and its insertion sit, which is why the rotator cuff case later in the lecture is shown on a coronal image.

The sagittal plane shows the cuff muscles arranged around the glenoid, and the axial plane shows the anterior and posterior labrum, which is the view that matters after a dislocation.

> The coronal shoulder MRI is where the supraspinatus and its insertion are assessed, which is why the deck's rotator cuff case is shown in that plane.

Library: Normal MRI appearance of the knee

![Labeled coronal MRI of the knee](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s32.jpg)

## Identify it

Structures labeled across the deck's three knee planes include the femur and tibia, the medial and lateral femoral condyles, the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments, the tibial and fibular collateral ligaments, the medial and lateral meniscus with their anterior and posterior horns, the patella and patellar ligament, the quadriceps tendon, the infrapatellar and prefemoral fat, the iliotibial tract, and the surrounding muscles and tendons including biceps femoris, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, sartorius, gracilis, popliteus, gastrocnemius and soleus.

## Key features

The cruciates are best followed on the sagittal images and the collaterals and menisci on the coronal, which maps onto the acute knee injury scenario later in the deck, where the suspected structure is a cruciate ligament.

> The cruciate ligaments are followed on sagittal knee images while the collaterals and menisci are assessed on the coronal.

Library: Normal MRI appearance of the wrist
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Labeled coronal MRI of the wrist](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s35.jpg)

## Identify it

Structures labeled across the deck's three wrist planes include the radius and ulna with the ulnar styloid, the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate and hamate, the metacarpals, the fibrocartilage and the scapholunate and radial and ulnar collateral ligaments, the interosseous muscles, the flexor and extensor tendon groups, the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis, the median and ulnar nerves, and the radial artery and deep palmar arch.

## Key features

The coronal plane lays the carpal rows out side by side, which is the plane in which a scaphoid fracture or a scapholunate problem is most visible, and it is why MRI is the fallback when a scaphoid is clinically suspected but radiographically silent.

> The coronal wrist MRI lays out the carpal rows and is the plane in which an occult scaphoid fracture becomes visible.

Library: How CT produces an image and when to order it
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide explaining computed tomography and its indications](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s40.jpg)

## Key features

CT combines many X-rays and uses a computer to build a rendering of the body, so it can give a much better picture of internal structures than standard radiographs. The lecture also notes that CT is useful for patients unable to tolerate MRI, such as those with a pacemaker or other implanted device, and that a CT arthrogram can be used to better evaluate a joint.

Indications the lecture lists:

- Occult fracture, meaning a fracture that does not appear well on X-ray
- Evaluating bones that would be obscured by soft tissue structures on plain films
- Evaluating complex fractures
- Situations needing an excellent view of both bone and soft tissue

Note that occult fracture appears on both the CT list and the MRI list. The deck resolves that in its scaphoid case, where repeat plain films come first, then MRI for the occult fracture itself, with CT used to get a more detailed look at the fracture and assess healing.

> CT is built from many X-rays, and it earns its place for occult or complex fractures, for bone hidden by soft tissue, and for patients who cannot have an MRI.

Library: CT appearance of the shoulder, knee and wrist
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![CT images of the knee in two planes](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s43.jpg)

## Identify it

- Bone appears bright and sharply defined, with cortex and trabecular pattern both visible
- Soft tissue appears in shades of grey, less differentiated than on MRI
- Images are cross sectional, and the same study can be reconstructed into more than one plane

## Key features

CT sits between the other two modalities in what it shows. It has the bone detail of a radiograph with cross sectional anatomy added, and it shows soft tissue better than a plain film but without MRI's soft tissue contrast.

That is exactly the profile the indications describe, which is why CT is the answer for a complex fracture and MRI is the answer for a torn ligament.

> On CT, bone is bright and sharply defined in cross section, which is why CT is chosen for complex and occult fractures rather than for soft tissue derangement.

Library: Imaging chronic knee pain in an older adult
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Standing radiographs of both knees from the deck's chronic knee pain scenario](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s48.jpg)

## Key features

The lecture's scenario is a 67 year old man with acute on chronic knee pain, no specific injury and no past injury history, aching for years and worse over the past three months, non-radiating, worse with activity and better with rest, partially relieved by over the counter NSAIDs and gels.

The question asked is which study is most appropriate, and the deck answers it with plain radiographs, including standing and weightbearing views of both knees along with lateral and sunrise views.

The reasoning is that everything in the history points at a degenerative joint rather than a soft tissue derangement, and joint space is the D of the ABCDs, which the lecture says to answer on a radiograph. Weightbearing matters because joint space narrowing can disappear when the joint is unloaded.

> A chronic, activity related, non-traumatic knee complaint in an older adult is worked up with weightbearing plain radiographs, not with MRI first.

Library: Imaging an acute knee injury with a pop and effusion
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![AP knee radiograph from the deck's acute knee injury scenario](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s52.jpg)

## Key features

The scenario is a 23 year old who planted his leg playing ultimate frisbee five days ago, felt a pop, had immediate pain and swelling, and still has persistent swelling although the pain has improved. No prior injury history.

The lecture asks two separate questions about this patient and gives two different answers:

1. The imaging modality to obtain next is a plain radiograph, because the first job is to exclude a fracture
2. The modality best suited to evaluate the most likely injured structure is MRI, because a pop with immediate swelling in a planting injury points at a cruciate ligament, and ligaments are soft tissue

That pairing is the whole lesson. The right first study and the right definitive study are not the same study, and the answer depends on which question is being asked.

## What the deck's own MRI shows

![Sagittal knee MRI with an ellipse drawn around the intercondylar notch and a caption naming the absent structure](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s53.jpg)

The lecture does not stop at ordering the study. The sagittal image it shows for this patient is captioned NO ACL, with a white ellipse drawn around the intercondylar notch where the ligament should run. The MRI therefore confirms the torn anterior cruciate ligament rather than leaving it as an inference from the pop and the effusion.

> Even when a ligament tear is the likely injury, the first study is a radiograph to exclude fracture, and MRI is what evaluates the ligament itself.

Library: Imaging a suspected scaphoid fracture and occult fracture follow-up
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Wrist radiographs from the deck's fall on an outstretched hand scenario](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s55.jpg)

## Key features

The scenario is a 48 year old soccer player who fell onto an outstretched hand, finished the game thinking she had sprained her wrist, and now has continued pain and swelling. Examination shows tenderness at the anatomic snuffbox and the scaphoid tubercle.

The best initial imaging is plain radiography, and in this case the films are normal.

The lecture is explicit that a normal film does not end the encounter:

1. Place the patient in a thumb spica splint to immobilize the joint
2. Re-evaluate in two weeks, because fractures are not always evident on the initial X-ray and repeat imaging lets an occult fracture reveal itself
3. If repeat imaging is negative but suspicion remains, MRI can be used to evaluate the scaphoid
4. CT is sometimes used to get a more detailed look at the fracture and to assess healing

> Snuffbox tenderness after a fall on an outstretched hand is splinted and re-imaged in two weeks even when the initial radiograph is normal, because the scaphoid fracture may be occult.

Library: Imaging suspected rotator cuff disease
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![AP shoulder radiograph from the deck's shoulder pain scenario](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s59.jpg)

## Key features

The scenario is a 52 year old man who does CrossFit three times a week, with a month of shoulder pain that aches, worsens with overhead motion and with movement generally, improves with rest, and hurts when he lies on that side.

The lecture again asks two questions and gives two answers. The best initial study to assess the presumptive diagnosis is a plain radiograph, and the study that best diagnoses the concern itself is MRI.

The logic matches the MRI indications given earlier. Overhead aggravation and night pain on that side point at the rotator cuff, the cuff is soft tissue, and soft tissue derangement that plain films cannot image adequately is exactly what MRI is for.

> Shoulder pain worse with overhead motion gets a radiograph first, but the rotator cuff itself is assessed on MRI.

Library: Imaging recurrent shoulder dislocation
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Shoulder imaging from the deck's recurrent dislocation scenario](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s62.jpg)

## Key features

The scenario is a 30 year old lacrosse player whose shoulder slipped out of place at a face off and went back in on its own, with some tingling down the right arm afterward. He reports previous dislocations, each self-reduced, with no further intervention. Radiographs are obtained first.

The lecture then asks what the next imaging modality should be in this patient's care. The answer follows from what recurrent instability damages, which is the labrum and capsule along with the bony margins of the glenoid and humeral head, and those are cross sectional and soft tissue questions rather than plain film ones.

The tingling down the arm is worth noting separately, because the shoulder material in this week's anatomy lectures puts the axillary nerve at risk in exactly this injury.

## What the deck's own images show

The lecture does not leave the bony damage unnamed. The slide that follows this scenario carries a radiograph with two boxed labels and arrows, one marking a Hill-Sachs defect on the humeral head and one marking a Bankart lesion at the glenoid rim, beside an axial CT of the same joint. Those two lesions are set out on the page Hill-Sachs and Bankart lesions after shoulder dislocation.

> A recurrent dislocator gets plain films first, and the next study is cross sectional imaging to assess the labrum, capsule and bony glenoid, which plain radiographs cannot show.

Library: Hill-Sachs and Bankart lesions after shoulder dislocation
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![Slide showing an axial CT of the shoulder beside a radiograph carrying two boxed labels with arrows, one marking the humeral head and one marking the glenoid rim](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s64.jpg)

## Identify it

- The slide pairs two studies from the recurrent dislocation case, an axial CT of the shoulder on the left and a radiograph on the right
- On the radiograph the Hill-Sachs label and its arrow point at the humeral head, at its upper outer margin
- The Bankart label and its arrow point at the lower rim of the glenoid

## Key features

| Lesion | Bone it sits on |
|---|---|
| Hill-Sachs | Humeral head |
| Bankart | Glenoid rim |

The pairing is the testable part, and the two are easy to swap. Hill-Sachs sits on the ball of the joint and Bankart sits on the socket.

The slide names both lesions and points to where each one sits, and gives no further definition, so anything beyond the bone each involves is outside this deck.

Both belong to the recurrent dislocation scenario, and together they explain why the lecture moves from plain films to cross sectional imaging in that patient. The glenoid rim and the humeral head are bony surfaces that a single projection shows poorly.

> Hill-Sachs sits on the humeral head and Bankart sits on the glenoid rim, which is the pairing the slide labels on its radiograph.

Library: Stress reactions and their imaging
Folder: MSK / Week 14 / Musculoskeletal Imaging Basics

![MRI of the lower leg from the deck's stress reaction scenario](library/images/msk-week-14/imag-s66.jpg)

## Key features

The scenario is a collegiate distance runner with two months of worsening right anterior shin pain during runs, now also present on long walks between classes, worse with running and better with rest.

The pathophysiology as the lecture states it: bone placed under stress during activity normally responds with osteoblastic activity laying down new bone where it was stressed. In a stress reaction, osteoclastic activity is occurring at a greater rate than osteoblastic activity, which leaves weakened bone, and that continues to the point of fracture if no intervention is made.

The imaging approach follows from that:

- Initial imaging is plain films, to evaluate for fracture
- The best imaging is MRI, because it best categorizes the extent of the stress reaction and will pick up stress reactions that have not yet resulted in fracture

> In a stress reaction osteoclastic activity outpaces osteoblastic activity, and MRI is the study that shows the reaction before it becomes a fracture.
